sessions.title: Lower your cortisol
script: [pause 1.5s]
For the next five minutes, you'll learn one rhythm. It's the simplest and most useful one in CortiFree. A short breath in, and a long breath out.
[pause 1.5s]
Sit on a chair or lie on your back, whichever you prefer. Let your shoulders drop.
Place one hand on your belly, just below your navel. The other can rest on your thigh, or on your chest.
You can close your eyes, or let your gaze rest on the floor in front of you.
[pause 3s]
Before we start, one simple idea.
Your body has two main modes. An alert mode, which speeds everything up so you can cope. And a recovery mode, which slows things down, digests and repairs.
When you breathe in, your heart speeds up very slightly. When you breathe out, it slows down a little. It happens on its own, with every breath.
So when you lengthen your exhale, you spend more time on the slowing side. Many people find it helps their body shift toward recovery.
It isn't magic, and there's nothing to get right. It's a signal you can send your body, again and again. You are safe.
[pause 2s]
Start by noticing your breath just as it is, without changing it.
Under your hand, your belly rises a little as you breathe in, and falls as you breathe out. Or maybe it's mostly your chest that moves. Both are normal.
Is your breath short or deep right now? Fast or slow?
[pause 2s]
Just take note. Notice the air too, a little cooler coming in, a little warmer going out.
It doesn't need to be calm already. We start from wherever you are.
And notice the small natural pause at the very bottom of the exhale, just before the air comes back. We're going to stretch it a little.
[pause 3s]
Here's the rhythm. You breathe in through your nose for about four seconds, and out through your mouth or nose for about six.
I'll give you one word for each phase, then leave you the silence. Let's do it together.
[pause 1.5s]
In.
[pause 3.5s]
Out.
[pause 5.5s]
In, your belly rising under your hand.
[pause 3.5s]
Out, slowly.
[pause 5.5s]
In.
[pause 3.5s]
Out, as if you were blowing on a candle without making the flame flicker.
[pause 5.5s]

[pause 3.5s]

[pause 5.5s]
If your mind wanders off, that's normal. Come back to the rhythm, without blaming yourself. Every return is part of the practice.
[pause 2s]
If it's comfortable, let the exhale stretch a little further. Seven seconds, maybe eight.
The breath in stays the same. Only the breath out gets longer.
Picture the air flowing out like a thin stream of water, fine and steady, down to the very last drop.
[pause 1.5s]
In.
[pause 3.5s]
Out, long and fine.
[pause 7.5s]
In.
[pause 3.5s]

[pause 7.5s]

[pause 7.5s]

If eight is too much, stay closer to six. The right rhythm never leaves you gasping for the next breath. And if you feel dizzy or uncomfortable, simply return to your natural breath. There's no hurry.
[pause 2s]

An easy breath in. A longer breath out, taking all the time it needs.
Under your hand, your belly rises... then falls, slowly.

[pause 3s]

This rhythm is yours now. A short breath in, a long breath out. No one can see it.

sessions.title: Your inner refuge
script: [pause 1.5s]

For the next seven minutes, we're going to build something you can keep. An inner refuge, a place where your body feels safe, and where you can return in a few seconds, even in the middle of a busy day.
[pause 1.5s]
Get comfortable, sitting or lying on your back. Let your back be supported, and let your hands rest wherever they feel good.
You can close your eyes, or lower your gaze to a point that isn't moving.
[pause 2.5s]
Let's arrive with a few slow breaths. Breathe in through your nose...
[pause 4s]
and let the air leave even more slowly, through your mouth...
[pause 6s]
Once more. The air comes in, cool... and goes out, warm, carrying a little of the day away with it.
[pause 5s]
One last time. And at the end of the exhale, let your body grow a little heavier, as if it were settling onto whatever is holding it.
[pause 4s]
Now, let a place come to mind where you feel safe.
It can be a real one. Your grandparents' kitchen, a little cove in Brittany, a bench in a park you know by heart. Or it can be completely imaginary, a cabin, a room that exists nowhere else.
[pause 1.5s]
Don't look for the perfect place. Take the first one that brings a sense of calm, even a faint one.
If several come up, choose just one for today. And if nothing comes, you can simply imagine a warm, quiet room, with a door that only opens for you.
If a place brings up difficult memories, set it aside and pick another, more neutral one. This refuge should feel simple and gentle.
[pause 3s]
You're there now. Start by looking around.
Which colors stand out? Greens, blues, the warm tones of wood or stone?
[pause 2s]
And the light. Is it morning, late afternoon, the soft glow of a lamp? Where does it come from, and how does it fall on things?
[pause 2s]
Let your inner gaze wander. Notice a detail close to you, a texture, a shape, an object. Then a detail farther away, on the horizon or at the far end of the room.
You can look up, too. A sky, a ceiling with wooden beams, branches swaying.
[pause 2s]
Every detail you add makes this place a little more solid. Take your time. And if the picture stays blurry, that's fine. Some people see very little, and feel a great deal.
[pause 3s]
Now, listen. What can you hear in this place?
[pause 2s]
Maybe running water, wind in the leaves, waves rolling in. The crackle of a fire, a clock ticking, birds in the distance.
Or a deep, reassuring silence, which has a texture of its own.
Notice whether these sounds are near or far, steady or coming and going. Let them wrap around you, with no effort at all.
[pause 2.5s]
Breathe in the air of this place. Is there a smell? Cut grass, sea salt, wood, warm bread, clean laundry.
If no smell comes, that's alright. Some places are felt more than they're smelled.
[pause 2s]
Feel the temperature on your skin. Is the air mild, or cool, just the way you like it? Maybe a ray of sunlight on your face, or the warmth of a blanket.
And under your feet, what's there? Sand that gives a little, soft grass, smooth floorboards, a stone warmed by the sun.
Take a few steps, if you like, and feel how the ground answers each one.
If you sit down in your refuge, feel what's holding you. An armchair, a rock, a soft cushion.
[pause 3s]
Here, nothing is rushing you. No one expects anything from you. No notifications, no appointments, no judgment.
Notice how your body responds to this safety. Where do you feel it?
[pause 2.5s]
Maybe in your shoulders, letting go. In your belly, unknotting. In your breath, fuller and slower. In your face, which no longer has to put on a brave front.
Let this feeling spread, like warmth slowly filling a room. You don't have to do anything to keep it. Just notice it.
[pause 2s]
Take the time to really savor it. The more clearly you feel it now, the easier it will be to find it again later.
If part of you stays a little on guard, that's normal. Welcome that part into this place as well. It's allowed to be here.
And if a thought from your day comes knocking at the door, that's normal too. You see it, you leave it outside, and you come back to one detail of your refuge. A color, or a sound.
[pause 3s]
Now I'm going to help you create a shortcut to this place.
Gently bring the tip of your thumb and your index finger together, on one hand or both. A small, discreet circle that no one will notice.
[pause 1.5s]
While your fingers are touching, breathe in the calm of your refuge. Its colors. Its sounds. Its temperature. The ease in your body.
As if you were recording all of it into this small gesture.
The gesture and the feeling, together, at the same moment.
Breathe in the calm...
[pause 4s]
and let it settle into your fingers...
[pause 6s]
Release your fingers. Breathe normally.
[pause 2s]
And make the gesture again. Thumb against index finger. Notice how the refuge comes back, maybe a little faster this time.
A color. A sound. The feeling under your feet. It's all there, in this small circle.
[pause 3s]
The more often you repeat this pairing, the more reliable the gesture becomes as a key. At first, it brings back a hint of calm. Over time, it can bring you back here within a few breaths.
Later on, before a meeting, in a waiting room, as you fall asleep, you'll be able to bring these two fingers together and find part of this place again.
You can practice a little each day, when things are going well. That way, the shortcut is ready on the day you need it.
[pause 2s]
Now release the gesture. Your refuge stays where it is. It doesn't disappear when you leave it.
You can also return to it simply by closing your eyes, without the gesture, whenever you have a little more time.
[pause 2s]
Slowly, begin to come back. Feel the support beneath your body, the floor, the chair or the bed.
Hear the sounds of the room you're actually in. The nearest ones first, then the ones farther away.
[pause 2s]
Take a slightly fuller breath. Move your fingers and your feet, and stretch if you feel like it.
[pause 2s]
And whenever it feels right, open your eyes. Your shortcut comes with you. Thumb to index finger, and your refuge is never far away.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Panic anchor
script: [pause 1.5s]
I'm here with you. Keep your eyes open, and stay with my voice.
What you're feeling is very unpleasant. It isn't dangerous, and it will pass.
Even if it feels enormous right now, a wave like this always comes back down.
[pause 2s]
Let's start with your feet. Place them flat on the floor. If you're sitting, feel the seat under you too. If you're standing, let your knees bend very slightly.
Now press down through your heels. The floor is solid. It isn't moving. It holds you, whatever your body is doing right now.
[pause 2s]
Bring your hands together, palm against palm, in front of your chest or resting on your knees.
Push them firmly into each other. Feel the strength in your arms, and the warmth building between your palms.
[pause 3s]
And release. Keep your hands together, just more gently now. Your feet and your hands are your anchors.
[pause 1.5s]
Now look around you. Let your eyes move slowly around the room, or the street.
Pick one object and name it, under your breath if you can. Just its name. A chair. A window. A bag.
[pause 2s]
Now a second object. Notice its color as you name it.
[pause 2s]
And a third one. Take your time, there's no right answer.
[pause 2s]
Naming what you see helps your attention come back here, to this place, and away from the alarm.
[pause 2s]
Now, the breath. You don't need a big breath in. Let the air come in however it comes.
Then blow out through your mouth, slowly, as if onto a candle you don't want to put out...
[pause 5s]
Once more. The air comes in on its own... and you let it flow out through your mouth, for a long time.
[pause 6s]
It's the exhale that matters. The inhale takes care of itself, you don't have to reach for it.
Feeling short of air is very common in moments like this. You are breathing. The air is moving.
[pause 1.5s]
One more exhale, soft and long, like a thin stream of air over the flame...
[pause 6s]
Now picture a wave. It rises, it swells, it can look very high.
Then it reaches its peak. And like every wave, it starts to come back down.
What you're going through follows the same movement. You may be right at the top, or already on the way down.
You don't have to stop the wave. You only have to stay on your feet while it passes.
[pause 3s]
Some sensations may still be there. A racing heart. Heat, tingling, a tight throat.
These are your body's alarm signals. They're loud, and they aren't dangerous. They rise, and then they settle on their own.
You don't need to fight them. Let them sit beside you while you keep breathing out, long and slow.
[pause 3s]
Come back to your feet. Press down into the floor a little.
Your hands are still together. Press a bit harder if it helps you come back here.
Find one object in front of you and name it once more. And one long exhale, through your mouth...
[pause 5s]
You're still here. You're getting through this, one exhale at a time.
Is anything different, even slightly? Your breath a little less short, your shoulders a little lower?
[pause 3s]
Or maybe not yet, and that's okay too.
[pause 2s]
You've made it through this wave, and that takes a lot of energy. You can stay seated a while longer, drink a glass of water, take things slowly.

If these attacks come back often, talk to a doctor or a health professional. Real help exists, and no one should have to handle this alone.
[pause 2s]

[pause 4s]

One last breath in...
[pause 3s]

Let the backrest support your lower back. Keep your shoulders low, even as your hands return to the keyboard.

Before you dive back in, one thing. Don't jump into every open tab at once.

sessions.title: After a tense meeting
script: [pause 1.5s]
The meeting is over. The door is closed, the call has ended. You're here now, and for the next five minutes, nobody needs anything from you.
If you can, step away from your desk for a moment. A hallway, an empty meeting room, even the restroom will do.
[pause 2s]
Sit or stand with your feet firmly on the floor. Feel the ground holding you up. Solid. Completely indifferent to whatever was just said.
[pause 1.5s]
Now let out a first breath, a little longer than usual... like a sigh you've been holding in for an hour.
[pause 4s]
Let's take a quick tour of your body, to see where that meeting has settled.
Start with your jaw. Are your teeth clenched right now?
[pause 2.5s]
Maybe your tongue is pressed hard against the roof of your mouth. Let a little space open between your teeth, and let your tongue rest softly, low in your mouth.
[pause 2s]
Move down to your shoulders. They may have crept up during the discussion, as if to protect you. Let them drop half an inch... then a little more.
[pause 2s]
And your belly. In a tense exchange, we often pull the stomach in without noticing. Let it soften, let it round out.
[pause 2s]
Look at your hands, too. Are they gripping a pen, or your phone? Open them wide, fingers spread, then let them rest.
[pause 2s]
Not everything has to relax at once. Simply noticing the tension is already the start of letting it go.
[pause 2.5s]
What lingers in the body after a hard meeting is energy that had nowhere to go. Your body got ready to react. So let's help it release some of that charge.
Gently shake out your hands, as if you were drying them after washing. Loose wrists, soft fingers.
[pause 2s]
Let the movement travel up into your forearms, then your shoulders. Nothing dramatic. Just enough to get things moving.
[pause 2s]
Keep going a few more seconds. You can shrug a few times too, or march gently in place if there's room.
[pause 4s]
And stop. Let your hands hang, or rest them on your thighs. Notice the tingling, the warmth, the blood moving again.
[pause 3s]
Now, a few long exhales. Breathe in easily through your nose...
[pause 3s]
Then out through your mouth, lips slightly parted, slowly, all the way to the end.
[pause 6s]
Once more. The inhale is ordinary...
[pause 3s]
it's the exhale that takes its time.
[pause 6s]
One last time. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and as you breathe out, imagine the air carrying away some of the heat of that discussion.
[pause 6s]
If you feel a little dizzy, just go back to your natural breathing.
[pause 2s]
Your mind may already be replaying the scene. A curt remark, a look, the perfect comeback that shows up too late.
That's normal. Your brain is trying to make sense of what happened, and to protect you next time.
You don't have to stop it. You can simply notice it... there it goes again, the replay.
[pause 2s]
Picture those exchanges on a screen at the far end of a theater. You're sitting in the very back row. You can see them, but you're no longer on stage.
[pause 2.5s]
If one sentence keeps looping, give it a simple label. Replaying. Then come back to the feeling of your feet on the floor.
You don't need to decide right now who was right. That debate can wait. For now, you're just watching from the back row.
[pause 3s]
Now, out of everything that was said, try to find what actually matters.
Not the tone. Not the way it was said. The substance.
A decision that was made, a fair concern, a deadline to meet, a point you genuinely disagree with.
Once you peel away the emotional wrapping, there are often only one or two concrete things left. What are they, for you?
[pause 3s]
Good. All that's left is to choose what comes next.
Maybe one action is clear. Send a recap, talk to a colleague, write down a question for later.
Or maybe the best action is not to respond right away... to sleep on it before you write that email.
Both are choices. What matters is that you're the one deciding, not the adrenaline.
[pause 1.5s]
If you feel the urge to reply right now, in the heat of the moment, that's often a sign it's wiser to wait a little.
[pause 1.5s]
Choose your next step. Just one. Put it clearly into words, in your head.
For example, I'll reply tomorrow morning, with a clear head. Or, I'll stop by Julie's desk before the end of the day.
[pause 3s]
Let your breathing return to normal. Notice whether anything has shifted in your jaw, your shoulders, your belly. Even slightly.
[pause 3s]

[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Screen detox
script: [pause 1.5s]
How many hours have your eyes spent on a screen today? A laptop, a phone, maybe both at the same time.
[pause 2s]
You may already feel it. Eyes that are a little dry and sting. A heavy forehead. A sort of buzzing, as if your mind keeps scrolling even after you've stopped.
For the next six minutes, we're going to give your eyes something else.
[pause 1.5s]
Let's start with your phone. Turn it face down on the table. Even better, put it out of reach, in a drawer or on another shelf.
If you're at a computer, switch off the monitor, or tilt the laptop lid partway down.
[pause 2s]
You might feel a little resistance. What if someone messages me? That's normal. It can wait six minutes.
That small tug is the habit of always being reachable. Every notification pulls at your attention, even the ones you never answer.
[pause 3s]
Now rub your palms together. Briskly, the way you would on a cold winter morning.
Keep going until you feel real warmth in the hollows of your hands.
[pause 2s]
Close your eyes. Then gently cup your palms over them. Your fingers rest on your forehead, the heels of your hands on your cheekbones.
No pressure on the eyes themselves. Just a pocket of warmth and darkness.
If you can, rest your elbows on the table, so your arms don't get tired.
If you wear glasses, you can take them off and set them aside. If you wear contacts, simply keep your eyelids relaxed.
[pause 3s]
This is called palming. It's a very simple way to rest your eyes, by giving them complete darkness.
Let the warmth of your hands spread over your eyelids. Then your brows, your temples, the bridge of your nose.
[pause 2s]
Do you still see spots of light, shapes, colors?
[pause 2s]
Let them fade on their own. You don't need to look for them.
The harder your eyes have worked, the longer they may need to really rest. Give them that time, without expecting anything in particular.
[pause 2s]
In this darkness, let your breathing slow down. You don't have to control it. Let it find a slightly calmer rhythm by itself.
Breathe in through your nose... and feel the cool air come in.
[pause 4s]
Breathe out slowly... and feel your shoulders drop a little.
[pause 6s]
If it helps, make the out breath a little longer than the in breath. Or don't measure anything at all.
[pause 3s]
Each exhale can soften the tiny muscles around your eyes a bit more. The ones that squint, stare and refocus all day long.
They can rest now too.
[pause 2s]
If a work thought shows up, an email to send, a file to finish, let it pass. It has no place here for now.
You can even say to it, silently, later. Then come back to the warmth of your hands, and the rhythm of your breath.
[pause 3s]
Keep your hands over your eyes, and now open your ears.
Listen to the sounds in the room. There are probably more than you thought.
The hum of a vent. A fridge or a computer whirring. Footsteps in a hallway, a voice in the distance, a car outside.
[pause 2s]
You don't need to name them, or to like them. Just let them come to you.
Notice the closest ones, then the farthest ones. And then the small silence between two sounds.
[pause 3s]
Some sounds are steady, like a backdrop. Others are brief, they arrive and disappear. For once, your ears are doing the work, and your eyes get to rest.
[pause 3s]
Slowly, let your hands come down and rest on your thighs, or on the table. Keep your eyes closed a little longer.
Now feel your body. Your weight in the chair. Your feet on the floor. Your back against the backrest.
And your hands. Empty hands, for once. No mouse, no phone, no pen.
[pause 2s]
Feel the air on your palms. The warmth that's still there. A faint tingling in your fingertips.
Maybe your hands want to do something. Let them do nothing. It's rare enough to enjoy.
[pause 2s]
Notice the smell of the room as well. Coffee, paper, the air from a window left open. A sense no screen ever reaches.
Touch, hearing, smell. All of them were on standby while your eyes did the work. You've just given them a little room again.
[pause 2s]
Now get ready to open your eyes. Before you do, turn your head slightly toward a window, or toward the far end of the room.
Open your eyelids slowly. Let the light come back little by little.
[pause 2s]
And find the farthest point you can see. A building, the sky, a tree, the back wall.
Rest your gaze there. Keep it soft, without searching for detail. Notice the space between you and that point.
[pause 3s]
Then bring your gaze to something at mid distance. A plant, a door. And back out, far away. Your eyes loosen up, like a muscle being stretched.
[pause 3s]
Blink several times. It helps keep your eyes moist, and in front of a screen we often forget to do it.
[pause 2s]
Before you go back to your screens, choose one simple rule for the next hour.
For example, every twenty minutes, look at something far away for twenty seconds. Or leave your phone in the drawer until your next break.
Just one rule, easy to keep. Which one is yours?
[pause 3s]
It may seem tiny. But repeated day after day, a small rule often changes more than a big resolution.
Your eyes now remember what it's like to look far away. You can come back to it whenever they ask.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Close the workday
script: [pause 1.5s]
Your workday is coming to an end. What if, tonight, you truly closed it, instead of letting it spill over into your evening?
It matters even more when you work from home, when your office and your living room are the same space.
[pause 2s]
Settle in at your workspace, one last time today. Feet on the floor, hands resting on your thighs.
You can close your eyes, or let your gaze rest on the edge of your desk.
Your head may still be full. Bits of conversations, numbers, things you mustn't forget. That's normal, after a whole day.
We're not going to empty it all at once. We're just going to tidy up, the way you'd clear a desk in the evening.
Think of these minutes as a bridge between your work self and the rest of your life.
[pause 3s]
Take an easy breath in through your nose...
[pause 3s]
then breathe out through your mouth, slowly, all the way.
[pause 5s]
Once more...
[pause 3s]
and let your breathing find its own rhythm, a little slower than it's been all day.
[pause 3s]
Notice the air coming in through your nose, slightly cool, and leaving a little warmer.
Feel the weight of your body in the chair. All day long, you've been turned outward. Messages, requests, other people.
Now, for a few minutes, you're turning back toward yourself.
Let your hands grow heavy on your thighs. Let your jaw loosen. These are the first signals to your body that the effort can stop.
[pause 3s]
Let's start by reviewing your day. Not to judge it, but to recognize what you did.
Look for three things you got done today. Just three. They can be very small.
A difficult email, finally sent. A problem solved. A colleague you really listened to. A boring task, crossed off the list.
Find the first one. Replay it for a moment. And acknowledge it. That's done.
[pause 3s]
Now a second one. Maybe something nobody noticed. It counts too.
[pause 3s]
And a third. If nothing comes, that's okay. Getting through the day is already something.
[pause 2s]
What does it feel like to count what got done, rather than what's missing? We do it so rarely.
[pause 2s]
These three things also say something about you. Your persistence, your attention to detail, your kindness toward others. Those qualities were there all day, even when you couldn't see them.
Take a moment to let them really count. No need for big pride. Just a simple thank-you to yourself for the effort.
[pause 3s]
Of course, there are things left. There always are. Tasks half-finished, replies pending, projects that won't budge.
Your mind tends to keep them open, like browser tabs running in the background all evening.
Let's close them, one by one. Picture tomorrow's list. A sheet of paper, a notebook, or a screen, whatever you prefer.
Take the first thing that's left, and write it on that list in your mind. Just a few words.
[pause 3s]
Then the next one. And the one after that. Take your time. You don't need to solve them. Just write them down.
Each time you add one, you can tell yourself... it's noted, I'll deal with it tomorrow.
[pause 3s]
Writing a task down somewhere, even in your mind, gets it out of your head a little. Your mind no longer has to keep repeating it so you won't forget.
Tomorrow, you'll be fresher, and better placed to handle it.
If there are a lot, that's normal. The list can be long. It'll be waiting for you tomorrow morning, and you'll come back to it with a rested mind.
And if one thing is truly urgent for tomorrow, circle it in your mind. You'll know where to start, without having to think about it again tonight.
If you like, you can write the list for real after this session. It often helps the mind let go.
[pause 2s]
Now, there may be something else. Not a task, but something difficult. Tension with someone, a frustration, a worry.
Choose one, not the heaviest. Just the one that's still with you right now.
Acknowledge it. You can tell yourself... yes, today, that was hard.
And maybe ask yourself, did I do my best, with what I had today? Often, the answer is yes. Even if the result wasn't perfect.
[pause 3s]
That difficulty belongs to work. Its place is at the office. Not in your kitchen, not in your bed.
Imagine setting it down on your desk, next to your keyboard. It'll stay there tonight. You can pick it back up tomorrow, if it's still useful.
What changes in your shoulders, in your chest, when you don't carry it with you?
[pause 3s]
If it keeps coming back, that's not a failure. You can simply set it down again, the way you'd put something back in its place.
[pause 2s]
It's time to mark the end. A concrete gesture, to tell your body the day is over.
When you work from home, this is often what's missing. No door to walk through, no commute, no colleagues saying goodnight. So it's up to you to create that boundary.
If you can, open your eyes. Save whatever needs saving. Then close your laptop. Listen to the soft click of the lid.
[pause 2s]
Notice the screen going dark, and the room growing a little quieter around you.
If you have a desk lamp, switch it off. Put your pen away, stack your papers.
You might also mute work notifications on your phone until tomorrow morning.
If you can't do this right now, picture it in detail. The lid closing. The light going out.
And say to yourself, silently or under your breath... my workday is done.
[pause 3s]
Take another breath. This one no longer belongs to work.
[pause 3s]
Now let's open up your evening. Simply ask yourself, what do I feel like doing tonight?
Not what you have to do. What you'd enjoy.
Maybe a meal you love. A call to someone. A walk outside, even a short one. A movie, a bath, a book, or nothing at all.
Even something small counts, like ten minutes on the balcony or a favorite song.
Let an image come. And let yourself look forward to it.
[pause 2s]
That wish matters. An evening that holds at least one moment you chose often feels more restful than one spent waiting for tomorrow.
Notice where that anticipation lives in your body. A little lift in your chest, a softening in your belly, a smile at the corner of your mouth.
[pause 3s]
To help the transition, you can change something concrete. Change your clothes, change rooms, open a window.
That small change tells your brain we're moving on to something else.
And if work thoughts come back during the evening, which they probably will, just remind yourself... it's noted, it's on the list. Then return to what you're doing.
[pause 2s]
Notice how you feel now, compared to the beginning. Without expecting anything. Maybe a little lighter. Maybe just tired, and that's okay too.
And if there's still a bit of tension, that's fine. This ritual works through repetition, evening after evening.
Gently move your fingers, your shoulders. Stretch, if your body wants to.
[pause 2s]
What's done is done. What's left is written down. What was hard stayed at the office.
The workday is over. Your evening begins. It belongs to you.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Unwind before sleep
script: [pause 1.5s]
Good evening. It's time to set the day down.
There's nothing special you need to do for these few minutes. Just listen, and let me guide you towards the night.
[pause 2s]
Settle into bed in whatever position suits you tonight. On your back, arms by your sides. Or on your side, one knee slightly bent.
Take a moment to move a little, if your body wants to. Stretch your legs. Wiggle your toes. Turn your head gently to one side, then the other.
[pause 2s]
Then find the place where everything stops. The hollow waiting for you in the mattress, warm and familiar.
You can close your eyes now. Or leave them half closed, if you prefer, your gaze resting nowhere in particular.
[pause 2s]
Simply notice what's here. The room. The darkness, or the dimmed light. The temperature of the air on your face, a little cooler on your nose and cheeks.
The weight of the duvet, resting over you like a calm, steady hand. The pillow under your cheek, or under the back of your neck.
[pause 4s]
The day was whatever it was. Long, perhaps. Full. Or just ordinary.
To help you leave it behind, here's an image you can borrow for a moment.
[pause 1.5s]
Imagine your day is a room, somewhere in your home.
A room with the light still on, a little untidy, with all the day's things lying around.
The emails. The conversations. The to-do list. The noise of the commute. The small annoyances. The questions that still have no answer.
[pause 2s]
You're standing in the doorway. You look at the room one last time, with no need to tidy anything.
Everything in there will stay there. Nothing will get lost. Tomorrow, if you need it, you'll know exactly where to find it.
[pause 2s]
Now reach for the light switch. And turn off the light.
The room goes dark. The day's things fade into shadow, one by one, like furniture under dust sheets.
[pause 2s]
Then, gently, you pull the door towards you.
It closes. You hear the soft click of the latch.
[pause 4s]
On this side of the door, there's only the night. The quiet. Your bed.
You have nothing left to carry until tomorrow. No more meetings, no more messages, no more answers to give.
If something from the day comes knocking, that's alright. You hear it, you notice it. And you leave it on the other side.
[pause 3s]
Now, come to your breath.
Just notice the air coming in and the air going out, without changing anything for now.
Maybe it's still a little quick, a little high in your chest. That's completely normal at the end of a day.
[pause 2s]
If you like, rest one hand on your belly, just below the navel. The other can stay where it is.
Under your hand, feel your belly rise as the air comes in, and fall as it leaves. Gently. Like a small boat on calm water.
[pause 3s]
Now let the out breath grow longer. Only the out breath.
There's nothing to count. Picture the air leaving like a balloon slowly letting itself down, without being squeezed.
You breathe in normally...
[pause 3s]
and let the air out for longer, all the way to the end, unhurried.
[pause 6s]
An out breath that's longer than the in breath can help the body slow down. It's a very simple signal, a way of telling it that the day is over.
The air comes in, cool...
[pause 3s]
and flows out, warm, like a long, silent sigh.
[pause 6s]
Once more. The air comes in without effort...
[pause 3s]
and leaves slowly, taking a little of the day's tiredness with it.
[pause 6s]
And at the end of each out breath, there's sometimes a tiny moment of stillness. A small dip, before the next breath arrives on its own.
You don't need to make it happen. Just notice it, when it's there.
It's a little like the quiet between two waves, when you're lying by the sea. You don't wait for it. It comes, and it goes.
[pause 2s]
If at any point you feel short of air, go straight back to your natural breath. Nothing should be forced.
[pause 4s]
Keep this slow breath in the background. And while it carries on, let's relax the body, starting with the face.
Your forehead first. Let it widen, as if someone were gently smoothing a thumb between your eyebrows.
[pause 2s]
Your eyes, behind your eyelids. They have nothing left to look at. They can rest deep in their sockets, heavy and still.
Your eyelids grow heavy too, like two small velvet curtains drawn for the night.
[pause 2s]
Your cheeks. Your mouth. Let your lips barely touch.
Your jaw, above all. That's often where the day hides. Let it loosen, teeth slightly apart.
Your tongue can come away from the roof of your mouth and rest, soft and heavy, at the bottom.
[pause 2s]
And all around your ears, your temples, your scalp, let a softness spread, like warm water flowing slowly over your head.
[pause 3s]
Your shoulders, now.
All day long, they've been carrying. A bag, a screen, responsibilities, other people's worries.
Tonight, they can come down. On an out breath, let them slide towards the mattress, a little lower. Then a little more.
[pause 3s]
Notice the space opening between your shoulders and your ears. The back of your neck lengthens. Your throat softens.
If there's still a knot somewhere, between your shoulder blades or at the base of your neck, don't try to undo it. Just send your breath its way, and let it melt in its own time.
[pause 3s]
Your arms follow. Your elbows. Your forearms. Your wrists.
And your hands. Let them open, palms up or palms down, whichever they like.
Notice your fingers one at a time. Thumb. Index finger. Middle finger. Ring finger. Little finger.
They have nothing left to hold, nothing to type, nothing to scroll. Only to rest.
[pause 2s]
You might feel a gentle warmth in your palms, or a faint tingling in your fingertips. Let it simply be there.
[pause 2s]
Your chest, now. It rises and falls without any help from you. Let it open a little, like a window left ajar on a quiet night.
Your belly becomes soft, round and loose. It doesn't need to hold itself in anymore. It can spread out freely under the duvet.
[pause 4s]
Now feel your whole body lying on the bed.
Feel the places where it touches the mattress. The back of your head. Your shoulder blades. Your lower back. Your heels.
[pause 2s]
With each out breath, you sink a little deeper. As if the mattress were growing deeper, softer, more welcoming.
You don't have to hold yourself up. The bed is holding you.
[pause 3s]
Your back can spread out. Your hips can grow heavy. Your legs can grow heavy, all the way down to your feet.
Your thighs sink into the sheet. Your knees let go. Your calves become soft and heavy.
Your ankles relax, and your feet fall slightly to the side, however they like.
[pause 3s]
Imagine sinking into warm sand in the evening sun. The sand shapes itself to every curve of your body.
It's warm under your calves, under your thighs, under your back. It holds you everywhere at once, and there's no effort left to make.
[pause 3s]
You might notice how different your body feels from a few minutes ago. Heavier. Wider. Slower. Or maybe not yet, and that's fine too.
[pause 4s]
Nothing left to do. Nothing left to decide.
Now let your breath return to its natural rhythm. You don't need to lengthen it anymore. It has found its own pace.
It comes and goes by itself, like the tide rising and falling on the beach.
You can simply watch it from a distance, the way you might watch waves without counting them.
[pause 4s]
Each breath a little slower than the last. Or maybe not. It doesn't matter. There's nothing left to check.
You drift gently, from one breath to the next, like a leaf floating down a quiet river, carried along by the current.
[pause 4s]
Listen, too, to the sounds of the night around you. Rain, perhaps. A car passing in the distance. The quiet of the house.
All these sounds belong to the night. They ask nothing of you. They might even rock you to sleep.
The rain falls on the roof, drop after drop, steady and soft. Each drop arrives, and then it's gone.
[pause 4s]
If thoughts pass by, let them pass. They're on the other side of the door.
You don't have to chase them away. They can wait until tomorrow, safely tucked away in that dark room.
[pause 3s]
If your sleep troubles go on for a while, a health professional can support you. Tonight, you can simply rest.
[pause 3s]
My voice will grow quieter now, and soon it will fade away. You can let it go, and stay right here, in the warmth of your bed.
[pause 3s]
The door is closed. The room is quiet.
[pause 3s]
Your body is heavy... and warm...
[pause 4s]
Your shoulders are resting. Your hands are resting.
[pause 4s]
The breath comes... and goes...
[pause 5s]
Soft... slow... still...
[pause 5s]
Everything slows down...
[pause 5s]
The bed holds you. The night is here.
[pause 4s]
Goodnight.
[pause 10s]

sessions.title: Heavy body, quiet mind
script: [pause 1.5s]
Tonight, your body may still be holding on to the day. Stiff shoulders, a clenched jaw, legs that won't keep still.
For these fifteen minutes, I'd like to offer you two very old, very simple sensations. Heaviness, and warmth.
It's a method that's been around for nearly a century, called autogenic training. The idea fits in one sentence. You silently repeat short phrases, and let your body respond in its own time.
[pause 2s]
Why heaviness and warmth? Because they're the natural sensations of a body letting go. When muscles release, your arms and legs feel heavier.
And when the body relaxes, blood flows more freely to the hands and feet, and they slowly warm up.
By thinking of these sensations, you walk that path in reverse. You invite your body to take the shape of rest.
You don't have to make anything happen. You say the words in your head and notice what follows. Sometimes a lot.
Sometimes almost nothing. Both are fine.
[pause 2s]
Lie on your back, if that's comfortable for you. Arms by your sides, a little away from your body, palms however they like.
Legs stretched out, slightly apart, feet falling naturally outward.
If your back pulls, you can slide a cushion under your knees. If you prefer sleeping on your side, stay on your side. The phrases work there too.
Take a moment to move one last time. A small stretch, a yawn if one wants to come, a little adjustment of the pillow under your neck.
[pause 3s]
After that, the idea is to stay still. Not rigid. Just resting, like a leaf that has landed on water.
Let your eyes close. Breathe normally. Don't try to breathe better.
Just feel the air coming in and going out, at its own pace. A little cooler as it comes in through your nose, a little warmer as it leaves.
[pause 3s]
Notice the places where you're supported, too. The back of your head in the pillow.
Your shoulder blades on the mattress. Your hips, your calves, your heels.
Everywhere your body touches the bed, there's support. And everywhere there's support, you can let a little more weight settle down.
[pause 5s]
You can begin with the core phrase. The one that opens and accompanies everything else.
Repeat it silently, slowly, leaving a space after each word. I am... completely... calm.
[pause 3s]
I am completely calm.
[pause 3s]
Don't ask yourself whether it's true. It isn't an order, and it isn't a lie.
It's a direction. Like pointing someone the way.
You can have a thousand things on your mind and still say, I am calm. The words open a door. The rest will follow, or not, tonight or another night.
[pause 2s]
I am calm. Let the words settle, like a pebble drifting slowly down to the bottom of a pond, and resting there.
[pause 3s]
If your mind wanders, toward tomorrow, toward a conversation, toward a list of things to do, that's completely normal. Come back to the phrase, without hurrying.
I am completely calm. Say it once more, more slowly, the way you'd say goodnight to someone you love.
[pause 5s]
Now, heaviness.
Start with your right arm. If your left side feels more natural, you can start there instead, whichever feels right to you.
Bring your attention to that arm. The shoulder. The upper arm.
The elbow. The forearm. The wrist.
The hand, right to the fingertips.
[pause 2s]
Feel how it rests on the mattress. Its weight.
The place where it touches the sheet. The fabric under your skin, cool or already warm.
And silently, repeat. My right arm is heavy.
[pause 3s]
My right arm is very heavy.
[pause 3s]
Imagine it filled with warm sand, flowing slowly from the shoulder down into the hand. The sand gathers in your palm, in your fingers, and the hand grows weighty and still.
Or imagine it's become so heavy that lifting it would take real effort. You don't need to try. Just imagine it.
My right arm is heavy, so heavy.
[pause 3s]
Like the arm of a child asleep in the back seat of a car. Completely limp. If someone lifted it, it would simply flop back down.
Notice whatever sensations arise. A tingling, a numbness, a feeling of sinking.
Or nothing in particular. All of it is right.
[pause 2s]
The elbow opens a little. The wrist softens. The fingers curl gently, all by themselves, like the fingers of a sleeping hand.
My right arm is heavy. And I am calm.
[pause 5s]
Now, the left arm. The shoulder, the upper arm, the elbow, the forearm, the wrist, the hand.
My left arm is heavy.
[pause 3s]
My left arm is very heavy. It sinks into the mattress, like a damp piece of clothing laid on the bed, following every fold of the sheet.
Feel the weight of the hand most of all. The back of the hand, or the palm, pressing into the sheet. The fingers spreading a little, on their own.
And the shoulder easing backward, as if it were opening. It doesn't need to stay ready anymore. It can rest now.
My left arm is heavy, heavy and peaceful.
[pause 3s]
Both my arms are heavy. Heavy and resting.
They have nothing left to carry, nothing left to hold. No bag, no phone, no steering wheel, no worries.
Maybe one arm responds more than the other. That's very common.
The body isn't symmetrical, and it doesn't have to be. Let each side go at its own pace.
I am calm. My arms are heavy.
[pause 5s]
Now the heaviness moves down into your legs.
The right leg first. The hip, the thigh, the knee, the calf, the ankle, the foot.
My right leg is heavy.
[pause 3s]
My right leg is very heavy. Like a log lying in the grass. It doesn't move anymore.
Feel the thigh spreading out, the back of the knee drawing closer to the mattress, the heel making a small hollow in the bed.
The foot tips gently outward. The ankle loosens. Even the toes can rest now.
My right leg is heavy, from the hip all the way down to the heel.
[pause 4s]
Now the left leg. From the hip all the way to the toes.
My left leg is heavy.
[pause 3s]
My left leg is very heavy. The heel sinks, the calf spreads, the thigh becomes weighty and soft.
Like after a long walk in the mountains, when you finally lie down and your legs feel as if they're made of lead. A good kind of tiredness. A tiredness that has earned its rest.
All day, your legs have carried you, up stairs, down streets, from room to room. Tonight, it's the bed that carries them.
My legs are heavy. My arms and legs are heavy.
[pause 3s]
Take a moment to feel all four limbs at once. Four quiet weights, resting on the bed, all around you.
And perhaps the middle of your body has softened a little too. Your back spreading wider. Your pelvis heavier.
As if the heaviness of your limbs had spread to everything else, little by little, the way water slowly soaks into a sponge.
I am completely calm.
[pause 6s]
Now, to this heaviness, you can add some warmth.
Not a strong heat. A gentle warmth, like a lukewarm bath, or an autumn sunbeam resting on your skin.
Come back to the right arm. Feel the skin of your hand, the inside of your elbow, the soft hollow of your wrist.
My right arm is warm.
[pause 3s]
My right arm is very warm. Imagine slowly lowering it into water at just the right temperature. The warmth rises from your fingertips up to your shoulder.
Or imagine sitting on a terrace late in the afternoon, with the sun resting on your forearm. You feel the skin growing warm, little by little.
Maybe your fingers tingle a bit. Maybe your palm feels thicker, fuller. That's relaxation finding its way through you.
[pause 3s]
My left arm is warm.
[pause 3s]
My left arm is very warm. Your hand may feel a little fuller, a little more alive. Like slipping on wool gloves on a cold winter morning.
The warmth glides along the forearm, wraps around the elbow, rises to the shoulder, and settles there, like a cat curled up in a ball.
My arms are warm. Heavy and warm.
[pause 5s]
The warmth flows down into your legs.
My right leg is warm.
[pause 3s]
My right leg is very warm. As if a soft blanket had just been laid over it, a blanket that had been left for a while in front of the fireplace.
The warmth wraps around the thigh, the knee, the calf. It moves through the ankle and down into the foot.
[pause 3s]
My left leg is warm.
[pause 3s]
My left leg is very warm. Right down into the foot, right down into the toes.
Cold feet are often what keeps us from falling asleep. Let the warmth settle there, gently, without forcing anything.
Imagine a hot water bottle at the bottom of the bed, resting against the soles of your feet. The warmth spreads into your heels, into your arches, in between your toes.
[pause 3s]
My arms and legs are heavy and warm.
Heavy, as if they were sinking into the mattress. Warm, as if they were wrapped in soft wool. Let those two sensations blend together.
I am completely calm.
[pause 6s]
Now, come to your belly.
Rest a hand on it if you like, just above your navel. Otherwise, simply bring your attention to that place.
Imagine a small source of warmth deep in your belly. Like a cup of herbal tea held in your hands, but on the inside.
My belly is warm. A gentle warmth glows deep in my belly.
[pause 3s]
My belly is very warm. The warmth slowly spreads, toward your ribs, toward your lower back, toward your hips.
That's often where the knots of the day like to hide, deep in the belly. Let the warmth surround them, without trying to undo them. They may loosen all on their own.
Your belly softens. It doesn't need to stay pulled in. It can round out and let go, like bread dough quietly rising somewhere warm.
My belly is warm, and my whole body softens around it.
[pause 6s]
And your breath, all this time?
[pause 2s]
You don't need to do anything with it. It carries on by itself, as it has since the start of the evening, since the start of your life.
The phrase is, it breathes me.
It breathes me. As if you were being carried by the breath, instead of steering it.
[pause 3s]
Your belly rises, and falls. Like a small boat on a very calm sea, lifting and sinking with the swell.
My breathing is calm and even. It breathes me.
[pause 3s]
You don't have to lengthen it, or slow it down. It knows exactly what your body needs. You can trust it, the way you'd trust the current of a slow, peaceful river.
Maybe you notice a tiny pause, right at the bottom of the out-breath. A moment where nothing moves, before the air returns.
There's nothing to do with that moment. Just let it be there.
If you feel dizzy or uncomfortable at any point, set the phrases aside and simply return to your natural breathing.
It breathes me, quietly, all on its own.
[pause 6s]
Before moving to your face, feel your shoulders and the back of your neck. The warmth from your arms may have risen up there too.
Your shoulders round and settle, as if they'd been wrapped in a wool shawl. Your neck lengthens on the pillow. Your head grows heavy, and the pillow receives it.
[pause 3s]
And now, your face.
Your whole body is heavy and warm. But your forehead can stay cool. Like stepping out onto a balcony on a summer evening, when a light breeze brushes across your face.
My forehead is pleasantly cool.
[pause 3s]
My forehead is cool. A cool forehead, a clear, light head, resting on the pillow.
Let your eyebrows soften too. Your eyelids grow heavy. Your jaw loosens, teeth slightly apart, tongue resting.
Your cheeks soften. Your lips barely touch. The tiny muscles around your eyes, the ones that have looked at screens all day, can finally rest.
Your whole face is relaxed. Forehead cool.
Cheeks soft. Mouth at peace.
[pause 6s]
Now, gather it all together. Let the phrases melt into one another, slowly, like colors spreading through water.
My arms and legs are heavy and warm.
[pause 3s]
My belly is warm.
[pause 3s]
It breathes me.
[pause 3s]
My forehead is cool.
[pause 3s]
I am completely calm.
[pause 5s]
Feel your whole body, heavy and warm, resting on the bed. Like a stone still holding the warmth of the evening sun.
The mattress holds all of you. You have nothing left to hold up. Not your arms, not your legs, not your head, not the day.
[pause 3s]
Go through it all, without hurrying. Your arms, heavy and warm. Your legs, heavy and warm.
Your belly, gently warm. Your breath, coming and going on its own. Your forehead, cool.
And everywhere, this calm settling in, like snow covering a garden during the night, without a sound.
[pause 5s]
If the words fade, let them fade. The sensations can carry on without them.
If anything bothers you, warmth that feels too strong, a heaviness that feels unpleasant, simply drop the phrase and come back to your natural breathing.
Tonight, there's nothing to come back to. No waking up, no getting ready. You can stay exactly as you are, and let sleep arrive whenever it wants.
If your body stays tense night after night, or if you've been sleeping badly for a long time, it's worth talking to a health professional.
[pause 6s]
Your body is heavy. It sinks, a little further, into the softness of the bed.
[pause 4s]
It's warm. A quiet warmth, from your shoulders all the way to your feet.
[pause 4s]
Your breath comes and goes. On its own. Like the sea, far away.
[pause 5s]
You are calm.
[pause 4s]
Heavy...
[pause 4s]
warm...
[pause 4s]
calm...
[pause 6s]
It breathes you...
[pause 10s]

sessions.title: Quiet a racing mind
script: [pause 1.5s]
It's busy up there tonight. Ideas follow one another, answer each other, circle back. And sleep is struggling to find a way in.
[pause 2s]
You haven't done anything wrong. A mind that races at bedtime is often a mind that hasn't had a minute to itself all day. It's making the most of the quiet.
During the day there's noise, screens, other people. At night, in the dark, there's only the mind left. So it unpacks everything.
[pause 2s]
So we won't ask it to be quiet. That never really works. The more you chase a thought away, the faster it comes running back.
We'll do something else. Let the thoughts be there, and learn not to follow them.
It's a skill, like any other. It's learned gently, night after night. And tonight, you don't need to master it. Just try it, a little.
[pause 2s]
Settle in first. On your back, or on your side, whichever you prefer.
If your eyes want to close, let them. If they'd rather stay half open in the dark, that's fine too.
Take a breath a little fuller than the others...
[pause 3s]
and let it go, without holding on.
[pause 5s]
One more. Fill up gently...
[pause 3s]
and empty out completely, like a long, slow sigh.
[pause 5s]
Then let your breath find its own rhythm again. You don't need to guide it anymore.
[pause 2s]
To begin, let's give your attention somewhere to land. Not in your head. Lower down. In your body.
Feel the weight of your body on the bed.
[pause 2s]
Your head, first. It's heavy in the pillow. You can feel the exact place where it rests. The back of your skull, your temple, or your cheek.
Your neck, with nothing left to hold up. The small muscles around your jaw, which can loosen a little, your teeth slightly apart.
[pause 2s]
Your shoulders. Your upper back. Notice how supported they are, without you having to do a thing.
Your arms, lying by your sides or on the covers. They're growing a little heavier, a little softer. Your hands, open or half closed, however they like.
[pause 2s]
Your pelvis, often the heaviest part. It sinks a little deeper than the rest, settling into its own small hollow in the mattress.
The backs of your thighs. Your calves. Your heels. All of it is resting. All of it is held.
And your feet, right at the end. Maybe a little coolness on your toes, or a soft warmth instead, tucked in under the duvet.
[pause 5s]
This weight is your anchor for tonight. It's always there. It doesn't think, it doesn't plan. It simply weighs.
And this bed will still be holding you in an hour, and at dawn. There's nothing you need to hold up yourself.
Each time you get lost in your thoughts, you can come back here. To the weight of your body on the bed.
[pause 3s]
Of course, thoughts will come. That's guaranteed. And that's fine. They'll be our practice.
When a thought arrives, give it a little name. A label, a single word, said silently, in a calm inner voice.
Not to analyse it. Just to recognise it. A bit like saying, oh, a bus, when a bus goes by in the street.
[pause 2s]
A few labels come up often.
If you're thinking about tomorrow, what you need to do, which order to do it in, you can say, planning.
If you're replaying a scene from the day, a conversation, a face, you can say, remembering.
If you're wondering what will happen, whether it'll go well, what you'd do if it went wrong, you can say, worrying.
There are others, if you like. Judging, when a small voice comments on what you did or didn't do. Rehearsing, when you're scripting a conversation that hasn't happened yet.
And if you're not sure, the word thinking works perfectly well. There's no wrong label.
[pause 3s]
Let's try it together. Let whatever comes, come. Don't go looking for anything in particular.
When a thought appears, name it. Planning. Remembering. Worrying. Thinking.
Then come back to the weight of your body on the bed.
[pause 3s]
For example, you think, I must call the garage tomorrow before ten. You notice, and you name it... planning. Then you feel your pelvis, heavy on the mattress.
Or you see your colleague's face in that meeting again. Remembering. And you come back to your heels, resting at the bottom of the bed.
Or a small voice tells you that you should have answered differently. Judging. And you feel your shoulders, broad and quiet against the sheet.
And maybe, all of a sudden, you find yourself preparing exactly what you'll say to someone tomorrow, word for word. Rehearsing. And you come back to your hands, resting, still.
[pause 2s]
That's all. A thought, a word, the body. And then again, as many times as you need.
[pause 5s]
Maybe the same thought comes back several times in a row. You name it each time. That isn't failing. That's the practice.
Maybe you were lost for a long while before you noticed anything. That's normal too. The moment you notice is the moment that counts.
[pause 2s]
When you name a thought, you take a small step to the side. You're no longer inside it. You're looking at it.
It's still there, but it's a little less sticky. A little further away.
A bit like the difference between standing in the rain and watching the rain from behind a window. Same rain. But you're dry, and warm, and you can let it fall.
[pause 3s]
To help you find that distance, imagine you're lying in a bedroom beside a country road, at night.
Every so often, a car passes in the distance. You hear its engine approaching, and maybe you see the headlights sweep slowly across the ceiling.
Then the sound fades. The light disappears. The room is dark and quiet again.
[pause 3s]
A little later, another one. A truck perhaps, heavier, slower. Then a scooter, high-pitched, in a hurry. Then nothing for a long while, just the hush of the countryside and the room around you.
You don't know where they're going. You don't need to know. They aren't your journeys.
[pause 2s]
Your thoughts are like those cars.
They arrive, they pass, they move on. You don't need to stop them. You don't need to get in.
You stay in your bed, warm and heavy. You hear them go by, far off, on the road, and you let them keep going.
[pause 5s]
Sometimes a car slows down. A thought insists, honks its horn a little.
You can give it its label. Worrying. Planning. And let it continue on its way.
It has its own destination. You stay here, warm, under the duvet, with nowhere you need to be until morning.
[pause 2s]
And if you notice you've climbed into the car, that you're already driving off with it toward tomorrow or yesterday... just step out.
Without blaming yourself for anything. Come back to your room. To your bed. To this body, heavy and quiet.
[pause 4s]
Now, feel the points of contact.
The sheet under your hands. Its texture. A little smooth, or a little rough. Cooler in some places, warmer where your skin has been resting for a while.
The pillow against your face or the back of your neck. Its softness. Its warmth, right where your head lies.
[pause 2s]
The duvet over your feet and legs. The slight weight of it. Like a wide, light hand resting on you.
Maybe the air is a little cooler on the tip of your nose, or on your forehead. And under the covers, a gentle warmth, settling in.
These sensations don't talk. They don't plan anything, and they don't replay anything either. They're simply here, now, keeping you company.
[pause 3s]
If you like, move one finger very slightly across the sheet. Feel the fabric glide under your fingertip. Then let your hand go still again, heavy, resting.
It's a very simple anchor, one you can return to at any moment of the night, even if you wake up later on.
[pause 5s]
When a thought comes, name it. And come back to the sheet. To the pillow.
A car goes by... its lights slide across the ceiling... and the room is quiet and dark again.
[pause 4s]
Now let's add something very small.
On each out-breath, let the air leave a little more slowly. Just a little. As if you were blowing on a cup of herbal tea that's too hot.
The in-breath stays natural. Only the out-breath stretches, without forcing.
If at any point it feels uncomfortable, or you're short of air, simply return to your usual breathing.
[pause 2s]
The air comes in...
[pause 3s]
and goes out, taking its time.
[pause 6s]
With each out-breath, your body weighs a little more on the bed.
On one out-breath, your shoulders. On the next, your arms. Then your belly, rising and falling all on its own. Then your legs.
As if each breath leaving set a little more of you down into the mattress.
[pause 5s]
A quiet warmth, perhaps, in your hands. In your belly. Or nowhere in particular. Either is perfectly fine.
Thoughts may still be passing. Further away. Less often. Or not.
You don't have to count them. You don't have to do better than last night.
[pause 3s]
Maybe you'll simply notice that the cars are passing less often. That the road is quieter. That the silences between them are growing longer.
And in those silences, there's you, lying here, heavy, still.
[pause 4s]
You don't need to fall asleep. Sleep will come when it's ready, in its own time, like the tide that always finds its way softly back up the sand. You're resting, and that's already plenty.
[pause 5s]
I'll speak less and less now. You know what to do, and it's very little.
A thought comes. A word. And back to the weight of the body.
[pause 4s]
If you've drifted off somewhere, no problem. The bed is still here. So is your weight.
A word, if a thought passes. Then the sheet under your hand.
[pause 5s]
Planning... and your pelvis, heavy.
[pause 4s]
Remembering... and your head, in the hollow of the pillow.
[pause 4s]
Worrying... and the breath flowing out, slowly, all by itself.
[pause 5s]
The out-breath, a little longer, a little softer.
Your shoulders sinking. Your legs, heavy. Your hands, warm.
The warmth under the covers, wrapping around you a little more with every breath.
[pause 5s]
If night-time overthinking has been spoiling your nights for a long time, a health professional can help. Tonight, you've already done a lot.
[pause 6s]
A car, far away...
[pause 3s]
then the quiet.
[pause 4s]
The road, completely silent, under a moonless sky.
[pause 5s]
The weight of the body... the sheet... the breath...
[pause 5s]
Nothing to do... nothing to hold on to...
[pause 10s]

sessions.title: Awake at 3am
script: [pause 1.5s]
Shh... it's alright.
[pause 1.5s]
You're awake, in the middle of the night. That's okay.
You haven't done anything wrong. Sleep comes in waves, and sometimes you drift up to the surface between two of them.
It happens to almost everyone. Even people who sleep like logs.
[pause 2s]
Don't reach for your phone. Don't check the time.
The number on the screen wouldn't tell you anything useful. It would only start the sums. How many hours are left, what time the alarm goes off.
Those sums can wait. There is no time right now. There's only the night.
[pause 2.5s]
If you're on your side, stay on your side. If you're on your back, stay on your back.
You don't need the perfect position. Just one that's good enough.
Adjust the pillow if you need to. Then let your head sink back into it, with all its weight.
Feel the pillow give a little under your cheek, under your temple. That's what it's there for.
[pause 4s]
Here's something true, and reassuring.
Lying still, eyes closed, in the quiet, is not wasted time.
Your body is already resting. Your muscles are softening. Your heart is slowing. Your breathing is settling.
Even awake, you're recovering. Not as much as in sleep, of course. But far more than you might think.
[pause 2s]
So for now, you don't have to sleep. You only have to rest.
And that, you know how to do. In fact, you're already doing it, right now, without any effort at all.
Nobody is grading you. There's no good night or bad night to hand in tomorrow morning. There's only this moment, lying here, in the quiet.
[pause 5s]
Maybe your mind woke up with you.
A conversation from yesterday. An email you need to send. A worry that grows bigger in the dark.
That's very common at night. Thoughts look larger, heavier, more urgent.
Not because they're more serious. Because it's dark, because you're tired, and a tired mind sees everything in deeper shades.
A bit like a shadow on the wall that looks huge because of where the lamp is.
Tomorrow morning, with a coffee and some daylight, the very same thought will be back to its normal size.
[pause 2.5s]
You can tell it, very gently... not now. We'll deal with this tomorrow.
The way you'd set something down on the nightstand, to pick it up when you wake.
It doesn't vanish. It simply waits for morning. That's where it belongs.
[pause 2s]
If it's something you mustn't forget, imagine writing it on a little yellow sticky note, stuck to the fridge door.
The note is there. It will remember for you. You don't have to hold on to it anymore.
[pause 2s]
If a thought comes back, that's fine. Set it down again. Not now. Tomorrow.
As many times as it takes. Without getting cross with it, or with yourself.
And each time you set it down, it gets a little easier. Like a small gesture your hands already know by heart.
[pause 5s]
Now, notice where you are.
The duvet, resting on you. Its light weight on your shoulders, your hips, your legs.
The warmth that gathered underneath while you were sleeping. Warmth that comes from you.
It wraps around your back, your belly, the tops of your thighs. A soft, even warmth that asks for nothing in return.
[pause 3s]
Feel your feet at the bottom of the bed. Maybe one patch of sheet is cooler, another warmer.
Your toes can uncurl. Your ankles can soften. Your calves grow a little heavier, sinking into the mattress.
[pause 2.5s]
Feel the softness of the fabric against your cheek, or the back of your neck.
Feel the mattress holding you. It asks nothing of you. It simply holds you.
Your hips sink in a little. Your back spreads out. All of your weight can settle there, with nothing held back.
[pause 3s]
Notice your hands, too. Under the pillow, on your belly, or by your sides.
Leave them where they are. They have nothing to carry tonight. No phone, no keys, no bag. Just the sheet.
Your fingers can open slightly. Your palms grow warm, heavy, and still.
[pause 3s]
You're sheltered. Outside, the night carries on without you. In here, it's warm and quiet.
There's nothing to keep watch over. Nobody needs you, right here, right now.
The house is asleep. The street is asleep. You can settle into this warmth, like a nest.
[pause 5s]
Your breath, now.
No need to change it much. Just let the out breath stretch a little, like a very slow sigh that leaves on its own.
[pause 2s]
Just a breath that goes out... a little more slowly than it came in.
[pause 6s]
The air comes in, without effort...
[pause 3s]
and it leaves, taking its time. Like a wave drawing back across the sand, in no hurry at all.
[pause 6s]
Then another wave rolls in...
[pause 3s]
and draws back, even more slowly than the last.
[pause 7s]
Each time the air goes out, something lets go a little. The shoulders. The jaw. The forehead.
The small space between your eyebrows. The hollows of your hands.
Your tongue can rest, soft, low in your mouth. Your lips can part, just barely.
Your eyelids are heavy and warm. They rest over your eyes like a tiny blanket.
[pause 4s]
If your mind wanders back to the day, that's fine. Just come back to the air going out. Slowly.
And if your heart is beating a little fast, let it. It will slow down by itself, in time with this quiet breath.
If a breath ever feels uncomfortable, or too long, simply go back to breathing naturally. Your body knows how.
[pause 5s]
And now, a small, surprising thing.
Instead of trying to sleep, you could try the opposite.
Staying awake. Peacefully. With your eyes closed.
Not by fighting. Not by forcing. Just by telling yourself, I'm staying awake, here, in the warm, and that's perfectly fine.
[pause 3s]
When you stop trying to sleep, the pressure drops. And often, without warning, sleep slips back in through the back door.
But that isn't the goal. The goal is simply to be here. Awake. At peace.
Keep your eyelids closed, heavy and soft.
[pause 2.5s]
You can even tell yourself, I'm keeping watch. Keeping watch over this quiet night.
Like a night guard with nothing to guard. Just sitting calmly while everything sleeps.
[pause 3s]
Listen to the night. The silence. Maybe the hum of the fridge. A car, very far away.
You stay awake... without doing anything with being awake.
No sounds to listen out for, no thoughts to sort through. Just being here, in the soft dark of the room, breathing.
If your eyelids grow heavy, you don't have to stop them. If they stay light, that's fine too.
[pause 3s]
If these night wakings happen often and weigh on your days, a health professional can help you make sense of them. But that's for tomorrow, too.
[pause 6s]
For now, there's only this.
The warmth. The breath. The night.
[pause 4s]
Your arms are heavy. Your legs are heavy.
Your head sinks a little deeper into the pillow.
[pause 4s]
Your face is smooth and still. Your belly rises, and falls.
Nothing to get right. Nothing to wait for.
[pause 5s]
The air comes in... and drifts away.
[pause 6s]
Again... and again... so gently.
[pause 7s]
Just staying here...
[pause 4s]
warm...
[pause 4s]
peaceful.
[pause 10s]

sessions.title: Gentle wake-up
script: [pause 1.5s]
You've just opened your eyes, or almost. Before you reach for your phone, stay lying down a little longer.
The notifications, the emails, the news. All of it can wait five minutes. This moment, between sleep and the day, is yours.
[pause 2s]
Waking up is a transition. If you jump straight into a screen, your body switches to alert mode before you're even out of bed. This morning, we'll take the slower road.
If your eyes are open, you can close them again. Not to fall back asleep. Just to stay inside a little longer.
[pause 2s]
Let's start with the bed. Its warmth, above all. The covers over you, their light weight on your shoulders and on your legs.
Where is your body warmest right now?
[pause 2s]
Maybe your belly, the backs of your knees, your feet.
And where is it cooler? Your face, a hand sticking out from the covers, the empty corner of the pillow.
[pause 2s]
Now notice the light behind your eyelids. Even with your eyes closed, you can sense it.
Is it fairly dark, gray, golden? Maybe it shifts a little, as the sun moves or someone turns on a light in the next room.
Listen to the sounds as well. The quiet of the bedroom, a bird, a car, the city getting started, the house creaking.
You don't have to do anything with them. Let them come to you.
[pause 3s]
All night long, your breathing looked after itself. Slow, steady, often quite shallow.
This morning, let's open it up gently. Breathe in a little more fully than usual, through your nose, and let your belly rise under the covers...
[pause 4s]
And breathe out, long and slow, through your mouth if you like.
[pause 6s]
Once more. Breathe in, and this time let the air rise into your chest, all the way up to your collarbones...
[pause 4s]
Breathe out, and let your body sink a little deeper into the mattress.
[pause 6s]
A third time, at your own pace. No forcing. The in breath opens, the out breath settles.
[pause 6s]
Good. Now let your breathing find its own rhythm again.
You might notice that these fuller breaths warm you up a little, from the inside. They get you ready to move.
[pause 2s]
Now let's wake up your hands and feet. Start with your fingers. Barely move them, as if you were playing a quiet tune on the sheet.
Then slowly open and close your hands, the joints still stiff with sleep.
[pause 2s]
Now your toes. Curl them up, then spread them wide. Once more.
You can draw small circles with your wrists and ankles, one way, then the other.
It's a way of telling your body, we're waking up, but there's no hurry.
[pause 2s]
And now, stretch. Like a cat getting up from a nap. There's no set order, and no right way.
You can reach your arms overhead and push your heels away, making yourself long.
You can roll onto your side, round your back, stretch one leg and then the other.
Hold each stretch for a couple of seconds, then let it go all at once, like a sigh.
Listen for what your body wants this morning. Maybe your back. Maybe your shoulders. Maybe a big yawn. Let it come, it's part of the stretch.
[pause 3s]
Now let everything go. Settle onto your back, or onto your side, whichever you prefer.
Notice the difference. Warmth moving through you, a little more space in your joints, a slightly clearer head.
[pause 2s]

If thoughts about the day start to arrive, the list, the time, what's coming, that's normal. You don't have to push them away. Just tell them, later. And come back to the warmth of the bed, and the breath coming and going.
[pause 2s]
Before you get up, choose a phrase for your day. Something short and simple that you can say to yourself again later.
For example, I have time to do one thing at a time. Or, I'm starting gently. Or a phrase that comes from you.
Say it once, silently, on an out breath.
[pause 3s]
Now open your eyes, if they aren't open already. Let the light in, little by little.
Roll onto your side. Press into the mattress with your hands, and slowly come up to sit on the edge of the bed.
[pause 2s]
Put your feet on the floor. Feel the coolness of the wood, the tiles or the rug under your soles.
Stay there for a breath or two before you stand.
[pause 3s]
Feel your weight settle into your feet. Your back lengthens, your head rests easily above your shoulders. You can stand up whenever you're ready.
Your day has started gently. Keep that pace for as long as you can.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Set your intention
script: [pause 1.5s]
Good morning. Today, we're going to choose a word. Just one. The word that will help you stay yourself, whatever the day has in store.
[pause 2s]
Sit upright, tall without being stiff. You might picture your spine as a stack of coins, balanced one on top of the other.
Rest your hands on your thighs, palms down, or open toward the sky, whichever you prefer.
Let your eyes close, or lower your gaze to the floor, about an arm's length in front of you.
[pause 2s]
Think of this as a small threshold between the night and the day. Before the messages, before the obligations, a moment to choose your direction.
[pause 2s]
Start by listening to your breath, without changing it. Where do you feel it most clearly this morning?
[pause 2s]
Maybe at the rim of your nostrils, with the cool air coming in. Maybe in your chest as it rises. Maybe in your belly.
Choose that spot, and stay with it for a few breaths.
[pause 4s]
Feel the small resting moment that comes on its own at the end of the out-breath. No need to stretch it. Just notice it.
If thoughts drift by, the shopping list, an email, yesterday's conversation, let them pass. Come back to the place where you feel your breath. Coming back is the practice.
Let your body settle as well. Feet on the floor, weight on the seat, hands heavy on your thighs. For now, there's nothing else to do but sit here and breathe.
[pause 3s]
Now I'd like you to ask yourself a question. Not what do I have to do today. You already know that, and your to-do list has it covered.
The question is more like this. How do I want to be, today?
In the way I speak to people. The way I work. The way I respond when something doesn't go to plan.
[pause 2s]
Or put another way. Tonight, as you get into bed, what would you like to be able to say about how you lived this day?
Let the question float. Don't hunt for the answer with your head. Wait for it to come.
This isn't one more goal to hit. It's more like a compass. A gentle direction you can come back to when the day pulls you off course.
[pause 3s]
Maybe a word has already appeared. If so, welcome it, even if it surprises you.
If not, here are a few suggestions. Listen, and notice which one resonates.
Patience.
[pause 1.5s]
Presence.
[pause 1.5s]
Courage.
[pause 1.5s]
Gentleness.
[pause 1.5s]
Clarity.
[pause 1.5s]
Lightness.
[pause 1.5s]
Trust.
[pause 2s]
There's no right or wrong word. What matters is the one that fits what you need today, not the one you think you ought to pick.
And if none of these speak to you, another word may come. Openness. Simplicity. Listening. Or even an image.
You may find yourself torn between two. Choose the one that feels a little kinder when you say it, the one that eases you rather than the one that piles on pressure.
[pause 3s]
Do you have your word? Say it to yourself once, slowly.
[pause 3s]

Behind every word, there's often a value. Something that matters to you. If you chose patience, maybe it's because you care about the quality of your relationships. If it's courage, maybe you want to move forward on something important.
Why this word, this morning? What does it protect, or what does it make possible?
[pause 3s]
Now look for this word in your body. What does patience, or trust, or lightness feel like, physically?
Maybe your shoulders drop a little. Your chest opens. Your jaw unclenches. Your breathing becomes slower, or fuller.
If nothing clear shows up, simply imagine you're already living this word. How would you be sitting? How would you be breathing?
Let your body take the shape of your word. Adjust your posture slightly, if you feel like it.
Notice where the sensation is clearest, and remember that spot. That's where your word lives.
[pause 3s]
Now think of one specific moment in your day when this word could be useful. Just one.
Maybe a meeting that's likely to drag on, if your word is patience. A conversation you've been putting off, if it's courage. Dinner with your kids or the people you love, if it's presence.
See that moment. The place, the time, the people around you.
[pause 2s]
Then imagine your word walking into the scene with you. It doesn't change anyone else. It changes something small in you. A second's pause before you reply, a softer look, a step forward.
If something difficult comes up in the scene, see yourself coming back to your word, the way you'd reach for the handrail on a staircase. One breath is enough.
Watch how the moment unfolds, with your word by your side. How do you feel at the end?
[pause 3s]
You didn't need to become someone else. Your word simply helped you stay a little more yourself.
[pause 2s]
Come back to your breath. Let's anchor your word over three out-breaths.
Breathe in easily...
[pause 3s]
and as you breathe out, say your word silently.
[pause 5s]
Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and on the out-breath, your word again. Let it sink down with the air.
[pause 5s]
One last time. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and your word, all the way through the out-breath.
[pause 5s]
Stay a moment with what's here. The word, the feeling in your body, the quiet of the morning.
[pause 3s]
You don't have to live this word all day long. You'll forget it, that's a given. What matters is coming back to it now and then.
And this word isn't there to judge you. If tonight you feel you lacked patience or courage, that's not a failure. Tomorrow, you can choose the same word, or another one.
[pause 2s]

To help you remember, give yourself a discreet reminder. Write the word on a sticky note and put it on your screen or your mirror. Make it your phone wallpaper. Or link it to something you do often, like opening a door or drinking water.
Each time you come across that reminder, one breath, and your word.
These small reminders matter. Without them, the morning's word gets lost in the noise of the day. With them, it comes back.
[pause 2s]
Gently, come back to the room. Move your fingers and toes. Sit up a little taller, and stretch your neck to one side, then the other.
[pause 2s]
Whenever you're ready, open your eyes. Your word is chosen. It's just waiting for you.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Natural energy
script: [pause 1.5s]
Good morning. Your body feels a bit sluggish today, and that's normal. Let's wake it up together, no coffee needed.
You can stand up, or stay sitting on the edge of the bed with your feet flat on the floor. Either works.
Let your arms hang loose. Lengthen a little, as if a thread were drawing the top of your head upward.
[pause 2s]
We'll start with the breath. Three brisk breaths in through the nose, and three firm breaths out through the mouth, like a big sigh you can hear.
Here we go. Breathe in sharply through your nose.
[pause 1.5s]
And blow it all out, in one go, through your mouth.
[pause 2s]
Again. Breathe in, quick and clean, opening the chest.
[pause 1.5s]
And let go. Let the air rush out like a balloon you've just released.
[pause 2s]
One last time. In...
[pause 1.5s]
and out.
[pause 3s]
