Now come back to your usual breathing. If you feel a little lightheaded, just breathe easily. It passes in a few seconds.
These three brisker breaths send your body a simple signal. The night is over, it's time to get going. Three is plenty.
Can you notice a difference already?
[pause 2s]
Maybe a bit more warmth in your face, a bit more air in your ribcage.
[pause 1.5s]
Now, a stretch. Breathing in, raise both arms toward the sky, fingers spread.
Press your palms gently upward. Feel your ribs widening, your belly lengthening, the space opening under your arms.
If you're standing, you can even rise up a little onto your toes.
[pause 3s]
Breathing out, let your arms float down slowly, like wings folding in.
[pause 2s]
One more time. Arms rise as you breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and come down as you breathe out.
[pause 3s]
Now for some tapping. With your right hand, palm soft, tap along your left arm. Work from the shoulder down to the wrist, then back up the inside of the arm.
No need to tap hard. Just enough to feel the skin waking up.
Tapping like this wakes up the circulation under your skin, a bit like shaking out a duvet to fluff it up.
[pause 2s]
Switch sides. Your left hand taps along your right arm, from shoulder to hand, and back again.
[pause 2s]
Now both hands to the top of your chest, below the collarbones. Light little taps with your fingertips, like soft rain.
Then your shoulders, and the back of your neck, where the night often leaves some stiffness.
[pause 2s]
Move down to your thighs, tapping the tops and the outsides down to your knees. If you're standing, only bend as far as is comfortable.
[pause 2s]
Stop. Let your hands rest. Feel the tingling, the warmth, as if your skin had just been switched on.
[pause 2s]
Now roll your shoulders backward. Big, slow circles. Up toward your ears, back, and down.
Three times...
[pause 5s]
then three times the other way.
[pause 5s]
Next, your neck. Let your chin drop gently toward your chest.
Roll your head toward your right shoulder, through the center, then to the left. A half circle, always through the front, never backward.
Only go where it feels good. Never into pain.
If your neck or shoulders are sensitive, just make the movement smaller. A little goes a long way.
[pause 3s]
Come back to center. Breathe normally, without changing a thing.
[pause 2s]
Take a few seconds to feel what's moving through you. Your hands, your arms, your face. Maybe a faint buzzing, a sense of being a little more here.
This isn't energy borrowed from somewhere else. It's your own, simply woken up.
[pause 3s]
Before you go, choose one concrete first step for your day. Open the curtains, drink a big glass of water, put on some music, step outside for some fresh air.
Just one thing, something simple you can do right now.
[pause 2.5s]
Have you got it? Then off you go. Your day starts now.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Morning gratitude
script: [pause 1.5s]
Hello, and good morning. Settle in just as you are, sitting on your bed, on a chair, or still lying down if you'd rather.
Let your hands rest wherever they're comfortable. Close your eyes, or simply let your gaze drift down toward the floor.
[pause 2s]
Take one breath that's a little fuller than the others...
[pause 3s]
And as you breathe out, let your shoulders drop a notch.
[pause 4s]
Now let your breathing do whatever it wants. Calm, or a bit quick, it doesn't matter. Just follow it for a few moments.
The air coming in, slightly cool in your nostrils. The air going out, a little warmer.
If thoughts are already drifting in, the day, the time, your list of things to do, let them pass through. You'll get back to them later. For now, just the breath.
[pause 3s]
Before we begin, a word about why.

Your attention has a natural habit. It spots what's wrong first. The problem to fix, the delay, the criticism. That helps keep you safe, but first thing in the morning, it can tint the whole day gray.
Gratitude is a way of training attention. It doesn't deny what's hard. It simply notices, as well, what's holding you up, all the things that so often go unnoticed.
This morning, I'd like us to look for three thank-yous. Not vague ones. Precise, detailed thank-yous that you can really feel.
[pause 2s]
The first one is very simple. Something material, something everyday, that you used this morning or during the night.
Your bed, for example. The mattress that held you up for hours, the duvet that kept you warm.
Or the hot water from the tap. All it takes is turning a handle, and it flows, at just the right temperature.
Choose your thing. Now make it precise. Its texture, its smell, the sound it makes. The exact moment you enjoyed it.
[pause 2s]
Imagine this morning without it, just for a second. A hard bed, a cold shower. Suddenly this small, ordinary thing takes on a different place.
Think of all the people who worked so it could be here. The ones who made it, shipped it, installed it.
And thank it, silently. A simple thank-you, like the one you'd give someone holding a door open for you.
[pause 3s]
The second thank-you goes to a person. Someone who matters to you, or someone who simply helped you recently. A loved one, a colleague, the person at the bakery who smiled at you.
Let their face appear. Their eyes, their expression, the way they hold themselves.
If several faces come to mind, choose just one for today. The others will have their turn another morning.
[pause 2s]
Remember a specific moment with them. Something they said, a gesture, a message that arrived at just the right time.
What does this person bring you? Laughter, calm, confidence, a helping hand?
[pause 2s]
Thank them silently, as if they were standing in front of you. You can even imagine their reaction as they hear it.
You don't need to tell them for this thank-you to count. Simply thinking it already shifts the way you see them, and your day, a little.
[pause 3s]
The third thank-you is for you. That may feel strange, and it's often the hardest one. Take your time.
It could be a quality. Your patience, your sense of humor, your curiosity, the way you look after others.

Or your body. Your legs that carry you all day long. Your hands that know how to do a thousand things. Your heart, which has been beating since your very first day, without you ever having to think about it.
Choose just one thing. And thank it, the way you'd thank a loyal friend.
[pause 2s]
Think of a recent moment when it helped you. Yesterday, maybe. One specific situation where this quality, or this body, was there for you.
If a little voice protests or plays it down, that's okay. Notice it, and come back to your thank-you.
[pause 3s]
Now let these three thank-yous come together. The simple thing. The person. What's in you.
Place a hand on the center of your chest, if you like.
[pause 2s]
What's happening there? Maybe a gentle warmth. A sense of openness, of softness. Maybe a smile finding its way onto your face.
[pause 2s]
Or maybe nothing special, and that's just as good. Gratitude doesn't need to be dramatic to count.
Research suggests that practicing gratitude regularly may help people feel a little more at ease. But this morning, there's no result to chase. Just this moment.
Breathe with whatever is here. Breathe in, and let your chest open a little...
[pause 3s]
Breathe out, and let that feeling spread toward your shoulders, toward your belly.
[pause 5s]
Stay here for a few more breaths. Nothing to add, nothing to look for.
The breath carries on, simply. Any warmth in your chest can stay there on its own, without you holding on to it.
[pause 5s]
Before you get up, choose one of these three thank-yous to carry with you. The one that touches you most this morning.
You can come back to it at some point today. On the train, at your desk, standing in line. It only takes a few seconds.
And if you feel like it, you could even say it out loud. Send a quick message to the person you thought of, for instance.
[pause 2s]
Gently, come back to the room. Move your fingers, stretch your back a little.
Open your eyes, and look around you. Maybe a fourth thank-you is already waiting for you somewhere.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Full body scan
script: [pause 1.5s]
Welcome to this body scan. For the next ten minutes, you're simply going to visit your body, one area at a time, from your toes to the top of your head.
[pause 1.5s]
Choose your position. Lying on your back, arms by your sides, legs uncrossed. Or sitting, your back upright and supported, feet flat on the floor, hands resting on your thighs.
Take a few seconds to adjust whatever needs adjusting. A cushion under your knees, a shoulder to shift, a waistband to loosen.
[pause 3s]
If you'd like, close your eyes. Otherwise, let your gaze rest on a spot on the floor or the ceiling, without staring.
Take a breath a little fuller than the others...
[pause 3s]
and let it go.
[pause 4s]
Then another, feeling your body lean a little more into whatever is holding it. Your back, your pelvis, your heels settling down.
[pause 4s]

Before we begin, an intention. In a body scan, you're not trying to relax at all costs, or to change anything. You observe. You notice what's here, like a curious explorer taking in a landscape without judging it.
You may feel warmth, coolness, pressure, tingling, an itch, heaviness. Or nothing at all. Feeling nothing is an observation too. Whatever you notice is just right.
And if your mind wanders off, as it almost certainly will, notice that, without scolding yourself, and come back to whichever part of the body we've reached.
If some part of your body is painful, you can observe it from a distance, gently, or move straight on to the next area. You decide how close to get.
[pause 3s]
Now let your breathing find its own rhythm. It doesn't need to be slow or deep. It's just as it is.
Simply notice where you feel it most clearly. Maybe at your nostrils, maybe in your chest, maybe in your belly. This breath will keep you company for the whole journey.
[pause 4s]
Bring your attention down to your feet. First your toes. The big toe, then the others, all the way to the little one.
Can you feel them without moving them?
[pause 3s]
Maybe they're touching each other. Maybe you can feel the fabric of your socks, or the air on your skin.

Then the soles of your feet. The padded part beneath your toes, the arch, the heel. If you're sitting, notice the pressure of the floor. If you're lying down, the weight of your heels on the mattress or the mat.
The tops of your feet now, with their fine tendons just under the skin. And your ankles, with their small round bones on either side.
[pause 2s]
Imagine breathing all the way down into your feet. As you breathe in, your attention travels down to them...
[pause 3s]
As you breathe out, they settle a little more, heavy and still.
[pause 5s]
Your attention moves up into your legs. Your calves at the back, often a little denser. Your shins at the front, right under the skin.
Your knees. The front, the kneecap. The sides. And the soft hollow behind each knee, a place we often forget about. It may feel a little warmer, a little softer than the rest.
Let your knees release, as if they no longer had to hold your legs together. The joints can open ever so slightly with each out-breath.
[pause 3s]
Then your thighs, the biggest muscles in your body. Feel their weight. The backs of your thighs against the chair or the floor. Maybe the temperature under the fabric of your clothes.
[pause 2s]
Take a moment to compare your left leg and your right leg. Does one seem heavier, warmer, more present than the other?
[pause 3s]
There's no right answer. It's just a way of sharpening your attention.
Simply observe. If you notice some tension, you can breathe with it, without demanding that it leave. Breathe in as you look at it, breathe out as you give it a little more room.
[pause 5s]
Now your pelvis. Your hips, on each side. Your seat, carrying much of your weight. Feel the points of contact, maybe one side pressing down a little more than the other.
Your pelvis is like a bowl that gathers the weight of your upper body. Let it grow heavy, widen, and rest completely on whatever is holding it.
[pause 3s]

Your belly, now. Notice how it moves with the breath, rising slightly, falling again. Notice too whether it feels tight or relaxed, warm or neutral, whether it's gurgling a little. All of that is part of the landscape.
The belly is often one of the first places stress settles. You don't have to force it to relax. Simply looking at it kindly already gives it a little room.
[pause 4s]
Then your lower back. The area that holds up your posture all day long. Feel the area around your kidneys, the muscles on either side of your spine.
Maybe stiffness, tiredness, warmth. Or a pleasant sense of rest. You don't need to do anything with what you find. You notice it, that's all.
[pause 5s]
Moving up to your chest. Feel your ribcage open a little as you breathe in, and close as you breathe out. Your ribs spreading apart, then drawing together.
[pause 3s]

If you can sense it, notice your heartbeat. No need to go looking for it. If it's there, it's there. This heart has been beating for you all along, day and night, without you ever having to think about it.
[pause 4s]
Then your upper back. The space between your shoulder blades, and the shoulder blades themselves. Feel them against the back of the chair or the floor.
And your shoulders. Where are they right now? High, low, rolled forward?
[pause 3s]
No correcting, just noting. If they decide on their own to drop a little, let them.
Imagine each in-breath gently filling the space between your shoulder blades, and each out-breath letting your shoulders slide down, a little heavier, a little wider.
A lot of tension quietly builds up here. You're giving it a moment's rest.
[pause 5s]
If you feel drowsiness creeping in, that's common when the body settles. You can open your eyes slightly, or take a fuller breath, to stay present.
[pause 2s]
Your attention now travels down both arms at once. Your upper arms. Your elbows, with their bony points. Your forearms, the skin a little thinner on the inside.
Your wrists. Then your hands. The backs of your hands, your palms. Each finger, from thumb to little finger. Your fingertips, often very sensitive. Maybe a pulse, a buzzing, some warmth.
[pause 3s]
Let your hands become completely idle. All day long they hold, type, and carry. For now, they have nothing to do.
[pause 5s]
Move up to your neck. The front, your throat, where the air passes through. The sides. And the back of your neck, which has been holding up your head since this morning.
[pause 2s]
Your face, now. Your jaw. Are your teeth touching, or not?
[pause 2s]
Your mouth, your lips. Your tongue, resting in your mouth.
If your teeth are touching, let a small gap open between them. Your jaw can grow heavy, as if sinking gently toward your throat. Feel the ease spreading in front of your ears, across your temples.
[pause 3s]
Your cheeks. Your nose, and the air moving through your nostrils, a little cooler on the in-breath, a little warmer on the out-breath.
Your eyes, beneath your eyelids. The tiny muscles around your eyes, which work so hard in front of screens. Your eyebrows. Your forehead, broad and flat.
Let your forehead widen and smooth out, like a sheet of paper unfolded flat on a table.
[pause 3s]
Then the sides of your head, your ears. The back of your skull, resting or balanced. And finally, the top of your head. Maybe a light sensation, tingling, air, or nothing in particular.
[pause 5s]
Now widen your attention to take in your whole body at once. From your toes to the top of your head. As if you were stepping back to look at the whole landscape you've just travelled through.
One body, breathing. With its tense areas, its calm areas, its neutral areas. Everything welcomed in the same way.
[pause 3s]
Feel the breath move through this whole body. On the in-breath, like a wave rising from your feet to your head...
[pause 4s]
On the out-breath, flowing back down to your toes.
[pause 8s]
Notice how this body feels now, compared to the start of the session. Not to judge whether it's better or worse. Just to see.
[pause 3s]
You've taken ten minutes to listen to it, without asking anything of it. That's a rare thing in a day.
[pause 2s]
Gently, let's come back. Let your breathing become a little fuller. Feel the weight of your body again, the points of contact with the floor or the chair.
Slowly move your fingers and toes. If you feel like it, stretch your arms, gently roll your head.
[pause 3s]
Become aware of the sounds around you. The room, the street, the silence.
When the moment feels right for you, open your eyes.
[pause 2s]

Throughout the day, you can keep a thread of this attention. When you stand up, walk, or sit down, simply notice one sensation, any sensation. It's a way of coming back to your body in just a few seconds.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Progressive muscle relaxation
script: [pause 1.5s]
Just relax. Easy to say. But if you feel you don't really know how, this session is made for you.
The idea is simple. You tense a group of muscles for a few seconds, then you let go. By feeling the tension, and then its absence, your body learns the difference.
[pause 2s]
Settle into a chair with your feet flat on the floor, or lie down on your back. Close your eyes if that's comfortable.
[pause 1.5s]
One important guideline for the whole session. Tense to about fifty percent of your strength. Not all the way. Enough to clearly feel the muscle working, but never to the point of pain.
If an area is injured or sore, or if you get a cramp, simply skip that step and imagine the movement instead. And while you're tensing, keep breathing normally. Don't hold your breath.
[pause 2s]
Before we begin, a quick check in. Where do you feel tense, right here, right now?
[pause 2.5s]
Your shoulders, your jaw, your belly, your hands? Just note it, without trying to change it. We'll come back to it at the end.
Take an easy breath in...
[pause 4s]
and let it go.
[pause 5s]
Let's start with your hands and forearms. Make two fists. Squeeze gradually, to about half your strength.
Feel the tension in your fingers, in your palms, then climbing into your wrists and along the top of your forearms. Observe it. It's hard, warm, maybe trembling slightly.
Hold it there...
[pause 5s]
And release. Open your hands, all at once. Let your fingers uncurl on their own, without stretching them out.
[pause 3s]
Notice what's happening in your hands now. Maybe tingling, warmth, heaviness. Your forearms softening.
That's the sensation we're here for. The letting go, right after the effort. Take your time to really savor it.
And compare your hands with the rest of your body, which hasn't done anything yet. Can you feel a difference?
[pause 2.5s]
Even a slight one counts.
[pause 3s]
Now your arms and shoulders. Bend your elbows and press your arms against your ribs, tightening your upper arms, your biceps.
At the same time, lift your shoulders toward your ears. Your whole upper body draws in, like when you're cold at a bus stop.
Feel the tension in your arms, across the tops of your shoulders, at the base of your neck. Hold it. Keep breathing...
[pause 5s]
And let go. Let your shoulders drop, your arms fall back onto your thighs or by your sides.
[pause 3s]
Feel your shoulders sink a little further, afterward. As if they were carrying on downward, all by themselves.
Your arms are heavy. Your shoulders are wide. And this area, which works nonstop all day, can finally settle. Each out breath lets it sink just a hair lower.
[pause 4s]
Now your face, in three steps. First, your forehead. Raise your eyebrows as high as you can, as if you were very surprised. Feel your forehead wrinkle, the skin drawing up toward your scalp.
Hold...
[pause 3s]
and release. Let your forehead become smooth and wide again.
[pause 2.5s]
Next, your eyes. Squeeze them tight, as if facing a dazzling sun, wrinkling your nose. Hold...
[pause 3s]
And release. Let your eyelids rest, barely closed. The area around your eyes softens.
[pause 2.5s]
Finally, your jaw. Gently clench your teeth, at half strength, and pull the corners of your mouth back. Feel the tension in your cheeks, in front of your ears, under your chin.
Hold, breathing through your nose...
[pause 3s]
And release. Your teeth part. Your lips may open slightly. Your tongue rests in your mouth.
[pause 4s]

If your mind has wandered during all this, to your day or to what's coming next, that's completely normal. The next contraction will bring you back into your body. That's one of the nice things about this method.
Feel your whole face, as if after a long sigh. Softer, heavier. No expression to hold for anyone.
[pause 3s]
Now your belly and back. Tighten your stomach muscles, as if you were bracing for a ball to land on your belly. Your stomach becomes firm and flat.
At the same time, if it's comfortable, draw your shoulder blades slightly toward each other, lifting your chest a little. Without arching hard, staying at half strength.
Feel your whole torso brace, front and back. Breathe as best you can, in small sips...
[pause 4s]
And release everything. Your belly softens. Your back settles against the chair, or the floor.
[pause 3s]
Let your breath find its place in your belly again. It rises, it falls. More freely than before, maybe.
Notice how it feels to have your whole torso relaxed, your pelvis sinking into the chair or the floor.
[pause 4s]
Now your legs and feet. First your thighs. Press your heels into the floor, and tighten your thighs and your glutes. Feel your legs become as hard as wood.
Hold, and breathe...
[pause 5s]
And release. Your thighs spread out, your glutes soften, your legs grow heavy. Maybe you can feel warmth spreading from your hips down to your knees.
[pause 3s]
And finally, your feet and calves. Pull your toes up toward your face, flexing your ankles. Feel the stretch along the back of your calves, the tension down the front of your shins.
Go gently. If a cramp starts, let go right away.
Hold a little longer...
[pause 3s]
And release. Your feet drop, your toes spread, your ankles relax.
[pause 4s]
Now there's nothing left to tense. Your whole body can rest.
Let's do a quick sweep, from the bottom up. Feet, relaxed. Legs, heavy. Belly, soft. Back, resting. Hands, open. Shoulders, low. Face, smooth.
[pause 3s]

Now imagine a wave of relaxation starting at your feet and slowly rising. It moves through your calves, your knees, your thighs. It flows through your pelvis and your belly, and up along your back. It runs down your arms to your fingertips, then rises into your neck and spreads across your face.
[pause 4s]
If any area is still tight, tense it gently one last time, then let it go with an out breath.
[pause 4s]
Think back to the area you noticed at the start. How does it feel now?
[pause 2.5s]
Looser, or still a bit tight? Both are normal. You've learned something about it.
Savor the contrast. A few minutes ago, your muscles were on alert. Now they're allowed to do nothing at all. What you're feeling right now is what relaxation feels like, in your own body.
The more you practice, the faster you'll recognize this feeling. And the more easily you'll find it again, even in a few seconds, in the middle of a busy day.
[pause 2s]
Stay a little longer in this pleasant heaviness. Nothing to do, nothing to get right. Just the weight of your body, the warmth in your hands, your breath coming and going by itself.
[pause 8s]
Gently deepen your breathing. Move your fingers and toes. Stretch, if your body feels like it, as if you were waking up.
Open your eyes, taking your time.
[pause 2s]
Tonight, or tomorrow, if you catch yourself tense and unsure how to let go, remember the trick. Squeeze a little... then release.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Shoulders and jaw
script: [pause 1.5s]
Hello. If you're here, maybe something is pulling at the back of your neck, or you've just caught yourself clenching your teeth.
[pause 1.5s]
Sit with your feet flat on the floor, your back upright but not rigid, your hands resting on your thighs.
For the next few minutes, stay within what feels comfortable. If a movement hurts, make it smaller, or simply imagine doing it.
[pause 2s]
Take an easy breath in through your nose...
[pause 4s]
and let it flow slowly out, a little longer than it came in.
[pause 6s]
A quick check in. Your shoulders, your neck, your jaw. Which of the three feels tightest today?
[pause 3s]
There's no right answer. Just notice where your attention goes first.
[pause 2s]
Let's begin with the shoulders. On your next breath in, lift them up toward your ears. Slowly, like a big, exaggerated shrug.
[pause 3s]
Keep them up there. Feel the effort in your upper back, along the sides of your neck.
[pause 2s]
And as you breathe out, let them drop all at once. Like putting down a bag that's far too heavy.
[pause 3s]
Feel the difference. The warmth, maybe a faint tingling, a sense of space opening up.
[pause 2s]
Once more. Breathe in and lift... hold for a moment...
[pause 2s]
And let everything go, blowing the air out through your mouth.
[pause 3s]
A third time, at your own pace. Lift, hold, and release.
[pause 5s]
Good. After this last release, let your shoulders find where they really belong. A little lower, a little wider than before.
[pause 3s]
Now the neck. Let your head tilt slowly to the right, your ear drifting down toward your shoulder. The shoulder itself stays low.
Only go as far as a gentle stretch along the left side of your neck. No further.
[pause 2s]
Stay there for two breaths. With every exhale, the weight of your head does the work for you. Imagine your breath softening that side of your neck, from your ear down to your collarbone.
[pause 6s]
Bring your head back to the center, slowly, as if it were floating.
[pause 2s]
And now to the left. Your left ear lowers, and the right side of your neck lengthens.
Breathe into that stretch. There's nothing to force. Does this side feel different? Looser, or stiffer?
[pause 6s]
Come back to the center. Let your chin sink a little toward your chest. Feel the back of your neck lengthen, all the way down into your upper back.
[pause 3s]
Then lift your head, one vertebra at a time, until it rests upright and balanced.
[pause 3s]
Now the jaw. It's one of the strongest muscles in your body, and it often works in secret. In the car, in front of a screen, during the night.
Open your mouth wide, slowly, as wide as feels comfortable. As if you were about to yawn.
[pause 2s]
If a real yawn comes, let it come. That's very good news.
Then close gently, without letting your teeth touch.
[pause 2s]
Once more. Open wide... feel your cheeks stretch, just in front of your ears... and release.
[pause 3s]
Now rest the tip of your tongue on the roof of your mouth, just behind your top teeth. No pressing.
Your lips stay closed, but your teeth part. Only a small gap, barely enough room for a grain of rice.
This is your jaw's natural resting position. The one it forgets when you're under pressure.
Let that space stay there. Breathe through your nose, cool air coming in, warmer air flowing out.
[pause 5s]
If you'd like, you can add a little massage. Place your fingertips on your temples and make small, very slow circles.
[pause 3s]
Then move your fingers down to just in front of your ears, on your cheeks. Clench your teeth lightly and you'll feel a muscle bulge there. That's the masseter.
Unclench, and massage that muscle in small circles with gentle pressure. If it feels tender, just stroke it lightly.
Keep going for a few breaths, at your own pace. Feel the warmth of your fingers sinking in, and the muscle softening a little under the pressure.
[pause 6s]
Let your hands come back to rest on your thighs.
[pause 2s]
Let's check in one more time. Shoulders, low. Neck, long. Jaw, loose, with your tongue resting on the roof of your mouth.
Has the spot you picked at the start changed? A little, a lot, or not at all. Whatever you find is fine.
[pause 3s]
Here's a small idea for the rest of your day. Pick something you do often. Opening a door, glancing at your phone, waiting for the kettle to boil.
Each time, simply ask yourself, am I clenching my teeth? And let that little space come back.
[pause 2s]
You can return to your day now, with your shoulders a little lighter.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Stress-relief yoga nidra
script: [pause 1.5s]
Welcome to this yoga nidra. It's a pause for deep recovery, like a nap, except that part of you stays listening. In a quarter of an hour, you'll get up rested and ready to pick up your day again.

This format is sometimes called non-sleep deep rest. Your body settles almost as it would in sleep, while a small part of you stays awake and listens. It's the nap you can't always take, offered to yourself in another way.
[pause 2s]
Lie down on your back, on a mat, a bed or a sofa. Legs stretched out and slightly apart, arms a little away from your body, palms facing up if that's comfortable.
If your lower back pulls, slide a cushion under your knees. If you tend to get cold, cover yourself with a blanket. The body cools down as it rests.
[pause 3s]
Make any last adjustments. Move your shoulders, your head, your pelvis a little, until you find a position you could stay in for a long time without moving.
Then close your eyes. From now on, the idea is to stay as still as you can. If you need to move, do it slowly, then come back to rest.
[pause 2s]

The only instruction in yoga nidra is to keep listening to my voice. No need to concentrate hard. Let the words come to you. If you drift off for a moment, that's fine. You'll pick up the thread again further on.
[pause 2s]
Take a big breath in through your nose...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out through your mouth, in a long sigh.
[pause 5s]
Once more. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and let the whole weight of your body sink into the floor.
[pause 5s]
Become aware of the sounds around you. The most distant ones first. A car, voices, the wind, perhaps. Let your listening reach far, beyond the walls, without looking for anything in particular.
[pause 3s]
Then the closer sounds, in the room. A humming fridge, a ticking clock, the faint rustle of your clothes. And finally, the sound of your own breathing, very close.
[pause 3s]
Let them all be there, without holding on to any of them. They pass by, like clouds. No sound is a disturbance. Each one simply becomes part of the background.
[pause 3s]
Now feel your body lying down. The points of contact with the floor. The back of your head, your shoulder blades, your elbows, the backs of your hands, your pelvis, your calves, your heels.
Feel the weight of each of these points. The floor holds you completely. There's nothing to hold back, nothing to hold up.
Say to yourself, silently... I am lying down, I am resting, I am listening.
[pause 4s]
Now comes the moment for your sankalpa. It's an intention. A short, positive phrase, said in the present tense, as if it were already true.
You may already have one. If not, here are a few for inspiration. I am calm and present. I am allowed to rest. I move through my days with more ease.
Choose one, or let your own appear. Don't look for the perfect phrase. Take the first one that feels right.
[pause 3s]
Now repeat it silently, slowly, with all your sincerity. A first time...
[pause 3s]
a second time, feeling it resonate a little more deeply...
[pause 3s]
and a third time, like a seed you place in soft earth.
[pause 3s]
Let your sankalpa settle. We'll come back to it at the end.
[pause 2s]

Now we're going to move your awareness around the body. I'll name a part of the body. When you hear it, simply rest your attention there for a moment, then follow my voice to the next. Without moving.
Right side. The right thumb. Index finger. Middle finger. Ring finger. Little finger.
The palm of the right hand. The back of the hand. The wrist. The forearm. The elbow. The upper arm. The right shoulder. The armpit.
The right side of the chest. The waist, on the right. The right hip. The right thigh. The knee. The calf. The ankle.
The right heel. The sole of the foot. The top of the foot. The big toe. The second toe. The third. The fourth. The fifth.
The whole right side, from fingertips to toes. Present, heavy, at rest.
[pause 2s]
Left side. The left thumb. Index finger. Middle finger. Ring finger. Little finger.
The palm of the left hand. The back of the hand. The wrist. The forearm. The elbow. The upper arm. The left shoulder. The armpit.
The left side of the chest. The waist, on the left. The left hip. The left thigh. The knee. The calf. The ankle.
The left heel. The sole of the foot. The top of the foot. The big toe. The second toe. The third. The fourth. The fifth.
The whole left side, from fingertips to toes. Present, heavy, at rest.
[pause 2s]
The back of the body. Both heels. Both calves. The backs of the knees. The backs of the thighs. The buttocks.
The lower back. The middle of the back. The right shoulder blade. The left shoulder blade. The whole spine. The back of the neck. The back of the head.
The whole back of the body, resting on the floor, like a print left in wet sand.
[pause 2s]
The face. The crown of the head. The forehead. The right temple. The left temple. The right eyebrow. The left eyebrow. The space between the eyebrows.
The right eyelid. The left eyelid. The right eye. The left eye. The right ear. The left ear.
The nose. The right nostril. The left nostril. The right cheek. The left cheek. The upper lip. The lower lip. The place where the lips meet. The chin. The jaw. The throat.
[pause 2s]
The front of the body. The right collarbone. The left collarbone. The center of the chest. The upper belly. The navel. The lower belly.
The whole front of the body, rising gently with the breath.
[pause 2s]
Now the larger parts. The whole right leg. The whole left leg. Both legs together.
The whole right arm. The whole left arm. Both arms together.
The whole back. The whole front of the body. The whole head. The whole body, together. The whole body, lying down, at rest.
[pause 3s]
Feel your body as one single presence, from feet to head. Feel the space it takes up in the room, its shape, its outline, completely still.
[pause 4s]
Now become aware of your natural breathing. Don't change it. Watch it the way you'd watch waves from the shore, asking nothing of them.
Feel the air come in through your nostrils, a little cooler. And go out, a little warmer.
Feel your belly rising and falling, all on its own.
Each in-breath brings a little freshness. Each out-breath invites you to settle a little more deeply.
[pause 4s]

Now follow the path of the breath. It comes in through the nostrils, down through the throat, gently fills the chest, then the belly. And it travels back the other way. Belly, chest, throat, nostrils. A quiet round trip, again and again.
[pause 4s]
Now we'll count the breaths backward, from eleven down to one. Silently, without changing the breath. I'll start with you, then you'll carry on alone.
Breathe in, and say to yourself, eleven.
[pause 3s]
Breathe out, eleven.
[pause 4s]
Breathe in, ten.
[pause 3s]
Breathe out, ten.
[pause 4s]
Breathe in, nine.
[pause 3s]
Breathe out, nine.
[pause 4s]

Carry on like this, at your own pace, down to one. If you lose count, which happens a lot, simply start again at eleven. There's nothing to get right. The counting is just a thread to help you stay present.
[pause 8s]
Each number a little calmer than the last. Each out-breath a little longer, a little softer.
[pause 8s]
Your body heavier and heavier, your mind quieter and quieter.
[pause 8s]
Let go of the counting, wherever you've got to. Come back to the breath, simple and easy. Let the body breathe in its own way.
[pause 4s]
Now we'll explore opposite sensations. Let them arise from memory, without forcing. If they don't really come, simply imagine them.

Awaken the feeling of heaviness. Your body is becoming heavy. Legs heavy, as if filled with sand. Arms heavy, resting. Head heavy, sinking into the pillow. Your whole body weighs down, as it does after a long day of walking.
Eyelids heavy. Shoulders heavy. Your back sinking into the floor, as if into warm sand. Everything is heavy, and everything is held.
[pause 4s]
And now, lightness. Your body is becoming light, very light. Like a cork floating on water. Arms light, legs light. As if the floor were barely holding you anymore.
Hands so light they could float away. Chest light, like a feather carried by the breath. Your whole body drifting, barely touching down.
[pause 4s]
Heaviness... and lightness. Let the two sensations come in turn, without preferring one. Heavy as a stone... light as a soap bubble.
[pause 4s]
Now awaken the feeling of warmth. Remember your hands around a mug of hot chocolate in winter. Or the sun on your skin, late on a summer afternoon. Warmth spreading through your whole body.
It starts in your belly, glows through your chest, flows down your arms to your hands, slips down your legs to your feet. A soft, enveloping warmth.
[pause 4s]
And now, coolness. Your feet in a river in springtime. The crisp air of a February morning on your face as you step outside. Your whole body becoming cool.
A clean coolness on your cheeks, your forehead, the backs of your hands. Like slipping between cool sheets on a summer night.
[pause 4s]
Warmth... and coolness. Your body knows how to move from one to the other. Now rest in a temperature that feels just right.
[pause 4s]

One last pair, closer to your everyday life. Remember a hectic moment, without choosing the worst one. A packed train platform, a phone that won't stop ringing, a morning where everything piles up. Just notice, for a moment, how your body remembers it. Maybe a shoulder creeping up, a breath growing shorter.
[pause 3s]

And now, let that image drift away. Remember a moment of calm. A Sunday morning with no alarm, a bench in the sun, the quiet of a house where everyone is still asleep. Let that calm settle into your body, and fill all the space.
[pause 4s]
Your body knows how to do both. It knows how to rev up, and it knows how to come back to calm. For now, it's resting in the calm.
[pause 4s]
Now I'll name some images, one after another. Let each one appear however it comes, blurry or sharp, then let it go. If an image doesn't speak to you, simply wait for the next.
[pause 2s]
An open window, on a summer morning. The curtain barely moving.
[pause 2s]
White sheets drying in the wind, in a garden.
[pause 2s]
A lighthouse at the end of a jetty, in Brittany. Waves breaking softly on the rocks.
[pause 2s]
A cup of tea steaming on a wooden table.
[pause 2s]
A field of lavender in the sun, the hum of bees.
[pause 2s]
Footprints in fresh snow, the soft crunch under your shoes.
[pause 2s]
A rowing boat, still, on a lake as smooth as a mirror.
[pause 2s]
A cat curled up on an armchair, purring.
[pause 2s]
Rain on a roof, at night, steady and gentle.
[pause 2s]
Warm bread coming out of the oven, its smell filling the kitchen.
[pause 2s]
A cobbled street shining after a shower.
[pause 2s]
An empty beach in winter, the wet sand reflecting the sky.
[pause 2s]
A fire in the hearth, the embers glowing.
[pause 2s]
A mountain path at sunrise.
[pause 2s]
A pine forest, the smell of resin, light falling between the branches.
[pause 2s]
The sky, just before the stars appear.
[pause 5s]
Now let all the images fade. Rest in the calm, dark space behind your eyelids. Nothing to look at, nothing to do. Just being here.
This space is wide, quiet, without edges. You can rest here as long as you like. All that's here is the breath, and this peaceful presence.
[pause 8s]
Now return to your sankalpa, the intention you chose at the beginning. The same phrase, with the same words.
Repeat it three times, silently, with sincerity.
[pause 8s]

Feel it settle inside you, somewhere deep and calm. It will keep making its way, quietly, even when you're no longer thinking about it. No effort, no pressure. Like a friend gently reminding you of what matters to you.
[pause 5s]
This yoga nidra is coming to an end. We're going to come back gradually.
If you dozed off at times, or don't remember everything, that's perfectly fine. Your body still benefited from the rest, even when your attention wandered away.
[pause 2s]
Become aware of your breathing. Let it deepen a little, become more present.
[pause 3s]
Feel your body lying down again, its weight, its points of contact with the floor.
Become aware of the room you're in. The temperature of the air. The light, perhaps, through your eyelids. The sounds around you.
[pause 3s]
Remind yourself what day it is, what time of day, what you're going to do next.
Let your attention widen, little by little, from your body to the room, from the room to the rest of your day.
[pause 2s]
Start to move gently. Fingers, toes. Slowly circle your wrists, your ankles.
If it feels good, stretch out full length, arms above your head, like a cat after a nap. Yawn if you feel like it.
Then roll gently onto your side. Stay there for a moment, eyes still closed.
[pause 4s]
When the moment feels right, use your hands to sit up. Open your eyes, slowly. Let the light come back in.
Take one last full breath, and feel the energy returning to your body.
[pause 3s]
You've given your body a real chance to recover. Take this calm with you, and return to your day refreshed and rested, at your own pace.
This practice is now complete.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: 5-4-3-2-1 grounding
script: [pause 1.5s]
You're here, and that's already a good step. Maybe your mind is racing right now, running a few steps ahead of the day.
For this exercise, keep your eyes open. You can do it sitting or standing, in your kitchen or on a train platform.
[pause 1.5s]
Place both feet flat on the floor. Feel the ground holding you, under your heels, under your toes.
Now let the air out through your mouth, slowly, as if you were blowing on soup that's too hot.
[pause 5s]
Once more. A long, easy out breath, without forcing the in breath at all.
[pause 5s]
Anxiety likes to live in tomorrow. What might happen, what might go wrong. Your senses only know about now.
So we'll use them like a rope, to pull you back here. Five things, then four, then three, then two, and finally one. Take your time with each step. There's no rush.
If a thought pulls you toward tomorrow, that's okay. Notice it, and come back to the step you were on.
[pause 2s]
Start with your eyes. Look for five things you can see.
They don't need to be special. The corner of a table, a power outlet, a mug, the sky through the window.
Rest your gaze on the first one. Look at it as if you had to describe it to someone who has never seen it.
What is its exact color?
[pause 2s]
Not just white, but off white, a slightly grey white, a white that shines where the light hits it.
Notice its edges. Are they sharp, rounded, a little worn?
[pause 3s]
Move on to the second thing. Take in its shape, its shadow, the small details you've never noticed. A scratch, a reflection, a speck of dust.
[pause 2s]
Then the third. And the fourth, maybe a little further away. Let your eyes travel slowly, without hurrying.
[pause 2s]
And a fifth. If your eyes want to go back to one of them, that's allowed.
[pause 3s]
Now, touch. Find four things you can feel against your skin.
The first may already be there. The weight of your body on the chair, or your feet inside your shoes.
Notice the pressure. Is it stronger on one side than the other? On your heels, or on the balls of your feet?
[pause 2s]
The second is the fabric of your clothes. On your shoulders, on your thighs. Is it soft, scratchy, snug, light?
[pause 1.5s]
For the third, you can place a hand on something. A table, your knee, the armrest. Feel whether it's cool or warm, smooth or rough.
[pause 1.5s]
And the fourth is more subtle. The air on your face, on the backs of your hands. Maybe a slight draft, maybe a little warmth.
[pause 3s]
Now, sounds. Listen, and find three of them.
Start with the most obvious one. A car, a voice, the hum of a fridge or a computer.
[pause 2s]
Then look for a more distant sound, right at the edge of what you can hear. Let your listening widen, as if your ears were opening a little more.
[pause 2s]
And finally, a sound very close to you. The rustle of your clothes when you move, or the quiet sound of your own breathing.
[pause 2s]
You don't need to name each sound precisely. Just notice that it's there, and then that it changes, or stops.
If a thought slips in among the sounds, let it drift into the background, like a radio playing in the next room.
[pause 2s]
Now, two smells. This is often the hardest step, so be patient with yourself.
Breathe in gently through your nose, without forcing it. Maybe there's a hint of coffee, laundry soap on your sweater, hand soap on your fingers.
You can bring your wrist or your sleeve up to your nose.
[pause 2s]

If you can't smell anything in particular, that's completely fine too. Then imagine two smells you love. Warm bread from a bakery in the morning. Freshly cut grass. The peel of an orange you've just opened.
Let the memory of those smells come back, as vividly as you can.
[pause 3s]
And finally, one taste. Notice what's in your mouth right now.
Maybe the trace of your last drink, toothpaste, or just a neutral taste.
Run your tongue over your teeth, along the roof of your mouth. Feel the saliva, the temperature inside your mouth.
If you have a glass of water nearby, you can take a slow sip, and follow its coolness until it fades away.
[pause 3s]
Each time you explore something with your senses, your attention steps out of the worried story. It's simple, and that's why it helps.
[pause 1.5s]
Now come back to your whole body. Your feet on the floor. Your hands resting. Your eyes taking in the room.
Let your out breath lengthen one more time, easily.
[pause 5s]
Take a moment to notice how you feel, without expecting anything. Maybe your anxiety has dropped a notch, or several. Maybe it's still here, but a little less overwhelming.
If you had to give it a score out of ten right now, what would it be?
[pause 3s]
Just compare it with earlier, without judging the number.
If nothing has changed, that isn't a failure. You spent a few minutes here, instead of in tomorrow. That's exactly what the practice is.
[pause 2s]
Keep this method in your pocket. In a waiting room, before a phone call, in the middle of a restless night, it's always there. It asks for nothing more than what's already around you.
Five things seen, four touched. Three heard, two smelled, and one tasted.
[pause 2s]
Before you go back to your day, choose one of the things you saw earlier, and look at it one last time. Let it be your little reminder. Here and now is where you actually live.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Leaves on a stream
script: [pause 1.5s]
Welcome. Take a moment to really arrive, right where you are.
Settle into a position where your body can stay still for a few minutes. Sitting, with your back upright but not stiff, or lying down if you prefer.
Let your eyes close, or lower your gaze toward the floor, slightly unfocused.
[pause 2s]
There's nothing to get right in these few minutes. Just be here, sitting, and watching.
Breathe normally. Simply notice the air coming in, and the air going out.
Maybe your breathing is fast, maybe slow. There's nothing to correct. Let it do whatever it wants.
[pause 2s]
Feel the places where your body is supported. The backs of your thighs, your back against the chair, your hands resting. Each out-breath settles you in a little more.
[pause 4s]
Today, I'd like us to practice something simple, and precious. Looking at your thoughts, instead of looking through them.
Usually, when a thought like, I'm going to mess this up, shows up, we take it as reality. We're inside it, like wearing glasses we've forgotten we have on.
This exercise comes from an approach called acceptance and commitment therapy. It invites you to take those glasses off and set them on the table for a few moments, so you can look at them.
The goal isn't to chase thoughts away, or to make them more pleasant. It's to change your relationship with them. Watching them pass, instead of being swept along.
[pause 2s]
Imagine you're sitting beside a small stream. Choose whatever place comes to you. A country brook, a mountain river, the edge of a canal in the city.
What's beneath you? Grass, a flat stone, a wooden bench?
[pause 2s]
Feel the temperature of the air on your skin. Maybe a little sunshine, maybe cool shade.
Listen to the water. It flows at its own pace, not too fast, not too slow. It makes a small, steady sound against the pebbles.
[pause 4s]
And on this water, leaves are floating by. Every so often, a leaf drifts in from the left, glides past you, and moves off to the right, until it disappears around a bend in the stream.
All kinds of leaves. Green, yellow, russet, large or tiny. Watch one or two float past, without doing anything.
[pause 5s]
Now gently turn your attention to what's happening in your mind.
Each time a thought appears, take it and place it on a leaf. Then let the leaf carry it away.

If the thought is made of words, you can imagine those words written on the leaf. I need to call the mechanic back. Onto a leaf. If it's an image, place the image on the leaf, like a small photograph.
Every thought gets its own leaf. Worries, shopping lists, memories, brilliant ideas, judgments, questions.
You don't sort them. You don't keep the good ones or chase away the bad ones. Everything goes onto the water in the same way.
[pause 5s]
Let each leaf go at its own pace. You don't need to push the current to make it go faster. And you don't need to hold a leaf back to look at it longer.
Some thoughts will come back. The same worry, five leaves later. That's perfectly fine. Place it down again, without irritation. The stream never gets tired.
If several thoughts arrive at once, put them all on one big leaf, or on several small ones. It's up to you.
And if there are no thoughts for a while, simply watch the water flow. The quiet stretches are part of the stream too.
[pause 4s]
At some point, and it's almost certain, you'll realize you're no longer by the stream. A thought hooked you, you followed it, and now you're preparing tomorrow's meeting or replaying a conversation.
This is exactly the heart of the exercise. The moment you notice is a small moment of waking up.
Without scolding yourself, come back to the water's edge. Take the thought that pulled you away, and place it on a leaf too.
[pause 4s]
There are also quiet thoughts, ones we don't even recognize as thoughts. I can't do this. This doesn't work for me. This is a bit silly.
They're thoughts like any others. They deserve their leaf. Watch them float away.
[pause 2s]

Sometimes a thought comes back with real force, sticky, insistent. What if I can't pay the bills this month? Notice how it tugs at you. You can even give it a bigger, heavier leaf. It still floats. It just takes a little longer to drift away.
Notice, too, the thoughts that comment on the exercise. Am I doing this right? My stream isn't realistic enough. One leaf for each.
And if an emotion shows up, impatience, boredom, a touch of sadness, you can name it, and place it on the water too.
The more you practice this, the more natural it becomes to tell yourself, oh, that's a thought. Not a truth, not an order. Just a thought.
[pause 3s]
Now carry on at your own pace. I'll guide you less. One thought, one leaf. The water flowing.
A thought arrives. You notice it. You place it on a leaf. And you watch it drift away, at the pace of the water.
[pause 8s]
If you've wandered off, no problem at all. Come back to the bank, one leaf, and the current.

If you're having trouble seeing the leaves, that's fine. Some people imagine bubbles rising instead, or clouds crossing the sky. The image doesn't matter much. What matters is the gesture. Notice, place, let go.
[pause 5s]
Notice that while the leaves pass, you stay on the bank. You're the one watching, not the leaf.
Thoughts come and go. You're here before, during, and after each one of them.
The bank doesn't leave with the current. It stays right where it is, steady, while the water flows by.
[pause 5s]
Maybe the stream is very crowded right now, with leaves everywhere. Or maybe there are long stretches with nothing at all. Either way, just watch the water.
If the current seems to stop, or a leaf gets stuck, notice that. It's often a sign that a small thought is here, the leaf isn't moving. Place that thought on another leaf.
[pause 6s]
Gently, let the image of the stream fade. The leaves carry on their journey without you, and that's just fine.
Come back to your breath. To the places where you're supported. To the weight of your hands.
[pause 2s]
Become aware of the room around you, and the sounds that are here.
Feel the air coming in through your nose, a little cooler, and flowing back out a little warmer.
[pause 3s]
Has anything changed? Maybe a little more space between you and whatever passes through you. As if your thoughts were stuck to you a little less tightly.
[pause 2s]
You may have had lots of thoughts, and been carried off often. That doesn't mean you failed. Every return to the bank was the exercise.
Gently move your fingers, your feet. Stretch if your body feels like it. And open your eyes, in your own time.
[pause 2s]
Today, when a thought gets loud, remember this little phrase. I notice I'm having the thought that... It's a leaf. You can let it drift.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Meet your emotion
script: [pause 1.5s]
Welcome to this moment for yourself. There may be an emotion keeping you company today, and you've chosen to stop and look at it, rather than run from it. That takes courage.
[pause 2s]
Get comfortable, your back supported, your feet on the floor. You can close your eyes, or rest your gaze on a spot on the floor.
Take two or three breaths a little fuller than usual, and let each out-breath set you down a little more into your seat.
[pause 6s]
Now feel your body breathing on its own. Your belly rising slightly. The air a little cooler as it enters your nose.
Stay here for a few moments, just with this movement.
[pause 4s]
If your mind is already wandering, that's normal. Just bring it back to the feeling of the air moving in and out.
[pause 2s]
Today we're going to practice RAIN. It's a four-step way of moving through a hard emotion without drowning in it.
R for recognize. A for allow. I for investigate. N for nurture.

This approach was popularized by the American psychologist Tara Brach. The idea is simple. Instead of pushing away what you feel, you make room for it, one step at a time. And often, it becomes easier to bear.
[pause 2s]
To practice, choose a situation that stirs you up a little, but not the heaviest thing in your life.
Tension with a coworker, a message that went unanswered, a worry about someone. Something in the middle, a five out of ten.
Let the scene come back to you. Where were you, who was there, what was said? Just enough for the feeling to wake up.
[pause 3s]
First step, recognize. Simply ask yourself... what's happening inside me, right now?
[pause 2s]
Let a word come. Worry. Disappointment. Anger. Shame. Sadness. There may be several, tangled together like threads.
You can name it silently, in a calm voice, like a friend noticing. Ah, there's anger here. Or, oh, that's fear.
If no word comes, just describe what you notice. Something tight. Restlessness. A heaviness. That's just as accurate.
Naming isn't solving yet. It's simply turning on the light in the room.
[pause 3s]
Second step, allow. This doesn't mean you approve of the situation, or that you like what you're feeling.
It means stopping, just for a moment, the fight against the fact that it's here. A bit like rain. You don't have to love the rain, but there's no point shouting at the sky.
You can whisper inside, yes, this is here. Or, okay, I see you.
[pause 2s]
Notice if there's resistance. An urge to think about something else, to justify yourself, to blame yourself for feeling this way. You can let that be, too. Yes, that too.
Often, it's the fight against an emotion that wears you out the most. When you stop pushing against the door, it sometimes weighs a little less.
[pause 3s]
Third step, investigate, with kindness. Now let's leave the story behind, and move toward the body.
Where does this emotion live? Take a little tour. Your throat, maybe tight. Your chest, heavy or pressed. Your stomach, knotted. Your shoulders, your jaw, your hands.
[pause 2s]
Choose the place where it's clearest, and rest your attention there, gently, the way you'd rest a hand on someone's shoulder.
Explore it with curiosity. Is it warm or cool? Hard like a stone, or shifting? Does it have a size, a shape, edges?
[pause 3s]
Notice, too, what the emotion is pushing you to do. Withdraw? Snap at someone? Grab your phone so you don't have to think about it?
You don't have to follow that push. Just see it.
If it gets too intense, you can come back to your breath or your feet on the floor at any moment. You're the one in charge.
[pause 3s]
Then ask this part of you, kindly... what are you afraid of? Or, what do you need me to understand?
[pause 3s]
Don't look for the right answer. Listen to whatever comes, a sentence, an image, or nothing at all. Simply asking is already a form of care.
Sometimes the answer turns up later, during the day or on a walk. You've already done your part by asking.
[pause 2s]
Fourth step, nurture. Now ask yourself... what do I need, right here, right now?
To be reassured? To be understood? To know it's not my fault? A bit of rest?
[pause 2s]
When you have an idea, even a vague one, try to offer it to yourself.
You can place a hand on your heart, or on the spot where the emotion is. Feel the warmth of your palm, the light pressure.
[pause 2s]
And offer yourself a few words, the ones you'd say to a friend going through the same thing. Of course this is hard. I'm here. You're doing your best.
If the words ring false, imagine instead someone who loves you, or once did, saying them to you, in their own voice.
And if what you need is more practical, a break, a phone call, a glass of water, a boundary to set, make a note of it somewhere inside. You can give it to yourself later.
[pause 3s]
Let these words, or this gesture, do their quiet work. There's nothing to force.
Notice even the smallest change. A shoulder softening, a slightly longer breath, warmth under your hand.
[pause 3s]
Now let go of all the steps. Nothing left to do, nothing left to explore.
Simply rest in being aware. There's the emotion, maybe softer, maybe the same. There are the sounds, the breath, the seat beneath you.
[pause 3s]
And there's you, noticing all of it. A bit like the sky, which holds the clouds without becoming the clouds.
You are not your anger, or your fear. You're the space they move through.
This emotion is a visitor. It arrived, it's shifting, and sooner or later it will leave, like every one that came before it.
[pause 4s]
Notice how you feel now, without looking for a result. Sometimes RAIN brings real relief. Sometimes, just a little more gentleness. Both count.
[pause 2s]
Gently, come back to the room. Move your fingers, your shoulders. Let the sounds around you come in.
Open your eyes when the moment feels right for you.
[pause 2s]
The next time an emotion floods you during the day, you don't need all the steps. Sometimes, pausing and saying yes, this is here, is enough to shift something.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Set your worries down
script: [pause 1.5s]
Some days, your head feels like an overstuffed bag. You've crammed in worries about work, money, health, family, and you carry it everywhere, even to bed.
This moment is here to open that bag, look at what's inside, and sort through it. Keep what you can act on. Set the rest down, at least for a while.
[pause 2s]
Get comfortable, sitting or lying down. Let your hands rest wherever they feel good.
You can close your eyes, or let your gaze rest on the floor.
If you're rushed or restless, that's completely fine. You don't need to be calm to start sorting.
[pause 1.5s]
Breathe in through your nose, calmly...
[pause 4s]
and let the air flow out through your mouth, a little longer, like a sigh at the end of the day.
[pause 6s]
Once more. Breathe in...
[pause 4s]
and breathe out, feeling your shoulders drop with the air.
[pause 6s]
Now let your breath find its own rhythm. Feel the weight of your body, the contact with the seat or the mattress. For the next few minutes, you have nothing else to do but sort, calmly.
[pause 2s]

This sorting draws on a very old idea, found in the Stoic philosophers as well as in today's therapies. Telling apart what depends on you from what doesn't. It sounds simple, and yet it can lighten the load a lot.
Let your current worries come up. Not to solve them right now. Just to take them out of the bag and set them in front of you.
A first one may show up straight away. Give it a short name. The overdue report. The doctor's appointment. My daughter's grades.
[pause 2s]
Once it's here, notice where it shows up in your body. A weight on your chest, a clenched jaw, a knotted stomach. Each worry often has its own little corner.
[pause 3s]
Then a second. And maybe a third. Big or small, it doesn't matter. A bill, an argument, a loved one's health, the state of the world.
Three or four is enough for today. You don't need to empty the whole bag.
[pause 3s]
Now imagine two circles drawn on the ground in front of you, as if in chalk.
A small circle in the middle. This is what depends on you. Your actions, your words, your choices, the way you take care of yourself.
And around it, a large circle. What doesn't depend on you. Other people's decisions, the past, the distant future, the weather, the economy, what people think.
That large circle is often the one that fills our nights. And it's exactly the one we have the least control over.
[pause 2s]
Take a moment to see these two circles clearly. Their color, their size, the surface they're drawn on.
You can even step into the center of the small circle. Feel your feet inside it. This is your ground, the place where your hands can actually do something.
[pause 3s]
Pick up your first worry. Hold it in your hands, like an object. And ask yourself one simple question. Is there something I can concretely do about this?
[pause 2.5s]
If yes, place it in the small circle. If not, place it in the large one.
Often, a worry has a bit of both. The doctor's appointment, for example. The result doesn't depend on you, but booking the appointment and preparing your questions does.
In that case, split it in two, and place each piece in its own circle.

A difficult bill, for example. The amount is fixed, but calling to ask for a payment plan is up to you. A loved one's health. You can't control it, but you can call them tonight and tell them you're thinking of them.
[pause 3s]
Do the same with the second worry. Then the third. Take your time. There are no wrong answers, only your honesty with yourself.
[pause 3s]

Notice what happens when you place a worry in the large circle. Sometimes a small relief, as if you were finally admitting it was never your job. Sometimes resistance. If I stop thinking about it, something bad will happen. And yet, thinking about something is not the same as controlling it.
If you're unsure about a worry, set it on the line between the two circles, and come back to it later. The sorting doesn't need to be perfect.
[pause 2s]
Now look at the small circle. This is where your strength lies.
Choose just one worry in this circle. And ask yourself, what would the next small action be? Not the whole problem. Just the first step.
Sending that email. Jotting down a few ideas on a piece of paper. Calling a friend for advice. Booking a time slot. Sometimes the most useful action is simply going to bed at a reasonable hour.
[pause 2s]
Once you've found it, picture yourself doing it. When, where, how. Feel what it's like to go from I'm worried, to I'm handling it.
If you can, pick a specific moment. Tomorrow at ten, before you open your inbox. The more concrete the step, the more easily your mind can let go of it at night.
[pause 3s]
Now turn toward the large circle. Everything in it, you may have been carrying for days, even weeks. And yet carrying it hasn't changed it.
Let's set it down. Imagine a place for that. A big wooden box by a fireplace, a rowboat tied up at the edge of a lake, a trunk in an attic. Choose whatever speaks to you.
[pause 2s]
Take the first worry from the large circle. Feel its weight in your hands. Then gently place it there.
You're not throwing it away. You're not pretending it doesn't exist. You're simply recognizing that it isn't yours to hold, right now.
If you chose the box, hear the soft knock of wood as the worry touches the bottom. If it's the rowboat, watch it drift out a little on the still water, held by its rope.
[pause 3s]
And the next one. Set it down. Maybe you notice a slight easing in your arms, your shoulders, your chest.
[pause 2s]
If a worry resists, if your hands don't want to let go, that's okay. Set it halfway down. Or tell it, I'll pick you up later, if I need to.
And if it comes knocking again tomorrow, that will be normal. You can set it down again, as many times as it takes.
[pause 2s]
Once everything is set down, gently close the lid. Or let the rowboat rock at the end of its rope. Your worries are there, sheltered. They don't need you in order to exist.
Take a moment to feel your empty hands. Open them, if you like, palms facing up. They can rest now too.
[pause 3s]
Now come back to your breath. Notice the space around you, now that your hands are lighter.
Breathe in, and feel your chest open a little...
[pause 4s]
breathe out, and let your body settle.
[pause 6s]
Breathe into this freed up space. There's nothing to fill it with. It's just a little room for you.

I'll guide a gentle rhythm now. A calm breath in, about four seconds. A slower breath out, about six seconds, without forcing. If the rhythm bothers you, just let the out breath be a little longer than the in breath.
[pause 1.5s]
In.
[pause 4s]
Out.
[pause 6s]
In.
[pause 4s]
Out, and let your shoulders drop a little further.
[pause 6s]
If you feel dizzy or uncomfortable, go straight back to your natural breathing.
[pause 3s]
Notice how you feel now. Maybe a little lighter. Maybe just clearer about what's ahead. The worries haven't disappeared, but they've been put away.
[pause 2s]
Gently, start to come back. Move your hands, your feet. Stretch if you feel like it.
Remember your small action, the one from the small circle. It's waiting for you, within reach.
You can write it down on paper or in your phone as soon as you open your eyes, so your mind doesn't have to hold on to it.
And for everything else, remember that box by the fire. It's always there, ready to hold what you don't have to carry.
You can do this sorting again whenever the bag fills up. A few minutes is often enough to see more clearly.
[pause 2s]
Open your eyes when the moment feels right for you.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Self-compassion break
script: [pause 1.5s]
If you've opened this pause, maybe something is weighing on you right now. You did well to stop for a moment.
[pause 2s]

Over the next few minutes, I'll guide you through three simple steps, inspired by the work of the psychologist Kristin Neff. Three inner gestures you can come back to anywhere. At your desk, in the street, or lying awake in bed.
[pause 2s]
Settle in just as you are. Sitting or standing, it doesn't matter. If you like, close your eyes, or simply let your gaze rest on the floor in front of you.
Take a breath in through your nose, without forcing it...
[pause 3s]
And let the air flow out slowly, like a long sigh.
[pause 4s]
One more time. Breathing in...
[pause 3s]
and letting go.
[pause 4s]
Now feel where your body is supported. Your weight on the chair or the floor. Your feet. Your hands, resting somewhere. Your body is being held up. You don't have to hold it.
[pause 2s]

Now choose something that's difficult for you at the moment. Something medium sized, not the heaviest thing in your life. A worry at work, some tension with someone close to you, a concern that's been going round in your head since this morning.
Let the situation come to mind. Who's involved, what was said, what worries you.
[pause 2s]
Then, gently, turn your attention to your body. Where do you feel this difficulty?
[pause 2s]
A tight throat, a weight on your chest, a knot in your stomach, a clenched jaw.
You don't need to change anything. You're simply noticing. Ah, there it is.
You can even rest a hand on that spot, as a way of telling your body, I feel you. If it gets too intense, come back to your feet on the floor.
[pause 3s]
Step one is acknowledging. Say to yourself, in simple words, this is a moment of difficulty.
Or, this is hard right now. Or, this hurts. Choose the words that feel true for you.
[pause 2s]
This isn't complaining, and it isn't being dramatic. It's the opposite of pretending everything's fine. You're looking honestly at what's here, without adding to it.
Naming what hurts often helps you step back a little.
[pause 2s]
Step two is remembering that you're part of something bigger. Difficulty is part of life. It isn't proof that you're getting things wrong.
Say to yourself, other people go through this too. I'm not the only one who feels this way.
[pause 2s]
Right now, somewhere, someone feels overwhelmed in front of a full inbox. Someone is waiting for a reply that doesn't come. Someone is being hard on themselves, alone in a kitchen, late at night.
You don't know these people, and yet you share something with them. What you're feeling is deeply human.
This difficulty doesn't set you apart. If anything, it connects you to everyone who has ever found life heavy.
[pause 3s]
Step three is kindness. If it feels comfortable, place a hand on your heart. Or both hands. Or a hand on your cheek, on your belly, wherever that touch feels good.
Feel the warmth of your palm. The gentle pressure. Your chest rising and falling beneath it.
[pause 2s]
This gesture isn't trivial. Warm, gentle touch can help your body feel safe, a little like a friend's hand resting on your shoulder.
And now say to yourself, softly, may I be kind to myself. May I give myself the patience I need.
Repeat it slowly, once or twice, in time with your breath. Breathing in, may I be kind to myself. Breathing out, the patience I need.
[pause 4s]
These words are only an example. What do you need, right here, right now? Comfort, courage, rest, a little understanding?
[pause 3s]
Imagine a friend going through exactly what you're going through. What would you say to them? Maybe, you're doing your best. Or, of course this is hard. Or simply, I'm here.
Take those same words, and offer them to yourself.
[pause 4s]

If nothing comes, that's fine. The intention is enough. And if an emotion rises, tears, a lump in your throat, that's normal too. You can slow down, open your eyes, or stop here. You're the one who decides.
[pause 2s]
Stay a moment longer with your hand where it is. Notice what's here now. Perhaps a little more space. Perhaps nothing has changed, and that's completely fine too.
[pause 4s]
Let your hand come down. Move your fingers a little, and your shoulders. Come back to the sounds around you.
When the moment feels right for you, open your eyes.
[pause 2s]
These three steps fit into three short sentences. This is hard. I'm not alone in this. May I be kind to myself. You can take them with you wherever you go.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Loving-kindness
script: [pause 1.5s]
This practice is very old. It's called metta, or loving-kindness. It means offering wishes of well-being, first to yourself, then to wider and wider circles of people.
It isn't a way of forcing a feeling. You can't produce love on demand. You're simply watering a seed, and letting it grow at its own pace.
Research suggests that practicing this regularly may help people feel more connected to others, and a little gentler with themselves. Two precious things when stress pulls us into isolation.
[pause 2s]
Settle in comfortably. Your back upright but not rigid, as if a thread were gently drawing the top of your head toward the ceiling. Shoulders relaxed, hands resting.
Let your face soften. Your forehead, the space between your eyebrows, your cheeks. You can even let a faint smile appear at the corners of your mouth, if it comes naturally.
[pause 2s]
Breathe in through your nose...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out, a little longer. Let that out-breath carry away a little of the day.
[pause 5s]
Once more. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out, letting your body settle a little more.
[pause 5s]
Now bring your attention to the area of your heart, in the center of your chest. You can rest a hand there, if it helps you feel it.
Breathe as if the air were flowing in and out through that spot. You don't need to feel anything in particular. Just spend a little time there, with curiosity.
[pause 3s]
Throughout the practice, if your mind wanders to your shopping list or tomorrow's meeting, that's normal. Simply come back to the phrases, without judging yourself.
And if a phrase passes by without you feeling it, that's fine. The next one arrives, like another wave.
[pause 3s]
We'll begin with you. It's often the hardest part, and that's exactly why we start there.
Picture yourself as you are right now, here, with your worries, your tiredness, your hopes. Or picture the child you once were, if it's easier to feel tenderness toward them.
Choose whichever image brings the most softness. There's no right one.
Or think of the person who got through this week, with everything it asked of you. That person deserves kindness too.
And silently offer yourself these phrases, slowly, letting each one resonate.
May I be safe.
[pause 2s]
May I be peaceful.
[pause 2s]
May I be healthy.
[pause 2s]
May I live with ease.
[pause 2s]
You can imagine these words as a hand resting on your shoulder. Or as the voice of someone who loves you, saying them to you.
[pause 3s]
If the phrases feel mechanical, or a bit strange, that's very common. You can adapt them. May I be protected. May I find some calm. May I take care of my body. May my life feel a little lighter.
What matters isn't the exact wording, but the intention. The intention of wishing someone well. And that someone, for now, is you.
Once more, at your own pace. May I be safe. May I be peaceful. May I be healthy. May I live with ease.
[pause 3s]
What's happening inside you right now?
[pause 2s]
A little warmth, perhaps. Or resistance, a voice saying I don't deserve this. If so, welcome that too. That voice needs kindness as well.
[pause 3s]

Now bring to mind someone you love easily. Someone whose name alone makes you smile. A loyal friend, a sister, a grandfather, a child. It can even be an animal, like the dog who greets you at the door every evening.
See them in front of you. Their face, their familiar expression, the way they move. Feel the tenderness that rises naturally when you think of them.
If memories come, a shared laugh, a hug on a station platform, let them feed the warmth.
Where do you feel that tenderness in your body? In your chest, your hands, around your eyes? Let it spread a little.
[pause 2s]
And offer them these wishes, as if you were whispering them.
May you be safe.
[pause 2s]
May you be peaceful.
[pause 2s]
May you be healthy.
[pause 2s]
May you live with ease.
[pause 3s]
Imagine these wishes really reaching them. See them a little more relaxed, a little lighter. Maybe they smile, without knowing why.
Notice how easy it is with this person. How the warmth flows without effort. It's this same warmth you can learn, little by little, to turn toward yourself and toward others.
Stay with that warmth for a breath or two before moving on.
[pause 3s]
Once more, for them. May you be safe. May you be peaceful. May you be healthy. May you live with ease.
[pause 3s]

Now think of a neutral person. Someone you see regularly but don't really know. The woman at the corner bakery. The morning bus driver. A neighbor you nod to on the stairs. A colleague from another floor.
If no one comes to mind, simply choose someone you passed today.
It doesn't matter if you can't picture them clearly. A rough outline is enough.

You know almost nothing about them. And yet, like you, this person has a whole life. People they love. Worries that wake them in the night. Small joys, disappointments. They too want to be happy. They too want to avoid suffering.
[pause 2s]
Think of everything you can't see. Maybe they slept badly. Maybe they're worried about a child, the rent, their health. Behind that ordinary face, there's a whole story.
Let yourself be curious about this person for a moment, the way you might wonder about a character in a book.
See their face, even if it's blurry, and offer them the same wishes.
May you be safe.
[pause 2s]
May you be peaceful.
[pause 2s]
May you be healthy.
[pause 2s]
May you live with ease.
[pause 3s]
You may feel less for this person. That's normal. You don't have to feel love. You're expressing an intention, and that intention counts.
Maybe the next time you see them, you'll look at them a little differently. With a little more curiosity, a little more warmth.
You can do this with anyone, really. It's a quiet practice you can take anywhere, in a queue or an open-plan office.
[pause 2s]
Now let your circle widen, little by little.
You can imagine this warmth as a soft light that starts in your chest and spreads outward, circle after circle, like ripples on water when you drop in a pebble.
First, everyone in your building, or on your street. Those who are sleeping, those who are working, those who are cooking dinner.
[pause 2s]
Then your neighborhood, your city. People on the subway, in hospitals, in schools. Those who are happy right now, and those going through a hard time.
Including the people working through the night so others can sleep.
[pause 2s]
Then your country. Then every country. People getting up as you go to bed, people speaking languages you don't know.
Including people you'll never meet, whose lives are just as real as yours.
Let the light travel at its own speed. There's no need to picture everyone. The intention reaches further than your imagination.
And beyond humans, all living beings. Animals, birds, everything that breathes and, in one way or another, seeks to be well.
May all beings be safe.
[pause 2s]
May all beings be peaceful.
[pause 2s]
May all beings be healthy.
[pause 2s]
May all beings live with ease.
[pause 3s]
And don't forget that you're part of this great circle. These wishes come back to you too, like a wave returning to the shore.
If a strong emotion rises, sadness, joy, tears, that's normal. These practices sometimes touch tender places. You can pause, come back to your breathing, open your eyes.
Bring your hand back to your heart, if you like, and let a slightly longer out-breath help you settle.
[pause 4s]
Now let go of the phrases. Simply rest in whatever is here. Perhaps a warmth in your chest, a softness in your face, a sense of openness.
Or perhaps nothing special, and that's fine too. You've planted something. Seeds don't grow before our eyes.
Notice, too, that this kindness cost you nothing. You lost nothing by giving it. Often, the person offering it is the first to feel it.
Kindness isn't a limited supply. The more you practice it, the more easily it comes, for others and for yourself.
[pause 2s]
