Let your breath come and go, like a calm wave. Enjoy this moment, without doing anything.
If you like, rest a hand on your heart again, and feel it beating beneath your palm. There's nothing to hold on to, and nothing to push away.
[pause 5s]
Take one more breath, just to savor this calm.
[pause 3s]
Gently, begin to come back. Take a slightly deeper breath.
Wiggle your fingers and toes. Stretch if you feel like it, slowly.
Listen to the sounds around you. Sense the room you're in.
And when the moment is right for you, open your eyes.
[pause 2s]
Today, if you pass someone in the street, at work, in a queue, you can silently send them one of these wishes. May you be peaceful. No one will know. And yet something will have shifted, in you.
And you can come back to this practice as often as you like, even for three minutes, on the bus or before you sleep.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Soften your inner critic
script: [pause 1.5s]
Inside each of us there's a little voice that comments on everything. It reads your emails over your shoulder, it counts your mistakes, it compares. Sometimes it whispers, sometimes it shouts.
Today, we're not going to try to silence it. We're going to get to know it, understand what it's after, and answer it with another voice, a gentler one, that's also yours.
[pause 2s]
Find a position where your body feels both steady and relaxed. Your back upright without stiffness, your shoulders dropping, your hands resting.
Close your eyes if you like, or simply lower your gaze.
[pause 1.5s]
Breathe in through your nose, calmly...
[pause 4s]
and breathe out through your mouth, as if you were fogging up a window.
[pause 5s]
Once more. And let the air leave a little more slowly than last time.
[pause 6s]
Now let your breathing return to normal. Choose a place where you can feel it clearly. Your nostrils, your chest, or your belly. Stay there for a few moments, with this simple coming and going.
[pause 3s]
If your mind wanders off, that's normal. Just bring it back, without comment. That's already a small training in kindness.
Each return to the breath is a bit like a hand on your shoulder. You don't scold yourself for wandering. You just come back.
[pause 3s]
Now let a typical sentence from your inner critic come to mind. One you know by heart, because you hear it so often.

Choose one that stings a little, but not the most painful one. It might be something like, you'll never manage it. Or, late again, it's always the same with you. Or, everyone's going to see you don't know what you're doing. Or simply, you should have done better.
Hear it in your head, in its exact words. Don't correct it straight away. Listen to it, the way you'd listen to someone talking in the next room.
[pause 3s]
Now notice the tone of this voice. Is it curt? Contemptuous? Impatient? Does it sound like someone you've known, a parent, a teacher, a former boss?
[pause 2.5s]
You don't need to analyze it. Just notice whether it feels familiar.
And notice what it does to your body. Maybe your chest tightens. Your head sinks into your shoulders. Your stomach knots, or you suddenly feel like disappearing.
[pause 2s]

It's interesting. A few words in your head, and your whole body reacts as if it were facing a threat. That's exactly what's happening. Your system goes on alert, as if you were under attack, except the attack is coming from the inside.
Take a moment to rest a hand on the place that's reacting most. Just to tell your body, I can see this hurts.
Let your breathing slow a little under your hand. You're not fighting the voice. You're looking after the one who hears it.
[pause 4s]
Now, a slightly surprising question. What is this voice trying to protect?
[pause 2s]
Because the inner critic, however harsh, often has an intention. A clumsy one, but a real one. It wants to spare you rejection. Embarrassment in front of others. Losing your place. Failing.
Maybe it learned, a long time ago, that to be accepted, you had to be flawless. And it's still trying to keep you safe, with the only tools it knows, which are fear and pressure.
Research on self-criticism suggests that this kind of pressure tends to drain motivation rather than build it. Encouragement usually works better than threats, for adults as much as for children.
[pause 1.5s]
Ask it silently, what are you afraid of, for me? And let the answer come, without searching for it. A word, an image, a sensation.
[pause 5s]
If something came up, you can acknowledge it. Ah, so that's it. You're afraid I won't measure up. You're afraid people will let me down.
And if nothing came, that's fine. Simply asking the question already changes your relationship with this voice a little.
Sometimes the answer arrives later, while you're doing the dishes or walking somewhere.
[pause 3s]

Now imagine that a very dear friend comes to see you. Someone you love deeply. With a lump in their throat, they tell you they'll never manage it, that they're always late, that it's always the same with them.
Would you answer, yes, that's true, you're hopeless? Of course not.
[pause 2s]
So what would you say? And in what tone? Maybe you'd put a hand on their arm. Maybe you'd tell them, you're exhausted right now. You're doing so much. Being late once doesn't define who you are.
Listen to your own voice when it speaks to someone you love. Its warmth, its patience, its quiet firmness too.
Notice that kindness isn't the same as letting yourself off the hook. A good friend can still encourage you to do better. They just don't crush you to get there.
[pause 2s]
Take a moment to feel that voice inside you. Picture your friend's face as they listen, and see it soften a little. Notice whether your own breathing changes when you speak this way.
[pause 4s]
Now let's rephrase your critic's sentence together. Not to deny it, or to pretend everything's fine. But to keep the useful idea, and change the way it's said.
Take the original sentence. Ask yourself what it really wants for you. Often, behind late again, there's something like, I'd like you to be reliable, so people can count on you.
So the kind voice might say, you care about being reliable, and that's a lovely quality. What would help you leave earlier tomorrow?

Behind you'll never manage it, there may be, I'm afraid you'll be disappointed. And the gentle voice would answer, this is hard, and you're allowed to take it step by step. You've already got through difficult things before.
[pause 2s]
Now it's your turn. Take your own sentence, and rephrase it the way you would for that friend. Keep what's true in it. Change the tone.
[pause 6s]
Take your time. If the words don't come, you can simply start with, I can see this is hard for you. The rest can follow.
[pause 3s]
Say this new sentence to yourself again, slowly, silently. Perhaps with your hand on your heart. Notice how your body receives it.
[pause 3s]

Maybe a little relaxation. Maybe some resistance, a part of you saying, that's too nice, I don't deserve it. That's very common, especially at first. It isn't a failure. It's like learning a new language. The first words sound strange, then they become familiar.
And if this practice stirs up strong emotions, that's normal. You can open your eyes, breathe, and stop here. You can come back to it whenever you like.
[pause 3s]
Stay a few more breaths in this space. The critical voice may still be there, somewhere. But you've heard something else.
You don't have to choose between the two once and for all. You're simply discovering that you get to choose the tone.
[pause 2s]
This gentle voice isn't borrowed. You already use it every time you comfort someone. It belongs to you too. You're simply allowed to turn it toward yourself.
[pause 3s]
Bring your attention back to your breathing, then to your whole body. Gently move your fingers and your toes. Stretch your neck.
When the moment is right for you, open your eyes and look around.
[pause 2s]
Today, when the critic speaks up, try asking yourself one question. Would I talk like this to someone I love? And if the answer is no, try the other voice.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Single-point focus
script: [pause 1.5s]
This is one of the simplest attention exercises there is. No visualization, no images to build. Just breaths, and numbers.
[pause 1.5s]
Sit in a steady position. Your back upright without being stiff, as if a thread were gently drawing the top of your head toward the ceiling. Your hands resting on your thighs.
Close your eyes if you like, or keep a soft, lowered gaze, resting about three feet in front of you.
Let the background sound wrap around you. It works like a curtain between you and everything else.
[pause 2s]
Take two slightly deeper breaths, to tell your body it's time to stop for a moment. Let the air come in fully...
[pause 3s]
and leave without hurrying.
[pause 5s]
Then let your breathing find its natural rhythm again. You're not going to control it. You're only going to count it.
[pause 1.5s]
First, find the place where you feel it most clearly. The tip of your nose, your chest, or your belly. Choose just one, and stay with it for the whole session.
[pause 2s]
Here's the instruction. With each out-breath, you silently count one number. The first out-breath is one. The next is two. And so on, up to ten.
When you reach ten, you start again at one.
The in-breath gets no number. It's a small neutral space, where you simply feel the air coming in.
The number lands on the out-breath, gently, like a pebble settling at the bottom of a pond.
[pause 1.5s]
And here's the most important rule. If you lose count, if you find yourself at fourteen or twenty-three, or you have no idea where you are, you go back to one. No commentary, no sigh.
Losing count isn't a failure. It's information. Your mind wandered off, and you've just noticed. That moment is exactly what we're training.
[pause 2s]
Let's do a first round together. I'll count with you, and you keep your own pace.
Breathe in... and on the out-breath, one.
[pause 3s]
Two.
[pause 3s]
Three.
[pause 3s]
Four. Really feel the end of the out-breath, the moment the air comes to rest.
[pause 3s]
Five. Let the in-breath come on its own before six.
[pause 3s]
I'll leave six, seven and eight to you. Your rhythm, not mine.
Keep going at your own pace up to ten, then come back to one.
[pause 4s]
Notice the quality of the counting. It can be very light, almost whispered inside. There's no need to say the numbers with force.
Some people like to see the number, others to hear it, others to feel it. Go with whatever comes naturally.
If your breathing speeds up or slows down, let it. The counting follows the breath, never the other way around.
[pause 4s]
Keep going. One out-breath, one number.
If you feel you're counting too fast, you're probably setting the number down before the breath has finished. Wait until the out-breath is complete, then count.
[pause 4s]
Where are you now?
[pause 2s]
The number doesn't matter. If you know where you are, carry on. If you don't, go back to one.
Maybe you've already lost count several times. That's true for almost everyone. It doesn't mean meditation isn't for you. It means you have a lively mind.
Every time you come back to one, that's a repetition, like working a muscle. Notice, let go, come back.
[pause 3s]
Sometimes a thought keeps running in the background while you count. You can count anyway. It may quiet down, or it may not. Your only job is the next number.
Now I'll speak less, and you count on your own. Just you, the breath, and the numbers from one to ten.
[pause 8s]
One number per out-breath. Nothing else to do.
[pause 5s]
You're still here. Whatever the number, or if there's no number anymore, simply start again at one on the next out-breath.
If you caught yourself planning, remembering, or commenting on the exercise, that's perfect. You noticed. Back to one.
And if you feel a flicker of annoyance with yourself, note that too, with a bit of humor. It's part of the landscape. Then pick up the count again.
[pause 5s]
Now let's switch to a variation. Instead of counting to ten, count only up to four, then go back to one.

This shorter cycle asks for a different kind of presence. There's less time to drift, and the return to one comes more often. On days when your mind is very busy, this can be the most helpful version.
It works at work too. One thing at a time, and when you drift, you go back to the start of the paragraph, no drama.
Try it now. One...
[pause 3s]
two...
[pause 3s]
three...
[pause 3s]
four. And again, from one.
[pause 6s]
Feel how each number is a small appointment. You arrive, you set the number down, you move on.
Notice the space, too, between the out-breath and the next in-breath. A small quiet moment, where nothing happens.
[pause 5s]
Now let the numbers fade away. Stop counting. Just stay with the breath for a few moments, in the spot you chose.
[pause 4s]
Notice what's here. Maybe a little more calm, maybe not. Maybe restlessness, or tiredness. All of it is valid. You don't have to get anything out of these minutes.
[pause 2s]
You can take this counting anywhere. In a waiting room, before a meeting, in the middle of an overloaded day. A few rounds of ten are enough to come back to yourself.
Take a deeper breath. Gently move your fingers, your shoulders.
[pause 2s]
When it feels right for you, open your eyes. Take this simplicity with you. One breath, then the next.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Before an important task
script: [pause 1.5s]
You have something important to do, and you chose to take four minutes before diving in. That's a good instinct.
[pause 1.5s]
Settle into your chair, both feet on the floor, your back supported. You can close your eyes, or simply lower your gaze toward your desk.
[pause 2s]
Let's take three breaths together, a little slower than usual.
Breathe in through your nose, easily...
[pause 3s]
And out through your mouth, slowly, as if you were blowing on a hot drink.
[pause 4s]
Once more. The air comes in...
[pause 3s]
and flows back out, a little more slowly.
[pause 4s]
One last time, in...
[pause 3s]
and as you breathe out, let your shoulders drop, just a little.
[pause 4s]
Good. Now let your breathing find its own rhythm again. It knows how.
If your mind is still on the last meeting, or on what's waiting for you tonight, that's normal. For these few minutes, bring it back here, to your chair, to this breath.
[pause 2s]
Before going further, something very practical. Your phone.
If you can, switch it to silent, or turn it face down. Better still, put it out of reach.
Think about the open tabs too, the inbox, the notifications blinking in the corner of your screen. Right after this session, you can close them, and keep only what this task really needs.
Every little alert pulls your attention somewhere else, and it takes a while to find its way back. Turning them off simply makes things easier for you.
[pause 2s]
Now, the task itself. Often, what makes the mind restless is vagueness. You think about that big project, about everything you have to do, and it feels enormous.
So try to describe your task in a single sentence. Simple, precise, starting with an action word.
For example... Write the introduction to the report. Or, prepare the three slides for Thursday's meeting.
Take a few seconds to find your sentence, and say it silently to yourself.
[pause 4s]
If it still feels too big, narrow it down. Something you could clearly move forward in the next half hour.
[pause 1.5s]
Good. Now go even smaller. What's the very first step? Not the second one, not the whole plan. Just the first move.
Opening the right file. Typing a heading. Reading the brief once through. Jotting down three rough ideas.
[pause 2s]
See that move in detail. Where are your hands? What's on the screen? What's the first word you type?
[pause 2s]
Picture yourself doing it, without hesitating, almost casually. The way you'd open a door you've walked through a hundred times.
[pause 3s]
Notice how doable that first step is. It doesn't need inspiration, or being in top form. It only asks you to begin.
[pause 1.5s]
And now, set an intention. Something like this. For twenty-five minutes, just this.
Twenty-five minutes is long enough to make real progress, and short enough for your mind to agree to it. You can set a timer if that helps.
During that time, if another thought pops up, an email to send, an errand to run, jot it down on a piece of paper next to you, and come back. Nothing is lost. It's simply parked for later.
[pause 1.5s]
And if your mind wanders off, that's normal. You'll come back to your sentence, to the next small move. No need to scold yourself.
No need to start over either. One breath, your sentence, the next small move. That's all.
[pause 2s]
Repeat your intention one last time, silently. For twenty-five minutes, just this.
[pause 3s]
One more breath. Feel your feet on the floor, your hands ready.
Open your eyes, if they were closed, and look at your workspace.
[pause 1.5s]
Your sentence is clear. Your first step is ready. You don't need to feel like it to get started.
Begin now.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Mindful breathing
script: [pause 1.5s]
Welcome to this practice. It's one of the oldest and simplest there is. Paying attention to your breath, and coming back to it each time you drift away.
Nothing to achieve. Nowhere to get to. Just breathing, and knowing it.
If this is your first time, know that your mind will wander often. That's not a problem to fix. It's the very material of the exercise.
[pause 2s]
First, take time to settle in. If you're on a chair, place your feet flat on the floor, a little apart. Move slightly forward on the seat, so your back can hold itself up without leaning.
If you're on a cushion, let your knees sink toward the floor, your hips slightly higher than your knees.
[pause 1.5s]
Let your spine lengthen, from the base of your back to the top of your head. Chin slightly tucked. A posture that's both dignified and relaxed.
Rest your hands on your thighs, or one in the other in your lap.
And close your eyes, or let your gaze rest on the floor about three feet in front of you, not fixed on anything.
[pause 3s]

Take a moment to feel your points of contact. Your feet on the floor, the weight of your body on the seat, your hands resting. These are solid supports. Your body is held. You don't have to hold it up. Let the ground do its job.
[pause 2s]

Do a quick sweep through your body to release whatever can be released. Your forehead. Your eyes. Your jaw, which we often clench without noticing. Your shoulders, which can drop a little. Your hands, open.
If an area stays tense, that's fine. Just notice it, and leave it be.
[pause 2s]
Take two slightly fuller breaths, through your nose if that's comfortable. Breathe in...
[pause 4s]
and let the out breath settle you a little more into your seat.
[pause 6s]
Once more...
[pause 9s]
Then let the breath return to its natural rhythm. You're not going to steer it. You're only going to observe it, the way you'd watch waves from the beach.
The breath doesn't need you in order to breathe. It does it day and night. You're simply keeping it company.
Why the breath? Because it's always available, and always in the present. You can't breathe yesterday, or tomorrow. Each time you feel it, you come back here, now.
[pause 2s]
Let's start by finding the place where you feel it most clearly.
It might be at the nostrils. The feeling of air coming in, going out, brushing your upper lip.
It might be in the chest. The ribs widening slightly, then drawing back in.
Or in the belly. A soft swelling on the in breath, a gentle falling back on the out breath.
Explore these three areas, one after the other, for a few breaths each.
[pause 8s]
Which one is clearest for you today?
[pause 2.5s]
There's no right choice. It may even change from day to day.
Choose one place, and keep it for the rest of the practice. This will be your anchor.
If you're unsure, simply choose the belly. It's often the steadiest place when the mind is busy.
[pause 3s]
Now try following one whole breath. Not just a moment of it, but its entire journey.
The beginning of the in breath, that almost imperceptible moment when the air starts to come in.
The middle, as the movement grows.
The end, as the in breath slows and completes.
Then the beginning of the out breath, its middle, its end, until everything comes to rest.
As if you were following a wave from the moment it forms out at sea to the moment it spreads across the sand.
[pause 5s]
You may notice that the in breath and the out breath aren't necessarily the same length. Often the out breath is a little longer, a little softer. No need to measure. Just feel the shape of each one.
[pause 5s]
Keep going like this. Each breath is a little different from the last. Longer, shorter, deeper, lighter. There's nothing to correct. Just notice.
If you notice a tendency to control the breath, to make it nicer, more even, that's very common. Let it go back to its own shape, even if it's a little uneven.
[pause 5s]
At some point, maybe already, you'll realize you're no longer with the breath. You're thinking about dinner, an email, a conversation from yesterday. Or you're commenting on the meditation itself.
That's exactly what a human mind does. It's not a mistake, and it doesn't mean you're meditating badly.
What matters is the moment you realize it. That little click. Oh, I drifted off.
That moment is precious. It's a moment of presence. Welcome it kindly, almost with a sense of satisfaction.
Then bring your attention back to the breath. Gently, without forcing. The way you'd bring back a puppy that has wandered off, without scolding it.
You can use a quiet word, right at the moment you notice. Thinking. Or, wandering. Then come back.
[pause 5s]
Drifting, noticing, returning. This cycle will repeat dozens of times. Each return is a repetition. That's how attention is trained, like a muscle, one repetition after another.
Someone who comes back a hundred times in twelve minutes hasn't failed at meditating. They've done a hundred repetitions.
[pause 2s]

Some thoughts are light. They drift past like a cloud. Others are sticky. A worry, a conversation you keep replaying. With those, you may come back ten times in a row. That's normal. Each time, the same gesture. Notice, and return to the breath, without arguing with the thought. You don't have to solve it now. If it's important, it will still be there later.
[pause 3s]

If you like, you can also note the breath itself, very lightly. The word in, on the in breath. The word out, on the out breath. An inner whisper, almost silent. It sometimes helps when the mind is busy. As soon as you no longer need it, let the words drop, and stay with the pure sensation.
[pause 6s]
If you find you're often carried away, you can make your attention a little finer. Don't just try to feel the breath in general. Look for the details.

If your anchor is at the nostrils, notice the temperature. The in breath is often slightly cooler. The out breath, slightly warmer. Notice too which side the air flows through more, the left nostril or the right.
If your anchor is the chest or the belly, notice the texture of the movement. Is it smooth, or jerky? Are there small waves within a single breath?

Maybe the air feels more humid on the out breath. Or the movement of the belly extends into your lower back. Notice, too, the moment the air touches the back of your throat. Tiny details you may never have noticed before.
[pause 6s]

And notice the pauses. Between the end of the in breath and the start of the out breath, there's often a tiny stillness. And another, often a little longer, after the out breath, before the air returns.
Don't create these pauses, and don't lengthen them. Just notice them when they're there. A small moment of calm, where the body quietly waits for the next breath.
[pause 6s]
You may discover that the breath, which seems so ordinary, is full of nuance. The closer you look, the more there is to see.
And if a strong sensation appears elsewhere, an itch, some tension, an ache in your back, you can notice that too. Give it a moment of attention. Move if you need to, mindfully. Then come back.
[pause 2s]
If you're feeling sleepy, straighten your posture a little, and open your eyes slightly. If you're restless, let the out breath help you settle, without forcing.
Either way, whatever is here is allowed to be here. Calm, restlessness, boredom, drowsiness. It's all part of the practice.
And if you're doubting, wondering whether you're doing it right, notice that too. Doubting. It's a thought like any other.
[pause 4s]
Now I'm going to speak less and less, and let you practice on your own. Your anchor, the whole breath, the fine sensations. And when you notice you've drifted, a simple return, no story.
You can choose a very simple marker. Feeling the end of each out breath. That's often where we get lost, and where it's easiest to come back.
[pause 10s]
Breathe in, and feel where the air begins...
[pause 4s]
breathe out, and feel where it ends.
[pause 6s]
Where is your attention right now?
[pause 3s]
Wherever it is, that's fine. Come back to the next breath. Just this one.
[pause 10s]
If you've drifted into a project, a conversation, a worry, simply note where you were, then come back to your anchor. The next breath is always a fresh one.
One whole in breath. One whole out breath. Nothing else to do.
[pause 8s]
No need to do more. Being here for this one breath is enough.
If you spent all that time in your thoughts, it doesn't matter at all. What counts is now. The breath is here, waiting for you without impatience.
Let it breathe on its own. You simply watch. Like a friend sitting beside someone who's asleep, attentive, doing nothing.
[pause 8s]
Maybe you notice your mind has settled a little. Or maybe not at all. That's not the measure of your practice. The practice is having come back, again and again.
This is the same move that helps when you're facing a difficult page or a long report. You notice you've drifted, and you come back to the line where you left off.
[pause 2s]
Now let your attention gently widen. From your anchor point, to the whole body breathing. Feel how the breath is present everywhere. In the belly, the chest, the back, the shoulders.
Rest for a few moments in this sense of the whole. A body breathing, simply.
[pause 6s]

You've spent these minutes with something very simple. And yet you've made many returns, many small fresh starts. That ability will stay with you, at work and everywhere else. Noticing that you've drifted, and coming back to what matters.
[pause 3s]
Notice how you feel now, compared with the beginning. Not to judge. Just to know. Maybe more space, more clarity, or nothing in particular. Whatever you find is fine.
[pause 2s]
This breath goes with you everywhere. In a queue, at your screen, before you reply to someone. One mindful breath is all it takes to come back here.
Three mindful breaths before opening your inbox, for example. Or before starting a task that needs your full concentration.
[pause 2s]
Now begin to come back. Take a deeper breath that fills your belly and chest.
[pause 5s]
Let sounds come back into your awareness. The sound of the water, and whatever is around it. Notice the temperature of the air on your face, the touch of your clothes, the light behind your eyelids.
Gently move your fingers and toes. Stretch if you'd like.
[pause 3s]
And when it feels right for you, open your eyes. Take a moment to look around before you get up. And let your next move be made with the same attention.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Quick body scan
script: [pause 1.5s]
Three minutes, just for you. Wherever you are, in your chair or standing up, is perfectly fine.
Close your eyes if you'd like, or let your gaze rest low, on the desk or the floor in front of you.
[pause 2s]
Breathe in through your nose...
[pause 4s]
and breathe out a little longer, like a quiet sigh.
[pause 5s]
Let's take a quick tour of the body, the way you'd pat your pockets before heading out.
Start with your feet. Feel them against the floor, the weight in your heels.
Your toes can soften inside your shoes.
[pause 2s]
Your calves, your knees, your thighs. Let them be heavy, simply resting, as if your legs had nothing left to carry.
Now your hips. Feel how your pelvis sits on the chair, the weight settling there, the seat holding you up.
[pause 2s]
Then your lower back. If you're slumped, lift up just a little, without stiffening.
All along your back, let the chair, or your own spine, do the holding. You don't have to hold yourself up alone.
[pause 2s]
Now your belly. Is it pulled in, tight?
[pause 2s]
You can let it go, let it be soft, rounding a little as you breathe in.
Your chest. Notice your breath lifting it, without trying to change anything. Just this movement, rising and falling.
[pause 3s]
Your shoulders. They often creep up without us noticing, especially in front of a screen.
Let them drop half an inch, and then a little more, as if someone had rested warm hands on them.
Your arms grow heavy, from your shoulders down to your elbows, from your elbows down to your wrists.
Your hands rest, your fingers uncurl. There's nothing you need to hold on to right now.
[pause 2s]
Your face. Your forehead smooths out, the space between your eyebrows widens. Your cheeks soften.
Your eyes rest behind your eyelids. And your jaw... are your teeth touching? Let a little space open between them, lips gently closed, tongue at ease.
[pause 3s]
And now your whole body at once, from your feet to the top of your head. One single presence, breathing.
[pause 3s]
Think of the spot that felt tightest a moment ago. Has it shifted at all? If not, that's okay. You noticed it, and that already counts for a lot.
[pause 2s]
Let's take one last breath together. Breathe in slowly through your nose, feeling your whole body...
[pause 4s]
And breathe out through your mouth, long and slow, letting go of whatever is ready to go.
[pause 6s]
Open your eyes if they were closed, or lift your gaze. Wiggle your fingers and toes, and roll your shoulders once.
You can come back to this little tour any time today, even for thirty seconds, between two emails.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Shake off stress
script: [pause 1.5s]
Sometimes, sitting still and breathing calmly just isn't possible. Your body is too wound up, and it needs to move. So let's move.
[pause 1.5s]
Stand up, if you can. Feet hip-width apart, knees soft and slightly bent, arms hanging by your sides.

One rule for the whole session. Stay within what's comfortable. No jumping, no jerky movements, never any pain. If your back or knees are sore, do all of this sitting down, and shake just your arms and shoulders. That works too.
[pause 2s]
Breathe in through your nose...
[pause 3s]
and blow out through your mouth, all the way.
[pause 3s]
Let's start with your hands. Let them hang, wrists loose, and shake them. As if your fingers were wet and there was no towel in sight.
Fingers completely relaxed, flapping about. Go a little faster, or a little slower. Find what feels good.
[pause 2s]
Now let the movement travel up into your wrists, your forearms, then your elbows.
Your whole arms are shaking now, floppy as ropes. In front of you, out to the sides, down low. Change direction whenever you like.
Do your shoulders want to join in?
[pause 2s]
Let them. They can bounce, shrug and drop.
[pause 3s]
Now the legs. Without leaving the floor, start bouncing gently on your heels. They lift just slightly and drop, again and again.
It's a small, springy bounce that comes from the knees. Feel the vibration travel up through your calves, your thighs, into your hips.
[pause 1.5s]
If you like, lift one foot and shake that leg, as if you were shaking sand out of your shoe. Then the other leg. Hold on to a wall or a chair if you need a little balance.
Come back onto both feet and keep bouncing. Let your breath stay free, through your nose or your mouth, however it comes.
[pause 2s]
Now let your whole body join in. Heels bouncing, arms shaking, shoulders moving, belly jiggling too.
Let your head follow along, without throwing it around. Just loose, carried by everything else.
And your jaw... let it hang. Mouth slightly open, cheeks soft and wobbling a little. It might feel a bit silly, and that's perfectly fine.
If a sound wants to come out, let it. A loud breath, a long sigh, a grunt, a laugh. Nobody's grading you.
[pause 1.5s]
Your body has built up momentum to face a danger that isn't coming. You're simply giving it a way to spend that energy.
Keep going at your own pace. Shake out whatever needs shaking. Your upper back, your hips, your hands again, wherever things feel stuck.
[pause 3s]
A few more seconds. Put a little more energy into it, if that feels good. One last burst, as if you were shaking off the last crumbs of the day.
[pause 2s]
And now, start to slow down. No sudden stop. The movement gets smaller, slower.
Your arms swing gently. Your heels barely bounce. Like a merry-go-round coming to the end of its ride.
Your shoulders settle, your knees soften, your hands slow down little by little. Smaller still. Just a slight tremble in your hands, in your knees.
And then... still.
[pause 3s]
Stay standing, knees still a little bent, arms hanging. Close your eyes if you feel steady, otherwise rest your gaze on the floor in front of you.
What's happening in your hands right now?
[pause 2s]
Maybe a tingling, a buzzing, a sense of aliveness under the skin.
Maybe warmth in your arms, in your face. Your heart beating a little faster, and starting to slow. You might feel it in your chest, or in your fingertips.
There's nothing to do with these sensations. Just watch them, the way you'd watch bubbles rising to the surface.
[pause 3s]
Feel your feet flat on the floor. Your weight sinking into the ground, spread between your heels and the balls of your feet.
Let your breath settle. No need to control it. Just notice how it finds its own way back toward a calmer rhythm.
[pause 2s]
Breathe in through your nose...
[pause 3s]
and let the breath out last a little longer, like a wave drawing back from the shore.
[pause 5s]
Once more. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and out, slowly.
[pause 5s]
Notice the contrast between the commotion a moment ago and this calm. Your body found it all by itself, once that energy had somewhere to go.
[pause 2s]
Open your eyes if they were closed. Take a few steps, look around you.
Next time you feel wired, remember this. You don't have to sit still to calm down. You can shake first, and then stop.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Belly breathing
script: [pause 1.5s]
When we're stressed, the breath tends to climb. It settles high in the chest, quick and shallow, the shoulders lifting with every inhale.
Babies breathe with their bellies without even thinking about it. So you already know how to breathe this way. We're simply going to find it again, one step at a time.
[pause 1.5s]
Lie down on your back, knees bent if that's more comfortable. Or sit upright, with your feet flat on the floor. Either way, loosen your belt or anything tight around your waist.
Close your eyes, or let your gaze rest on a fixed point.
[pause 3s]
Now place one hand flat on your upper chest, just below your collarbones. And the other hand on your belly, around your navel.
Your hands are going to be your witnesses. They don't push. They listen.
For now, don't change anything about your breathing. Let it be exactly as it is.
[pause 2s]
Watch your two hands. Which one moves more as you breathe in? The top one, on your chest? The bottom one, on your belly? Or both, a little?
[pause 3s]
There's no wrong answer. If it's mostly your chest moving, that's very common. It's often the sign of a busy day, or of a long habit.
Take a few more breaths to really feel what's happening under each hand.
[pause 4s]
Now let's invite the belly to take part. Imagine a soft balloon just behind your navel.
On your next breath in, through your nose, let that balloon gently fill. Your lower hand rises. Your upper hand stays almost still.
This isn't an effort from your stomach muscles. It's closer to the opposite. You release your belly and let it round out to make room for the air.
Beneath your lungs sits a large, dome shaped muscle, the diaphragm. As it moves down, it gently nudges your belly forward. That's all that's happening.
[pause 1.5s]
Try again. Breathe in, and feel your lower hand rise, like a small boat lifted by a gentle wave.
[pause 3s]
Now the out breath. This part, you don't have to do. Let the air flow out through your nose, or through slightly parted lips.
Your belly sinks back by itself, like a balloon deflating without being squeezed. Your lower hand gently lowers.
[pause 4s]
Breathe in, and the belly fills...
[pause 3s]
breathe out, and it settles back, with no help.
[pause 4s]
If your upper hand is still moving a lot, that's fine. It comes with practice. You can also let your shoulders get really heavy, as if they were melting into the floor or the back of the chair.
And if you feel dizzy or uncomfortable at any point, just go back to your natural breathing. The goal isn't to breathe more, or harder.
[pause 2s]
Now let's slow things down a little. Not by taking in more air, but by taking more time.
The in breath becomes slow and smooth. And the out breath can stretch out a bit longer still, like a peaceful sigh.
Roughly three or four seconds in, and four to six seconds out. Only if it feels pleasant. Otherwise, keep your own rhythm.
Your belly rises only slightly more than before. You don't need big breaths. A small wave in the right place is better than a big, forced one.
[pause 1.5s]
Let's do a few rounds together. Breathe in through your nose, and let your belly round out under your hand...
[pause 4s]
and breathe out. Your belly settles back, effortlessly, like a sheet drifting down onto a bed.
[pause 6s]
Again. Breathe in. The balloon fills from the bottom up, and your chest stays quiet...
[pause 4s]
and breathe out, slowly. Notice that still moment at the end of the breath, before the next one arrives by itself.
[pause 6s]
Keep going at this pace, following your lower hand. The belly rises... and falls. Nothing else to do.
[pause 6s]
If your mind has wandered off, to a to-do list or a conversation, that's normal. Notice it, and gently bring your attention back under your lower hand.
Feel the warmth of your hand on your belly. The fabric under your fingers. The movement lifting your palm, then letting it sink again.
[pause 3s]
Notice the sides of your waist, too. As you breathe in, they widen a little, like an accordion opening. As you breathe out, they draw back in.
Each out breath can carry away a little of the tension in your belly. The muscles let go, and space opens up for the next breath in.
[pause 3s]
Let your jaw unclench and your shoulders drop. The quieter your upper body, the more easily your breath finds its way down to your belly.
Many people find that this slow, low breathing helps them feel more settled. Just let yourself feel what it's doing for you, today.
[pause 5s]
Now let your hands rest wherever they'd like. By your sides, or on your thighs.
Your belly may keep breathing on its own, or your breath may drift a little higher again. Notice, without correcting.
[pause 3s]
How do you feel, compared to when you started? Slower, heavier, calmer? Or about the same?
[pause 3s]
Every session is practice, and your body is learning even when you don't feel a big difference.
Deepen your breath a little. Move your fingers and your feet. Open your eyes whenever the moment feels right for you.
[pause 2s]
For the rest of your day, here's a simple idea. Three or four times, at a red light, waiting for the train, or after hanging up the phone, place a hand on your belly.
And ask yourself where your breath is, right here, right now. Then let it drop back down, just a little.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Knotted stomach
script: [pause 1.5s]
A ball in the pit of your stomach. A knot that tightens, a belly that clenches before a meeting, an appointment, a difficult conversation.
A lot of people feel stress right here. If that's you today, you're in the right place.
[pause 2s]
Settle into a seat with your back supported, or lie down with your knees bent. Loosen anything tight around your waist, if you can.
Let your eyes close, or let your gaze rest softly downward.
Take an easy breath, and let the out-breath linger a little...
[pause 5s]
First, rub your hands together. Palm against palm, quite quickly, like on a cold winter morning at the bus stop.
Feel the friction, and the warmth building in your palms and fingers.
[pause 3s]
Keep going a little longer... and stop. Hold your hands slightly apart for a moment, and feel that warmth between them, like a small cushion of warm air.
[pause 2s]
Now rest both hands on your belly. One just above your navel, in the soft hollow below your ribs. The other just below. Or wherever feels right.
Feel the warmth of your palms passing through the fabric, reaching your skin.
Your hands aren't trying to fix anything. They're just there, like a friendly hand resting on a shoulder.
[pause 3s]
Take a few natural breaths, without changing anything. Feel how your belly moves under your hands. Maybe a lot, maybe very little. Maybe it feels frozen, as if it were holding its breath.
[pause 3s]
All of this is normal. When we're tense, the belly often closes up to protect itself. It's an old reflex, one that has long helped the body get ready to act.
[pause 1.5s]
Now, with curiosity, go and meet the sensation. As if you were discovering it for the very first time.
Where exactly is it? Higher up, under your ribs? In the middle, around your navel? Lower down?
[pause 2.5s]
How big is it? A marble, a tennis ball, a clenched fist? Does it have clear edges, or is it more spread out, a little blurry?
Is it hard, or more heavy? Warm, or cool? Does it pull, prickle, weigh down, flutter?
Does it stay still, or does it move, pulse, tighten and loosen?
[pause 2s]
You don't need precise words. Just observe it the way you'd watch a cloud. Its shape, its color, its outline.
[pause 3s]

And what's around it? Look for a place in your belly, or in your back, that feels neutral, or even comfortable. There's often one, right next door. Notice that the unpleasant sensation doesn't take up all the room.
Maybe your lower back, resting against the chair or the floor. Maybe your hips, or the warmth of your hands themselves. Let your attention rest there for a moment...
[pause 3s]
then gently come back to the knot.
If your attention drifts toward what's worrying you, toward the scenarios and the what ifs, that's normal. Come back to the sensation itself, in your body, right now.
[pause 2s]
And now, breathe as if your breath could wrap itself around this sensation.
As you breathe in, imagine the air traveling down to it and surrounding it, gently, on every side. Without pushing it, without chasing it away.
As you breathe out, simply leave it there, held in a little more space.
Let's try it. Breathe in... the air flows down and wraps around it.
[pause 3s]
Breathe out... it leaves a little room around it.
[pause 5s]
Once more. Breathe in slowly... like a soft cloth settling all around it.
[pause 3s]
Breathe out... and the sensation floats in a little more space.
[pause 5s]
Keep going like this, at your own pace. If you feel any discomfort or dizziness, just return to your natural breath.
Let your belly swell just slightly under your hands, just enough to feel it taking part. Nothing more.
[pause 3s]
Now bring your attention to the muscles of your belly. The ones that tighten without your say-so, like an inner belt.
With each out-breath, invite those muscles to loosen by one notch. Not all at once. Just one notch.
Breathe out... the belly softens a little.
[pause 4s]
Breathe out again... the belt loosens a tiny bit more.
[pause 4s]
Imagine the warmth of your hands slowly melting into those muscles, like butter on warm toast.
The upper belly, just below your breastbone, can soften. The sides, at your waist, can widen. The lower belly can become softer, heavier.
And behind you, your lower back can let go too. Your belly and your back form a single cylinder. When one softens, the other often follows.
If the sensation is still there, that's completely fine. We're not trying to make it disappear. We're making room for it.
[pause 3s]
And now, a phrase to offer it, silently. You can repeat it with me, or just listen.
You're allowed to be here.
[pause 3s]
This ball, this knot, is your body trying to protect you, in its own way. It's reacting to something that matters to you.
You're allowed to be here. I'm here too, with you.
[pause 3s]
What happens when you stop fighting it? Maybe it shifts a little, softens, moves somewhere else. Maybe not. Both are normal.
[pause 3s]
Stay a few more breaths like this, warm hands on your belly, breath coming and going beneath them.
Nothing to achieve. Just being here, with your belly, with kindness. The way you'd sit beside a worried friend, without trying to talk them out of anything.
[pause 6s]
Before we finish, let your hands stay where they are a moment longer. Don't take them away just yet.
Feel the contact, the light weight of your palms, the warmth that lingers. Like a thank-you to your body, which is doing its best.
Notice how your belly feels now. Maybe a little softer, calmer. Or not yet. You've offered it a moment of attention, and that already means a lot.
[pause 2s]
And if stomach pain is strong, frequent, or unusual for you, talk to a doctor. This practice isn't a substitute for medical advice.
[pause 1.5s]
When the moment feels right, let your hands slide gently to your sides. Take a slightly fuller breath. Move your fingers, your shoulders.
Open your eyes, and come back to the room around you.
[pause 2s]
Later today, if the knot comes back, you know what to do. Rub your hands together, rest them on your belly, and tell it, silently, that it's allowed to be here.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Release your back
script: [pause 1.5s]
Hours in front of a screen, on the commute, on the sofa... Your back carries all of it, without ever complaining out loud. For the next few minutes, the floor is going to do the carrying instead.
[pause 2s]
For this practice, lie on your back on a mat, a folded blanket, or a rug. A firm floor works better than a soft bed.
Bend your knees and place your feet flat on the floor, about hip-width apart, toes pointing forward.
If your head tips back and your chin lifts toward the ceiling, slide a book or two under your head, so the back of your neck stays long.
Rest your hands on your belly, or let your arms lie on the floor slightly away from your body, palms however you like.
[pause 2s]

One note before we begin. This isn't a treatment session. If you have back pain, an injury, or any doubts, adapt the position, and feel free to ask a health professional for advice. And if lying down isn't possible for you, you can follow along sitting, with your back against a chair.
[pause 3s]
Let your eyes close, or simply look at the ceiling with a soft gaze.
Take a slightly fuller breath...
[pause 3s]
And as you breathe out, let a sigh escape, like when you finally set your bags down.
[pause 4s]
This position is called constructive rest. Bending your knees lets your lower back settle more easily. There's nothing to hold.
If your knees want to fall out to the sides, let them lean against each other, or bring your feet a little closer together.
Take your time finding the spot where your legs almost balance on their own. Your thighs can let go, your hips can soften. Your legs aren't doing any work at all.
[pause 4s]
Now bring your attention to the back of your body. Start by finding the points of contact, the places where your back actually touches the floor.
The back of your head, resting on the floor or the book. Both shoulder blades. Maybe the middle of your back. Your pelvis. The soles of your feet.
[pause 3s]
Notice too the places that don't touch. Often the hollow of your neck, or the curve of your lower back. There's nothing to fix. These curves are natural.

Just feel the contrast between what's resting and what's floating. The floor, maybe a little cool under your hands. The fabric of your clothes against your skin. The pressure, stronger in some places, lighter in others.
[pause 4s]
Now come all the way down to the base of your spine, to the sacrum. That's the flat, triangle-shaped bone at the back of your pelvis, just above your tailbone.
Feel how it rests on the floor. Imagine it getting heavy. A little heavier with every out-breath, like a warm stone resting in the sand.
[pause 4s]
You don't need to press. Just let the weight do its work. Maybe you can feel a slight warmth there, where your pelvis meets the floor.
[pause 3s]
And as your sacrum grows heavier, bring your attention to your lower back, around the kidneys.
Imagine this area widening. Spreading out to the right and to the left, like dough left to rest.
[pause 3s]

The muscles on either side of your spine can loosen, softening toward the floor. Maybe the curve of your lower back eases a little closer to the mat, without you pushing it. Or maybe not. Either is fine.
If you feel stiffness or discomfort, don't fight it. Breathe around it, and let it be there.
[pause 4s]
Now let's travel up the spine, one vertebra at a time, the way you'd climb a staircase very slowly.

The lumbar vertebrae, at waist level. Five broad, sturdy vertebrae that carry much of your weight all day long. Let your attention rest on each one in turn, without worrying about counting them exactly.
[pause 3s]
Then the middle of your back, behind your stomach. This is where your ribs attach to your spine. Maybe you can feel their slight movement with every breath.
[pause 3s]
Keep climbing, vertebra by vertebra, up to the space between your shoulder blades. Each vertebra can settle onto the floor, one after another, like pearls on a necklace being laid on a table.
Is there a part of your spine that feels stiffer, or more present?
[pause 3s]
Rest your attention there a little longer. Imagine that with every out-breath, a tiny bit of space opens between those vertebrae.
[pause 4s]
Then the base of your neck. Your neck, long, resting on its support. And the back of your skull, heavy, held.
Your head weighs about as much as a bowling ball. For once, you don't have to hold it up.
[pause 4s]
Now come to your shoulder blades, those two large flat bones at the top of your back.
Imagine them spreading out across the floor. Sliding gently away from each other, outward, opening up space between them.
[pause 3s]
Your upper back widens. Your shoulders move away from your ears. Your arms grow heavy, almost draping from your shoulders down to the floor.
Feel your whole upper back as one wide surface, spread out and held by the floor.
[pause 4s]
Now let's breathe into the back. You're used to feeling the breath at the front, in the chest or belly. But your lungs also fill the back of your ribcage.
On your next breath in, see if you can feel your back against the floor. Maybe it presses down just a touch more. Maybe your ribs spread slightly backward and out to the sides.
As you breathe out, your back settles again, a little heavier.
[pause 4s]
Breathe in, and feel your back widen against the floor...
[pause 4s]
Breathe out, and let it give in completely.
[pause 6s]
Imagine your breath reaching into your lower back too, massaging it from the inside, ever so gently, with every breath.
Breathe in... your lower back opens a little, like a sponge filling with water.
[pause 4s]
Breathe out... it rests, wider, heavier.
[pause 6s]
If your mind slips off toward your to-do list, that's normal. Come back to the contact with the floor. It's always there.
Stay like this for a few breaths, not looking for anything. The floor is holding you. You don't have to hold yourself up anymore.
[pause 10s]
Now take a moment to feel your back as a whole. From your sacrum to the back of your head. Wide, long, resting.
Compare it with the start of the session. Is your back touching the floor in new places? Does it feel wider, heavier, calmer?
[pause 3s]
Just notice, without expecting anything.
[pause 4s]
It's time to come back, taking care of your back as you do. Start by moving your fingers and toes. Breathe a little more deeply.
[pause 2s]
Let your knees fall gently together to the right, or to whichever side suits you. And roll your whole body onto that side, all in one piece, like a log.
Stay lying on your side for a moment, your head resting on your arm. Take a breath or two here.
[pause 4s]
Then use your hands to push yourself up, pressing into the floor. Your head comes up last, without any rush.
[pause 3s]
Once you're sitting, pause for a moment. Feel your back lengthening upward, and see whether it keeps some of that width.
[pause 2s]
Throughout your day, every time you get up from your chair, you can recall this feeling. A wide, supported back that doesn't have to hold everything up on its own.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: After a mistake
script: [pause 1.5s]
Something went wrong. You forgot something, sent an email too fast, said something that hurt, missed an appointment. And ever since, it's been going round and round in your head.
[pause 1.5s]
Before anything else, notice this. If you're upset with yourself, it's because it matters to you. People, good work, the trust others place in you. This discomfort comes from something precious.
Over these six minutes, we won't erase what happened. Instead, you'll look at it clearly, without beating yourself up, and see what you can do with it.
[pause 2s]
Settle in. Place your feet flat on the floor, and let your hands rest on your thighs.
Breathe in gently through your nose...
[pause 4s]
and out through your mouth, a little longer.
[pause 5s]
Once more, at your own pace. Let the out breath carry away some of the tension in your shoulders.
[pause 6s]
And a third breath, just for you. There's nothing to fix during this one.
[pause 6s]
Feel your feet in contact with the floor. It's solid. Whatever happened, the ground is still there beneath you.
[pause 2s]
Now let the mistake come back to mind. Not replaying it on a loop. Just placing it in front of you, like a photo on a table.
And notice what it does in your body. Shame and guilt often have a precise address. Heat rising in your face. A hollow feeling in your stomach. Shoulders curling forward, as if you wanted to hide.
Where is it, for you?
[pause 2.5s]
You can simply name what you find. Heat. Tightness. Heaviness. Without trying to push it away.
[pause 3s]
Now listen to what you've been telling yourself since the mistake. Maybe, I'm useless. I'm hopeless. I always ruin everything.
Look closely at the difference between two sentences. The first is, I made a mistake. The second is, I am a mistake.
The first is about an action. One specific moment, which can be understood and repaired. The second is about the whole of you, and it leaves no way out.
[pause 1.5s]
Guilt says, what I did wasn't right. It moves you to make amends. Shame says, I'm worthless. It makes you want to hide, or freeze.
[pause 1.5s]
If you hear that second sentence in your head, try rephrasing it. Bring it back to its true size. I forgot that file. I spoke too harshly. I made a mistake, on that day, in those circumstances.
Notice what changes in your body when the sentence shrinks back to its real size. Often, your chest breathes a little easier.
[pause 3s]
Now imagine a friend who knows you well and cares about you, no matter what. They've heard the whole story. They sit down beside you.
They don't tell you it's nothing. They don't pretend. But they speak to you warmly.

Maybe they say, you were running on no sleep that day, you had a thousand things on your mind. Or, everyone gets things wrong, it doesn't take anything away from who you are. Or, I can see you're upset with yourself, and that shows how much this matters to you.
[pause 2s]
Listen to what they would say, in their own words. And let those words actually reach you.
Let them land the way a warm hand would on your shoulder. You don't have to agree with every word. Just let yourself hear them.
[pause 5s]
Notice if something loosens a little. Your shoulders, your belly, your breathing. Even a slight shift counts.
And notice that you can hold two things at once. Regret for what happened, and kindness toward the person who did it. One doesn't cancel out the other.
[pause 3s]
Now that you're a bit calmer, you can look at the situation with clearer eyes. What can be repaired?
[pause 2.5s]

Sometimes it's a sincere apology. Sometimes a message to correct some information, a phone call, an offer to catch up on what was delayed. And sometimes nothing can be repaired, and the only possible action is to do things differently next time.
Choose one single action. Small, concrete, doable. Picture yourself doing it. The time of day, the first words you'll say or write.
If it helps, decide when you'll do it. Today, tomorrow morning, right after lunch. Writing it down can help, too.
[pause 3s]
Then ask yourself, gently, what is this mistake teaching me? Maybe that you need to write important things down. To say no more often. To slow down before replying when you're running on empty.
One lesson, just one, is enough. You don't need to put yourself on trial.
Mistakes are how every human being learns. Including the people you admire most.
[pause 2s]
If you like, place a hand on your heart or your arm, and tell yourself, I made a mistake, and I still deserve kindness. Or, in your own words, I'm learning, like everyone else.
[pause 4s]
If strong emotions come up during this practice, that's normal. You can open your eyes, come back to your feet on the floor, or take a break. There's no rush.
Stay for a few more breaths with whatever you're feeling now. Without forcing yourself to feel better. Just being here, on your own side.
[pause 6s]
You've acknowledged the mistake. You know what you can repair. You've taken something from it. Whatever's left, you can leave behind.
[pause 2s]
Feel your back again, your hands, the sounds in the room. Have a little stretch if you feel like it.
And when the moment is right for you, open your eyes.
[pause 2s]
You're allowed to turn the page. Not because it didn't matter, but because you've done what needed doing.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Someone who matters
script: [pause 1.5s]
Hello. This practice is a little different from the others. There's no problem to solve here, and no tension to undo. You're simply going to think about someone who matters to you.
[pause 2s]
When stress builds up, we tend to close in on ourselves. Remembering the connections that hold us up is a very simple way to feel supported, even when things are hard.
[pause 2s]
Settle in comfortably, with your back supported. Your eyes can close, or rest softly on a point in front of you.
Breathe in through your nose, and let your belly swell a little...
[pause 4s]
And breathe out slowly, as if you were blowing across a cup of hot tea.
[pause 5s]
Once more. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and let it go.
[pause 5s]
Now let your breathing find its own rhythm. You don't need to guide it anymore. Just feel the air coming in, cool, and going out, a little warmer.
Notice where your body is resting, too. Your weight on the seat, your hands in your lap. There's nothing to get right here. Only a memory to let in.
[pause 2s]
Bring to mind someone who helped you at some point, in one way or another. Not necessarily the person closest to you. Maybe a grandmother, a childhood friend, a colleague, a teacher, a neighbor.
Don't look for the perfect person. Take the first one who comes, the one who brings a small smile inside.
If several faces appear, choose just one for today. The others can come back another time.
[pause 2s]
And if no one comes right away, that's fine. You can think of someone who did you a simple kindness. A stranger who helped with a heavy suitcase, a pharmacist who took the time to listen.
[pause 3s]
Now try to see this person in detail. Their face. The color of their eyes. The shape of their smile, or that little crease between their eyebrows when they're thinking.
What are they wearing, in your memory? Where are they?
[pause 2s]
Maybe in a kitchen, on a park bench, behind a desk, on the other end of the phone.
And their voice. The sound of it, the way they say your name. A phrase they often use.
[pause 2s]
Let this presence settle near you, as if they had just sat down in the room. Notice what that already changes, simply imagining them here.
[pause 3s]
Now remember one particular moment when this person really mattered. One specific day.

Maybe they listened when things weren't okay. Maybe they believed in you before you believed in yourself. Maybe they did something quiet and kind. Dropped off some soup, gave you a ride, sent a message at exactly the right time.
[pause 2s]
Bring that moment back as concretely as you can. Where were you? What time of day was it? What did they say, or do?
[pause 3s]
And what did you feel, in that moment? Relief, maybe. Surprise. The feeling of mattering to someone.
[pause 2s]

You can also ask yourself what this person passed on to you. A way of laughing at small troubles. Pride in doing things well. The idea that you were allowed to make mistakes. Perhaps even today, without realizing it, you carry a little of them in the way you are.
[pause 4s]
Now bring your attention to your chest. Is there something there? A warmth, a slight opening, a kind of fullness?
[pause 3s]
Gratitude is often felt in the upper body. Sometimes around the heart, sometimes in the throat, sometimes just as a smile at the corner of your mouth.
If you feel something, let it take up a little more room. Like a light being turned up slowly on a dimmer switch.
[pause 2s]
And if you don't feel anything in particular, that's completely fine. Thinking of them with care is already a lot. The feeling may come another time.

Sometimes an unexpected emotion rises, too. Nostalgia, or sadness, if this person is far away, or no longer here. That's normal. Meet it gently, and if it's too much, come back to your breath or open your eyes.
[pause 3s]
Now, silently, say thank you to them. A real thank you, in your own words.
You might say what you've never said out loud. Thank you for being there that day. Thank you for your patience. Thank you for believing in me.
[pause 3s]
If the words don't come, you can simply send them a look, a nod, the warmth you're feeling. They would understand.
Imagine they can hear you. See their face as they receive your words. Maybe they smile, or look surprised, a little moved.
[pause 2s]
If you like, rest a hand on your chest as you thank them. As if to keep this moment close.
[pause 4s]
Stay with this warmth for a few more breaths. Notice how simply thinking about someone can change the atmosphere inside you.
[pause 4s]
You're part of a web of connections. People have supported you. And you too, without always knowing it, have mattered to others.
Research suggests that regularly bringing this kind of gratitude to mind can help us feel more connected to others. And connection is one of our best buffers against stress.
[pause 2s]
Gently, let the image fade. Come back to your breath, to your body resting here, to the sounds around you.
Move your hands and feet a little. And when the moment feels right, open your eyes.
[pause 2s]
One last idea to take with you. What if you told them today? A message of a few words is enough. You might be surprised by the difference it makes, on both sides.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: For those who care for others
script: [pause 1.5s]
You spend a large part of your days looking after other people. A child who wakes up in the night, an aging parent, a partner who's unwell, patients, pupils. These few minutes are for you.
[pause 2s]

Caring for others wears you down. Not because you're not good enough. Simply because giving, day after day, takes an enormous amount of energy. Feeling that strain isn't a weakness. It's a sign of how much you give.
If you've managed to find a few minutes on your own, good. And if you're listening in a waiting room, or with a child playing next to you, that's fine too. Work with what's possible.
[pause 2s]
Make yourself as comfortable as you can. Let your back lean into something. For once, you're the one being held.
Take a breath that's a little fuller than usual...
[pause 3s]
and let it out slowly, without holding anything back.
[pause 4s]
Once more. And as you breathe out, let your shoulders drop a little.
[pause 4s]
Let the out-breath be a little longer than the in-breath, like a quiet sigh of relief.
[pause 3s]
Bring your attention to your hands. These hands that carry, wash, cook, reassure. For now, they have nothing to do. Let them rest, open or lying on your thighs.
Your breath takes care of you too, without you having to think about it. In and out, day and night. Let it do its work for a few moments.
[pause 3s]
Now notice the tiredness that's here. Where do you feel it most?
[pause 2s]
Maybe a heaviness in your legs, stinging eyelids, tension between your shoulder blades, or a fog in your head.
You might place a hand where the tiredness is strongest, the way you would for someone else.
You don't have to fight it, or hide it. Here, nobody needs you to be on top form. You can simply tell yourself... yes, I'm exhausted, and that makes sense after everything I carry.
[pause 2s]

If other emotions come along with the tiredness, irritation, sadness, sometimes even resentment toward the person you care for, let them be here too. They aren't bad feelings. They're human feelings, telling you that your resources have limits.
Let them simply be here for a few breaths, without sorting them. You can tell yourself... this is heavy right now. And that's understandable.
[pause 3s]
Now let's try a very simple practice with the breath. It rests on one idea. Your compassion needs to flow in both directions. Toward the other person, and toward you.
To begin, focus only on the in-breath. With each breath in, imagine you're taking in some kindness for yourself. A warmth, a soft light, or just the word rest. Whatever you need, right here.
Breathe in for you.
[pause 4s]
And again. Feel that kindness spreading through your chest, your belly, all the way into your tired arms.
[pause 4s]
You're allowed to receive. Even if you're not used to it. Even if a small voice tells you others need it more than you do.
[pause 2s]
Now bring to mind the person you care for. Or several people, if that's your situation. See their face, as it is today.
And add the out-breath. As you breathe in, you take in kindness for yourself. As you breathe out, you send kindness toward them.
One for me, one for you.
[pause 3s]
You don't need to picture anything specific. The intention is enough. You can imagine the air that surrounds you both. The same room, the same air, shared.
If thinking of this person stirs up worry, come back first to your in-breath, for you. Your own steadiness comes first.
Breathe in for you. Breathe out for them.
[pause 5s]

You can adjust the balance depending on what you feel. If your reserves are especially low, keep several breaths for yourself before sending one their way. If it's worry for them that's strongest right now, direct more of your breath toward them.
There's no right ratio. Let your breathing find its own balance, like a tide coming in and going out.

Carry on like this for a few breaths. Breathing in, kindness for me. Breathing out, kindness for you. If your mind drifts to your to-do list, that's normal. Bring it back, without blame, to the next breath.
[pause 5s]
Here's a phrase that may help ease the guilt of never doing enough. Listen to it, and repeat it silently if it speaks to you.
I'm doing my best. I can't control everything.
[pause 2s]
Their suffering isn't entirely in my hands. My love, yes. My presence, yes. But not everything else.
[pause 2s]
This is sometimes called finding the right distance. Staying close and attentive, without carrying on your shoulders what isn't yours to carry.
You can care deeply, and still put some things down.
Let these words settle. What do they do in your body?
[pause 2s]
Maybe relief, maybe some resistance. Both are normal.
If you prefer, find your own words. I'm already doing a lot. I'm here, and that already counts for so much. I'm not responsible for everything.
If a strong emotion rises, tears perhaps, let it pass through. You can also open your eyes and take a break. There's nothing to get right.
[pause 3s]
Before we finish, think of one small thing you could do for yourself today. Really small, and realistic, given the day ahead of you.
A hot coffee without rushing, for once. A ten minute walk outside. Calling a friend. Asking someone to take over one task. Going to bed a little earlier.
Choose one, and picture it already done. It isn't a luxury. It's what allows you to keep on giving.
If you like, place a hand on your heart as you choose. Like a small promise to yourself, with no pressure. And if the day has other plans, you can try again tomorrow.
[pause 3s]
Stay a moment longer with your breath, without guiding it at all. Notice how you feel now, without expecting a miracle.
[pause 3s]
Gently bring your attention back to the room. The sounds, the light, your body resting on the seat.
Move your neck a little, your shoulders. And when the moment is right, open your eyes.
Remember this today. Taking care of yourself is part of your role. You can't pour from an empty cup.
And tonight, if you think of it, take a few breaths like this once more. One for me, one for you.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Close the day gently
script: [pause 1.5s]
Here you are, in bed. The day is behind you, or very nearly.
If the light is still on, you can switch it off now, or dim it to its softest.
[pause 2s]
Settle in the way you like to fall asleep. On your back, on your side, the duvet pulled up as far as you like.
Feel the weight of your head in the pillow. The mattress under your back, under your hips, under your heels.
[pause 2s]
For a few minutes, let's close this day together. The way you close a book, slipping a bookmark between the pages.
Not to judge it. Not to replay every move. Just to put it away before you sleep.
There's nothing to get right here. If you fall asleep along the way, that's perfect too.
[pause 2s]
Begin with a few slow breaths. Breathe in through your nose, unhurried, and feel the air gently filling your chest, then your belly...
[pause 4s]
and let it flow out, even more slowly. Like a long sigh at the end of the day.
[pause 6s]
Once more. Cool air coming in...
[pause 3s]
warm air going out.
[pause 5s]
One last time. And as you breathe out, let your shoulders sink back into the pillow.
[pause 5s]
Then let your breath find its own rhythm again. You don't need to look after it anymore.
[pause 4s]
Now you're going to rewind your day. Like a film playing backwards, a little faster than usual.
There's no need to stop on every scene. The images roll by, and you watch them pass.
If your mind wants to linger somewhere, to analyse or comment, that's fine. You notice, and you let the film roll on.
You're not the judge of this day. Just the audience, sunk into a soft seat at the back of the cinema.
[pause 2s]
Start with right now. You, in this bed.
Just before that, brushing your teeth. The bathroom light. Warm water running over your hands.
[pause 1.5s]
Before that, the evening. Dinner, maybe. A screen, a conversation, the clatter of dishes.
Coming home. The key in the lock. The bag dropped on the floor. Maybe kicking off your shoes, at last.
[pause 1.5s]
Late afternoon. The sky through the window, the light shifting.
The afternoon. Faces, voices, tasks. Some done, some not.
Lunch. What you ate, who you were with, or whether you were alone.
[pause 1.5s]
The morning. The commute. The first coffee. The first few minutes after waking.
And right at the start, waking itself. You, in this same bed, this morning.
[pause 2s]
The loop is closed. A whole day, from this morning all the way back to this pillow.
[pause 4s]
Maybe one scene in that film caught your eye. A hard moment.
Words that stung. Something that went wrong. Tiredness. A worry that wouldn't let go.
You don't need to live it again. You can simply acknowledge it. That was hard today.
[pause 2s]
Has that memory left a trace somewhere in your body? A weight on your chest, a tight throat, a knot in your stomach.
[pause 3s]
Rest a hand there, if you'd like. Just a warm hand, not trying to fix anything.
Feel the warmth of your palm seeping gently through the fabric. Let your breath move slowly beneath your hand.
[pause 3s]
You're allowed to find it hard. And you got through it. You're here, warm, tonight.
[pause 1.5s]
Now imagine picking up that moment and placing it in a box. A plain cardboard box.
You close the lid. You set it at the foot of the bed, or on a shelf, far from your pillow.
It will still be there tomorrow, if you need to deal with it. But not tonight.
If other difficult moments show up, they can go in the same box. There's room for all of them.
[pause 4s]
And now, the gentlest part.
You're going to look for three good things in this day. Just three.
They don't need to be big. Often the best ones are tiny.
A patch of sunlight on the pavement. A message that made you smile. A song on the radio. The first coffee, nice and hot.
Take your time. Let whatever comes, come, without hunting for the best answer.
[pause 3s]
Here's your first good thing. It doesn't matter what it is.
See it again for a moment. Where were you? What could you see, what could you hear?
[pause 3s]
And notice how it feels, right now, to think back on it. Maybe a little warmth in your chest. The start of a smile.
Savour it, like a square of chocolate you let melt slowly on your tongue.
[pause 2s]
We often walk straight past these small moments. The brain is built to remember what went wrong. So tonight, you show it the rest as well.
[pause 4s]
Now, a second good thing.
Maybe something someone did for you. Or something you did for someone else.
Or simply a moment when you felt at home in yourself, even for a minute.
[pause 2s]
Go over the details. A colour, a smell, the sound of a voice, the temperature of the air.
Keep it close. Let it take up a little room, a few seconds longer than usual.
If a smile comes, let it form. If nothing stirs, that's fine too. Simply thinking back on it already counts.
[pause 3s]
And a third.
If nothing comes, that's alright. The good thing can be this one. You're lying here, warm, taking care of yourself.
That's already a lot.
[pause 2s]
Or maybe something small arrives. A taste, a bit of light, a quiet moment between two tasks. Welcome it.
Rest your attention on it, the way you'd rest your hand on a warm mug, just to feel the heat.
[pause 3s]
Your three good things are here, resting gently beside you, like three small lights.
There's no need to hold on to them. They've already changed the colour of this day, just a little.
[pause 3s]
Before you close the book, one last gesture.
Say thank you. To yourself, quite simply.
Thank you for getting through today. Thank you for what you did, and even for what you tried.
You can say it in your own words, silently. Softly, the way you'd say it to a tired friend.
[pause 2s]
Thank you to your legs, for carrying you all day. Thank you to your hands, for all they did. Thank you to your mind, which thought so hard, and can finally rest.
You did your best with what you had today. And tonight, that's enough.
[pause 2s]
If your nights stay difficult week after week, do talk to a health professional about it.
[pause 4s]
Now the page is turned.
Your body can grow heavy. First your feet, sinking into the mattress.
Then your calves. Your knees. Your thighs, heavy and warm under the duvet.
[pause 3s]
Your hips settle. Your lower back spreads out. Your belly rises and falls, all on its own.
Your shoulders sink. Your arms slide down along your sides. Your hands are loose, open, soft.
[pause 3s]
The back of your neck lets go. Your jaw unclenches. Your forehead smooths out.
Your eyelids are heavy, so very heavy.
[pause 3s]
Your breath slows, without any help from you.
In... and out... like a very slow wave on the shore.
[pause 5s]
The warmth of the duvet. The quiet of the room.
[pause 3s]
Nothing left to do. Nothing left to tidy away.
[pause 4s]
You can drift, very gently, toward sleep.
[pause 5s]
The day is put away...
[pause 3s]
and the night begins.
[pause 10s]

sessions.title: Count down to sleep
script: [pause 1.5s]
Tonight, we're going to count. Not sheep. Breaths.
From fifty down to one, one number on each out-breath.
It's a very simple task, almost boring. And that's exactly what a mind needs when it still wants to work.
We give it a small job. Enough to keep it busy. Not enough to wake it up.
A bit like handing a rattle to a child who isn't ready to sleep yet. They hold it, they look at it, and without noticing, their eyes begin to close.
[pause 2s]
Before we start, settle in for the night.
Lie down in the position you usually fall asleep in. Pull the duvet up to wherever you like it. Find the hollow in the pillow, the one that already knows the shape of your head.
Let your arms rest wherever they're comfortable. If anything bothers you, a crease in the sheet, a strand of hair, a leg at an awkward angle, take a moment to sort it out now.
After that, you won't need to move. The bed will take care of the rest.
[pause 4s]
There's one rule, just one. If you lose count, it doesn't matter at all.
If you can't remember whether you were on thirty-two or twenty-eight, pick whichever number you like and carry on from there.
If your breath doesn't line up with my voice, that doesn't matter either. Your breath is right. Follow it, and let my voice trail along behind, like a quiet sound in the background.
And if you fall asleep before the end, that's perfect. Few people make it all the way down.
It isn't a contest. Nobody's checking. There's no right way to count, only yours.
[pause 2s]
To begin, three breaths, a little slower than usual.
Breathe in gently through your nose, feeling the cool air coming in...
[pause 3s]
and let the air flow out for a long time, warm now, through your nose or your mouth.
[pause 6s]
Again. Breathe in, feeling your belly rise under the duvet...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out, feeling it fall, very softly, like a balloon slowly emptying.
[pause 6s]
One last time. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out, letting the full weight of your body drop into the mattress.
[pause 6s]
Now let your breath return to its natural rhythm. Stop steering it. It knows what to do. It does this every night without you.
On each out-breath, I'll say a number. You can repeat it in your head with me, like an echo.
And between the numbers, I'll invite you to let go of one small part of your body.
Here we go.
[pause 3s]
Fifty. The air leaves, and your shoulders drop a little, away from your ears.
[pause 3s]
Forty-nine. Your forehead smooths out, like a sheet pressed flat by hand. The space between your eyebrows grows wider.
[pause 3s]
Forty-eight. Your jaw loosens. Your teeth part. Your tongue rests, soft and heavy, at the bottom of your mouth.
[pause 3s]
Forty-seven. Your hands open, very gently, fingers slightly apart. There's nothing left for them to hold.
[pause 3s]
Forty-six. The back of your neck settles into the pillow, and the pillow takes the whole weight of your head.
[pause 3s]
Forty-five. Your chest softens. It doesn't need to hold itself up anymore. It barely rises at all.
[pause 3s]
