Forty-four. Your belly is soft. It rises and falls by itself, like a slow wave rolling up the sand.
[pause 3s]
Forty-three. Your back spreads out on the mattress, one vertebra at a time, from the top all the way down.
[pause 3s]
Forty-two. Your hips sink a little deeper. Your thighs grow heavy, warm and still.
[pause 3s]
Forty-one. Your calves, your ankles, your feet let go, down at the bottom of the bed. Even your toes are resting now.
[pause 3s]
Forty. Your whole body is resting. From head to toe, there's nothing left to carry.
[pause 5s]
Now we'll leave a little more space.
I'll only say every other number. The one in between, you count on your own, on the next out-breath.
Meanwhile, my voice will stay here, very low, telling you gentle things. You can listen to it, or let it drift past.
No need to be precise. If you skip a number, or count the same one twice, let it be. The numbers are there to carry you, not to keep an eye on you.
[pause 3s]
Thirty-nine.
[pause 5s]
On the next breath, you'll count thirty-eight on your own. Or maybe you won't. It makes no difference at all.
[pause 4s]
Thirty-seven. Imagine each number is a step, and you're walking down a staircase covered in thick, soft carpet.
Your feet make no sound. The handrail is smooth and warm under your hand. You go down without hurrying, one step for each breath.
[pause 5s]
Thirty-five. With each step it gets a little darker, a little softer, a little warmer.
As if you were heading down to a room where someone has already switched on a small lamp and drawn the curtains. The bed is made. The sheets are cool and clean.
[pause 5s]
Thirty-three. Your body is as heavy as a sack of sand set down on the floor. Once it's down, it doesn't move. It simply takes the shape of whatever is beneath it.
[pause 5s]
Thirty-one. Your head sinks into the pillow, as if into fresh snow. Silent. Soft. All around you, the world goes quiet.
[pause 5s]
Twenty-nine. If thoughts pass by, let them pass. They can make noise in the distance, like a street behind a closed window. You only have one number to hold, nothing more.
[pause 5s]
Twenty-seven. Your eyelids are heavy. They rest like two little curtains drawn for the night. Behind them, everything is dark and gentle.
[pause 5s]
Twenty-five.
[pause 4s]
Halfway. Notice how much slower your breath is than at the start. You did nothing to make that happen. It slowed down by itself, number by number.
[pause 4s]
From here, you carry on by yourself.
My voice will only give you a few landmarks now and then. In between, count at your own pace, each time the air leaves.
If you drift off track, pick up anywhere. The number doesn't matter. What matters is the breath going down, and you going down with it.
[pause 4s]
As you count, imagine a smooth stone sinking slowly to the bottom of a lake. It drifts down, silently, through calm, warm water.
It has nothing to do to sink. It simply lets itself be carried downward, further and further from the surface.
Up there are the day, the noise, the screens. Down here, there's only light slowly fading, layer after layer, from pale blue to deep blue.
[pause 4s]
Your body is like that stone. Heavy, smooth, still.
You sink with each breath, a little deeper into the mattress.
At the bottom of the lake there's fine sand, and the stone settles into it without a sound. It has arrived. It can stay there all night long.
[pause 6s]
Twenty, more or less. Or somewhere else. It doesn't matter.
[pause 3s]
Your arms are so heavy you could forget where they are. They feel warm, as if they were resting in a patch of sunlight.
Your legs too. They melt into the sheets, as if they were part of the bed.
And that heaviness rises slowly, from your feet to your knees, from your knees to your belly, from your belly to your chest. A quiet warmth, taking all the time it needs.
[pause 5s]
Now picture a tall building in the evening. Every window is lit.
And one by one, floor by floor, the lights go out. Gently. In no particular order.
Each window that goes dark is a thought going to bed.
[pause 3s]
The office on the third floor. The kitchen on the fifth. A bedroom right at the top. The building grows dark and quiet, just like you.
[pause 6s]
Fifteen, perhaps.
[pause 3s]
The numbers are getting blurry. They're spreading out. Some of them disappear.
That's normal. In fact, it's a sign you're drifting.
If you're still counting, count more slowly. If you've stopped, there's no need to start again.
[pause 5s]
Outside, perhaps, a few snowflakes are falling through the night. They land on rooftops, on cars, on branches. Without a sound. Each in its turn.
[pause 4s]
Think of an hourglass. The sand falls, grain by grain. At the bottom it forms a small, soft, motionless heap.
Your breath is like that sand. It flows, slowly, and it settles.
[pause 6s]
Twelve, or thirteen. Your breathing has become so light you can barely feel it, just a small coming and going at the edge of your nostrils.
[pause 3s]
Your jaw is loose. Your cheeks are loose. Your whole face has softened, like the face of someone already asleep.
Your hands lie heavy and warm on the sheet. You couldn't quite say where your fingers end and the fabric begins.
[pause 5s]
The next number can come. Or not. Your breath simply carries on, patient and steady, without you having to look after it.
There's nothing left to hold on to. Not the numbers, not the day, not tomorrow.
Just the breath, coming in...
[pause 3s]
and going out.
[pause 6s]
If your nights are often difficult, consider talking to a health professional one day. For now, let the numbers carry you.
[pause 5s]
Ten...
[pause 5s]
Your shoulders are heavy. Your hands are heavy.
Your head is resting. Your whole back is resting.
[pause 6s]
Heavy... warm... slow...
[pause 4s]
The bed holds you. The night wraps around you.
[pause 5s]
Nothing to do... nothing to hold...
[pause 5s]
Keep counting... or let it all go...
[pause 10s]

sessions.title: Cognitive shuffle
script: [pause 1.5s]
Tonight, let's play a little game. A very quiet game, played with your eyes closed, lying in bed.
[pause 2s]
First, settle in as if you were going to sleep. Turn onto whichever side you like. Let your head find its place in the pillow.
Pull the covers up to wherever feels right. Let your arms rest wherever they want to, without arranging them.
[pause 3s]
If your mind is reasoning tonight, arguing, planning tomorrow, this game is for you.
As you fall asleep, your thoughts change shape. They come loose. An image of a cat, then a staircase, then a colour, with no link between them.
Some researchers think you can imitate that moment. By picturing random objects, unrelated to one another, you give the brain the impression that sleep is already on its way.
And above all, you keep it just busy enough to let go of its ruminating. It's hard to replay an argument while you're picturing a giraffe.
[pause 2s]
The rule is simple. I'll give you a word, and we'll take it one letter at a time.
For each letter, I'll suggest a few objects beginning with that letter. You picture one for a few seconds, then move on to the next.
You don't need to see them clearly. A blurry image is enough. Even just the idea of an image is enough.
This isn't a memory test, or an imagination contest. If an object doesn't come, move on to the next one. If a different object turns up instead, take it. It'll do just fine.
And above all, don't try to connect them. No story, no logic, no reason. An apple, then a piano. That's all there is to it.
[pause 2s]
Before we start, two easy breaths.
Breathe in through your nose, without forcing...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out gently, letting your body sink a little further into the mattress.
[pause 5s]
Once more. The air comes in, cool in your nostrils...
[pause 3s]
and flows out, a little warmer, a little slower.
[pause 5s]
Then let your breath find its own rhythm again. You don't need to look after it anymore.
[pause 2s]
The first word is beach. B, E, A, C, H.
We'll start with the letter B.
[pause 2s]
A balloon. A red balloon, its string trailing, floating against a white ceiling. See the light shining on its round surface.
[pause 2s]
A bicycle. An old blue bicycle leaning against a garden wall. A few drops of rain still resting on the saddle.
[pause 2s]
A button. A big wooden coat button, with four little holes in the middle.
A bowl of cherries. Dark red, shiny, stalks sticking up every which way. A small white napkin folded beside it.
[pause 2s]
A loaf of bread. The crust golden and crackly, a dusting of flour on top. Maybe its warm smell, fresh from the oven.
A boat. A narrowboat moored on a canal, pots of geraniums on the roof, a bicycle propped against the cabin.
[pause 2s]
A butterfly. Its wings slowly opening and closing on a warm stone wall.
A blanket. A thick wool blanket, folded over the arm of a sofa, its fringe a little tangled.
A bucket. A red plastic bucket, upside down on the sand, a little spade lying next to it.
[pause 2s]
If a thought from the day slips in between two objects, that's fine. Let it be, and come back to the letter. Always the letter.
[pause 3s]
The letter E.
An egg. A brown egg in an egg cup, a tiny feather stuck to the shell. A slice of buttered toast waiting on the plate beside it.
[pause 2s]
An envelope. A brown paper envelope, no address, lying on a desk by a window.
An eraser. A white eraser, worn down at one corner, with a few grey crumbs around it.
[pause 2s]
An elephant. An old grey elephant, standing quite still, flapping just one ear.
An easel. A wooden easel in an empty room, a blank canvas resting on it, a brush on the ledge.
[pause 2s]
An elm leaf. Yellow, a little curled, lying on a park bench after the rain.
An earring. A single silver earring, forgotten on a bedside table, catching a little light.
An eiderdown. Big and puffy, spilling over the side of an old bed.
[pause 4s]
The letter A.
An apple. A green apple on a wooden table, smooth and cool under your hand.
[pause 2s]
An anchor. A big rusty anchor lying on a quay, a coil of thick rope next to it, gulls standing about.
An apricot. Orange, slightly fuzzy, still warm from the sun.
[pause 2s]
An accordion. Folded, silent, in its case lined with red velvet.
An armchair. A deep, faded armchair by a window, a cushion squashed in one corner.
[pause 2s]
An acorn. A small acorn with its little cap, resting in the palm of a hand.
An aquarium. One small orange fish turning slow circles, bubbles rising one by one to the surface.
An attic. Dusty and quiet, a single beam of light falling across the wooden floor.
[pause 3s]
You might notice your mind hopping from one object to the next. That's exactly what we're after. There's no right answer.
[pause 3s]
The letter C.
A cat. A ginger cat curled up on a windowsill, its tail wrapped around its nose. Its side rising and falling, very slowly.
[pause 2s]
A candle. A white candle, the flame standing straight, a drop of wax sliding slowly down the side.
A cup. A blue china cup, a spoon resting on the saucer.
[pause 2s]
A cloud. A single white cloud, alone in a pale sky, changing shape so slowly you can hardly tell.
A carrot. Fresh from the ground, a little soil still clinging to it, its leafy top bright green.
[pause 2s]
A cello. Propped in a corner, one string slightly loose.
A cushion. Round and velvet, a deep green, with a small dent where someone's head has been.
A cardigan. Grey, soft, hung on the back of a kitchen chair, the sleeves dangling.
[pause 2s]
If a letter gets you stuck, skip it. There's no penalty, nothing to get right.
[pause 4s]
The letter H.
A hat. A straw hat hanging on a hook by the back door.
[pause 2s]
A hammock. Strung between two apple trees, swaying ever so slightly, a book left open in the bottom.
A hedgehog. A small hedgehog snuffling through fallen leaves at dusk, its tiny black nose twitching.
[pause 2s]
A honey jar. Golden, a wooden dipper resting inside, a slow thread of honey falling back down.
A harp. Tall and still, in the corner of a quiet room.
[pause 2s]
A hot-water bottle. Wrapped in a knitted cover, warm against your hands.
A haystack. Golden in a field at the end of the day, a few loose strands lifting in the breeze.
[pause 3s]
That's the end of the word. You don't need to remember anything you saw. It's already fading, like the images of a dream on waking.
The balloon, the elephant, the cat... They can go back to wherever they came from.
[pause 2s]
Is your body a little heavier now? Your breath a little slower? The thoughts from earlier, a little further away?
[pause 5s]
Let's take a second word. This time, we'll go more slowly. Fewer words, more space between the images.
The word is soft. S, O, F, T.
[pause 2s]
The letter S.
A sock. A thick wool sock, drying on the radiator, its heel a different colour.
[pause 3s]
A seashell. A pale pink shell, ridged and smooth, lying on wet sand.
A saucer. A white saucer, a teaspoon on top, a few grains of sugar left behind.
[pause 3s]
A snowman. Slightly lopsided, a scarf around his neck, alone in a quiet garden. His carrot nose points a little toward the sky.
A sailing boat. Small and white, far out on a calm sea.
[pause 3s]
A slipper. A sheepskin slipper, warm inside, waiting by the side of a bed.
A sofa. Deep and worn, the cushions sagging just where you would sit.
[pause 4s]
The letter O.
An orange. Round, its peel slightly bumpy under your fingers. Maybe its scent, as your thumb sinks in to peel it.
[pause 3s]
An owl. Perched on a branch, perfectly still, its eyes half closed. Its feathers puffed up against the cool night air.
An oar. A wooden oar resting across a rowing boat tied to a jetty.
[pause 3s]
An olive. A single green olive in a little earthenware dish.
An oven glove. Checked red and white, hanging from a hook.
[pause 3s]
An onion. Golden, its skin as thin as paper, crackling a little under your thumb.
An otter. Floating on its back on a still river, its paws folded on its chest.
[pause 4s]
The letter F.
A feather. A white feather drifting slowly down through the air, swaying from side to side, landing without a sound.
[pause 3s]
A fern. Its fronds uncurling in a shady corner of a garden.
A fig. Purple, soft, split open a little at the top, showing the pink inside.
[pause 3s]
A fence. A low wooden fence, its paint peeling, a cat walking slowly along the top.
A fireplace. Embers glowing low, a log settling with a soft crackle, the warmth reaching your feet.
[pause 4s]
The letter T.
A teapot. A round brown teapot, a wisp of steam rising from its spout.
[pause 3s]
A tulip. A single yellow tulip, very upright, in a narrow vase.
A towel. A thick white towel, folded on the end of a bed, still warm from the dryer.
[pause 3s]
A teddy bear. Sitting alone on a shelf, one ear coming unstitched, looking slightly to one side.
A tortoise. Moving across a lawn so slowly, its shell warm from the afternoon.
[pause 4s]
From now on, you can carry on by yourself.
Pick a word of your own, a gentle word with nothing worrying about it. Garden. Pillow. Cherry. Whatever comes.
Take its first letter. Let an object come. Then another. Then another.
[pause 3s]
For example, with the letter G. A goldfish in a round bowl. A pair of gloves on a bench. A guitar against a wall. A gate at the end of a lane.
[pause 3s]
Then the letter A. An almond. An apron hanging on a hook. An apple tree in blossom, petals falling on the grass.
[pause 3s]
Take your time with each one. A few seconds. Long enough to see it, even vaguely. Then let it go, without regret, and take another.
When you run out of ideas, move to the next letter. And if you forget the word, make up a new one. It doesn't matter at all.
[pause 4s]
If your nights stay restless for a long time, think about speaking to a health professional. Tonight, just let the images come.
[pause 6s]
A letter... an object...
[pause 4s]
then another...
[pause 4s]
no link... no effort...
[pause 5s]
a blurry image... drifting away...
[pause 5s]
and your body, carried... very gently...
[pause 10s]

sessions.title: One minute to breathe
script: [pause 1.5s]
Stop for a moment. Right where you are, just as you are.
Standing, sitting, in a hallway... anywhere works. You can keep your eyes open.
[pause 1.5s]
Breathe in gently through your nose...
[pause 4s]
And let the air out even more slowly, as if through a straw...
[pause 6s]
Now, let's take a quick look inside. Three questions, one word each.
Your body. What stands out? Tight, hot, tired... Just one word.
[pause 2.5s]
Your emotion. Irritation, worry, nothing much? One word, no judgment.
[pause 2.5s]
Your mind. What is it busy with, right now? One more word.
[pause 3s]
Simply naming it already gives you a little distance.
One more slow breath. In...
[pause 4s]
And out, no rush, all the way to the end.
[pause 6s]
Now, move on. What's the next small thing to do? Not the whole day. Just the very next step.
Picking up that call. Opening that door. Answering that one message.
[pause 2s]
You have it? Then go, with this calmer breath.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Box breathing
script: [pause 1.5s]
Sit or stand tall, feet flat, shoulders settled. Let's go.
Box breathing has four sides, and each side lasts about four seconds. Firefighters, nurses and pilots use it to keep a clear head under pressure.

You breathe in, you hold, you breathe out, and then you rest with empty lungs. All through the nose, without straining, as if you were tracing a square in your mind. One side goes up, one runs across, one comes down, one runs back.
I'll give you one word for each side, and the silence will do the counting. Start by gently letting your air out.
[pause 2s]
Breathe in.
[pause 3.5s]
Hold.
[pause 3.5s]
Breathe out.
[pause 3.5s]
Rest, empty.
[pause 3.5s]
Again. Breathe in.
[pause 3.5s]
Hold, throat soft.
[pause 3s]
Out, shoulders dropping.
[pause 3s]
Wait, nice and easy.
[pause 3s]
Now I'll say even less. Keep the same square, and I'll just mark the corners.
[pause 1s]
In.
[pause 3.5s]
Hold, shoulders loose.
[pause 3s]
Out.
[pause 3.5s]
Wait.
[pause 3.5s]
If the hold feels uncomfortable, make it shorter. A smaller square is still a square. And if you feel dizzy or uneasy, simply go back to your natural breath.
While you trace the square, your mind has a simple job to do. There's less room left for whatever was worrying you.
Notice the four corners. The top of the breath, the bottom of the breath, and those small plateaus in between, where everything is still.
Now one last square, all your own, at your own pace.
[pause 6s]
Then let it go. Your breath returns to its natural shape, on its own.
You've found your footing again, with a slightly clearer mind. You can head back in now.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Stressed in public, discreetly
script: [pause 1.5s]
No one around you will notice a thing. Keep your eyes open and stay just as you are.
Everything we'll do is invisible. From the outside, you simply look like someone waiting.
[pause 2s]
Let's start with your feet. Standing or sitting, press them lightly into the floor, as if you wanted to push it down by a millimeter.
Feel the pressure under your heels, then under the balls of your feet. The ground pushes back. It's holding you up.
[pause 1.5s]
Release... and press again, gently.
That simple contact reminds your body that it's standing somewhere real, here and now.
[pause 3s]
Now your hands. They can stay in your pockets, on your lap, or around a rail.
Press the tip of your thumb against your index finger. A small, firm squeeze, for a couple of seconds.
Then against your middle finger. Your ring finger. Your little finger.
[pause 1.5s]
And back the other way, feeling each contact. The warmth, the texture of the skin, the fingernail under your thumb.
If your thoughts are racing, this gives them a rhythm to follow. One finger, then the next.
[pause 2s]
Let your gaze rest on something neutral. A coat button, the corner of a poster, a mark on the floor.
No need to stare. Let your eyes settle there, the way they do when you look out of a train window.
The edges of what you see can widen a little. Your brow softens.
[pause 3s]
Now the breath. Your mouth stays closed, so no one hears a thing.
Breathe in easily through your nose, without lifting your chest...
[pause 3s]
and let the breath out last a little longer. The air slides out through your nostrils, slowly, silently...
[pause 5s]
Once more. An ordinary breath in...
[pause 3s]
and a breath out that takes its time.
[pause 5s]
At the end of the exhale, your shoulders drop by half an inch. Invisible to everyone else, but not to you.
A longer exhale gently tells your body it can slow down.
[pause 2s]
Keep this quiet rhythm and listen to what's around you.
Pick out a first sound. The hum of an engine, a distant voice, someone typing.
Don't judge it. Just notice it.
[pause 2s]
Then a second one, closer. Footsteps, the rustle of a jacket.
[pause 2s]
And a third, quieter one. The kind you only hear when you really listen.
[pause 3s]
Three sounds, and here you are, in this place, rather than inside a busy head.
The noise and the crowd haven't changed. But you've found your anchors again. Your feet, your fingers, your gaze, your breath.
[pause 2s]
You can do this anywhere. In a line, in a meeting, in a packed elevator.
Even thirty seconds can help. A press of the feet, a round of the fingers, one long exhale.
[pause 1.5s]
Go back to what you were doing, at your own pace. Your anchor travels with you.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: When anger rises
script: [pause 1.5s]
Anger has just surged up in you. A word, an email, a situation that crossed a line.
It's allowed to be here. Often, it's a sign that something important to you has been touched.
We're not going to make it disappear. We'll only take care of what you do with it in the next few minutes.
[pause 2s]
First, find where it's burning in your body.
Maybe in your jaw, clenched, teeth pressed together.
Maybe in your fists, or in your forearms, ready to spring.
Or in your chest. Heat, pressure, a pounding heart.
Sometimes it's a knot in the stomach, or a face that's burning.
[pause 2s]
You don't need to change anything yet. Just notice the hottest spot. Simply locating it already gives you back a little control.
[pause 2s]
Now, your hands. If they're clenched, open them slowly, one finger at a time.
Rest them on your thighs, palms facing up, or let them hang loosely by your sides.
[pause 2s]
Feel the air on the inside of your hands. Open hands are not the same as clenched fists. Your body notices the difference.
[pause 2s]
Let's cool things down a little with the breath.
Breathe in through your nose, normally.
[pause 3s]
Then blow out slowly through your mouth, lips slightly rounded, as if you were cooling a spoonful of soup that's far too hot.
Not hard. Just a thin stream of air, long and steady...
[pause 6s]
Again. Breathe in easily...
[pause 3s]
and blow on the soup, nice and long...
[pause 7s]
A third time. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and out. Notice the end of the exhale, that little moment when the air is out and nothing is urgent.
[pause 4s]
The long exhale is like your body's brake pedal. Every slow breath out presses on it a little more.
Keep this rhythm going while we take a closer look at the anger.
[pause 1.5s]
Behind it, there's almost always a need. Something that matters to you and wasn't respected.
Maybe respect. Someone spoke to you in a way that isn't okay with you.
Maybe fairness. What happened feels unjust.
Maybe rest. You're running on empty, and this was the last straw.
Or something else. Being heard, being recognized, feeling safe.
Which word feels right to you? Say it silently, once or twice.
[pause 3s]
Naming that need doesn't mean your anger is wrong. It helps you see what you actually want to protect.
[pause 1.5s]
Take another long exhale, like blowing on the soup. Feel your shoulders come down a notch, and your jaw loosen a little.
[pause 5s]
Now you have a choice. And that choice belongs to you.
You can respond now, if you feel calm enough to say what matters without hurting anyone.
You can respond later. In an hour, tomorrow, after a walk or a night's sleep. Nothing forces you to react in the heat of the moment.
If it's an email, you can even write your reply without sending it, and reread it once you've cooled down.
You can also decide not to respond at all, if it isn't worth it.
[pause 1.5s]
All three options are valid. Let the one that feels most right, here and now, come to you.
Notice what your body says about it. Often, the right option is the one that lets you breathe a little more freely.
[pause 3s]
Before you carry on, one last breath. In through the nose...
[pause 4s]
and blow out, long and slow, keeping your hands open...
[pause 7s]
The anger may still be there, a little less fierce. That's normal. It tends to come down in stages.
You know what you need, and you know you get to choose your response.
[pause 1.5s]
You can go back to your day now, in your own way.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Too much at once
script: [pause 1.5s]
It's a lot right now. Too many things at once, and all of them feel urgent.
Feeling overwhelmed like this is normal. It isn't a lack of ability. It's simply too much for one head to hold at once.
For the next four minutes, set it all down. None of it is going to fly away.
[pause 3s]
Let's start with three long exhales.
Breathe in through your nose, without forcing...
[pause 3s]
Then blow out through your mouth, slowly, emptying all the way...
[pause 6s]
A second one. The air comes in...
[pause 3s]
and goes out, more slowly than usual...
[pause 6s]
The third one. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and let the exhale carry away a little of the tension in your forehead and shoulders, right to the end.
[pause 5s]
When everything speeds up, slowing your breath is one of the few things you can do straight away.
[pause 1.5s]
Now, your hands. Rest them flat on a table, on your thighs, or one inside the other.
Notice their weight and their temperature. Are your fingers cold, warm, a little numb?
[pause 2s]
Now choose a fixed point in front of you. A corner of the wall, a door handle, something on your desk.
Let your gaze rest there. It doesn't need to jump from screen to screen anymore.
[pause 3s]
Hands resting, eyes resting. You have something steady to lean on.
Things can move forward without your body rushing off in every direction. For now, it can stay right here.
[pause 2s]
Now let's empty your head. Not to organize anything, just to let out what's spinning.
Silently, name everything that's on your mind, in any order, without sorting. A word or two for each thing.
The report that's due. The message you haven't answered. The groceries. That appointment. That conversation that keeps nagging at you.
Let your own things come up, big ones and tiny ones alike. Each one gets its name, just once.
If you like, you can count them quietly on your fingers.
Work. Home. The people waiting to hear from you. The worries about later on. Anything can come up.
[pause 3s]
If more keep coming, keep going. You don't have to do anything with these thoughts right now. Just acknowledge them.
Notice that once they're named, they often take up a little less room. They're still there, but they're not all shouting at once anymore.
Your mind was trying to hold everything in memory at the same time. Now that it's all been named, it can loosen its grip a little.
[pause 1.5s]
Take one long exhale...
[pause 6s]
Now, just one question. Out of all of that, what's the one thing that really matters in the next hour?
Not necessarily the biggest one, or the one others find most urgent. The one that would bring you the most relief once it's done. Or the one that truly can't wait.
Let the answer come. If you're torn between two, pick the simpler one. You can always change it later.
[pause 3s]
You have your one thing. Now picture the very first small step to get going on it.
Really small. Opening the document. Writing the first line of the email. Finding the number in your phone.
See yourself doing it. Where are your hands? What's on the screen, or in front of you?
[pause 2s]
Notice how doable that one step is, even now, even tired.
One small, clear step is often what gets everything else moving again.
[pause 1.5s]
The rest of the list hasn't disappeared. It's waiting its turn, and it will get it, one thing after another.
You don't have to carry it all at once. Just this one step. When it's done, you'll choose the next one the same way.
[pause 1.5s]
One last long exhale, hands resting, eyes on your fixed point...
[pause 5s]
And now, go and take that first step. Everything else can wait its turn.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: After an argument
script: [pause 1.5s]
An argument has just happened. With someone who matters to you, and that's exactly why it's so unsettling.
You don't have to sort anything out in the next few minutes. Just come back down, and see things a little more clearly.
[pause 2s]
Settle in wherever you are. On a chair, standing against a wall, it doesn't matter. If you need to change rooms, now is a good time.
[pause 3s]
Let's start by noticing what's happening inside you, without changing anything.
Your heart may be beating faster, or harder. You can feel it in your chest, in your throat, sometimes even in your temples.
There may be some heat. In your face, at the back of your neck, in your hands.
And in your head, the scene is probably replaying. The words that were said, the tone, that look.
Your hands may be trembling a little too. A lump in your throat, an urge to cry or to shout.
[pause 2s]
All of this is normal. It's your body, still on alert, ready to defend itself. It needs a little time to realize the tense moment is over.
Let's help it along with a few long exhales. I'll guide you.
[pause 1.5s]
Breathe in through your nose, simply...
[pause 4s]
Then blow out through your mouth, slowly, a little longer than the inhale...
[pause 6s]
Again. Breathe in...
[pause 4s]
And as the air leaves, let your shoulders drop. They may have crept up toward your ears during the argument.
[pause 6s]
A third time. In...
[pause 4s]
The air goes out, your shoulders come down another notch, your hands unclench.
[pause 6s]
A fourth one, even slower. In...
[pause 4s]
And out... feel your belly soften at the very end of the exhale.
[pause 6s]
Good. Keep breathing like this, at your own pace, with an exhale that takes its time.
[pause 2s]
Comebacks will probably keep popping up. I should have told them... Next time, I'll say...
That's what the mind does after a conflict. It hunts for the perfect line. It replays the match.
You don't need to follow these comebacks, or push them away. Just notice them, the way you'd watch cars go by from the sidewalk.
[pause 2s]
Oh, there's one. It passes. And you come back to your exhale.
You can even label it with one word... replaying. And come back to your breath.
[pause 3s]
Every time you return to the breath, you give your body a little more time to settle.
If one line keeps coming back, again and again, you can answer it silently. I hear you. Not now.
[pause 3s]
Now turn toward yourself. Not toward what the other person did, but toward what's happening inside you.
What are you feeling, right now, underneath the agitation?
[pause 2s]
Maybe sadness. Hurt. Fear. Exhaustion. Sometimes several at once.
Put a word to it, the one that feels true.
[pause 2s]
Notice where it sits in your body. Your throat, your chest, your belly. You can rest a hand there, if that helps.
[pause 2s]
And behind that feeling, what do you need? To be heard? Respected? Some calm? Recognition for everything you do?
[pause 3s]
That need is legitimate. It doesn't make you difficult. It simply tells you what matters to you.
[pause 2s]
Take a long exhale, and let that need stay where it is, acknowledged.
[pause 3s]
Now, if you feel up to it, take a small step to the side. Picture the scene from the other person's place.
Not to say they were right. Just to see a slightly bigger picture.
What might they have been feeling during the argument? Frustration? Worry? Feeling like they didn't matter?
[pause 2s]
And what do they need, on their side?
[pause 2s]
Often, the two needs turn out to be less opposed than they seemed. Two people who each wanted, in their own way, to feel respected or reassured.
You don't have to guess right. A best guess is enough.
And if it's too soon to put yourself in their shoes, that's okay. You can come back to it later.
[pause 3s]
Breathe. An easy breath in...
[pause 3s]
and a long breath out, gently emptying.
[pause 5s]
Now picture the moment when you reconnect. Later on, when the time is right.
What could your first sentence be? A calm one, that opens things up instead of starting the fight again.
Maybe... I don't like how things went earlier. Or, I'd like us to talk about it again, more calmly. Or simply, I care about you, even when we disagree.
[pause 2s]
Choose your own, in your own words. One sentence is enough to begin.
A sentence about you, about what you feel and what you need, is often easier to hear than a reproach.
Say it to yourself silently, slowly, and notice what it does in your body.
[pause 3s]
And nothing says you have to fix everything right away.
Sometimes it takes a few hours, or a night, for both of you to come back down. That delay isn't a failure. It's often what makes a real conversation possible.
[pause 2s]
Take one more long exhale. Feel your feet on the floor, the weight of your body, your back straightening a little.
[pause 3s]
Notice where you are now, compared to the beginning. Maybe a slightly slower heart, a slightly less crowded head. Or still some agitation, and that's okay too.
[pause 3s]
You've made some space between the argument and whatever comes next. That space is what will let you choose your words.
Go back to your day, gently, with your sentence in your pocket for the right moment, whenever it comes.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: After bad news
script: [pause 1.5s]
Something hard has just happened. A call, a message, an announcement.
You don't have to understand or decide anything right now. Just take this time for yourself.
[pause 2s]
If you can, sit down. Or lean your back against a wall.
If you're outside, find a bench, a low wall, a quieter corner. Put your phone down if you can, screen facing the table, or tucked in your pocket.
[pause 2.5s]
Let's start by looking around you. Slowly, let your eyes travel around the place you're in.
The walls, their color. A window, the light coming in. A piece of furniture, a familiar object.
[pause 2s]
Let your eyes rest on three things, one after another, without hurrying.
Name them silently, simply. The lamp. The door. My mug.
[pause 3s]
It helps your mind remember where you are. After a shock, everything can feel unreal. Looking at what surrounds you is a gentle way back into the present.
[pause 1.5s]
Now feel the floor beneath your feet. It's there, steady. Feel the seat holding you, the backrest behind you.
You're here, in this room. What just happened is real. And you are here too.
Both are true at the same time. The news, and this floor holding you up.
[pause 2s]
Notice the temperature of the air on your hands, on your face. The touch of your clothes. These small, ordinary things are still here.
[pause 3s]
Let your breathing slow down a little, if it's willing. There's no goal here.
Just a breath in, whenever it comes...
[pause 3s]
and a breath out, a little longer, if that's possible.
[pause 5s]
Another one. The air comes in however it can...
[pause 3s]
and goes out, without effort, without trying to do it right.
[pause 5s]
If your breath stays short or ragged, that's okay too. Your body is reacting to something big. You don't have to correct it.
If you like, press your feet a little more firmly into the floor, and let the exhale leave through your mouth, like a sigh.
[pause 5s]
Whatever you're feeling right now is normal.
Maybe a kind of numbness, as if everything were wrapped in cotton wool, with no clear thoughts. That's a very common reaction to shock.
Maybe tears are rising. You can let them come. They belong here.
Maybe anger, disbelief, an urge to run away.
Or thoughts racing in every direction. What if, what now, how will I cope. You don't have to answer them yet.
Or maybe nothing at all, for now. A big blank. That happens too, and it doesn't mean this doesn't matter.
[pause 2s]
There's no right way to react. All of these are ways for your body to absorb the blow.
And they may shift through the day, coming and going in waves. That's normal too.
You don't have to choose how to feel. Just let whatever is here exist, for the length of this pause.
[pause 2.5s]
If you'd like, place a hand on your heart. Or on your belly. Wherever feels most right.
Feel the warmth of your hand, its gentle weight. Like a friend's hand resting on you.
[pause 2s]
And say to yourself, softly... This is hard, what's happening to me. I'm here for myself.
Or another phrase that speaks to you more. I'll take this one step at a time. It's okay for this to hurt.
[pause 4s]
Keep your hand there a little longer, if it feels good. Breathe beneath it.
Feel your chest or your belly moving softly under your palm. You're keeping yourself company.
This gesture may seem very small. Yet many people find it soothes a little, like having someone there.
[pause 3s]
Now, just one question. Not for tomorrow, not for the week. Only for the next hour.
What do I need, in the next hour?
[pause 3s]
Maybe a glass of water. Something to eat. Some fresh air. Lying down. Letting someone know you won't be able to do what was planned.
Choose just one thing. Simple, concrete, doable. One, not a list. The rest will come later.
This isn't a small detail. Looking after your body now is what will help you face what comes next.
[pause 3s]
Think of a person, too. Someone you could call or text, if you need to share some of this weight.
Someone close, a friend, a neighbor. You don't have to explain everything. Something hard is happening, can you call me... That's enough.
Choose that person now, even if you only reach out later. See their face, hear their voice, just for a moment.
[pause 3s]
And if no one comes to mind, or if it feels too heavy, support lines exist, and your doctor can be a source of support too.
You don't have to carry this alone. Asking for help isn't a weakness. It's one way of taking care of yourself.
[pause 3s]
Come back to your breath, just as it is now. Feel your feet on the floor again, and the seat beneath you.
You don't need to feel better right away. What happened will take time, and that's normal.
The next few hours may have their ups and downs. You can come back to this pause as many times as you need.
[pause 2s]
For now, you've done something important. You stopped, and you took care of yourself for a few minutes.
When the moment comes, move toward what you need in the next hour. One thing at a time.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Before a party or a date
script: [pause 1.5s]
In a few hours, or maybe a few minutes, you'll be meeting people. A party, a dinner, a first date. And something inside you is tightening.
Maybe your throat, your stomach, slightly clammy hands. Maybe that small voice suggesting you cancel.
[pause 2s]
All of this is deeply human. Feeling nervous before seeing people doesn't mean you're strange, or that the evening will go badly. It just means it matters to you.
So to begin, there's nothing to fix. Only a little room for what you're feeling.
[pause 2s]
Settle in wherever you are, sitting or standing. You can keep your eyes open, or let them half close.
If your heart is beating fast, let it beat. That's your body getting ready, like before a game or an exam. There's nothing dangerous about it.
[pause 2s]
First, let's talk to the body, because the body is what sounded the alarm.
Breathe in calmly through your nose, no bigger than usual...
[pause 3s]
Then breathe out through your mouth, slowly, as if you were fogging up a window. Let the out breath last longer than the in breath.
[pause 6s]
Once more. Breathe in, normally...
[pause 3s]
And breathe out, long and soft, all the way to the end.
[pause 6s]
Now look at your hands. Are they clenched?
[pause 2s]
If they are, open them. Gently spread your fingers, then let them fall back, loose, onto your thighs.
Notice the warmth coming back into your palms. Let your shoulders drop half an inch. Unclench your jaw, let your tongue rest.
One last long out breath, and let your body sink a little into the seat.
[pause 5s]
Breathing out slowly is a simple way of telling your nervous system it can slow down. You don't have to believe it. You just have to do it.
[pause 3s]
Now let's see what your mind is doing. There's a good chance it's already playing a little movie.
The moment you walk in and nobody talks to you. The awkward silence. The joke that falls flat. The other person looking bored.
These images feel real, and the body reacts to them as if they were.
[pause 2s]
And yet they all have one thing in common. None of them has happened yet. They're predictions.
So let's try something. Each time one of these scenes plays, simply say to yourself, silently, prediction.
They'll think I'm boring. Prediction. I'm going to blush. Prediction. I won't know what to say. Prediction.
You're not trying to prove it's false. You're just noticing that it's a guess your brain is making, not a fact.
[pause 3s]
And remember the times you dreaded an evening, and it actually went well, or at least better than you expected. Your brain tends to forget those.
Tonight too, there's a good chance reality will be simpler than the movie.
[pause 2s]
Here's something many people find reassuring. Tonight, most of the people you meet will mostly be thinking about... themselves.
About their outfit, about what they're going to say, about that person they don't know. Some of them will have the same knot in their stomach that you have.
Psychologists even have a name for it. The spotlight effect. We feel as if we're under the stage lights, when in fact other people notice us far less than we think.
[pause 2s]
You're not on stage. You're one person among others, all of whom would like to have a nice time.
And if you blush, or search for your words, most people won't even notice. The ones who do often find it rather endearing.
[pause 2s]
So let's change the goal. Instead of trying to come across well, to be funny, interesting, perfect, try a lighter intention. Curiosity.
Being curious about at least one person. Who they are, what lights them up, how they see things.
When your attention goes out toward someone else, it steps away from that spotlight pointed at you. And awkwardness often loosens its grip.
Put this intention into your own words. For example, tonight, I want to get to know someone. Or, tonight, I'm listening.
[pause 3s]
To make it easier, prepare one simple question you can pull out of your pocket if a silence settles in.
An open question, one that invites a story. What's been keeping you busy lately? How do you know everyone here? What was the best thing you did this summer?
Pick one. Say it once in your head, in your own voice, calmly.
[pause 2s]
Now picture the person answering, and you listening, really listening, nodding along. Nothing else to get right.
[pause 3s]

One small gesture for the moment you arrive. Just before you ring the bell or push the door open, pause for a couple of seconds. Feel your feet in your shoes, open your hands, and let out a long breath.
Then walk in and look for a first face to smile at. You don't need to shine. A hello, a name, your question, and you're on your way.
And if a silence happens anyway, it's not a disaster. You can take a sip, smile, or ask your question. Silences are part of every conversation.
[pause 2s]
Come back to your breath. A long out breath. Hands open. Feet grounded.
[pause 4s]

And keep one last thing in mind. You're allowed to leave whenever you want. If after an hour you've had enough, you can say goodbye and go home. That's allowed, and it doesn't make you any less likeable.
Knowing the door is open often makes it easier to walk through it.
[pause 2s]
You're going with your nerves, your question, and your curiosity. That's more than enough.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Urge surfing
script: [pause 1.5s]
If you're starting this session, maybe an urge is here right now. The urge to pick up your phone, open the cupboard, light a cigarette, check your messages one more time.
That makes this the right moment. You don't need to wait until you're calm. We practice precisely while the urge is here.
And if there's no urge at the moment, remember the last time it was strong, and let the memory of it come back a little.
[pause 2s]
Sit down with your feet flat on the floor. If the object of your urge is within reach, move it a little further away, or turn it face down, just for the length of this session.
You haven't promised anything. You're not giving anything up forever. You're observing for a few minutes, that's all.
If part of you feels it's hopeless, that you'll give in anyway, that's okay. You can do this exercise with that doubt along for the ride.
Take a slow breath in...
[pause 3s]
and let the air flow out easily.
[pause 4s]
Let's start by giving this urge a name. Something simple. Urge to scroll. Urge for something sweet. Urge to smoke. Urge to check.
Then ask yourself, what is it promising me?
[pause 2s]
Often, it's not the thing itself. It's a break. A reward. A little forgetting. The end of some discomfort.
Follow me, and you'll feel better. Listen to that promise without believing it, without arguing. Just hear it.
And maybe notice what set it off. Tiredness, boredom, tension, an unpleasant email. Urges rarely come out of nowhere.
Spotting the trigger is already useful. Next time, you might answer the real need instead. Rest, move, take a breather.
[pause 3s]
Now look for where the urge lives in your body. An urge isn't just an idea. It's also a collection of sensations.
Maybe restlessness in your hands, fingers that want to move. Tension in your jaw. A hollow feeling in your stomach. Warmth in your chest, your mouth watering, impatience in your legs.
Take the time to do the full tour. Where is it strongest?
[pause 2s]
And give its intensity a score from one to ten. One is barely there. Ten is almost irresistible. Remember that number.
[pause 3s]
Here's the image we'll use. Imagine your urge is a wave, out at sea.
Every wave has the same life. It forms, it swells, it reaches a peak, then it breaks and dissolves onto the sand. No wave rises forever.
Urges often work the same way. Many people notice that they peak and then fade within a few minutes, if they aren't fed.
When we give in right away, we never get to see the wave go down on its own. So the brain comes to believe the urge is an order. Today, you're showing it something different.
Your breath is your surfboard. You don't need to stop the wave, or throw yourself into it. Just stay standing on the board, and let it carry you.
[pause 3s]
Bring your attention to your breathing. Air coming in, air going out. Let the out-breath be a little longer, like your balance settling.
And at the same time, keep an eye on the place in your body where the urge is showing up.
Maybe it's rising right now. The sensations grow stronger, the thoughts speed up. Just this once. It doesn't count. Come on, quickly.
Those thoughts are part of the wave. You can hear them, like the sound of the water, without answering them.
Stay on your board. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
breathe out. You have nothing else to do.
[pause 4s]
If you catch yourself bargaining, telling yourself fine, right after the session, notice it with a little smile. That's the wave talking too.
[pause 3s]
Look closely. Does the sensation pulse, or is it steady? Does it move around?
[pause 2s]
Does it have a shape, a temperature? The closer you look, the more the urge becomes a set of small, shifting sensations, rather than a command you can't refuse.
If the urge is very strong, remember this. It's uncomfortable, but it isn't dangerous. You can ride it out.
Your body knows how to do this. A sensation, even a strong one, rarely stays at its peak for very long. Sooner or later, it moves, it changes.
[pause 2s]
At some point, the wave reaches its peak. You might feel it. A moment where it's at its most intense, and then a slight shift.
If you're there now, this is the time to be especially gentle with yourself. Feet on the floor, long out-breath. You're still standing.
If it helps, count your out-breaths silently up to five, then start again. Each out-breath is a small paddle stroke that keeps you balanced on the crest.
If your hands are fidgeting, lay them flat on your thighs and feel their warmth. Give your body something simple to do while the wave rolls beneath you.
[pause 5s]
And then, almost without warning, the wave starts to go down. The tension eases a little. The thoughts slow down. The urgency loses its voice.
Follow this ebb with the same curiosity you gave the rise. Where does your body relax first? Your hands? Your jaw? Your stomach?
[pause 3s]
If the urge rises again, that's normal. The sea has more than one wave. You simply climb back on your board and start surfing again.
With practice, many people find the waves get a little lower, or come a little less often. But today, it's just about this one.
[pause 2s]
Now rate the intensity again, from one to ten, and compare it with your number from the beginning.
[pause 2s]
Maybe it's dropped a lot, maybe just one point. Maybe it has changed shape. All of this is useful information. Your urge isn't a straight line. It's a movement.
[pause 3s]
And here's the heart of it. You didn't have to fight, or obey. You watched.
Now you can choose freely. Maybe you'll set the urge aside. Maybe you'll still have that square of chocolate, but you'll really savor it, by choice rather than on autopilot.
Both options belong to you. The goal isn't perfection. The goal is to put some space back between the urge and the action. And you've just created that space.
Every wave you surf makes the next one a little more familiar.
[pause 2s]
Take one last breath, feel your feet, look around you, and pick up the thread of your day.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Name it to tame it
script: [pause 1.5s]
Welcome. In this session, I'll show you a very simple tool you can take anywhere. Putting a word on what's happening.
[pause 1.5s]
Sit with your back upright but not rigid, your hands resting on your thighs, or one in the other.
Close your eyes if that feels okay, or lower your gaze toward the floor.
Let your body take its place. Shoulders dropping, face softening, belly letting go.
And let go of the idea of doing it well, too. There's nothing to achieve here, only things to notice.
[pause 2s]
To begin, rest your attention on your breath, wherever you feel it most clearly. Maybe at the tip of your nose, maybe in your chest, maybe in your belly rising and falling.
Follow one in breath from beginning to end. Then one out breath, all the way to the little resting moment that follows it.
[pause 4s]
You can already try, very gently, noting the breath itself. Rising, on the in breath. Falling, on the out breath. Just to get a feel for the idea.
[pause 5s]
Your breath will be your point of return, your home base. Every time you drift away from it, you can come back.
Here's how mental noting works. When something pulls your attention away from the breath, you notice it, and you give it a word. Just one, simple and soft.
A door closing, for example, is hearing. An itch is sensation. A thought about your to-do list is planning.
Then, without lingering, you come back to the breath.
Think of it as a light tap on the shoulder. You notice, you name, and you let go.
[pause 1.5s]
One word every few seconds is plenty. This isn't a labeling race. Between two notes, there's the breath, calm, carrying on.
The word doesn't need to be perfect. It's just a way of saying, ah, this is what's happening. Say it silently, in a calm, almost tender tone, the way you'd greet a neighbor on the stairs.
Many people find that naming what they feel helps them step back a little. You're no longer inside the thought. You're watching it pass.
Researchers have observed that putting feelings into words can soften their intensity a little. That's what we'll explore today, lightly.
[pause 3s]
Let's start with the body. Stay with the breath, and let sensations show up.
Maybe the contact of your hands on your thighs. You can note, touch.
[pause 2s]
Maybe warmth in your palms or at the back of your neck. Warmth. A little coolness on your face. Cool.
A tingling in your foot. Tingling. Tension in your back. Tension.
Each time, one word, and back to the breath. There's no need to analyze the sensation, or change it.
[pause 2s]

If a sensation is unpleasant, discomfort in your knee, stiffness in your neck, you can note that too. Discomfort. Stiffness. Then see whether it changes by itself. Often it pulses, shifts, eases a little.
[pause 4s]
Now open your listening to sounds. When a sound reaches you, simply note, hearing.
You don't need to say car, or bird, or neighbor. Just hearing. The sound arrives, you note it, it leaves.
Notice how sounds appear and disappear without any help from you. Hearing. Back to the breath. Hearing. Back.
[pause 3s]
Notice the silence between two sounds, too. If it comes naturally, you can note it. Silence.
If you find yourself waiting for the next sound, listening out for it, you can note, waiting. Then come back to the breath.
[pause 4s]
Now, thoughts. This is often where anxiety hides, so it's an important step.
When a thought carries you off, try to see what kind it is. If you're preparing something, organizing your week, making a list, that's planning.
If you're picturing what could go wrong, that's worrying. If you're telling yourself you're doing this wrong, or that someone else was wrong, that's judging.
If you're replaying a memory, remembering. If you're making up a scene, imagining.
[pause 1.5s]
The word creates a little distance. Worrying is no longer, something terrible is going to happen. It's just your mind doing what minds do.
And when you don't know what to call it, thinking is more than enough.
Sometimes you only notice the thought after a minute, after a whole journey. That doesn't matter at all. Note it wherever you find it, and come back.
Does the thought keep the same strength once it's been named? Or does it deflate a little?
[pause 4s]
Now, emotions. They often blend with thoughts and sensations. When you notice one, give it its name.
A clenching that feels like fear. Fear. Impatience, irritation. Irritation. A light heaviness. Sadness. A gentle moment. Calm, or joy.
You can feel them in the body, too. Fear in the stomach, irritation in the shoulders. Note the emotion, then come back to the breath.
There's no wrong emotion to note. They all have the right to be here, for as long as they last.
If an emotion is strong, you can note it several times, slowly, in rhythm with the breath. Fear... fear... Like a hand resting on the shoulder of someone who's trembling.
[pause 4s]
Now let's bring it all together. The breath is still your home base. And anything that pulls you away from it, a sensation, a sound, a thought or an emotion, gets its little word.
I'll speak less now. If you get lost for a long time, that's fine. The moment you notice, you can even note lost, or returning. And you return.
[pause 6s]
Touch. Hearing. Planning. Breathing.
[pause 5s]
If you're noting too quickly, slow down. Let the breath make at least one full round between two words.
Keep your words light. If you catch yourself searching for the exact word for ten seconds, just note searching, and smile.
[pause 4s]
Sometimes nothing shows up. The breath is simply here. You can note breathing, or note nothing at all.
[pause 4s]
Breathing. Hearing. Thinking. Returning.
[pause 6s]
If the same thought keeps coming back, you can note it each time, with the same gentleness. Worrying. Worrying. It often ends up losing its momentum.
And if you notice you're noting in a harsh, impatient voice, soften your tone. The word matters less than the kindness you place it with.
Maybe notice the pleasant moments too. A softening in your shoulders, a moment of calm. They deserve their word as well. Ease. Calm.
[pause 4s]
Now let go of the technique. No more noting. Simply let things appear and disappear, without naming them.
Notice how everything moves. Sensations, sounds, thoughts, nothing stays in place for very long.
You simply stay here, in the middle of whatever passes through. No need to grab hold of anything.
[pause 6s]
Take a moment to feel how you are now. Maybe a little more space. Maybe not. That's okay.
[pause 2s]
Gently come back to the room. Feel your feet, your hands, your back. Take a slightly deeper breath, and stretch if you feel like it.
Open your eyes when the moment feels right for you.
[pause 2s]
You can practice this anywhere. On the train, in a queue, while walking. A few words, a few breaths, and you get a little perspective back.
During your day, when anxiety rises, you can take back just one word. Fear. Worrying. Simply saying it inside can remind you that you can watch the storm, without being the storm.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Living with uncertainty
script: [pause 1.5s]
Waiting is one of the hardest things there is. Waiting for test results, for an answer after a job interview, for news about someone you love, for a decision that isn't up to you.
Time seems to stretch. Your phone becomes a magnet. And your mind just won't stop searching.
[pause 2s]

If you're going through one of these times, know this first. What you're feeling is normal. The human brain doesn't like uncertainty, and it often experiences it as a threat. This isn't a flaw in you. It's part of being human.
This session won't give you the answer. But it can help you live inside the waiting a little differently.
It can help you stay with, I don't know, without rushing to fill it with stories you make up.
[pause 3s]
Get comfortable. Sitting or lying down, whatever feels right. If you can, put your phone away for these few minutes, or turn it face down on the table.
Close your eyes if you like, or keep a soft gaze resting in front of you.
And let your shoulders drop a little. They may have been carrying this waiting all day.
[pause 2s]
Start by noticing your breathing, just as it is. Maybe it's short, high up in your chest. That often happens when we're waiting.
Without forcing anything, let the out-breath lengthen a little. Like a slow sigh, gently emptying your lungs...
[pause 5s]
Once more. The in-breath comes on its own...
[pause 3s]
and the out-breath takes its time.
[pause 5s]
Now place a hand on your belly, if that's comfortable. Feel it rise under your palm, then fall again.
This movement doesn't depend on any answer. It's here, now, faithful. You can lean on it.
If at any point focusing on your breath feels uncomfortable, just let it go back to normal, and bring your attention to your feet instead.
Lengthening your out-breath is a concrete way of telling your body it can ease off its vigilance a little. Nothing to achieve. Just let it happen.
[pause 3s]
Now watch what your mind is doing with this waiting. Let it talk for a bit, without following it.
Maybe it's producing scenarios. The worst ones first. What if it's serious. What if they never call back. What if everything falls apart.
Maybe perfect scenarios too, ones you don't dare believe in. Or endless calculations. If they didn't call yesterday, that must mean... If she said that, it means...
Maybe you're replaying conversations, hunting for clues, checking again and again.
[pause 2s]

Notice what these thoughts do in your body, too. A knot in your stomach, raised shoulders, a need to move, to refresh your inbox, to call someone and talk it through one more time. That's the waiting making itself felt. Nothing abnormal.
Just notice that they're here. The way you'd watch cars go by from a window.
[pause 4s]
All these scenarios have something in common. They're your mind's attempts to get back in control.
When we don't know, it feels as if imagining every possibility will get us ready. As if it will hurt less if the worst happens. As if thinking hard enough were already a kind of doing.
It's a touching intention, really. Your mind is trying to protect you.
But you may have noticed that these scenarios don't bring the answer any closer. They make you live through things ten times over that may never happen at all.
You can thank your mind for its efforts. Thank you, I can see you're trying to help. And gently tell it that, for now, it can rest a little.
Another approach is to call each scenario by its name as it arrives. Ah, the disaster movie. Ah, the clue hunt. Recognizing it means you're already not quite inside it.
[pause 3s]
Here's a sentence I'd like you to try. Repeat it silently, slowly, in rhythm with your breath.
I don't know yet.
[pause 3s]
And I can stay with that.
[pause 4s]
What do these words do in your body?
[pause 2s]
Maybe a slight resistance, as if part of you were protesting, no, I need to know. That's normal. You can welcome that protest too.
Maybe also a small loosening. As if, for the first time in days, you didn't have to find the answer right away.
[pause 2s]
Say it again, in your own words if you prefer. I don't know, it's uncomfortable, and I'm still here.
[pause 3s]
Not knowing isn't an empty space you have to fill. It's a space you can breathe in, while you wait.
You can feel it like an open hand. You're not squeezing the future to force it to answer. You're letting it come, whenever it comes.
If your mind comes back with a new what if, that's normal. You don't have to win against it. Just return to the sentence, at your own pace.
[pause 4s]
Now let's turn toward what is certain. Not what will happen tomorrow, but what is here, right now.
What's certain is that you're breathing. Feel the air come in, and go out.
[pause 3s]
What's certain is that your body is supported. The chair, the bed, the floor. Feel the weight you're trusting them with.
[pause 2s]
What's certain are the sounds around you. The hum of an appliance, a car, distant voices. Listen to them for a few moments.
[pause 5s]
What's certain is the temperature of the air on your hands, the texture of your clothes, the light behind your eyelids.
What's certain is this exact moment. This one. It doesn't hold the answer yet, and yet it's livable. You're living it right now.
[pause 4s]
And there are other certainties, deeper ones. The people who matter to you. The hard times you've already been through, even when you didn't know how they would end.
Remember a period of waiting, in the past, that came to an end. One way or another, you faced it. You found resources.
Whatever answer arrives, you'll still have those resources to meet it. And you don't need to prepare for it completely today.
[pause 2s]
Take a moment to feel that steadiness. Maybe in your back, in your feet, in the way you're sitting. You've held on before, and you're holding on now.
[pause 4s]
Finally, let's think about the waiting itself. It may last a few more hours, or a few more days. And that time belongs to you too.
What could you do today that would be useful or enjoyable, even a little?
[pause 2s]
A walk around the neighborhood. Calling someone who makes you laugh. Clearing out a drawer. Cooking something simple. Moving forward on a small project. Watching a movie you know by heart.
Choose one thing, just one. Picture yourself doing it. The place, the movements, how it feels.
[pause 3s]
This isn't running away. It's a way of living during the waiting, instead of putting your life on hold.
And if the urge to check is strong, you can set specific times to look at your messages, say at noon and at six. In between, your phone can stay in another room. It gives the waiting some structure.
You can also write your worries down on a piece of paper once a day, then fold it away. They don't disappear, but they have a place, somewhere other than your head.
[pause 2s]
Come back to your breath, and to your hand on your belly if it's still there.
Be gentle with yourself during this time. If you're sleeping less well, if you have less patience, that's understandable. You're carrying something heavy, even if no one can see it.
And if the waiting becomes too heavy to carry alone, you're allowed to talk about it. A friend, someone close, or a professional can help you through it.
[pause 2s]
Notice how you feel, without demanding anything. The uncertainty may still be here, but you've spent a few minutes breathing with it, instead of fighting it.
Gently, move your fingers and toes. Open your eyes when the moment feels right for you.
[pause 2s]
And each time your mind slips back into its scenarios today, you can return to these two sentences. I don't know yet. And I can stay with that.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: When sadness visits
script: [pause 1.5s]
Maybe sadness is here today. A tiredness of the heart, a heaviness that won't lift, the loss of something or someone, or just a grey day without any clear reason.
[pause 2s]
First of all, you don't need to feel better right away. This session isn't here to cheer you up at all costs. It's here to keep you company.
You're allowed to be sad. You're allowed to cry, if tears come. And you're also allowed to not feel anything in particular.
[pause 2s]
Sometimes we learn to hide our sadness, to tuck it away quickly so we can keep going. Here, there's nothing to hide. No one is watching. There's only you, and this moment.
And if part of you thinks this is a bit pointless, or wonders whether you're really allowed to be sad over something so small, that part can stay too. There's no such thing as a small sadness.
[pause 2s]
Settle into a place where you feel sheltered. A couch, your bed, a corner of the floor with a cushion.
If you're a little cold, grab a blanket, a throw, a soft sweater. Sadness can make the body feel cold, and it's good to offer it some warmth.
Let your body sink into whatever is holding it. You don't have to sit up straight or put on a brave face.
[pause 2s]
Close your eyes if you like, or let your gaze rest on something soft.
Notice the places where your body is supported. The back of your head, your back, your legs. Let them hold a little of your weight, a little more with each out-breath.
[pause 4s]
Breathe the way you're breathing. Maybe your breath is short, or there are sighs. Let them come. A sigh is often the body setting down a little weight.
Feel the air come in...
[pause 3s]
Feel the air go out. Nothing to get right.
[pause 4s]
If your mind drifts into memories or thoughts, that's okay. You can gently come back to the movement of the air, without blaming yourself.
[pause 2s]
Now, if you feel like it, try to notice where the sadness lives in your body.

It often has favorite places. The throat, with a lump that tightens. The chest, heavy, as if something were resting on it. The eyes, stinging or burning. Sometimes the stomach, hollow, or the shoulders, slumping.
Take a little tour, without hurrying. And when you find a place where it's clearest, stay with it.
[pause 3s]
Notice its shape, its size, its density. Is it tight, heavy, empty, warm? Does it move, or is it still?
[pause 3s]
You don't need to understand it. Just look, with attention that's as gentle as you can make it.
If it feels like too much at any point, you can open your eyes, look around the room, and feel your feet. You're always free to step back.
If you can't find a specific place, that's okay. Sadness is sometimes everywhere and nowhere, like a grey color laid over the whole body. Then you can simply feel your whole body, just as it is.
[pause 4s]
Now let your breath move toward that place. As if each in-breath were bringing it a little air, a little space.
And on the out-breath, don't try to make it leave. Just let it exist. You can be here.
[pause 4s]
Often, we tense up around sadness, to contain it, so we don't fall apart. Is there that kind of tension around it right now, in your jaw, your forehead, your hands?
[pause 3s]
See if you can loosen, just a little, whatever is squeezing around it. The sadness can stay. It's only the struggle you're setting down.
Soften your forehead, as if you were smoothing out a sheet. Unclench your teeth, let your tongue rest. Open your hands, palms up if that's comfortable.
A body that's a little less tense lets what needs to pass, pass more easily.
[pause 4s]
If tears come, let them. There's nothing weak about them. They rise and fall like waves, and afterward the body is often a little calmer.
If nothing comes, that's fine too. There's no right way to be sad.
[pause 2s]
Thoughts sometimes come along with sadness. This will never pass. I should be over this by now. I'm too sensitive.
Notice them, like heavy clouds. They're part of the weather right now. They don't tell the whole truth about you, or about the future.
Emotions, even heavy ones, change over time. They have their own rhythm, like the seasons, and you don't have to hurry that rhythm along.
[pause 3s]
Now I'd like to offer you an image. Imagine that someone dear to you is sad, sitting on a bench, or on the edge of a bed.
You come and sit down beside them. You don't say, come on, it'll pass. You don't try to distract them or give them advice.
You're simply there. Your shoulder close to theirs. Maybe your hand on their back. You stay, without hurrying, for as long as it takes.
Feel what it's like to offer that kind of presence.
[pause 3s]
Maybe notice what happens in your own body as you picture this scene. Some softness, some warmth, a little tenderness. These are resources you already carry inside you.
Maybe you've lived this from the other side. Someone who stayed close to you on a hard night, without saying anything, and whose simple presence changed everything. Remember what that felt like.
[pause 4s]
And now, imagine that this person is you. That you can sit beside your own sadness, the way you would for someone you love.
Not to fix it. Just to keep it company. You, beside yourself.
What would the part of you that comforts say to the part of you that hurts? Maybe nothing. Maybe just, I'm staying.
Let those words, or that silence, do their work.
[pause 4s]
If it's comfortable, place a hand on your heart, or on the spot where the sadness is. Your other hand can rest on your belly, or on your cheek.
Feel the warmth of your hands. Their light weight. Many people find this gesture soothing, simple as it is, like a hug you give yourself.
And offer yourself a few words of support. Choose the ones that ring true for you.
[pause 2s]
This is a hard moment.
[pause 3s]
I'm not the only one who feels this. So many people know this kind of pain.
[pause 3s]
May I be gentle with myself, right now.
[pause 3s]
I'll take all the time I need.
[pause 3s]
If these phrases feel strange, just keep your hand where it is, and breathe beneath it. Sometimes the gesture speaks better than words.
This hand on the heart comes from self-compassion practices. It doesn't try to erase the pain. It reminds you that you can be on your own side, even in the hard moments.
[pause 3s]
Now, if you have the energy, one last question, to ask very gently. What is this sadness telling me about what matters to me?
[pause 3s]
We only grieve what we care about. A person we love. A bond that has been damaged. A project we believed in. A part of ourselves we've left behind.
Your sadness may be the trace of that attachment. The shadow cast by something precious.

If you've lost someone, this sadness speaks of the love that goes on, even when the person is no longer here. If it's a dream slipping away, it tells you how much it meant. Sadness and attachment are often two sides of the same coin.
Let whatever comes, come. A face, a place, a word. And if nothing comes, that's okay. You don't need an answer today.
[pause 4s]
Gently come back to your breath. To the feeling of your hand, if it's still there. To the warmth of the blanket.
The sadness may still be here. Maybe a little lighter, maybe the same. But you didn't leave it alone. You offered it your presence, and you offered that presence to yourself as well.
Notice what it's like to have been present with yourself for these few minutes. Even if it felt imperfect, it was a real act of care.
[pause 3s]
Take your time coming back. Move your fingers a little. Breathe a little more deeply.
You can stay warm and cozy for a while after this session, if you need to. Make yourself a cup of tea. Send a message to someone you trust. Step outside for some air, even for five minutes.
And if you can, eat something simple and warm today. Taking care of the body is also taking care of the heart.
Be patient with yourself in the days ahead. Sadness sometimes needs to come back a few times before it softens. You can return to this session whenever you feel the need.
[pause 2s]
Open your eyes when the moment feels right for you.
[pause 2s]

And if this sadness settles in for a long time, if it lasts for weeks or keeps you from living your daily life, please talk to a doctor or a health professional. Asking for help is also a way of taking care of yourself.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Worry appointment
script: [pause 1.5s]
Welcome to your worry appointment. The name might sound strange. Why make an appointment with the things that worry us?
[pause 1.5s]
Because worries have a habit of showing up whenever they like. In a meeting, in the shower, in the middle of a movie, at three in the morning. And every time, we get swept along.

The idea behind this technique, widely used in cognitive behavioral therapy, is simple. Instead of worrying all day long, you worry on purpose, for a limited time. And the rest of the time, you're allowed to tell your worries, not now, I'll see you at the next appointment.

Many people find that with a little practice, worries take up less room in their day. Ideally, you'd do this appointment every day at the same time, preferably in the late afternoon, and not right before bed.
Why not right before bed? Because your mind needs a little time to settle afterward. Your bed should stay a place for rest, not for sorting.
[pause 2s]
If you'd like, grab a sheet of paper and a pen, or open a note on your phone. Writing helps get worries out of your head. But you can also do all of this in your mind.
Sit in a way that keeps you alert but comfortable. Keep your eyes open if you're writing, or close them if you prefer.
[pause 2s]
Take a calm breath...
[pause 4s]
Plant your feet. Feel your back. The appointment begins.
[pause 3s]
For the next few minutes, you have permission to worry. Really. No need to talk yourself out of it, or to tell yourself it's no big deal.
Let all the worries that are spinning right now come up. The big ones, the small ones, the recurring ones, the new ones, the silly ones too.

Work. A project, a deadline, a tense relationship with a coworker. Money. A bill, an overdraft, an upcoming expense. Health, yours or a loved one's. Family, your relationship, your friends. Your home. The future.
[pause 2s]
Write them down, or name them silently, one by one. One line, a few words per worry. No details, no solutions for now. Just a list.
If a worry seems too embarrassing or too small to note, note it anyway. Every worry is welcome here. The more honest the list, the more useful the sorting will be.
If it starts to feel like too much, you can slow down, set your pen down, and feel your feet on the floor for a few seconds before carrying on.
[pause 4s]
Keep going. Are there any others, hiding behind the first ones?
[pause 2.5s]
Things you avoid looking at? If so, add them too.
[pause 3s]
Notice how your body reacts while you make this list. Maybe some tightening, a quickening. That's normal, and it will settle. Let your out breath lengthen a little.
[pause 3s]

Now look at your list as a whole. Sometimes just seeing your worries written down, in black and white, makes them smaller, or clearer. What was going round and round in your head fits, in the end, into a few lines.
[pause 3s]
Now you're going to sort each worry with one single question. Is this a real problem, happening now? Or a hypothetical problem, one that might happen someday?
A real problem is something like, my car is making a weird noise. I haven't answered that email. I have an unresolved argument with my sister. It's here, today.
A hypothetical problem often starts with what if. What if I lose my job. What if it's a serious illness. What if my kids don't turn out okay. It isn't happening. It might, perhaps, someday.
[pause 2s]
Go back through your list from the start, and for each worry, mark an R for real, or an H for hypothetical. If you're not writing, sort them in your mind, to the left or to the right.
A quick test can help. Can I do something about this in the next few days? If so, it's probably a real worry. If the answer is no, I can only wait or imagine, it's probably a hypothetical one.
[pause 4s]
Take your time. Some worries are a mix. What if my presentation goes badly, is hypothetical. But I haven't prepared my presentation yet, is real. You can separate them.
This sorting isn't a test. If you're unsure, put a question mark and move on. What matters is seeing more clearly, not being right.
[pause 3s]
Let's start with the real worries. For each one, look for a concrete next step. Not the whole solution, just the next step.
The car noise. Call the garage tomorrow morning. The waiting email. Reply in two lines at ten o'clock. The argument. Send a message suggesting you talk this weekend.
Make each step very precise. What, and when. If you're writing, note it next to the worry.
[pause 2s]

If the problem is huge, like a move or a conflict at work, break it down. The next step isn't resolve the conflict. It's write three sentences to prepare for the conversation. Small, doable, scheduled.
And if a real problem has no immediate solution, the step can be asking for help, or setting a time to think it over later.
Notice what it's like to turn a vague worry into a small, precise action. Often, the body relaxes a little as soon as it knows what it's going to do.
[pause 4s]

Now for the hypothetical worries. You can't solve these today, because they don't exist yet. Going over and over them doesn't stop them from happening. It just makes you carry their weight in advance.
And often, what we dread doesn't happen the way we imagined. Think of something you were worried about a year ago. Did it happen exactly that way?
[pause 3s]
And if something hard did happen, you faced it with the resources you had at the time.
Take them one by one. Simply acknowledge each one. This is a worry about the future. It's here because this matters to me.
Then let it be. If you're writing, you can draw a light line through it, or fold the page over on that side. If you're doing this in your mind, imagine placing it on a shelf.
You're not denying it. You're choosing not to deal with it now, because there's nothing to do with it, here, today.
[pause 4s]
If some hypothetical worries resist, ask yourself, is there one small, real thing I can do to prepare, or to take care of myself? If so, move it to the real side. If not, leave it on the shelf.
Over time, you may notice that some hypothetical worries come back often. They're old regulars. You can greet them, without throwing the door wide open.
[pause 2s]
The appointment is coming to an end. Let's close it, for real.

If you've been writing, fold your sheet in half, or close the note, and put it away in a drawer, a bag, somewhere separate. If you did it all in your head, imagine closing a notebook and setting it down on a table, far from you.
[pause 2s]
