Find yours. One short sentence you can come back to during the exam.
[pause 4s]
Take one last long out-breath. Feel your feet, your hands, your back.
[pause 4s]
Look around you. The others are probably just as nervous as you are. Everyone in this room is sharing this moment with you.
You don't have to be perfectly calm to do well. You just need to be present enough to read, think and write.
Your body is ready, your preparation is there, and you have a plan if you get stuck. The rest will happen on the page.
Go for it.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: When you're procrastinating
script: [pause 1.5s]
If you're listening to this, there's probably a task you keep putting off. Maybe for an hour, maybe for weeks.
[pause 1.5s]
Let's start with something simple. This isn't laziness, and it isn't a character flaw. Everybody procrastinates. Students, managers, artists, and very organized people too.
Often, procrastination has little to do with time or willpower. You put a task off because it stirs up something unpleasant. So you do something else instead, and for a while, that feels like relief.
Today, instead of forcing yourself or beating yourself up, let's look at this with curiosity.
[pause 2s]
Get comfortable. You can close your eyes, or let your gaze rest on the floor.
Take a slightly fuller breath...
[pause 3s]
And let it go, without effort.
[pause 4s]
One more. Feel your body on the chair, or the couch, wherever you are.
[pause 4s]
You don't need to feel motivated for this. You only need to be here, with whatever is going on inside you.
[pause 2s]
Now think of the task you've been avoiding. Bring it clearly to mind. The file on your desk, the email you haven't written, the form to fill in, the pile of laundry, the chapter to review.
See it as if it were right in front of you. Imagine you're just about to start it, right here, right now.
You don't have to actually start. Just imagining it is enough.
[pause 2s]
And notice what happens in your body. Not in your head. In your body.
Maybe a small tightening in your stomach. A heaviness in your chest. A sudden urge to pick up your phone. Your shoulders tensing, a sigh rising.
There's no right answer. Just notice what's there, even if it's subtle.
If you barely feel anything, notice the urge to move on to something else. That's useful information too.
[pause 3s]
Now try to put a word to what you're feeling. What emotion is hiding behind that reaction?
[pause 2s]
Maybe it's boredom. The task is dull and repetitive, and everything in you is asking for something more alive.
Maybe it's fear of failing, or of doing it badly. Fear of what others will think, or of your own judgment. As long as you don't start, you can't fail.
Maybe it's fog. You don't really know where to begin, or what done even looks like. And the mind hates vagueness.
Or maybe it's something else. Tiredness, irritation, a sense that it's unfair.
Choose the word that feels most accurate, and say it gently to yourself. Boredom. Fear. Fog. Or your own word.
[pause 3s]
Good. Simply naming an emotion often loosens its grip a little. It's no longer a vague cloud. It's something specific, something you can look at.
[pause 1.5s]
Now let's do the exact opposite of what procrastination does. Instead of running away from this feeling, you're going to stay with it for a few seconds.
Find the place in your body where it's strongest. And breathe with it. Imagine your breath reaching that spot, surrounding it, making a little room around it.
It doesn't need to disappear. You can let it be there, just for a moment.
[pause 4s]
Yes, it's unpleasant. But it's bearable. Maybe it shifts a little, or changes in intensity.
Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and as you breathe out, let a bit of space open up around it.
[pause 5s]
If it gets too intense, come back to your feet on the floor, or open your eyes. You're always in charge.
You've just done something important. You felt what you were avoiding, and you're still here. Discomfort isn't dangerous. It's just uncomfortable.
[pause 2s]
Now, back to the task. We're going to make it ridiculously small. So small that your mind can hardly argue with it.
Not, write the report. Instead, open the document and type the title.
Not, clean the apartment. Instead, pick up the three things lying on the table.
Not, review the chapter. Instead, read the first page and highlight one sentence.
Not, reply to that difficult email. Instead, write the greeting and one first sentence, even a clumsy one.
[pause 1.5s]
Find the tiny version of your task. The one that fits into two minutes. The one so small it almost makes you smile.
[pause 3s]
Got it? See yourself doing it. Your hands, the exact movement, the place where you are.
[pause 2s]
Here's the rule. Two minutes. No more commitment than that. If you want to stop after two minutes, you're allowed to. You'll have kept your promise.
Very often, the hardest part is the first minute. Once you're moving, momentum does the rest. And if that doesn't happen today, those two minutes still count. They're done.
Starting is often the part the mind dreads most. Once the first step is behind you, the task usually looks smaller than it did from the outside.
[pause 1.5s]
Make one simple commitment. Right after this session, with no transition, you'll do those two minutes. Not after a coffee, not after checking your messages. Straight away.
Say it to yourself. Right after this, two minutes.
[pause 3s]
And if the feeling comes back when it's time to start, which it probably will, you now know what to do. You recognize it, you make room for it for one breath, and you take the first step anyway.
[pause 1.5s]
Take one last breath. Feel your feet, your back, your hands.
[pause 3s]
Notice that you have nothing to prove. You just have one small thing to do.
Open your eyes, if they were closed. Your tiny task is waiting. Two minutes, now.
Go.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Visual anchor
script: [pause 1.5s]

This time, you're going to meditate with your eyes open. If closing your eyes makes you restless, or puts you to sleep, this practice is for you. It's also a way of meditating you can use at work, without anyone noticing.
[pause 1.5s]
Start by choosing a simple object in front of you. A mug, a plant, a pen, a stone, the flame of a candle if you have one. Ideally something still, at a comfortable distance, a little below eye level.
Take your time choosing it, and moving it into place if you need to.
[pause 3s]
Settle in so your head is upright and your neck relaxed. Your eyes don't need to stare hard. Your gaze is soft and resting, the way you'd watch the countryside from a train window.
You can blink as much as you need. We're not trying to stare without blinking, just to keep the object as a point of reference.
Take an easy breath...
[pause 3s]
and as you breathe out, let the small muscles around your eyes soften. Your forehead, your eyebrows, your eyelids.
[pause 3s]
There's nothing to get right here. Just looking, with a little more attention than usual.
[pause 2s]
Now look at your object as if you were seeing it for the very first time. As if you didn't know what it was for, or what it was called.
Start with its overall shape. Its outline. Is it rounded, angular, irregular?
[pause 2.5s]
Where does it end, and where does everything around it begin? Slowly trace the outline with your eyes, as if you were drawing it in one continuous line.
[pause 3s]
Then its colors. Not just white or green, but every shade. Where the color is lighter, where it deepens. Maybe tones you'd never noticed before.
If a word pops up, blue, beige, let it pass, and come back to what you actually see, beyond the word.
[pause 2s]
Now move in closer to the details, with your eyes only. A scratch, a small mark, the texture of the surface. Does it look smooth, grainy, matte, glossy?
[pause 2s]
Notice the shadows. Which side is the light coming from? How does the object's shadow fall across the table? Maybe its edges are sharp, or maybe they're soft and blurry.
And the reflections. A small point of light on the rim of a mug, the sheen on a leaf, the flicker of a flame that never stops moving.
Let your gaze explore slowly, unhurried, like a hand discovering the object with its fingertips.
[pause 4s]
At some point, you'll notice you're not really looking anymore. Your eyes are still open, but your mind is somewhere else. A shopping list, a conversation, a worry.
Or the mind starts commenting. It's a mug, I know what it is, I get it. That's very common too.
As soon as you notice, come back to the object. Pick one specific detail, and rest your gaze on it, like returning to the page where you left off reading.
No need to judge yourself. The mind wanders, you come back. That's the very movement of the practice.
You can even note where you went. Planning, remembering, worrying. One word, then back to the detail.
[pause 4s]
Keep exploring. If you feel you've seen everything, look again. There's always another shade, another angle, a speck of dust.
You might notice the image shifting slightly as you look at it for a long time. The edges blur, the colors seem to shimmer. That's normal, it's just your vision at work. Simply blink and come back.
[pause 3s]
Now, without moving your eyes, let your field of vision widen. Your gaze stays on the object, but your attention opens to everything around it.
The table, what's to the left, to the right. The top of your visual field, the bottom. All the way to the edges, where shapes go soft and blurry.
[pause 2s]
You see everything at once, without lingering on anything. A panoramic view, like a wide angle lens.
You can even feel your breathing and your hands resting at the same time, without your gaze leaving the object. Seeing and feeling, together.
[pause 2s]
Many people find this wide gaze soothing, and that it brings a sense of space. Is that true for you?
[pause 3s]
If a movement catches your attention, someone walking by, a screen lighting up, let it be part of the scene, without following it.
Stay in this open view for a few more moments.
[pause 5s]
Notice how this wide view resembles the attention a long task needs. Centered, but not tense.
[pause 1.5s]
And now, gently bring your attention back to the object. Like a zoom lens closing in. The edges become simple background again, and the object returns to the center.
Look at it again. Does it seem different from before? More present, sharper, more familiar? Or exactly the same? Whatever you see is fine.
[pause 2s]
Rest your gaze on a single detail, the one you like best. And stay with it for a few breaths.
[pause 6s]
This object, or any other, can become an anchor in your day. Between two emails, in the middle of a meeting, you can rest your gaze on one detail for thirty seconds, and come back to yourself.
[pause 2s]
Now close your eyes for a moment. Notice any image that may linger behind your eyelids. Notice your eyes resting.
[pause 4s]
Take a slightly fuller breath.
[pause 4s]
Then open your eyes again, slowly. Let the light come back in. Look around the room, and notice what you see now.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Unlock creativity
script: [pause 1.5s]
Stuck on a project? An idea that won't come, a problem that won't budge?
[pause 2s]
You may have noticed that the best ideas rarely show up when you force them. They tend to arrive in the shower, on a walk, while you're doing the dishes.
That's no accident. When we push hard, the mind tends to narrow. When it loosens up, it makes unexpected connections more easily. So that's what you're going to do now. Loosen up.
[pause 2s]
Get comfortable, sitting or lying down, whichever you prefer. Keep a pen and paper within reach, for the end.
Close your eyes, if that feels okay. Let the sound of the water settle around you. It flows, with no goal and no effort.
[pause 2s]
Take a big breath in through your nose...
[pause 3s]
and let it out through your mouth, with a gentle sigh.
[pause 5s]
One more. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and let go. Feel your shoulders drop.
[pause 4s]
If part of you is still in that file, in front of the screen, leave it there for now. It'll still be there in seven minutes.
Now let your breath come and go at its own pace. Like the stream. Nothing to steer.
[pause 3s]
Let's take a quick tour of your face. Your forehead, often furrowed when you're searching for something. Let it widen. Your eyebrows, your jaw. Let all of that soften a little.
A tense head tends to produce tense ideas. A relaxed face is already a step toward more flexibility.
[pause 3s]

Now put your question, or your project, into a single sentence. It doesn't need to be perfect. For example, how can I make this presentation come alive? Or, what's the right title for this piece? Or, how do we get unstuck on this problem with the team?
An open question often works better than a statement. Start with how, or what if, or what would.
Find your sentence, and say it to yourself, slowly.
[pause 4s]
Say it once more. Feel it, as if you were setting it down somewhere. On a table, or at the water's edge.
[pause 2s]
And now... let it go. Completely.
You don't have to think about it anymore. It's been set down. Your mind can keep working on it in the background, without you.
If it comes back, that's fine. Notice it, and gently set it down again.
Like letting go of a balloon. You watch it rise, without holding on.
[pause 4s]
Now open your attention to everything that's here. Without choosing anything in particular.
The sounds. The flowing water, the noises in the room, maybe a car in the distance.
The sensations. The weight of your body, the temperature of the air on your skin, your hands.
The breath, carrying on by itself.
[pause 2s]
There's nothing you need to do with any of it. Just let things come, and let them pass. As if you were sitting on a riverbank, watching leaves drift along the surface.
[pause 5s]
Notice how there's no effort here. No answer to find. Only this moment, as it is.
If you feel the urge to get back to work right away, to search, just notice it. Wanting to search. And come back to the sounds, to the water.
[pause 3s]
Now you're going to do something we usually try not to do. Let your mind wander. On purpose.
Usually in meditation, we come back to the breath. This time, let your mind go wherever it wants. A memory, an image, a color, a place, a conversation, a piece of music.

Follow it, the way you'd follow a cat through a garden, with no idea where it's heading. One thought leads to another, then another. Let the associations happen, even the strangest ones, even the ones that seem completely unrelated.
[pause 4s]

You can also wonder, without looking for an answer. How would a child see this? Or someone in a completely different line of work, a chef, a gardener, an architect? Let the images come, however far fetched.
Nothing is silly here, and nothing is off topic. You're simply daydreaming.
[pause 2s]
If you find yourself worrying, about a problem or an overdue task, that's no longer daydreaming. Come back to the water for a moment, then let your mind drift somewhere lighter.
[pause 6s]
Keep drifting. If you notice you've started thinking in a tense, analytical way, let yourself slip back into the daydream. Lighter. Looser.
If an image amuses you, play with it. Make it bigger, change its color, turn it upside down.
[pause 6s]
And if your mind becomes very calm, almost empty, that's fine too. Emptiness is often the space ideas need.
[pause 4s]
Now, very gently, without leaving this relaxed state, bring your question back. Just brush against it. As if you were glancing at it sideways, without looking at it head on.
Say it once, silently. And notice what shows up.
[pause 4s]
Maybe a word, an image, a feeling. A memory that seems totally unrelated. A half formed idea. Even another question.
Don't sort. Don't judge. Don't tell yourself that's rubbish, or that'll never work. Welcome whatever comes, the way you'd gather shells on a beach, without knowing yet which ones you'll keep.
If your inner critic wakes up, the one that says been done, too simple, ridiculous, thank it politely. It'll get its turn later, when it's time to sort. For now, it's playtime.
[pause 4s]
If nothing comes, that's normal too. The idea may arrive later, in the shower, on the bus, on a walk. You've planted something, and it will grow at its own pace.
Ask the question one more time, differently. What if... And let things come.
[pause 5s]
Maybe an idea appears from a completely different angle. Something that seems absurd sometimes holds a lead. Welcome it with curiosity. You'll evaluate later, not now.
[pause 2s]
How do you feel? Maybe lighter, more open, with a little pleasure in playing with ideas. Or maybe nothing special. That's fine too.
[pause 3s]
We'll come back soon. Take a deeper breath. Feel the weight of your body, the contact with the floor or the seat.
Start to move your fingers and toes a little.
[pause 2s]

And here's the most important part. As soon as you open your eyes, before doing anything else, write down everything that came up. A word, an image, a phrase. Even what seems pointless. Daydream ideas evaporate quickly, like dreams when you wake up.
Don't write it up, don't organize it. Just get it down, uncensored.
[pause 2s]
Open your eyes when it feels right for you. Pick up your pen. And let it flow, like the water.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Making a decision
script: [pause 1.5s]
You have a choice to make, and maybe you've been going around in circles for a while. Pros, cons, back to the pros. The more you think about it, the less clear it gets.

That's normal. When a decision weighs on us, the mind speeds up and hunts for the perfect answer. It compares, it anticipates, it imagines the worst. And often it ends up exhausted, without having decided anything.
[pause 2s]
Today we'll do it differently. First, slow down. Then listen to three sources of information. Your head, your body, and what matters to you.
One important note. You won't need to decide by the end of this session. The goal is to see more clearly. The decision will come when it comes.
[pause 2s]
Settle into a position where you feel steady. Back supported, feet on the floor, hands resting.
Close your eyes, or gently lower your gaze.
For a few minutes, the decision can wait. There's nothing you need to solve right now.
[pause 2s]
Let's start by slowing your breath. You'll breathe in through your nose for about four seconds, without forcing, then breathe out slowly for about six.
Breathe in...
[pause 3.5s]
and out, slowly.
[pause 5.5s]
Again. In...
[pause 3.5s]
and out, as if you were slowly letting the air out of a balloon.
[pause 5.5s]
Once more, at your own pace. If it feels too long, shorten it. And if you feel any discomfort, simply return to your natural breathing.
[pause 6s]
On the out-breath, let your belly soften, and your jaw too. A slow breath tells your body there's no immediate danger.
Now let your breathing go back to normal. Has something already slowed down a little? Your heart, your thoughts, that sense of urgency?
[pause 3s]
Urgency makes it feel as if you have to decide right now, this minute. But most decisions can wait a few calm minutes. You're giving yourself that time.
[pause 2s]
Now name your decision in one sentence. Simple and clear. For example, should I take this new job? Or, should I move, or should I stay?
If there are more than two options, pick the two main ones for this exercise. We'll call them option A and option B.
Say your sentence silently. Then give each option a short name. A word or two.
[pause 3s]
Start with your head, briefly. Let the main arguments run past, one or two for each option, without debating them. You already know them by heart.
Then set them down beside you, like files on a table. They're still available, but they're not the only information you have.
[pause 2s]
Let's begin with option A. Imagine you've chosen it. It's done. The decision is made, and you're living with it.
Picture yourself a few weeks from now. An ordinary morning. Where are you? What do you do when you get up? Who are you spending your day with?
Make the scene concrete. The places, the faces, the rhythm of your days. As if you were really there.
[pause 3s]
Now bring your attention to your body. Don't analyze, just observe. What happens when you step into this choice?
Maybe an opening in your chest, a sense of space, of lightness. Or maybe a knot in your stomach, a tight throat, shoulders tensing up.
Maybe a mix of both. Excitement tinged with fear, for example. That's common when a choice helps us grow.
Simply notice. And if you like, name one or two words to yourself. Light, tight, warm, heavy.
If nothing clear shows up, stay in the scene for another breath or two. Sensations are sometimes quiet, like a whisper.
[pause 3s]
Your body doesn't give you the answer on its own. But it offers information your head doesn't always see.
Now let that image dissolve. Come back to your breath for a few breaths, like washing your hands between two experiences.
Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and as you breathe out, let option A drift away. You're not losing it, just setting it aside.
[pause 4s]
Now on to option B. This time, imagine this is the one you chose. Not the other. This one.
Picture yourself in the same way, a few weeks from now. An ordinary morning. Where are you? What are you doing? Who's around you?
Take the time to step into this life, with as much detail as the first. If a thought keeps nagging, yes, but, note it without following it. It will be useful later.
[pause 3s]
And again, listen to your body. What changes? Is your breathing fuller, or shorter? Is there tension, release, relief?
Gently compare it with what you felt for option A. Without jumping to conclusions. Just notice the difference, if there is one.
And if both feel the same, or blurry, that's information too. Maybe the two options are equally good, or maybe you need to know more.
[pause 2s]
Come back to your breath for a few moments.
If your mind has drifted back into the arguments, that's normal. It loves doing that. Simply come back to the feeling of the air coming in and going out.
[pause 4s]
Now, another question, a deeper one. Set aside the pros and cons, and what other people might think.

Ask yourself, what really matters to me, in my life, right now? Not a goal, but a direction. Freedom, maybe. Security. Being close to the people I love. Learning. Creating. Being useful. Being honest with myself.
Let two or three words come. The ones that truly resonate, not the ones that would look good on paper.
[pause 3s]
Now look at your two options in the light of these values. Which one brings you closer to what matters to you? Which one looks more like the person you want to be?
It isn't necessarily the most comfortable option. Sometimes what matters takes courage. And sometimes, on the contrary, the simplest choice is the one that respects you most.
[pause 3s]
One last exploration. If you feel you can't decide yet, ask yourself what's missing.
A concrete piece of information? A number, a date, an answer from someone?
A conversation with someone you trust?
Simply time, to let things settle?

Or maybe permission to get it wrong. No decision is ever completely safe, and most can be adjusted along the way. Sometimes what's missing is simply accepting that some uncertainty will remain, whatever you choose.
Notice what's missing, if anything. And perhaps one small action to get it.
[pause 3s]
Now let all of this settle. You've listened to your head, your body, and your values. You've explored the question in a different way than going around in circles.
Maybe one option is becoming clearer. Maybe not yet. Both are fine.
You're under no obligation to decide now. Decisions often ripen in calm, once we stop forcing them. You can let this one find its way, on a walk, or overnight.
You can also set a time to decide. Tomorrow evening, or by the end of the week. It's often a relief to know when, even before you know what.
[pause 2s]
Take a deeper breath. Feel your body's points of support. Gently move your hands, your shoulders.
Open your eyes when it feels right for you. And if one option felt lighter or truer, write it down somewhere. It's a marker, not a verdict.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Meditating amid noise
script: [pause 1.5s]
We often imagine you need silence to meditate. A quiet room, a closed door, nobody around. But life rarely looks like that.
The open plan office, the train, the apartment with thin walls, the street under your window, the construction next door. If you wait for silence, you may be waiting a long time.
The good news is, you don't need it. Today, the sounds around you are going to become your meditation. Not an obstacle to get around, but the anchor itself.
If you're on public transport, keep an ear out for your stop. And of course, never practice with your eyes closed while driving.
[pause 2s]
Settle in however you can. Sitting or standing, it doesn't matter. Let your back lengthen a little, and your shoulders settle.
Close your eyes if you can, or lower your gaze toward the floor.
Take a slightly fuller breath...
[pause 3s]
and let it go.
[pause 4s]
One more. As you breathe out, let your hands and your jaw soften.
[pause 4s]
There's nothing to prepare. Your ears are already open. They're working all the time, even when you're not paying attention.
[pause 2s]
Now open your listening. There's no need to search. Sounds come to you on their own.
Start with the loudest, most obvious sounds. The ones that take up the most space.
Maybe voices, one conversation blending into others. An engine, a ringtone, a keyboard clattering, a building site, the hum of the ventilation.
Or the steady background sound you're hearing right now, like fine rain.
[pause 2s]
Let them arrive. Where do they come from? In front, behind, to the left, to the right, above you?
[pause 2.5s]
Notice their distance, too. Some are very close, almost touching you. Others arrive from far away, muffled, as if through a window. The space around you takes shape, just through your ears.
[pause 3s]
You don't have to like them. Just notice them.
Loud or soft, pleasant or not, every sound counts as an anchor.
[pause 2s]
Now go a little further. Behind those loud sounds, there are others. Quieter, more subtle. The ones we never hear because we never pay attention to them.
The hum of an appliance. A bird in the distance. The rustle of your clothes as you breathe. Your own breathing, perhaps. A ticking clock, a creak, a door somewhere.
As if you were turning down the volume on the foreground to hear the background.
[pause 4s]
Notice how rich the soundscape is. There are layers, distances, textures. Some sounds are continuous, others come and go.
You might also notice where your ear tends to go. Often it's drawn to voices. That's common. We're very tuned in to other people.
[pause 2s]
Now let's try something more subtle. Listen to a sound, any sound, without giving it a name.
Usually, as soon as we hear a noise, the mind sticks a label on it. Car. Coworker. Drill. And the label often comes with a judgment. Annoying. Unbearable. Him again.

This time, try to hear the sound before the label. As if you didn't know what it was. Just a sound. Its pitch, low or high. Its volume. Its rhythm. Its texture, rough or smooth. Like strange music you're hearing for the very first time.
[pause 3s]
If you like, pick a sound that lasts. A fan, an engine, this white noise. Follow it for a few moments. Is it really steady? Or are there small variations, ripples, rises and falls?
[pause 4s]
You'll probably notice the mind naming things anyway. That's its reflex. No problem. Notice the label, let it drop, and come back to the raw sound.
A sound rises, it lasts, it fades. Another takes its place. Nothing stays. Everything passes.
This coming and going is exactly what trains attention. Staying present while everything keeps moving.
You don't have to go looking for sounds, or hold on to them. You're simply here, and they pass through your space of listening, like people walking down a street.
Some pass quickly, some linger. Either way, you stay where you are.
[pause 3s]
Sometimes a sound triggers a reaction. A laugh that's too loud, an alarm, a motorbike, a phone call that goes on forever. And something in you tightens.
That's completely human. Irritation is part of the practice too.
When it happens, notice the reaction itself. Where is it in your body? A clenched jaw, a frown, a held breath, a rush of heat?
[pause 2.5s]
You can name it gently. Irritation. Then take one breath with it.
[pause 3s]
And come back to the sound. Not to the story about the sound, the one that says they could at least talk more quietly. Just the sound. Its volume, its rhythm, its texture.
[pause 3s]
Often, it isn't the noise itself that wears us out. It's the fight against the noise. Wanting it to stop. When you stop fighting, the sound may stay exactly the same, but it takes up less space.

You may also notice that the same sound can seem neutral one day and unbearable the next. The sound hasn't changed. Your state has. Tiredness, stress, hunger. That's useful to know, without blaming yourself.

If you work somewhere noisy, this is something concrete you can use. Instead of fighting every noise, you notice it, let it pass, and come back to your task. Just as here, you come back to the next sound.
[pause 2s]
If your mind has drifted into a thought, a list, a memory, that's normal. The next sound that arrives is an invitation to come back. There's always another one.
That's the real strength of this anchor. It's everywhere, all the time.
No app, no headphones, no silence required. Just what's already here.
[pause 3s]
Now listen even more closely. Between sounds, there are sometimes small gaps. A split second when a voice stops, when an engine fades away, before something else begins.
Even in a noisy place, these gaps exist. Little breaths in the soundscape.
Try to notice them. The moment just after a sound, before the next one. These small silences are often very brief. No need to catch them. Just be curious.
[pause 5s]
And notice, too, that all these sounds appear in a kind of listening space. A space that welcomes them all, loud and soft, pleasant and grating, without being damaged by any of them.
You, the one listening, are a bit like that space. Sounds pass through. You remain.
[pause 4s]
Stay a few more moments, listening. The full and the empty. The sounds, and the silences between them.
[pause 8s]
We'll finish soon. Take a deeper breath. Feel your body, its points of contact, the floor under your feet.
Let the sounds carry on around you, without changing anything.
[pause 2s]
Open your eyes, if they were closed. Look at where you are.
[pause 2s]
The noise is still there. But maybe your relationship with it has shifted a little. It's no longer just something that bothers you. It's something you can listen to.

Next time you're somewhere noisy, you can remember this. No need to escape. Just listen, one sound after another. At work, on the train or at home, a few seconds of listening are enough to come back to yourself.
[pause 1.5s]
Before you get on with your day, pick one sound from your usual surroundings. The coffee machine, the printer, the street. It can become your cue to come back to listening, just for a second.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Your inner compass
script: [pause 1.5s]
There are times when everything speeds up. The days blur together, the lists grow longer, and we run on autopilot. We do a lot, but we're no longer quite sure why.
This session is a pause to find your compass again. Not to add one more goal, but to remind yourself what truly matters to you. What gives you a direction, even when the path is unclear.
[pause 1.5s]

A quick note before we begin. A goal is something you tick off, like getting a degree or finishing a project. A value is a way of moving forward, like being caring, curious, or honest. You can live it today, in a tiny action, even when your goals are still far away.
[pause 2s]
Take a moment to settle in. Sitting or lying down, in a comfortable position you can hold for a while. You might want a pen and paper nearby, for the end.

Feel the weight of your body, the places where it touches the floor or the seat. Let your shoulders drop, your jaw loosen. You don't have to produce anything in these minutes. Just listen to what comes.
Close your eyes if that feels good.
[pause 2s]
Let the sounds of the forest settle around you. The leaves, the birds, the air moving between the trees.
For these few minutes, the rest of your list can wait. It will still be there afterward, and you might see it differently.
[pause 2s]
Take a slightly deeper breath. Let the air fill your belly, then your chest...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out slowly, letting your body settle.
[pause 5s]
Once more. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and out, more slowly.
[pause 5s]
Now let your breath find its natural rhythm. Simply notice the movement of breathing, somewhere in your body. The belly, the chest, or the nostrils.
For the next few minutes, this breath will be your place to come back to. If you get lost in thought, or an emotion feels like too much, you can always return to it.
This isn't an exercise in hard thinking. Let the answers come on their own, rather than building them.
[pause 3s]
Now let a memory come up. A moment when you felt fully yourself. Alive, in the right place, in tune with who you are.

It doesn't have to be a big moment. It can be very simple. A conversation where you were truly honest. An afternoon spent helping someone. A project you threw yourself into, heart and soul. A walk with a friend. A time you dared to say no. A meal where you made everyone around the table laugh.
Let whatever memory comes, come. No need to look for the best one. The first one is often the right one.

If nothing comes, that's okay. Think of a recent moment when you were proud of yourself, not for a result, but for the way you acted. Or think of someone you admire. What touches you about them? Often, what we admire in others says something about our own values.
[pause 4s]
Now step into this memory. Where were you? What time of day was it, what season? Who was there?
[pause 3s]
Find the details again. The light, the sounds, the smells. What you were doing with your hands. What you were saying, or not saying.
And notice how you felt. Maybe a warmth in your chest, a sense of lightness, of momentum, of rightness.
Take your time. There's no rush to move on. Let the memory become as vivid as it wants to be.
Let those sensations come back a little, now, in your body.
[pause 5s]
Now ask yourself what qualities were present in that moment. Not what you achieved, but the way you were.
Was there generosity? Courage? Curiosity? Honesty? Creativity, presence, humor, care for others, freedom, perseverance?
Was this moment about connection with others? About learning? Adventure? Fairness? Beauty?
[pause 2s]
Let two or three words come. The ones that ring true. Keep them in mind for later.
[pause 3s]
These qualities didn't depend only on the circumstances. They were in you that day, and they still are today, even if everyday life sometimes buries them.
You may already know them. But finding them again in a specific memory brings them back into focus, like a photo getting sharp again.
[pause 2s]
Now let this memory gently fade. Come back to your breath for a few breaths. Listen to the forest. Feel your body resting.
[pause 5s]
If your mind has wandered into the past, into regrets or comparisons, that's normal. Notice it, and come back to the breath, to the forest.
[pause 3s]
Now let's take a little trip through time. It's an exercise of imagination. If at any point it feels uncomfortable, you can simply come back to your breath.

Imagine you're celebrating your eightieth birthday. You've lived a long life. The people who matter to you have gathered for the occasion. Maybe in a garden, a big hall, a family home. Choose the place you like.
See the scene. The tables, the light, the faces. Family, friends, maybe colleagues, people you've crossed paths with who made a difference.
Come closer. Notice the atmosphere. Laughter, glasses clinking, maybe some music. You're there, with a few more wrinkles, surrounded by people. Take the time to look at the faces, one by one.
[pause 4s]
At some point, someone stands up to speak about you. Someone who knows you well. They're going to say a few words about the person you've been.
Not about what you owned, or your titles, or your salary. About who you were for others, and for yourself.
What would you like them to say? If you could choose their words, which would you choose?
[pause 2s]
Maybe, we could always count on you. Or, you never stopped learning. Or, with you, we felt free to be ourselves. Or, you did things with heart, even the small ones.
Or, you knew how to listen. You were there when things were hard.
Listen to what comes. Let this person speak, in your imagination.
[pause 4s]
Maybe someone else takes the floor. A child, a lifelong friend, a colleague. What do they say about you?
[pause 4s]
Notice what it feels like in your body to hear these words. Maybe some emotion, a lump in your throat, a smile. Welcome whatever is here, gently.

Notice, too, what you don't hear. People rarely wish to hear that they always answered their emails within the hour, or never took a day off. That contrast can be revealing. It shows the gap between what keeps us busy and what truly matters to us.
Day to day, the urgent tends to take up the most room. This moment is about giving the important its place back.
[pause 3s]
Now bring it all together. The memory from earlier, the qualities that were present. And the words you heard at this celebration.
What keeps coming back? What are the two or three words that sum up what matters most to you?
[pause 3s]
These are your values. Not rules to follow, or goals to tick off. More like directions. Like north on a compass. You never actually reach it, but it tells you which way to walk.
Choose your words. Two or three. Say them to yourself, slowly.
If several words are similar, group them together. If you're torn between two, keep both for now. There's no perfect list, and your values can change over the course of your life.
[pause 4s]
How does it feel to hear them? Do they ring true?
[pause 2s]
If one of them doesn't really speak to you, you can change it.
A value that fits often brings a small echo in the body, a sense of, yes, that's it.
[pause 3s]
Now look at your current life in the light of these values. Your typical week. Your work, your relationships, your free time, the way you take care of yourself.
Where are you already living in line with them? Even a little. Take a moment to acknowledge that. It matters.
[pause 4s]
And where has your life drifted away from them? Where have autopilot, stress, and obligations pulled you off course?
Look at this without judging yourself. With kindness, the way you would for a friend. Everyone drifts. It's human. Life moves fast, and the constraints are real.
If a harsh voice starts up, the one that says you should have, you can thank it, and come back to curiosity.
The gap isn't a failure. It's information. It shows you where you could come back to.

Maybe you care about connection with the people you love, but your evenings disappear in front of a screen, exhausted. Maybe you care about creativity, but your days leave no room to create. Simply notice. One or two places are enough.
[pause 4s]
Now, one last question. What would be one small step, this week, to bring you closer to one of these values?

Not a life overhaul. A tiny, concrete step. Calling someone you love. Saying what you think in a meeting. Taking an hour for a project close to your heart. Turning down a request that doesn't fit you. Walking outside for twenty minutes, without your phone.
The smaller the step, the more likely it is to happen. And a step taken is worth more than a big plan you keep putting off.
What would your step be? Choose just one, something you can do in the next seven days.
[pause 4s]
Imagine yourself doing it. Where, when, with whom. Make it concrete.

And if an obstacle comes up, tiredness, lack of time, the fear of bothering someone, what could you do? Plan an even smaller version, just in case. A message instead of a call. Ten minutes instead of an hour.
And notice how it feels to see yourself acting on what matters to you.
[pause 4s]
Now come back to your breath. Let everything that came up settle inside you.
[pause 3s]
Notice how you feel now. Maybe calmer, more aligned, or a little stirred up. All of it is welcome. Reconnecting with what matters can be moving.

Your compass is here. It has always been here, even when you weren't looking at it. On overloaded days, you can ask yourself, what really matters, here, right now? No need to turn your life upside down. One direction, one step, then another.
These values help you focus, too. When everything seems urgent, they help you choose what to do first, and what to say no to.
[pause 2s]
Take a deeper breath. Feel the places where your body is supported.
[pause 3s]
Listen to the sounds of the forest for one more moment. Then to the sounds of the room around you.
[pause 3s]
Gently move your hands, your feet. Stretch if you'd like.
When it feels right for you, open your eyes. And if you can, take that piece of paper and write down your values, and the small step you chose. Written words tend to stay with us longer.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Open awareness
script: [pause 1.5s]
Welcome to this practice of open awareness. If you've practiced attention to the breath before, you know the idea of an anchor. A single point you keep coming back to.
Today, we'll start from there, then gradually widen, until you're welcoming everything that appears. Sensations, sounds, thoughts, emotions.
We won't choose an object anymore. We'll let experience come as it is, without holding on to it or pushing it away.
[pause 2s]
This is a subtler practice. It takes a bit of getting used to, and it's normal to get lost in it. Each time that happens, you'll have a simple way to find your bearings again.

Why this practice? With focused attention, you learn to steady the mind. With open awareness, you learn something else. To see what's happening inside you while it's happening, without immediately being swept along.
Noticing irritation the moment it arises, for example, rather than ten minutes later.
[pause 2s]
Settle into a stable, alert posture. Back upright, without stiffness. Shoulders relaxed, hands resting. Face soft, eyes gentle.
Posture matters a little more than usual here. Without a specific object, the mind tends to doze off or daydream. An upright back helps you stay present.
[pause 2s]

Take a moment, too, to leave behind whatever you were doing just before. The tasks, the conversations, the screens. They'll still be there later. For the next few minutes, you have nowhere else to be.
Close your eyes, or keep a low, diffuse gaze.
There's nothing to get right in these fifteen minutes. Just being here, and seeing what happens.
[pause 2s]
Take a few fuller breaths to arrive. Breathe in through your nose...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out slowly.
[pause 5s]
Once more, letting the out-breath settle you a little further.
[pause 5s]
Feel the air a little cooler coming in, a little warmer going out.
Then let the breath return to its natural rhythm.
[pause 3s]
Let's begin with the anchor you know. Find the place where the breath is clearest. The nostrils, the chest, or the belly.
Rest your attention there, simply. The in-breath, the out-breath. The movement coming and going.
[pause 4s]
For a few moments, let your attention steady itself on this point. If the mind wanders, bring it back, as usual. No need for perfection. We're just building a base.
Steady attention isn't tense attention. Hold it the way you'd hold a small bird in your hand. Firmly enough that it doesn't fly away, gently enough not to crush it.
If your mind is very busy today, stay a little longer with the breath before widening. There's no rush to open up.
[pause 6s]
Feel the steadiness of the breath. It's here, reliable, in every moment. It will be your refuge throughout this practice. If at any point you feel lost, you'll know where to come back to.

Notice what it's like to have an anchor. A kind of stability, a center. It's on this stability that the openness can rest. Without it, you scatter. With it, you can welcome everything without being carried away.
If a word helps, note gently, in... out. Then let the words fade.
[pause 5s]
Now, without leaving the breath, let your attention widen to the whole body.
As if your flashlight, until now pointed at a single spot, became a soft light that fills the whole room.
Feel your body sitting, as a whole. The weight on the chair or cushion. Your feet on the floor. Your hands resting.
[pause 3s]
And let sensations come, wherever they appear. You don't need to seek them out one by one, as in a body scan. Simply notice the ones that show up on their own.
A tingling in your hands. Pressure in your back. The warmth of your palms. An itch. Tension in your neck. The touch of your clothes.
And subtler sensations. The breath gently moving the fabric on your chest. Your pulse, somewhere, perhaps in your hands or your neck. Air on your bare skin.
[pause 5s]
A sensation appears. It lasts a while. It changes, or disappears. Another takes its place.
The breath is still here, in the middle of it all. One sensation among others.
Let your attention wander wherever it's called, without clinging to anything.
[pause 3s]
Feel how attention can be both wide and precise. Wide as an entire room, and yet able to notice the slightest tingle.
If you notice you've started searching the body, actively hunting for sensations, relax. Let the sensations come and knock at the door instead.
If a sensation is unpleasant, you can notice it with the same openness. Tension. Discomfort. And see how it changes. If it becomes too strong, you can move, mindfully.
Notice too that the body isn't a solid block. Up close, it's a collection of constantly changing sensations. Lively areas, areas that are almost silent. Nothing is fixed.
[pause 5s]
Now open up your listening as well. Let sounds enter your field of attention.
Nearby sounds. Your breathing, a creak, the rustle of clothing.
More distant sounds. The street, a neighbor, a car, the wind, a bird.
You don't need to look for them. They arrive. You receive them.
[pause 4s]
A sound arrives, and for a moment it fills everything. Then it's gone, and something else takes its place.
Notice the silences too, if there are any, between sounds. They're part of the landscape, just as much as the noise.
Sounds and bodily sensations now share the same space. Nothing is more important than anything else. A sound may appear, then a sensation, then the breath, then another sound.
[pause 5s]
Notice how sounds arise, last a moment, then fade away. Just like sensations. Everything appears, and everything passes.

If a sound feels pleasant, notice the wish to hold on to it. If it feels unpleasant, notice the wish for it to stop. That small preference is also something that appears. You can watch it pass, like everything else.
There's no clear boundary between inside and outside. A sound from the street and a sensation in your hand show up in the same way. They appear in your experience.
If you catch yourself following a sound, picturing the car, the person talking, that's the mind telling a story. Come back to the sound as it is, then open again.
[pause 4s]
Now, a more delicate step. Let thoughts become part of what you're observing too.
Usually in meditation, when a thought appears, you notice it and return to the anchor. This time, the thought itself becomes an object of attention, like a sound or a sensation.
An image appears. A memory. A plan for tomorrow. A comment about the practice. A phrase going round and round.
[pause 3s]
Try to see the thought as an event. Something that appears in your mind, lasts a little while, and leaves. Without following it. Without stepping into its story.
You can use a light, quiet note. Thinking. Planning. Remembering. Imagining. A gentle label, then let it pass.
You can even try to catch a thought at the very moment it arises. Where does it come from? It pops up, without warning. And where does it go when it disappears?
No need to answer. Just be curious.
[pause 5s]
It's a bit like sitting by the side of a road, watching the cars go by. You see them, you notice their color, their speed. But you don't get in.
And if you do get into a car, if a thought carries you off for a while, that's okay. When you notice, you step out, and find yourself back at the side of the road.
No need to scold yourself for getting in. Just step out.
[pause 3s]
You may notice that some thoughts are words, like an inner voice. Others are images, scenes. Some are very clear, others barely sketched. All of them pass.
Sometimes there's no thought at all for a moment. A small gap, a stillness. Notice that too, without clinging to it. It passes, like everything else.
[pause 5s]
Emotions may appear as well. Impatience, boredom, a hint of sadness, joy, peacefulness. They often have a color in the body. Warmth, heaviness, tightness, lightness.
Welcome them in the same way. There's impatience. There's calm. No need to change them, or understand them. They come, and they go, like everything else.
You might notice that emotions rarely stay exactly the same for long. Even strong ones shift, swell, and soften.
You may also notice how an emotion changes when you look at it this way. Sometimes it swells for a moment, then dissolves. Or it stays, but takes up less space.
[pause 3s]
Notice the nuance. Not, I am impatient. But, there is impatience. That small shift leaves a little room. The emotion is here, and you can see it.

If a difficult emotion shows up, a worry for example, you can come back to the breath and your points of contact for as long as you need. Welcoming doesn't mean putting up with everything. You're always free to steady yourself first.
[pause 5s]
Everything is here now. The breath. Sensations. Sounds. Thoughts. Emotions. Everything appears and disappears in the same space.
Nothing to choose. Nothing to hold on to. Nothing to push away.

You're no longer directing your attention like a spotlight. You're more like a mirror, reflecting whatever passes in front of it without holding on. The mirror has no preferences. It welcomes light and shadow alike.
[pause 6s]
And now, if you can, notice the space itself. What welcomes all of this. The awareness that knows there's a sound, that knows there's a thought.
It doesn't get agitated when thoughts are agitated. It doesn't make a sound when sounds are loud.
Like the sky. Clouds pass, storms pass, the sky remains.
[pause 6s]
Simply rest here. In the knowing.
[pause 8s]
Nothing to do. Just being aware.
Breath, sounds, thoughts. Everything passes. You remain.
[pause 10s]
If you notice you've been carried away, by a thought, a daydream, or a bit of drowsiness, that's completely normal. This practice is subtle. Without a specific object, the mind easily drifts.
Here's what you can do. First, come back to the breath. A few breaths on your anchor. Just long enough to find some stability again.
Then, when you feel settled again, gently open back up. The body, the sounds, the thoughts, whatever shows up.
The breath first, then the opening. You can go back and forth like this as many times as you need. It's not a failure. It's the very way to practice.
[pause 3s]

Over time, this back and forth becomes smoother. You learn to sense the moment when openness turns into scattering, and to return to the center before being completely swept away. It's learned practice by practice, without forcing.
A useful marker. If you're no longer quite sure what you're observing, that's often a sign it's time to come back to the breath for a while.
[pause 2s]
I'm now going to stay very quiet, with just a few words now and then. Stay open to whatever appears. And if you get lost, the breath, then the opening.
[pause 10s]
Body, sounds, thoughts. Whatever comes, let it come. Whatever goes, let it go.
[pause 8s]
You're still here, sitting, breathing. Where is your attention right now?
[pause 3s]
Don't correct anything. Simply notice. Then open up again.
[pause 8s]
If you drifted for a long time without realizing it, smile inwardly. It happens to everyone who practices, even after years. The breath, then the opening.
[pause 8s]
Maybe there were moments of great clarity. Maybe there were also lots of thoughts. Both are part of the practice. There's no such thing as a good session or a bad one.
What matters is the quality of your attention. Curious, open, without judgment. That's something you can come back to at any moment.
Notice that, even in the midst of agitation, something in you always knew what was happening. That presence never really disappears. We forget it, and then we find it again.
[pause 4s]

Take a moment to notice the state you're in now. Maybe a sense of space, of lightness. Maybe tiredness, or restlessness. There's nothing to keep and nothing to chase away. It's simply what's here, and you know it.
[pause 4s]
Gently, begin to come back toward the breath. A familiar anchor, to prepare you to return. Feel a few breaths, in the place where you feel them best.
[pause 6s]
Then feel your whole body. Its weight, its points of support, its shape in space. Let the sounds of the room come back to the foreground.
[pause 3s]
Take a deeper breath. Move your fingers, your toes, your shoulders. Stretch if you'd like.
[pause 3s]
You may feel yourself shifting from a very open awareness to a more focused one, the kind you'll need to take action.
[pause 2s]
This open way of seeing can stay with you through your day. In a tense moment, you can remember that thoughts and emotions pass, like sounds and clouds. You don't have to get into every car.
For example, before replying to a message that irritates you, take one breath, and notice. There's irritation. That simple observation often leaves you free to choose your response.

At work, too. When a task takes sustained effort, open awareness helps you spot tiredness or irritation before it takes over. Then you can take a real break, instead of pushing through or drifting off without realizing it.
And nothing stops you, on a busy day, from giving yourself thirty seconds of this openness. Feeling your body, hearing the sounds, watching thoughts go by. Then picking up where you left off.
[pause 2s]
When it feels right for you, open your eyes. Let your gaze take in the room, as widely as you welcomed everything else.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: The first coffee
script: [pause 1.5s]
You've got a cup in your hands, or you're about to pick one up. Coffee, tea, hot water, a plain glass of water... anything works.
For the next five minutes, this drink is your meditation. Nothing else to do but drink it, properly.
[pause 1.5s]
If your phone is in front of you, turn it face down, or move it a little further away. Your messages can wait for the length of one cup.
Sit down if you can. Feet on the floor, back supported.
[pause 2.5s]
Hold the cup in both hands. Wrap them all the way around it, fingers almost touching.
Let a first breath out, a long one, like a sigh that says, right, here I am.
[pause 4s]
And another, if you like. Your shoulders drop a little, hands still resting around the cup.
[pause 4s]
Feel the warmth in your palms. Where is it strongest?
[pause 2.5s]
Maybe in the hollow of your hand, maybe at your fingertips. Notice how it spreads, up into your wrists, sometimes as far as your forearms.
[pause 2s]
Notice the weight of the cup, too. Its texture. Smooth, a little rough, a tiny flaw in the glaze, the curve of the handle.
These are things you touch every single day, without ever really feeling them.
[pause 3s]
Now bring the cup up toward your face, without drinking just yet.
Feel the steam on your skin, under your nose, on your lips.
[pause 2s]
Breathe in slowly through your nose. Let the aroma in.
No need to fill your lungs. A slow, light breath is enough for the scent to arrive.
[pause 3s]

What can you smell? Something roasted, toasty, maybe a little chocolatey. Or something floral and grassy, if it's tea. And if it's water, almost nothing... and that almost nothing is something you can notice too.
[pause 2s]
Breathe in again, more softly. Sometimes a second note appears, quieter than the first.
[pause 3s]
Notice what's happening in your mouth as well. Saliva gathering, your body getting ready. It already knows what's coming.
[pause 2s]
Now, the first sip. A small one. Hold it in your mouth for a moment before you swallow.
Feel the temperature first. Hot, scalding, lukewarm.
Then the taste. Where does it land first? The tip of your tongue, the sides, the back?
[pause 2.5s]
Bitter, sweet, sharp, smooth... You don't need the right word. Just taste.
[pause 2s]
And when you're ready, swallow. Follow the path it takes. Down your throat, then that warmth sliding behind your breastbone, all the way to your stomach.
[pause 2s]
That small bit of attention changes everything. The same sip, gulped down over email, leaves no trace at all.
Stay a moment with the aftertaste. Whatever is left on your tongue once the sip is gone.
[pause 3s]
Put the cup down, or keep it in your hands, and look up.
If there's a window, look outside. The sky, its exact color this morning. A rooftop, a tree, a building across the street, someone walking past.
If there's no window, look at the light in the room. Where it falls, what it touches.
No need to think about what you see. Just look, as if for the very first time.
[pause 4s]
Second sip. Is it different from the first? It often is. A little less hot, the flavor a little more present.
[pause 2s]
And maybe, somewhere in the background, part of you is getting impatient.
An urge to check the time. To run through today's list. To finish quickly and get on with things.
That's completely normal. In the morning, the mind loves to get ahead of itself.
Just notice that urge to hurry. You can even say to it, silently, I see you.
Then come back to the cup. To the warmth in your hands. That's all.
[pause 3s]
Take another sip or two, at your own pace. A sip, a glance outside. A sip, a breath.
Each time your mind races off toward the day ahead, the cup is right here to bring you back.
[pause 4s]
Notice how you feel now, compared to when you started. Maybe a little more settled. Maybe much the same. Both are fine.
[pause 2s]
What you just did, you can do again tomorrow. And the day after.
You have a drink every morning anyway. The moment is already part of your routine. All you need to add is your attention.
Even three mindful sips are a real practice. A way of starting the day by actually being in it, instead of already chasing after it.
[pause 1.5s]
Finish your cup however you like. And when you get up, take a little of this calm with you.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Waking up anxious
script: [pause 1.5s]
You woke up with that knot in your stomach. Your heart a little fast, your mind already racing, before you've even put a foot on the floor.
If that's how it is this morning, you're in the right place. And it's one of the most common ways to wake up.
[pause 2s]
Notice one thing, to begin with. Nothing has happened yet. The day hasn't started. For now, there's just you, here, and this feeling.
You can stay lying down or sit up, whichever you prefer. Keep your eyes open, resting on something calm. The ceiling, a corner of the wall, the light at the window.
[pause 2s]

A quick word about what's going on. In the morning, your body is starting up. To pull you out of sleep, it naturally turns up its level of activation. Your heart speeds up a little, your mind becomes alert.
That's a normal process, and it's there to help you get going.

But when you're going through a busy or difficult stretch, that start up can feel a lot like worry. Your body is on alert, and your mind goes looking for a reason. The ten o'clock meeting, the email you haven't answered, yesterday's conversation.
[pause 2s]
So what you're feeling isn't necessarily a message about your day. Partly, it's just your body waking up a little too loudly.
Just knowing that can ease things a bit. You don't have to work out what's wrong right away. You can look after your body first.
[pause 2s]
Let's help it turn the volume down. Place one hand on your belly, just below your navel. The other can rest on your chest, or on the bed.
Feel the warmth of your hand. Its weight. It's there, and it isn't going anywhere.
[pause 2s]
Breathe in normally through your nose. No need to take in a lot of air...
[pause 3s]
Then breathe out slowly through your mouth, as if you were cooling a spoonful of hot soup. Longer than the in breath.
[pause 6s]
Again. Breathe in simply...
[pause 3s]
and let the out breath stretch out, easy, all the way to the end.
[pause 6s]
Under your hand, your belly sinks back down.
Notice the small release that often comes at the end of the out breath, in your shoulders or your jaw.
[pause 2s]
Why the out breath? Lengthening it sends your body a signal of safety. A bit like gently easing your foot off the accelerator.

Keep going at your own pace. The in breath stays natural, and it's the out breath that grows longer. If it helps, you can count silently, giving the out breath a couple of counts more than the in breath.
If it feels difficult, or you feel dizzy, just go back to your normal breathing. There's nothing to get right.
[pause 6s]
Now look at the anxiety a little more closely, without diving into it. The way you'd glance out the window to check the weather.
You can give it a simple name. Worry. Tension. Dread about the day. Whatever word fits.
Naming it silently is already a tiny step back from it.
[pause 2s]
Then find where it lives in your body. Your stomach? Your throat? Your chest? Your jaw?
[pause 3s]
Notice its shape. Is it a weight, a knot, a restlessness, a heat?
You don't have to make it go away. It can stay right there, while your hand keeps breathing along with you.
[pause 3s]
Now, a useful distinction. On one side, what's actually going to happen today. On the other, what your mind is busy imagining.
Think about what's on your mind. Then ask yourself, what do I know for certain, right now, concretely?
[pause 3s]
Maybe, I have a meeting at two o'clock. That's a fact.
And then there's the story wrapped around it. It's going to go badly. I won't cope. Everyone will see. Those are scenarios. Guesses your mind produces, especially when your body is on alert.
[pause 2s]
You don't have to argue with these thoughts. Just recognize them. Ah, that one's a scenario.
And come back to the fact, which is usually smaller, simpler, and more doable.
[pause 3s]
There's another truth here too. You've already made it through days you were dreading. And here you are.
This morning, you don't need to have all the answers before you get up. You only need the next step.
So we're not going to plan the whole day. We're going to choose one thing. The very first, and the smallest possible.
[pause 2s]
Drink a glass of water. Open the window and feel the fresh air on your face. Put on your slippers. Switch on the kitchen light.
Pick one. Whichever feels easiest, right here, right now.
[pause 3s]
Picture yourself doing it. The cool glass in your hand, or the air drifting into the room.
This tiny step matters more than it seems. It brings your body back into concrete action, where worry has less of a grip.
[pause 3s]
Before you get up, take two more breaths with that long out breath. Hand on your belly.
[pause 8s]
Has anything shifted, even slightly? Sometimes the knot loosens a little. Sometimes it stays, and that's okay too. You can get up and take it with you.
[pause 2s]
If anxious mornings like this come back very often or weigh on your daily life, it's worth talking to a health professional.
For this morning, there's only one thing to do. That first small step. Then the next one. One thing at a time.
Okay. Sit up slowly, put your feet on the floor, and go do your first small thing.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Preview your day
script: [pause 1.5s]
This morning, before the day sweeps you along, let's take a quick tour of it. The way you'd look at a route on a map before setting off.
The idea isn't to plan everything. It's to spot the tricky stretch, and to arrive there with a plan.
It's not about worrying ahead of time. Quite the opposite. A moment you've already looked at squarely is often less scary than one you avoid imagining.
[pause 2s]
Sit down, back supported, feet flat. You can close your eyes, or rest your gaze softly on a point in front of you.
We'll take three easy breaths. In through the nose...
[pause 3s]
and out, a little more slowly.
[pause 4s]
Once more. Feel the air coming in...
[pause 3s]
and your body settling into the chair as you breathe out.
[pause 4s]
One last one, at your own pace. Then let your breathing carry on by itself.
[pause 4s]
Feel what's supporting you. Feet on the floor, thighs on the seat, back against the chair. This is your base. You can come back to it at any moment.
If your mind is already busy this morning, that's normal. It has a lot on its plate. This exercise gives it some structure. We look, we choose, we prepare.
[pause 2s]
Now run through your day in your head. Quickly, like a film on fast-forward. No need for detail.
Start with the rest of your morning. Shower, breakfast, getting dressed. Maybe a commute. The street, the bus, the train, the car.
Then arriving. At work, at school, or at your desk if you work from home. The first tasks, the first conversations.
Move on to lunchtime. Where will you eat? Who with?
[pause 2s]
Then the afternoon. Meetings, calls, things that are due.
And the end of the day. Heading home, the evening, the moment you finally put your bag down.
Notice how many different moments fit into a single day. It's rarely just one big block.
If some hours are hazy, that's fine. Stick to the main stages. And as you pass over each one, notice how you feel. Neutral, curious, tense, impatient.
[pause 3s]
As you skimmed through, one moment may have caught your attention. The one where you felt a slight tightening, a flinch, an inner oh no.
It might be a meeting, a call you're dreading, a delicate conversation, a big task, or simply the evening rush.
Pick just one. Ideally something moderately difficult, not the worst thing in your week.
Place it. What time is it? Where are you? Who's there?
[pause 3s]
Notice how your body reacts just from thinking about it. Shoulders creeping up, stomach tightening, jaw clenching. That's information, nothing more.
Before going further, let one long out-breath soften whatever tensed up. Shoulders dropping. Jaw loosening.
[pause 4s]
Now let's rehearse that moment together. Like an athlete picturing the race before the start.
See yourself arriving in that situation. This time, pay attention to your posture. Your back is upright, your feet steady on the ground. Your shoulders are low. Your hands relaxed.
Your breathing is slow. Before walking in, or just as it begins, you take one long, quiet out-breath. Nobody notices.
[pause 2s]
Let the scene unfold. What people say to you, how you reply. You take a moment before speaking. Your voice is steady.
Notice the details. The light in the room, the chair you're sitting in, the mug in front of you. The more precise the scene, the more familiar it will feel when the moment comes.
Maybe there's a tense moment. A comment, a tricky question, something unexpected. See yourself taking it in, pausing briefly, and answering at your own pace.
You don't have to be flawless in this scene. Just present and calm, in your own way.
If your mind heads for the worst, gently steer the scene back to a simple, realistic version. Not perfect, not a disaster.
[pause 3s]
Now let's turn that into a simple plan, in two parts. If this happens, then I do that.
The first part is the signal. The moment you notice the pressure rising. If I feel my throat tighten. Or, if someone talks over me. Or, if I see that pile of files.
The second part is your response. Something tiny and concrete. Then I plant my feet and breathe out slowly. Then I take a sip of water before answering. Then I start with one task, the smallest one.
Choose a response you can actually do on the spot, discreetly, even with other people around. A breath, a gesture, a phrase you say to yourself.
[pause 2s]
Now make your own plan. Pick your words. Keep it short.
Say it once, silently, slowly. If... then...
[pause 4s]
A small prepared phrase like this can really help. When the moment comes, you don't have to search for a solution in the middle of the pressure. It's already there, ready to use.
Run through the scene one last time, with your plan. The signal arrives... and you use your response. Simple.
[pause 3s]
The more you rehearse it like this, the more natural it becomes. Like a route you take every day, one your feet know by heart.
[pause 2s]
Before we finish, one more quick tour. This time, look for something pleasant.

There's almost always something, even on a packed day. A coffee with a colleague. Lunch. A call with someone you love. The ride home with a good podcast. That first step into your living room in the evening.
Pick it, and picture it already. The taste, the laughter, the light, the relief.
Decide to really savor it when it comes. Not thinking about what's next. Just living it.
[pause 3s]
Now come back to what's supporting you. Feet, thighs, back. The breath coming and going.
You've taken a full tour of your day. You know where the tricky stretch is, and you have your plan. You also know where the good moment is waiting.
And if the day turns out differently than expected, your plan still works. The signal might show up somewhere else, at another time. The response stays the same.
Whatever else happens, you'll adapt, the way you always do.
[pause 2s]
Take one last breath, long and easy. Feel your body in the chair, ready to get up.
Gently move your hands, your shoulders. Open your eyes.
And keep your little phrase in your pocket. If... then... It's there when you need it.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Mindful morning stretch
script: [pause 1.5s]
Welcome to these eight minutes for loosening up your body. If you feel stiff this morning, or if sitting still to meditate feels like a struggle, this session is for you.
Here, we meditate by moving. Movement becomes the anchor, and the breath sets the pace.
One rule, and only one, before we start. Never into pain. Always stay within what's comfortable. If a movement doesn't suit you, make it smaller, or just do it in your imagination.
And if standing isn't possible for you, you can follow the whole session on a chair, sitting slightly forward, away from the backrest.
[pause 2s]
Stand with your feet hip width apart. Toes pointing forward. Knees soft, not locked.
Let your arms hang by your sides. Feel the weight of your hands at the ends of your arms.
[pause 2s]
Bring your attention to your feet. Heels, soles, toes. Where is most of your weight resting?
[pause 2s]
Maybe more on one foot than the other, more on your heels than on the balls of your feet.
Sway very slightly, forward and back, then side to side, and find the center. The place where you can stand without effort.
This gentle swaying already wakes up your ankles and the muscles of your legs. They're the ones carrying you through this session.
[pause 2s]
Take a breath. Just notice what it's like this morning. Short, long, high in the chest, low in the belly.
[pause 3s]
From here on, let the breath guide every movement. The in breath opens and lifts. The out breath releases and lowers.
If you slept in a slightly awkward position, you may notice a particular stiffness, in your neck or lower back. Keep it in mind, and take extra care of that area.
[pause 1.5s]
First movement. As you breathe in, slowly raise your arms out to the sides, then up over your head.
Your palms can meet, or stay shoulder width apart.
[pause 2s]
As you breathe out, let your arms come back down the same way, like a big wave.
[pause 3s]
Again. Breathe in, arms rising. Feel the space opening between your ribs, the air filling the top of your chest.
[pause 2s]
Breathe out, arms lowering. Your shoulders stay well away from your ears.
[pause 2s]
Do two or three more of these waves at your own pace. Match the speed of your arms to the length of your breath. If the in breath is short, the movement is short.
There's no need to fill your lungs to the max. We're looking for a smooth movement, not a feat.
[pause 8s]
Now, side bends. Breathe in, and raise your right arm over your head. Your left hand slides down the outside of your left thigh.
As you breathe out, lean gently to the left. Like a tree bending in the wind.
Feel the stretch all along your right side, from your hip to your fingertips.
Keep both feet firmly grounded. Don't try to go far. A small arc is plenty.
Breathe here. With each in breath, imagine the air flowing into the ribs on the stretched side.
[pause 5s]
Breathe in, and come back to center. Breathe out, arm lowering.
[pause 2s]
Now the other side. Breathe in, left arm rising. Breathe out, leaning to the right.
[pause 2s]
Does this side feel different? Looser, or stiffer?
[pause 2.5s]
The body is never perfectly symmetrical, and that's absolutely fine.
[pause 3s]
Breathe in, back to center. Breathe out, arm lowering.
[pause 2s]
Now, a forward roll down. Bend your knees a little more. This matters, to protect your lower back.
As you breathe out, let your chin drop toward your chest. Then your shoulders round, and your back rolls down, one vertebra at a time.
Your arms hang heavy toward the floor. No need to touch your toes. Stop wherever feels comfortable, even halfway.
[pause 3s]
Let your head hang, neck relaxed. You can nod a small yes, then shake a small no, to release the back of your neck.
Breathe into your back. Feel it lengthen and widen with every in breath.
If you like, bend one knee and then the other, alternating, to gently stretch the backs of your legs. No bouncing.
[pause 5s]
To come up, press firmly into your feet. Over several breaths, roll your back up, one vertebra at a time. Your head comes up last.
Take your time. If you feel a little dizzy as you come up, stay still for a moment, knees soft, and breathe normally.
[pause 5s]
Now, some gentle twists. Let your arms hang loose, relaxed like scarves.
Turn your upper body gently to the right, then to the left. Your arms follow, lightly tapping against your body as they swing.
Your feet stay put. Your hips can follow a little. Your gaze goes along with the movement.
Let the rhythm find itself. Like a child playing at swinging their arms.
Your breath follows freely. There's nothing to count.
[pause 3s]
Notice the feeling in your lower back, around your waist. That's often where the night has left some stiffness, and the movement eases it, little by little.
[pause 4s]
Slow down gradually. Smaller and smaller twists, until you come to rest at the center.
Take a moment to feel your lower back, still now. It often feels warmer and looser than at the start.
[pause 3s]
Now, a chest opener. Bring your hands behind your back. Interlace your fingers if you can. If not, hold one wrist, or grip both ends of a towel.
As you breathe in, gently draw your hands down and away from your back. Your shoulder blades move toward each other. Your chest opens forward, as if you were turning it toward the sun.
Keep your neck long, chin level with the floor.
Breathe here for a few breaths. Feel the fronts of your shoulders stretching, right where all those hours hunched over a screen tend to settle.
[pause 6s]
As you breathe out, release your hands. Let your arms come back to your sides.
Roll your shoulders once or twice, to finish.
[pause 3s]
Now, stay still. Remain standing, eyes closed or gaze resting on the floor.
Feel what's happening in your body after moving. Tingling in your hands. Warmth in your back. Your heartbeat, a little more noticeable.
Maybe there's more space in your chest, more length along your sides.
[pause 3s]
Feel your feet again. Is your weight spread differently than it was at the start?
[pause 2.5s]
Notice your breath too. It may have found a fuller rhythm, without you even trying.
This body that felt stiff a few minutes ago is now a little more alive. You didn't force anything. You simply listened to it.
Your body has its own wisdom. It knows what does it good, when you give it time to tell you.
[pause 3s]
Take one last full breath, raising your arms one more time, if you feel like it.
[pause 3s]
And as you breathe out, let them float back down, slowly.
[pause 4s]
Feel your feet on the ground one last time, before picking up the thread of your morning.

Carry this looser body with you into your day. And when the stiffness creeps back, at your computer or on your commute, remember that a single side bend, a single roll down, a single breath can bring back a little of this ease.
Even two minutes of stretching tomorrow morning can change the way you start your day.
[pause 1.5s]
Have a good day. Take it gently.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Slow weekend morning
script: [pause 1.5s]
It's the weekend. Or a day off, a morning with no alarm and no appointments.
Today, there's no rush. Nothing to do, nowhere to be. For these ten minutes, you have permission to accomplish absolutely nothing.
[pause 2s]
You might still be in bed, in an armchair, by a window, out on a balcony. Choose wherever your body wants to be. And settle in as if for a long while.
If someone is still asleep beside you, or the house is waking up around you, that's fine. You can listen quietly. This moment is still yours.
[pause 2s]
Start by noticing where you are. The surface holding you up. The temperature of the air. What you're wearing. Pajamas, a blanket, an old sweater.
There's no ideal posture this morning. If you want to pull your knees up, lean back against a cushion, let your head tilt to one side, go ahead.
Let your body find its most comfortable position, the one you'd choose if nobody were watching.
[pause 3s]
Now, a curious observation. Even though nothing is urgent, part of you may still be running.
Listen from the inside. Have your thoughts already started planning? Groceries, laundry, messages to send, all the things you should do this weekend to make the most of it?
[pause 2s]
Is your body a little ahead of itself? A slight tightness in your chest, a clenched jaw, an itch to get up and do something?
[pause 2s]

That's very common. After a busy week, the body holds on to its momentum, like a train that keeps rolling after the engine's been switched off. Alert mode doesn't shut down all at once, just because it's Saturday.
You don't have to chase it away. Just notice it. Oh, look. I'm still running.

You might even notice, with a bit of humor, all the little voices saying you should get up, tidy up, get things done. They're used to running the week. This morning, they can sit next to you, without taking the wheel.
There's nothing wrong with you for still feeling the pull. It's just the rhythm of the week, taking a little while to wind down.
[pause 2s]
So, let's slow down. Very gradually.
First, the breath. No technique here. Just let each out-breath last a tiny bit longer, like a lazy sigh.
Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and let the air drift out without hurrying, all the way to the end.
[pause 6s]
Again. The in-breath comes on its own...
[pause 3s]
and the out-breath takes its time.
[pause 5s]
