And at the end of the out-breath, there's sometimes a small moment of stillness, before the next in-breath arrives. You don't need to make it happen. Just notice it, if it's there.
Place a hand on your belly if you like, and feel it rise and fall, slowly. Like a wave stretching up the sand, then drawing back without any hurry.
[pause 5s]
Now, your movements. If you move, move at half your usual speed.
If you're holding a mug, bring it to your lips as if in slow motion. If you change position, do it as if you were underwater.
Try it with your hand now. Lift it very slowly, just a few inches, and set it back down.
[pause 4s]
Notice everything you felt during that simple movement. The lightness, the weight, the air on your skin.
At weekends, we often fill our free time just as quickly as everything else. Slowing your movements is a way of telling your body, today, we have time. Really.
This slowness might feel strange at first. Maybe even a bit uncomfortable. That's a sign you're stepping out of autopilot.
If the urge to hurry comes back, notice it, and slow down just a little more. Not out of discipline. Out of curiosity.
[pause 3s]
And now, let yourself savor what's here. The sensations of the morning, one at a time.
The light, first. If your eyes are open, look at it. How does it come into the room? Through the window, between the curtains, as a beam or a soft veil?
[pause 2s]
Notice its color. In the morning, it's often softer, more golden, or a pale, peaceful gray. Watch how it rests on things, the wall, the floor. The shadows it draws.
Maybe a speck of dust is dancing in a sunbeam. Maybe a reflection is trembling on the ceiling. Tiny shows that play out every morning, often with no one watching.
If your eyes are closed, feel the light through your eyelids. A tint, a brightness.
[pause 4s]
Then the warmth. Where is your body nice and warm? Under the blanket, around a mug, where the sun touches your skin?
[pause 2s]
Let yourself enjoy that warmth, simply. Like a cat settling into a patch of sunlight. It has nothing else to do. Neither do you.
Notice the contrast, too. One part warm, another cooler. Your nose a little chilly, your feet tucked under the covers. Those small differences make the warmth even more pleasant.
[pause 3s]
And the sounds. Listen to the morning. At weekends, it often sounds different.
Maybe fewer cars. Birds more noticeable. Neighbors laughing, a child playing, a market setting up, church bells in the distance. The coffee machine gurgling, the cat jumping off the sofa.
You don't need to name them. Let them come to you, and go again. The near ones, the far ones, and the silence in between.
Choose one sound, and follow it until it fades. Listen right to the end, the moment it melts into everything else.
[pause 5s]
Sounds make a lovely anchor on a slow morning. They arrive without any effort, and they're always new.
[pause 2s]
And maybe a smell. Coffee, toast, fresh air drifting in through a half-open window. Or just the familiar smell of home.
Breathe in gently, without searching. Let the smell come to you, rather than going looking for it.
[pause 4s]
Now I'll guide a little less. There's nothing in particular to notice anymore.
Let your attention open up, like a window flung wide. Everything can come in. Sounds, sensations, light, passing thoughts.
Nothing to hold on to, nothing to push away. Just be here, in the middle of it all.
You could imagine sitting on a riverbank. Everything that passes, sounds, thoughts, sensations, drifts by on the water. You watch, and let it flow.
If you catch yourself planning, smile at the habit, and come back to the morning.
You can let your gaze rest somewhere, without fixing on anything. Or close your eyes. Your body is heavy, your breath finds its own way.
[pause 8s]
One breath... and you stay right here.
[pause 6s]
Notice that this moment doesn't need anything more. No goal, no progress to make. Just the morning, and you in it.
All is well. There's nowhere else you need to be.
If a thought carries you off, it's nothing. You notice, you come back. And the morning is still here, waiting for you.
Maybe the light has already shifted a little since we began. Maybe a new sound has appeared. The morning moves slowly around you, and all you have to do is let it.
[pause 8s]
Gently, bring a little attention back to yourself. And ask yourself a question, without rushing for an answer.
What would really do me good today?
[pause 3s]
Not what would be productive. Not what you should do. What would actually do you good.
Maybe a long walk. A bath. A book. Seeing a friend. Cooking without watching the clock. Or nothing at all, which is a perfectly good answer.
You can also ask what your body needs. To move, to rest, to eat something delicious, to be outside? And what does your heart need? Quiet, laughter, company?
Listen to what comes. Sometimes it's a specific wish, sometimes just a feeling. More air, more calm, more connection.
If nothing comes, that's fine. The question can keep working quietly in the background while you have breakfast or take a shower.
[pause 4s]
Hold that wish lightly. It's not another task to tick off. It's an invitation.
It doesn't matter if the day doesn't go exactly the way you picture it. The point isn't to get your weekend right. It's to stay a little closer to yourself.
And if, later on, you feel the pace picking up again for no reason, you can come back to what you did this morning. A lazy out-breath. A slow-motion gesture. One sound you really listen to.
[pause 2s]
Before you move, stay here a moment longer. Notice what it feels like to have taken this time. Even if nothing special happened.
Maybe that's exactly the point. That nothing happened.
[pause 3s]
You've just given your body something rare. Time without a goal. It often holds on to that, a kind of ease that lingers for a while.
When you feel like it, and not before, start to move. Slowly. Stretch, if you're in the mood.
Arms overhead, a long yawn, your whole body lengthening.
[pause 3s]
And try to give yourself mornings like this more often. Even ten minutes, on a Tuesday, before the house wakes up.
For now, step into your day at the pace of this morning. There's no race to win today.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Walking meditation
script: [pause 1.5s]
This meditation is done while walking. Outdoors, on your way to work, in a park, or simply at home, pacing back and forth across your living room or along a hallway.
[pause 1.5s]
First, a safety note. Keep your eyes open the whole time. If you're outside, stay aware of what's around you. Sidewalks, bikes, cars.
At crossings, look, and cross as you normally would, with your full attention on the road. And of course, never while driving.
Your inner chatter can quiet down. The world around you stays switched on.
If you're outside, listen with one earbud, or at low volume, so you can still hear the street.
[pause 2s]
To begin, stand still for a moment. Feet hip-width apart, arms by your sides.
Notice your posture too. Knees soft, pelvis settled, shoulders dropping naturally. Your head light, as if balanced on top of your spine.
[pause 2s]
Feel the weight of your body sinking down into your feet. How is it spread? More on your heels? More toward the front? More on one foot than the other?
[pause 3s]
Sway gently, forward and back, side to side. Then find the center, the point where your weight is spread roughly evenly over both feet.
Feel the ground beneath you. Hard, soft, flat, uneven. The contact of your sole, your sock, or bare skin.
Take a moment to really feel it. This contact with the ground will be your anchor throughout.
[pause 4s]
Take a breath or two here. Your gaze resting a few yards ahead, not fixed on anything.
[pause 3s]
This short pause helps your mind change gears. You shift from I need to get there, to I'm walking right now.
[pause 2s]

Now, let's start walking. Very slowly at first. Much more slowly than usual. If you're on the street and this pace feels awkward, just walk a little slower than normal, and keep your attention in your feet.
Shift your weight onto your left leg. Feel your right leg becoming light.
Your right heel lifts. Then the sole. Then your toes leave the ground.
Your foot moves forward through the air, a few inches.
And comes down. Heel first. Then the sole rolls down. Then the toes.
Your weight glides forward, onto that right foot. And your left leg, in turn, becomes light.
[pause 2s]

Breaking it down like this may feel mechanical at first, a bit like learning to walk all over again. That's normal. You're discovering a movement you've made all your life, without ever really watching it.
[pause 3s]
Keep going like this, step by step. Heel, sole, toes. Lift, move, place.
You can say it silently, if it helps. Lift... move... place.
[pause 3s]
Notice all the tiny adjustments your body makes to keep its balance. Ankles, calves, hips. An incredible feat of coordination you perform thousands of times a day without a thought.
Notice, too, the moment when both feet are on the ground at once, just before your weight tips forward. A tiny instant of double support, and then the movement carries on.
[pause 4s]
If you're at home and you reach the end of the room, stop for a moment. Feel your feet, still. Then turn around slowly, staying present through the whole turn. And set off again.
The turn is part of the walk too. Your weight shifting, your feet pivoting, your eyes discovering the other side of the room.
[pause 2s]
Now, let's link your breath to your steps. Not rigidly. Just noticing the connection between them.
For example, you might breathe in over two steps, and out over two steps. Or in over a few, and out over a few more. Find whatever feels natural.
Breathe in, as your feet carry you forward...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out, over the next steps.
[pause 3s]
If your breath needs more or less, let it decide. Your steps adapt to your breath, not the other way around.
Does your breathing slow a little as your steps become steady? Or does it stay the same?
[pause 3s]
Either is fine.
[pause 2s]
Keep walking with this rhythm. Breath and feet moving together, like two musicians playing the same tune.
If counting steps feels too much like school, drop the numbers. Just feel the in-breath carrying a few steps, and the out-breath carrying a few more.
[pause 4s]
You may have noticed that your mind has already wandered off. Toward your day, a memory, a conversation, a project.
That's perfectly normal. It's what minds do. There's nothing to fix.
The moment you realize it, that's already a moment of presence. Simply come back to your feet. To the next heel touching the ground.
You can even note, in one word, where your mind went. Work. Memory. Worry. Then pick up your stride again, no commentary needed.
[pause 4s]
Now widen your attention a little. Your feet stay as a reference point, in the background. But you open up your other senses too.
Sounds first. What's close by, your own footsteps, the rustle of your clothes. Then further away. Voices, a door, wind in the trees, traffic, a bird, a fridge humming.
Let them come, without holding on to them.
Notice how they change as you move. Some come closer, others fade and disappear behind you.
[pause 3s]
The air on your skin. On your face, on your hands. Cool, mild, damp, dry. Maybe a bit of a breeze. Maybe sunshine on one cheek.
And smells, if you notice any. Coffee from a café, damp earth, cut grass, warm bread from a bakery, or the familiar smell of your hallway.
No need to stop to take them in. They come to you, step by step.
[pause 3s]

And colors. Look around as if you were discovering this place for the first time. The green of the leaves, the gray of the pavement, the red of a mailbox, the blue or white of the sky. At home, the color of a book, a cushion, a plant.
Let one color draw you in. Really look at it for a few seconds, while you keep walking.
[pause 3s]
If you're outside, notice the other people passing by. Each with their own day, their own thoughts, their own pace. You're part of this great morning movement, simply by walking.
[pause 3s]
All of this is part of your walk. You walk, and the world flows in through your senses.
If at any point it feels like too much at once, come back to your feet. Heel, sole, toes. That's your anchor, always available.
[pause 4s]

Thoughts will almost certainly come back, again and again. Each time, it's the same. You notice, and you come back to your feet. No frustration, no judgment. The way you'd gently bring back a puppy that's wandered off.
This coming back is the real heart of the practice. It's not a failure. It's the exercise itself.
Maybe your mind is calmer now, or maybe it's still very busy. Either way, your walk is exactly what it needs to be.
[pause 3s]
Now you can let your pace pick up. Gradually return to your natural walking speed. Your everyday pace.
This is where the real challenge begins. At this speed, the mind is used to slipping into autopilot.
Let's see if you can keep a little presence. Not as much as when you were walking slowly. Just a thread.
Keep feeling your foot meet the ground with each step, even at this faster pace. The natural swing of your arms. Your breath adjusting to the new rhythm.
[pause 2s]
You could choose a cue to bring you back to the present. For example, every time you pass a tree, a red light or a doorway. That cue becomes your bell. One mindful step, then you carry on.
[pause 3s]
How are you holding yourself right now? Is your head pushed forward, as if it wanted to arrive before you?
[pause 2s]
Let it come back over your shoulders. Your gaze opens out toward the horizon.
Let your arms swing freely too, rather than burying them in your pockets or clenching them around your bag.
An open posture often changes how you meet what comes next. Your body straightens, and your mind follows.
[pause 2s]
A few more steps, at your own pace. Feet, breath, sounds, light. Everything is here, all at once.
If you reach a street to cross, set the meditation aside while you cross. Look, wait, cross. Then pick up the thread again.
[pause 4s]
This session is coming to an end, but your walk can carry on.
If you're outside, you can keep this attention all the way to where you're going. The station, the office, the bakery. At least now and then, come back to a step, a sound, a color.
If you're at home, come to a gentle stop. Stand for a few seconds. Feel your weight settle back into both feet, still.
[pause 3s]
Notice your body after this walk. What feels calmer, more awake, more present.
[pause 2s]
This morning, you walked without rushing toward what's next. You lived in the journey, instead of just getting through it.
From today, every journey can become a small meditation. Even two minutes, between your front door and the end of the street. Or along an office corridor, between two meetings.
All you need is to remember your feet. They're always there, with every step, to bring you back here.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Make peace with your body
script: [pause 1.5s]

You and your body may not always get along. There's the mirror, the photos, the clothes that feel tight. Sometimes there's illness, pain, a tiredness that won't lift. Or simply the feeling that it doesn't do what you'd like it to.
[pause 1.5s]

This practice doesn't ask you to love your body overnight. That would be asking too much. It invites you to try, for a few minutes, a different way of looking at it. Less like a judge, more like someone saying thank you.
[pause 2s]

Find a position that's truly comfortable. Lying on your back, curled up in an armchair, wrapped in a blanket if you like. Adjust anything that bothers you. A cushion under your knees, a looser waistband.
Close your eyes if that feels pleasant. Otherwise, let your gaze rest on a neutral spot.
[pause 2s]
Breathe in gently through your nose...
[pause 4s]
and breathe out, letting the weight of your body sink into whatever is holding you.
[pause 6s]
One more breath, a little slower. Let it reach down into your belly...
[pause 4s]
then leave, without any hurry.
[pause 6s]
Now let your breathing happen on its own. Simply feel the movement it creates. Your belly or your chest rising, then falling.
Feel too the places where your body meets what supports it. Your heels, your back, the back of your head. There's nothing you need to hold up.
[pause 3s]
Before we begin, you might notice something. As soon as the body comes up, thoughts often arrive all by themselves. Too much of this. Not enough of that. I should. If only.

You don't have to silence them. You don't have to believe them either. You can just recognize them, like people passing in the street. Oh, there's the judgment about my stomach. Oh, there's the comparison.
Then, without arguing with them, come back to sensation. Not to the image of your body, but to what it feels, from the inside.
Each time a judgment pulls you back to the mirror, that's okay. Just return to what you can feel. Warmth, weight, contact.
[pause 4s]
Let's start with your feet. Feel their contact with the floor, the bed, or the fabric of your socks. Maybe warmth, coolness, a slight tingling.
Wriggle your toes a little, if you like, just to feel them more clearly.
[pause 2s]

These feet have carried you for years. They took your first steps. They took you to school, to work, to appointments that mattered. They've walked on sand, on wet pavements, perhaps down hospital corridors.
They did all that without asking for thanks. So, silently, simply tell them... thank you for carrying me.
[pause 4s]
Move gently up to your legs, your knees, your hips. All this architecture that lets you get up in the morning, climb the stairs, run for a bus.
If part of your legs hurts, or doesn't work the way it used to, you can still greet it. Thank you for everything you've done, and for what you still do.
You can rest a hand on your thigh as you say it, as a small gesture of respect.
[pause 3s]
Now move to your hands. Feel them, resting. The palms, the fingertips, the small sensations living there.
Think of everything they do each day. They type on a keyboard, open doors, chop vegetables, hold a phone, write your name. They stroke a cat, hold a child's hand, comfort someone who's crying.
And your arms. They've carried shopping bags, moving boxes, maybe a sleeping baby. They've let you hold people close.
Thank you, hands. Thank you, arms. For everything you do that I so rarely notice.
If your hands are stiff or sore today, you can thank them anyway, and let them rest completely.
[pause 2s]
Can you feel a little warmth in your palms? Or simply their weight?
[pause 2.5s]
This is how gratitude for the body begins. By actually feeling it, rather than looking at it from the outside.
[pause 2s]

Now bring your attention to the center of your chest. Somewhere underneath, your heart is beating. You may not feel it directly, and that's okay. You can rest a hand there if you like, to feel a little closer.

This heart has been beating since before you were born. Around a hundred thousand times a day. It has never stopped to rest. It beat through your calmest nights and your hardest days. It's beating right now, for you, asking nothing in return.
And your breath. These lungs filling and emptying, thousands of times a day. Even when you're angry with your body, it keeps on breathing for you.
[pause 2s]
Take a moment to recognize this loyalty. Thank you, heart. Thank you, breath.
You can let these words ride on your breath. Thank you, on the in breath...
[pause 4s]
thank you, on the out breath.
[pause 6s]
Now, if you feel able, choose an area of your body you have a more difficult relationship with. Somewhere you judge, or hide, or that hurts.
If that feels too charged today, you can stay with your heart or your hands. You have nothing to prove.
[pause 2s]
If you do choose an area, simply rest your attention on it, delicately. The way you'd approach a slightly timid animal. Not too fast.
Notice the emotions that come. Embarrassment, sadness, sometimes anger. They often have a long history. Let them be here, without judging yourself for feeling them.
[pause 3s]
Then, if you can, send this area a little kindness. You can rest a hand on it. Or imagine a warmth wrapping around it, like a soft, warm blanket.
Breathe gently toward it. As if each breath in brought a little more room, and each breath out let a little tension go.
[pause 4s]
And tell it, in your own way, I'm sorry I've been so hard on you. Or, you're part of me. Or simply, I'm here.
You don't need to believe it completely. It's an intention, a seed. It will grow in its own time.
[pause 5s]

If strong emotions have come up, that's completely normal. The body holds a lot. You can stop at any moment, open your eyes, come back to your breathing. And if your relationship with your body has been painful for a long time, talking to a professional can really help.
[pause 2s]
Now take a moment to feel your body as a whole. From your feet to your head. Not a perfect body. A living body, breathing, feeling, keeping you company.
This body has changed, and it will keep changing. It has been through years, scars, transformations. And it has never stopped being yours.
[pause 3s]
Notice whether there's a little more gentleness than at the start. Or perhaps not. Both are okay.
You won't keep this softer way of seeing all the time. Old judgments will come back. But each time you thank a part of yourself, even briefly, you're training a different habit.
[pause 4s]
Gently begin to move. Your toes. Your fingers. Maybe a small stretch, like a cat waking up, just whatever feels good.
Listen to the sounds around you. Sense the light through your eyelids.
Take a slow breath, and feel your whole body breathing with you.
[pause 5s]
And when the moment is right for you, open your eyes.
[pause 2s]
Today, the next time you catch yourself judging your body, try this little phrase. Thank you for carrying me. This body isn't your enemy. It has been your ally from day one.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Lonely tonight
script: [pause 1.5s]
Tonight, loneliness is making itself felt. Maybe the flat is too quiet. Maybe your phone hasn't buzzed all evening. Or maybe there are people all around you, and you still feel on the outside.
[pause 2s]
You did well to come here. For these few minutes, we're going to keep this feeling company, instead of running from it.
[pause 2s]

First, something important. Loneliness hurts, and that's no accident. The need for connection is as basic as the need to eat or sleep. When it isn't met, the body registers it as an alarm. What you're going through isn't a flaw. It's a human signal, and a completely legitimate one.
[pause 2s]
Settle in wherever you are. On the sofa, in bed, against a cushion. If you have a blanket or a hot drink nearby, bring them closer. Your comfort matters.
Let your eyes close, or keep a soft light somewhere in view.
[pause 2s]
Breathe in slowly...
[pause 4s]
And let the air out, without hurrying.
[pause 5s]
Once more, feeling your chest rise...
[pause 4s]
then fall.
[pause 5s]
And a third one, very gentle, letting your shoulders grow a little heavier.
[pause 6s]

Notice where your body is in contact with things. The weight of your legs. Your back leaning against something. The texture of the fabric under your fingers. Tonight, something is holding you up, quite literally.
[pause 2s]
Listen to the sounds as well. A car in the distance, the hum of the fridge, maybe rain. The world is still there, all around you.
Let those small sounds keep you company for a moment. You don't have to do anything with them.
[pause 4s]
Now, if you're willing, look for where loneliness lives in your body. It often has a shape. An emptiness in the chest. A tight throat. A coldness, or a heaviness in the arms.
There's no right or wrong way for loneliness to feel. Whatever you find is welcome.
[pause 3s]
Don't try to make it go away. Just rest your attention on it, gently. As if you were sitting down next to someone who's sad, without saying a word.
You can place a hand there. Feel the warmth of your palm. You're the one offering this touch, and it counts.
[pause 3s]
Breathe toward that place. Imagine that with each breath in, a little space opens up around the feeling. Like opening a window in a room that's been closed for too long.
[pause 5s]
You can tell yourself softly, I feel lonely tonight, and it's hard. Use whatever words feel like yours.
Saying it plainly often softens it a little. You're no longer pretending, and no longer fighting it.
[pause 4s]
Now widen your view a little. Imagine your street, your neighborhood, your city, seen from above, at night. Thousands of lit windows.
Some dark, some glowing blue from a screen, some warm and yellow.
[pause 2s]

Behind many of those windows, someone is feeling just what you're feeling right now. A student far from home, eating a bowl of pasta in front of a laptop. An elderly man watching television without really seeing it. A young mother rocking her baby at two in the morning, feeling invisible. Someone who's just moved to a city where they don't know a soul.
[pause 2s]
None of these people know each other. And yet tonight, they share something with you. Loneliness, strangely enough, is one of the most widely shared experiences in the world.
And it says nothing about your worth. It only says that a need is waiting to be met. Even people surrounded by others feel lonely on certain evenings.
You're not the only one feeling this. Let that idea settle.
[pause 4s]
Let's send them something. Not a message, not a call. A simple wish, from your heart.
Think of all those lit windows, and silently tell them, may you feel less alone tonight. May someone be thinking of you. May you find a little warmth.
[pause 3s]

And now turn that same wish toward yourself, since you're one of those windows too. May the loneliness weigh a little less tonight. May I find warmth, inside me and around me. May I know that I matter.
[pause 3s]
If these words sound strange, that's normal. Just hold on to the intention, like a candle being lit.
You might picture that small flame passing from window to window, right across the city.
This flame doesn't rest on you alone. Every window that receives it keeps it going in turn. And perhaps, somewhere, someone is thinking of you in the very same way.
[pause 4s]

Now let a memory of connection come back. A moment when you felt a real bond with someone. It doesn't have to be a big moment. A fit of giggles with a colleague. A noisy family dinner. A long conversation on a train platform. A knowing look shared with a stranger.
[pause 3s]
Relive that moment in detail. Where were you? What were the sounds, the smells, the light? Who was there, and what was being said?
[pause 3s]
And above all, find what you were feeling. That warmth, that lightness, that sense of belonging.
Where does that warmth sit in your body? Maybe in the very same place as the emptiness from earlier. Let it settle there for a moment.
[pause 3s]
Your body remembers this feeling. It's capable of feeling it. And it will feel it again.
Let yourself rest in it for a few breaths, the way you'd lean against someone you trust.
[pause 5s]
If this memory also brings some sadness, because that person is far away, or that time has passed, let it be here. Sadness and warmth can live side by side.
[pause 3s]
Before we finish, think of one tiny act of connection you could do tomorrow. Nothing spectacular.

Send a message to someone you've been thinking about. Really say hello to the person at the bakery, looking them in the eye. Invite a colleague for a coffee. Call a grandparent. Sign up for that activity you've been tempted by for ages.
Choose one. Picture yourself tomorrow, doing it. It isn't much, and that's often how connections start again.
[pause 3s]
If that feels like too much tonight, simply keep the idea in mind. That's already a beginning.
Studies on social connection suggest that it's often these small, everyday interactions, repeated over time, that build a sense of belonging.
[pause 2s]
For now, gently come back to your breath, the air flowing in and out. You're here, with yourself, and that is a real presence.
Stay a moment longer with your hand resting on you, and your breath coming and going. Notice how you feel now. Without needing the loneliness to be gone.
[pause 4s]
If it's still here, that's okay. Tonight, you didn't leave it on its own. You kept it company.
You can tell yourself, if it feels right, I'm staying with myself tonight.
[pause 3s]
And if this feeling of loneliness comes back often, or weighs very heavily, talking to a health professional can be a real source of support.
[pause 2s]
Gently, come back to the sounds of the room, the contact of your body. Move your hands a little.
And whenever you like, open your eyes, or let yourself drift toward sleep if it's time.
[pause 2s]
Tonight, thousands of people believe, just like you, that they're alone. You're not set apart from anyone. And somewhere, someone will be glad to hear from you tomorrow.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Letting go of a grudge
script: [pause 1.5s]
A grudge is a bit like a stone in your shoe. At first, you feel it with every step. Then you get used to it, and you limp a little without noticing. You forget that you could take it out.
Over the next ten minutes, you'll look at a grudge you've been carrying, and see whether you can lighten the load a little. For you. Not for the other person.
[pause 2s]

One important note before we begin. Choose a light or moderate grudge. A hurtful remark from a colleague, a friend who didn't keep their promise, a family member who broke your trust. Not a situation involving violence, and not a trauma. Wounds like those deserve to be explored gently, with the support of a professional.
And nothing obliges you to forgive. Not today, not ever. Here, you go at your own pace, and you can stop at any time.
[pause 2s]
Settle into a steady position. Feet on the floor, back supported, hands resting on your thighs or your belly.
If you like, close your eyes. Otherwise, keep a soft gaze, resting downward.
Breathe in through your nose, deeply but without forcing...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out slowly, through your mouth.
[pause 5s]
Once more. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and out, letting your jaw loosen.
[pause 5s]
Now let your breath find its own rhythm. Rest your attention on your belly, rising slightly as you breathe in, and softening as you breathe out.
[pause 2s]
Feel the weight of your body. Your hips on the seat. Your feet on the floor. You're here, safe, in the present moment. What happened belongs to the past. All you're going to do now is look at it.
If at any point what comes up feels too strong, come back to this anchor. Your feet, your belly breathing. It will always be there.
Let's try it right now. Press your feet gently into the floor... then let go. That's your safe place for the whole session.
[pause 3s]
Now let the situation come to mind. The person, the moment, the words or actions that hurt you.
You don't need to relive it all in detail. One image is enough. A fragment of the scene, like a blurry photo.

And notice what happens in your body as you think about it. A grudge often has a physical signature. A clenched jaw. Heat in the chest. Fists that want to close. A knot in the stomach, pulling tighter.
[pause 2s]
You can name what you feel. Anger. Sadness. Disappointment. Humiliation, perhaps. Every emotion has the right to be here.
Let these emotions exist without feeding them. You don't need to replay the scene to feel them. If it gets intense, take one breath down into your belly, then look again.
[pause 3s]
Now acknowledge the hurt. Not to dwell on it, but to do it justice.
Say to yourself silently... what happened hurt me. I had every right to be hurt. My reaction makes sense.
[pause 2s]
Often, we hold on to a grudge because it feels as if no one has ever acknowledged what we went through. So start there. You acknowledge it.
Perhaps what hurt was a need that wasn't respected. The need for respect, for being listened to, for being taken into account. That need was legitimate. It still is.
Place a hand on your heart if it helps, and let that acknowledgment reach you.
[pause 3s]
Now look honestly at what this grudge is costing you. You.

How many times have you gone back over that scene? In the shower, on the train, as you're falling asleep? How many imaginary conversations have you had with this person, searching for the perfect comeback?
[pause 2s]
And in your body, every time you think about it, the tension comes back. Your heart speeds up, your muscles tighten. As if the event were happening again, over and over.

Notice, too, whether this grudge spills over into other parts of your life. A greater wariness of other people. An irritability that flares up without warning. A subject you avoid, a place you no longer go.
Meanwhile, the other person probably feels none of this. You're the one carrying the weight. Like holding a bag of stones at arm's length, hoping it will feel heavy to someone else.
[pause 2s]
Just notice that, without blaming yourself. Holding a grudge is a very human way of protecting yourself. It may have served you, for a while.
You can thank that protection, silently. Thank you for looking out for me. And gently ask yourself... do I still need to hold it this tightly?
[pause 3s]
So what is forgiveness, really? Not what we often think.
Forgiving isn't excusing. What happened wasn't acceptable, and it still isn't.
Forgiving isn't forgetting. You can keep the memory, and the lesson that comes with it.
Forgiving doesn't necessarily mean reconciling. You can forgive someone and decide not to see them again. You can forgive and keep your boundaries, firmly.
Forgiving doesn't mean forcing yourself to feel affection, either. You can stay neutral toward this person. You can even go on not liking them.
[pause 1.5s]
Forgiving means putting the weight down. Deciding that this story won't take up so much room inside you anymore. Taking back the energy it's been using up.
It's a gift you give yourself, far more than one you give them.
Sometimes it helps to remember that the other person was also acting with their own limits, their fears, their tiredness. That doesn't excuse them. It simply makes them human, like you.
Take a breath with that idea. Not to change your mind about what happened. Just to see whether the fist inside you can loosen, even a notch.
[pause 4s]
Now see whether you can take one tiny step in that direction. Not a grand gesture. Just an opening.

You can choose a phrase, if one of them speaks to you. I choose to put this weight down, a little. Or, I don't condone what you did, but I no longer want to carry it. Or, I'm freeing myself from this story, at my own pace.
If no phrase feels right, simply keep the intention. The wish, however timid, to feel freer one day.
And if you sense it isn't the right time, that the anger still needs to exist, that's completely fine too. You can say, not yet. And that in itself is a form of honesty with yourself.
[pause 2s]
Imagine setting the bag of stones down on the ground, beside you. It's still there, and you can pick it up again if you want. But for now, your arms can rest.
Feel your arms, your shoulders, your hands, as if they really had just let go of something heavy. Let them soften, in rhythm with your breath.
[pause 5s]
Now, one last step, a more delicate one. In some situations, we also carry part of the responsibility. A reaction that was too sharp, a silence, a boundary we didn't manage to set.
If that's the case for you, if part of this story belongs to you, look at it with the same gentleness.
You did what you could, with what you knew, with what you were feeling at the time. You can tell yourself... I forgive myself for my part, too. I'm learning.
And if no part of it is yours, which happens too, you can simply thank yourself for taking the time to look at all this.
If strong emotions come up, tears, sharp anger, let them pass through like a wave. That's normal. Breathe, come back to your feet, open your eyes if you need to.
[pause 3s]
Now stay for a few moments without doing anything. Notice your body. Your jaw, your chest, your belly. Is there a little more space than at the beginning?
[pause 3s]
If there's a little space, breathe into it. A breath in that goes a little further. A breath out that sets down a little more.
[pause 4s]

And if nothing has changed, that's normal too. Letting go of a grudge is a process, not a switch. It happens in layers, like peeling an onion. You may need to come back to it several times. Each time, the weight gets a little lighter.
The anger may come back tomorrow. That isn't going backwards. It's just another layer showing itself.
On that day, you can simply come back to your feet, to your breath, and repeat the phrase that spoke to you today. No need to start from scratch.
[pause 2s]
Gently bring your attention back to the room. The sounds, the temperature of the air, the feel of your clothes against your skin.
Move your fingers and feet a little. Roll your shoulders, once or twice.
And when the moment is right for you, open your eyes.
[pause 2s]
If this story comes back to visit you today, remember the image of the bag set down on the ground. You don't have to carry it all the time. You have the right to feel freer.
And tonight, before you fall asleep, you can take one single breath and think... I'm putting it down, a little.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: A difficult person
script: [pause 1.5s]

There's probably someone in your life who tests you. A colleague who talks over you in meetings. A neighbor who makes noise at midnight. A brother in law with an opinion on everything. An ex you still have to coordinate with about the kids.
Just thinking about them, something may already be tightening. That's normal. These relationships cost us a lot of energy, often far beyond the time we actually spend with the person.
[pause 1.5s]
This practice won't change that person. It doesn't ask you to like them, or to accept everything. It offers something quieter. Loosening, a little, the grip this relationship has on you.

To do that, we'll use loving kindness, in several stages. First for yourself, then for someone you love. Only once you've built that solid base will we approach the difficult person. And always at your own pace.
[pause 2s]
Settle into a comfortable, stable position. Feet flat, back supported, hands resting on your thighs, palms up or down, whichever you prefer.
Close your eyes, or let your gaze rest on the floor, about a meter in front of you.
[pause 1.5s]
Take a full breath in through your nose...
[pause 3s]
and let it flow out through your mouth, slowly.
[pause 5s]
A second time. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out, letting your shoulders move away from your ears.
[pause 5s]
One last time, at your own pace. Then let your breathing return to its natural rhythm.
[pause 5s]
Feel where your body is supported. Your feet, resting on the floor. Your thighs, on the seat. Your back, against the chair. Let your weight sink a little into whatever is holding you.
Then find your breath in one precise place. Maybe the cool air coming in through your nostrils. Maybe your belly rising and falling.
Keep this anchor in mind. If at any point the practice becomes too uncomfortable, you can always come back here. Your feet on the floor, your breath coming and going.
Take a moment to really feel it. A few breaths where you do nothing but notice the air coming in and going out. This is your home port.
[pause 6s]
We'll begin with you. Because you need to feel safe before venturing onto difficult ground. And because you, too, deserve kindness.
Place a hand on your heart, if that feels good. Feel its warmth.
And silently offer yourself these wishes, slowly.
[pause 1.5s]
May I find peace.
[pause 2s]
May I be free from fear.
[pause 2s]
May I take care of myself gently.
[pause 2s]
May I live with more lightness.
[pause 3s]
Let each phrase sink in, like a stone drifting slowly to the bottom of a lake. You don't need to feel anything strong. Just offer the intention.
Think of everything you're carrying right now. The responsibilities, the worries, the tiredness. And all the energy this difficult relationship takes from you, too.
[pause 2s]
Once more, for yourself. May I find peace. May I be free from fear. May I take care of myself gently. May I live with more lightness.
[pause 3s]
Do these phrases warm anything, even slightly?
[pause 2s]
And if it feels neutral, just keep the rhythm of the words, like a lullaby.
Imagine these wishes wrapping around you like a warm coat, one you'll keep on for the whole practice.
[pause 3s]
Now bring to mind someone you love easily. Someone with whom everything is simple. A friend, a child, a grandmother, a partner.
See their face. Their smile, their eyes. Imagine them sitting beside you, their presence warming you.
If it helps, remember one particular moment you shared. A laugh, a meal, a walk. Let that memory feed the warmth.
Notice the details. The light, the sounds, their laugh. The more concrete it is, the warmer it tends to feel.
[pause 2s]
Let the tenderness rise naturally. And offer them these wishes.
[pause 1.5s]
May you find peace.
[pause 2s]
May you be free from fear.
[pause 2s]
May you take care of yourself gently.
[pause 2s]
May you live with more lightness.
[pause 3s]
Notice how easily these words come for this person. Notice the warmth in your chest, maybe a smile. This warmth is your resource. You'll take it with you into the next stage.
[pause 2s]
Before going further, check in with how you feel. If you're already tired, or feeling raw, you can stay here, with this warmth. That's a complete practice in itself.
[pause 2s]

Now, if the moment feels right, we'll bring in the difficult person. One important note. Choose someone moderately difficult. Not the person who has hurt you most in your life. Not someone who has put your safety at risk. Someone who irritates you, frustrates you, stresses you, but around whom you can stay safe.
If no one feels manageable enough today, you can stay with the person you love, or come back to yourself. That's completely valid.
Practicing with someone easier is still real practice. It builds the strength you'll need later.
[pause 2s]
If you've chosen someone, let their image appear. Not too close. You can imagine them on the far side of a room, or behind a pane of glass. You keep whatever distance suits you.
See their face. Their usual expression. Maybe a typical situation, a phrase they often say.
Remember, you can keep them at a distance. You're in charge of how close this gets.
[pause 3s]
Now notice what's happening in your body, without changing anything.
Maybe your jaw clenches. Your stomach tightens. Your breathing gets shorter, or your chest closes. Maybe a flush of anger in your face, or an urge to get away.
[pause 2s]
Simply name what you observe. Irritation. Tension. Wariness. Weariness.
Naming it helps create a little room between you and the reaction.
Notice the thoughts that arrive, too. The reproaches, the things you wish you'd said, the scenes replaying in your head. You don't have to follow them. Recognize them, and come back to your body.
[pause 2s]
And offer yourself a little kindness first. Your hand on your heart. A slow breath. You can tell yourself, this relationship is hard for me. My reaction makes sense.
If you like, breathe like this. Breathing in, kindness for you...
[pause 4s]
breathing out, a little space around the tension.
[pause 6s]
Now, if you can, look at this person from a slightly different angle. Not to excuse their behavior. Just to see a little more widely.
This person, like you, has a body that gets tired. A heart that beats. Nights when they sleep badly.
Mornings when they wake up already worried.
They were a child once, too. A child who wanted to be loved, comforted, understood.
[pause 2s]
They may have worries you know nothing about. Fragile health, a relationship falling apart, enormous pressure at work, a difficult childhood.
Imagine them, for example, in the morning, in front of the mirror. Without their role, without their armor. Just someone starting their day, with their doubts.
[pause 2s]
Like you, they want to be happy. Like you, they want to avoid suffering. And often, their difficult behavior is a clumsy way of protecting themselves, or of coping with their own pain.
You don't have to find that fair. You can simply notice it. They're a human being too, with their wounds, just like me.
Take a breath with that idea. Does anything shift, even slightly, in your belly or your shoulders?
[pause 4s]
Now, if you feel able, try offering them some simple wishes. You can start with just one. And if it's too much, you can stop at any time.
[pause 1.5s]
May you find peace.
[pause 2.5s]
May you be free from what makes you suffer.
[pause 2.5s]
May you find a calmer way of being with others.
[pause 3s]
Take your time between each phrase. You can say them half heartedly, without conviction. The intention matters more than the feeling.
Notice what that does. Maybe resistance, a voice saying they don't deserve it. Maybe a small, unexpected loosening. Or both at once.
Keep one simple idea in mind. A person at peace generally does less harm to those around them. Wishing them peace is also, in a way, wishing yourself more peaceful relationships.
[pause 2s]
If the anger is too strong, you can go back to wishes for yourself. May I find peace around this person. May I be free from fear. That's a perfectly valid way to practice too.

And remember, wishing someone well doesn't stop you from setting clear boundaries. You can offer them these wishes and still say no, still protect yourself, still ask for respect. Kindness isn't the same as giving in.
[pause 2s]
If you can, offer these wishes once more, even half heartedly. May you find peace. May you be free from what makes you suffer.
[pause 3s]
And if intense emotions come up, that's normal. These relationships often touch sensitive places. Come back to your feet, to your breath, and open your eyes if you need to.
[pause 3s]
Now gently let the image of this person move away. They leave the room. You no longer need to hold them in mind.
Come back to yourself. Place both hands on your heart, or on your belly. Feel their warmth.
Let your hands tell your body, we're back with someone who's on our side.
Breathe slowly, and let your body know that this part is over. You're safe here.
[pause 3s]
You've just done something brave. You looked directly at a relationship that weighs on you, and brought a little openness to it, however small.
Offer yourself these wishes one last time. May I find peace. May I be free from fear. May I take care of myself gently. May I live with more lightness.
[pause 4s]
Stay in this space for a few moments, without doing anything. Notice your body now. Your jaw, your belly, your shoulders. Is there a difference from the moment that person first appeared?
[pause 3s]
Maybe a little more space. Maybe nothing in particular. That's okay. This kind of practice often works over time, in small touches.
Whatever you notice, you can meet it with the same kindness you offered yourself at the start.
Notice, too, what you've learned about yourself. Perhaps a need that isn't being respected in this relationship. Calm, recognition, space. That need deserves your attention.
The next time you see this person, you don't have to act any differently. But you may feel just a little more distance. Half a second more before you react. That can change a lot.
Because in that half second, you get to choose your response, instead of simply reacting.
[pause 1.5s]
And if this relationship ever becomes truly too heavy, or causes you lasting pain, you have the right to seek support, from someone close or from a professional.
[pause 3s]
Gently, bring your attention back to your breath. Then to the room. The sounds, the light behind your eyelids, the temperature of the air.
Wiggle your fingers and toes. Stretch, if you feel like it.
And when the moment is right for you, open your eyes.
[pause 2s]
Today, if this person puts you on edge again, try to remember, silently, that they want to be happy too, just like you. And give yourself, first of all, one kind breath.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Bedtime body scan
script: [pause 1.5s]
For the next twenty minutes, you have only one thing to do. Lie still, and listen.
We'll travel through your whole body, slowly, very slowly, from your feet to the top of your head.
And in each place, we'll switch it off. The way you switch off the lights in a house at night, room by room, before going to bed.
[pause 2s]
Why does this help? Because attention can't be everywhere at once. While it wanders slowly through your body, it's no longer circling around tomorrow.
And a body that's looked at with kindness tends to let go all by itself.
It's very likely you'll fall asleep before the end. In fact, that's the plan. If it happens, let my voice carry on without you. It doesn't need you to listen.
[pause 3s]
Lie on your back if you can. It's the simplest position for a body scan.
But if you fall asleep more easily on your side, choose your side. Your sleep comes before the method.
Let your arms rest by your sides, or your hands on your belly.
Legs stretched out, slightly apart. Feet falling loosely, each to its own side.
[pause 2s]
Take a moment for any last adjustments. Pull the duvet up to your chin, if you like. Plump the pillow. Brush a strand of hair from your face.
Shift your shoulders a little so they find their place. Gently roll your head to the right, to the left, then back to the center.
Look for the position where nothing pulls and nothing pinches. The one you could stay in for hours.
[pause 3s]
And when everything is in place, let yourself become still.
If something itches or bothers you later on, you're allowed to move. Scratch, adjust, then come back to stillness. This isn't a test.
[pause 2s]
Listen for a moment to the sounds around you. The rain outside, perhaps. A car somewhere far off. The soft hum of something in the house.
[pause 4s]
There's nothing you need to do with them. They can stay there in the background, like a rug of sound for you to rest on.
Close your eyes, if they aren't closed already.
[pause 2s]
Begin by listening to your breath, without changing it.
Where do you feel it most? Maybe at the edge of your nostrils, slightly cool air coming in, slightly warmer air going out. Maybe in your chest. Maybe in your belly.
[pause 3s]
There's no right place. Just choose the one where the breath feels easiest to follow.
Now let that breath slow down a little.
Breathe in easily, without puffing up your chest. Just what you need...
[pause 3s]
And breathe out for a little longer. As if the air were taking the stairs instead of the elevator. Step by step, in no hurry at all.
[pause 6s]
Once more. The air comes in without effort, like a wave sliding gently up the sand...
[pause 3s]
and flows out, slowly, all the way to the end, like the wave drawing back.
[pause 6s]
With each out-breath, your body grows a little heavier. A little more settled.
You don't need to count. You don't need to get it right. Your breath will find its night rhythm on its own.
If at any point you feel short of air, simply return to natural breathing.
[pause 2s]
Notice the small pause right at the bottom of the out-breath. That very quiet moment when the air has left, and nothing is rushing in yet.
You can rest in that hollow. Just for a moment. Then the in-breath returns by itself, without you having to reach for it.
[pause 5s]
Now let's begin the journey. Right at the bottom. With the feet.
Bring your attention to your right foot.
Start with the big toe. Its shape, its nail, its weight. The touch of the sheet or the duvet, right at the tip.
Then the second toe, next to it. The third, a little smaller. The fourth. And finally the little toe, right at the edge of the foot.
[pause 2s]
Maybe you can feel them clearly. Maybe you can hardly feel anything. Both are normal. It's enough just to rest your attention there, like a light hand.
Feel the tiny spaces between your toes. The air, or the warmth, tucked in there.
Feel the sole of the foot. The padded part just below the toes, which has carried you with every step today.
The curve of the arch, softer, touching nothing at all.
The heel, round and firm, resting on the mattress, carrying the whole weight of the leg.
Feel the top of the foot, where the duvet rests. The fine little bones under the skin. And the ankle, round and bony.
[pause 2s]
Now imagine a small light glowing in that foot. A night-light, soft and golden.
And gently, as you breathe out, that light dims. It fades. Then it goes out.
The right foot is switched off. It has nothing left to do tonight. It rests in the dark, peaceful.
Maybe it feels heavier than the other. Or warmer. Or different, in a way that's hard to describe. Just notice, without trying to understand.
[pause 5s]
The left foot, now.
The big toe first. Its weight, its warmth. Then the second toe. The third. The fourth. The tiny one, at the edge.
Let each toe loosen, drifting just slightly away from its neighbor, like children falling asleep side by side.
The sole of the left foot. The arch, light, suspended. The heel, well settled, sinking ever so slightly into the bed.
The top of the foot, under the light weight of the covers. The left ankle.
Here too, there's a small light. Let it dim... gently... until it goes out.
The left foot is switched off.
[pause 5s]
Both feet are resting in the dark now. Heavy. Warm. Still.
All day long, they've carried you. Along sidewalks, up stairs, down hallways. Tonight, they have nothing left to carry.
Imagine them sunk into fine sand, still warm from a summer's day. The sand covers your toes, your heels, your ankles, and holds the warmth around them.
A slow warmth that doesn't move. That wraps around. That makes your feet so heavy they seem to become part of the sand.
[pause 4s]
Moving up to the calves.
Feel your right calf. Its roundness. Its weight on the mattress. The muscle inside, which can loosen like a rope being slackened.
Feel the shin, at the front, just under the skin. And the back of the leg, softer, spreading a little across the sheet.
Let the calf become soft, like dough left to rest somewhere warm.
And on the out-breath, let the light in the right calf go out too.
[pause 3s]
The left calf. Its weight. Its warmth. The muscle unwinding, fiber by fiber.
The shin, at the front. The back of the leg, growing a little heavier with every breath.
And the light dimming... dimming... and going out.
You may know this feeling, after a long walk, when you finally sit down and your legs grow heavy, almost numb. Let that good heaviness come.
[pause 5s]
Your feet, your ankles, your calves. Your whole lower legs are switched off.
Notice how far away this part of your body feels now. Blurrier. Like a shore you leave behind by boat, fading into the mist.
[pause 3s]
The knees, now.
Feel your right knee. The front, the kneecap, under the duvet. The back of the knee, that soft little hollow that may be touching the mattress.
Let that hollow soften. Let the knee grow heavy.
And the light in the right knee goes out.
[pause 2s]
The left knee. The kneecap. The hollow behind. Everything that bends and straightens all day, and tonight can stay still.
How many times did these knees bend today? To sit down, to stand up, to climb a step, to pick something up. They can rest now.
The light dims... and goes out.
[pause 4s]
The thighs.
These are big muscles, often tense without our noticing. Feel your right thigh. Its length. Its weight, spreading across the bed.
Feel the front of the thigh, under the duvet. The inner side, more tender. The back, resting along its whole length on the mattress.
Let it grow heavier still. As if it were sinking a little into the mattress.
The light in the right thigh goes out.
[pause 3s]
The left thigh. Heavy. Broad. Let go.
Feel the skin of your thigh against the sheet. The fabric slightly cool on one side, the warmth of the duvet on the other.
Let this big muscle unfold and soften, like a wool sweater laid over a chair at the end of the day.
It too switches off.
[pause 4s]
And now, the pelvis.
Feel your hips. The hip bones, on either side. Your buttocks, carrying a large part of your weight.
Feel your lower belly, below the navel. The inside of the pelvis, like a wide bowl.
Let all of it settle. Sink down into the mattress, like sand drifting to the bottom of the water.
The pelvis is the body's center of gravity. When it lets go, everything else often follows. The legs widen. The lower back spreads. The belly softens.
And the light in the pelvis dims, slowly... and goes out.
[pause 6s]
The whole lower half of your body is switched off now. From your toes to your hips.
It's dark and soft down there. All is calm. Nothing moves.
[pause 3s]
If you got lost along the way, if you're thinking about something else, that's fine. Just come back to wherever my voice is.
The mind wanders, that's its nature. A shopping list, a conversation, a song. Each time you notice, bring it back, without scolding. The way you'd call back a puppy that's wandered off the path.
And if you feel sleep arriving, if your thoughts turn strange or drift apart, let them. It's often a sign that the night is already carrying you off.
[pause 5s]
Moving up to the belly.
Feel your belly rising as the air comes in, and falling as it goes out.
It doesn't need to be flat, or held in. It can be round, soft, relaxed. Let it be exactly as it is.
[pause 3s]
Feel your navel, and the space around it. The hollow under your ribs. The sides of your waist, sinking a little into the bed.
You might imagine a small warmth in the middle of your belly, like a hot-water bottle resting on it. It spreads gently, out to the sides, round to your back.
A round, patient warmth. Like a mug of herbal tea held between your hands.
And on an out-breath, the light in the belly dims... and goes out.
[pause 5s]
The back, now.
Start with the lower back. That curve just above the pelvis, which may be touching the mattress, or may not.
Let it spread. Lengthen. As if each vertebra were moving ever so slightly away from the next.
The middle of the back. The ribs, at the back, moving gently with the breath.
The upper back. The shoulder blades, lying flat on the bed, like two folded wings.
[pause 2s]
Your whole spine, from bottom to top, resting on the mattress. Supported. Held. You don't need to hold yourself up anymore.
If you feel a tighter spot, somewhere between your shoulder blades or in your lower back, send your out-breath there. Imagine the air reaching it, and warming it a little.
The light in your back goes out. Vertebra by vertebra. Like lamps along a long hallway being switched off one by one, starting from the far end.
[pause 5s]
And the chest.
Feel your chest rising and falling, gently, under the duvet.
Feel your ribs, like a supple cage opening and closing.
Maybe you can feel your heart beating, somewhere in there. You don't need to do anything with it. It does its work quietly, as it does every night.
[pause 3s]
Let your chest soften. Widen a little.
We often keep the chest a little closed, a little guarded, without realizing it. Tonight, you're safe. It can open, just slightly, like a window left ajar to the night.
And the light in the chest dims... and goes out.
[pause 3s]
Your belly, your back, your chest. Your whole torso is switched off.
Only a few rooms in the house are still lit. We'll go there gently.
[pause 3s]
The hands.
Feel your right hand. The thumb first. Its fleshy base, its nail, its tip.
The index finger. The middle finger, the longest. The ring finger. And the little finger, right at the edge.
Let each finger uncurl just a little, open up, and stop holding on to anything.
The palm. The hollow of the hand, warm and soft. The back of the hand. The wrist.
These hands have done so much today. Held, carried, typed, opened, closed. Tonight, they can open and hold nothing at all.
Maybe you can feel something in your fingertips. A faint tingling, a pulse, some warmth. That's life flowing quietly, all the way to the edges.
The light in the right hand goes out.
[pause 3s]
The left hand. Thumb. Index finger. Middle finger. Ring finger. Little finger.
The palm, the back of the hand, the wrist.
Let it become heavy and limp. Like an empty glove lying on a table.
And the light in the left hand goes out.
[pause 4s]
The arms.
The forearms first. Feel their weight on the mattress, or on your belly.
The elbows, a little pointed, leaning into the bed. The upper arms, up to the shoulders.
Let them grow so heavy you could forget they're there.
Like heavy branches laden with snow, no longer trying to lift. They bow. They settle.
The light in both arms dims... and goes out.
[pause 4s]
And the shoulders.
The shoulders are often the attic of the day. We pile everything up there. Responsibilities, tension, things we mustn't forget.
Tonight, you can clear out the attic.
No need to sort. No need to tidy it all. You just open the skylight and let the night air in.
[pause 2s]
Let your shoulders drop, away from your ears. Let them widen, flatten onto the mattress.
Feel the tops of your shoulders, that little ledge where we carry bags and worries. Let it melt, like butter spreading slowly in a warm pan.
And on a long out-breath, the light in your shoulders goes out.
[pause 6s]
Only the head is left. The last room with the light on.
Start with the back of your neck, resting on the pillow.
Let your head weigh its full weight. The pillow takes all of it. You don't need to hold it up anymore.
Feel the front of your neck too. The throat. The place where you swallow. Let it soften, open, as if a collar that was too tight had just been undone.
The light in your neck goes out.
[pause 3s]
The jaw.
Feel where it hinges, just in front of your ears.
Let your teeth part a little. Let your tongue rest on the floor of your mouth, soft and wide.
Let your lips barely touch.
The whole lower face grows heavy, easy, a little slack. Like just before a yawn.
The light in your jaw goes out.
[pause 3s]
Your ears, now. They've heard so much today. Voices, engines, notifications, slamming doors.
Tonight, they don't need to stay on guard. The sounds of the night can reach them, or not. They're resting.
Your cheeks, growing round and heavy. Your nose. The air brushing the edge of your nostrils.
[pause 2s]
Your eyes, now. Feel your eyelids resting on your eyes, like two petals.
Behind your eyelids, your eyes can rest. They have nothing left to look at. No screen, no face, no road.
Let them sink back gently, heavy and still.
The light in your eyes goes out.
[pause 5s]
And the forehead.
Feel the whole surface of your forehead. Your eyebrows. The space between them, where worries sometimes settle.
Let your forehead smooth out. Widen. Like the surface of a lake when the wind has dropped.
Your temples. The top of your head. The back of your head.
Imagine all the skin of your scalp relaxing, like after a head massage at the hairdresser's. A fine, light ease, flowing slowly down to the back of your neck.
And very gently, the last light in the house dims... dims a little more... and goes out.
[pause 8s]
Now all the lights are out.
Your body is no longer made of separate parts. No more feet, legs, arms on their own.
There is just one quiet mass, heavy and warm, resting in the dark.
Like a hill under snow, at night. Still. Silent. Peaceful.
[pause 4s]
Perhaps you can no longer quite tell where your hands end and the sheets begin. Where your feet stop. That's normal. That's the body falling asleep.
Let this quiet mass spread out, melt into the mattress, into the warmth of the duvet, into the darkness of the room.
[pause 4s]
The breath carries on by itself, inside this quiet mass. Rising... falling...
Like the sea, far away, beyond the dunes. You can't see it. You can barely hear it. But it's there, steady, and it never stops.
[pause 5s]
You have nothing to do. Nothing to watch over. The house is asleep.
And if a thought still drifts by, it passes far away. Like a car's headlights gliding across the ceiling, then gone.
You don't need to follow it. It leaves on its own, and the dark comes back, soft and deep.
[pause 5s]
Feel the warmth that has settled everywhere. In your feet, in your legs, in your belly, in your hands.
An even, quiet warmth, like a bed you've already been sleeping in for hours.
Feel the weight, too. That good, heavy weight holding you against the mattress. You couldn't fall.
The mattress holds you. The duvet covers you. The night keeps watch over the house.
[pause 5s]
There's no time anymore. No list. Nothing to get ready.
Only the breath, slow... and the warmth... and the dark.
[pause 6s]
If you've been finding it hard to sleep for a long time, it may help to talk to a health professional. For now, just rest.
[pause 5s]
Heavy... and warm...
[pause 4s]
Each breath carries you a little further.
[pause 4s]
Further... deeper... softer.
[pause 6s]
Everything is switched off...
[pause 6s]
everything is still...
[pause 6s]
the night can begin...
[pause 10s]

sessions.title: The lighthouse keeper
script: [pause 1.5s]
Settle in comfortably, in the position you like to fall asleep in. Pull up the duvet, and let your head sink into the pillow.
Tonight, I'm going to tell you a story. A very simple story, where almost nothing happens.
[pause 2s]
You don't need to follow it to the end. You don't need to remember any of it.
If your attention drifts away, let it go. If you fall asleep in the middle, that's just as it should be.
Simply let my voice keep you company, like the sound of the sea heard from far off, through an open window.
[pause 4s]
It's the end of a September day, on the coast of Brittany.
The sky is clear. It rained a little in the morning, and now the air is rinsed clean, very bright, with that smell of salt and seaweed you only find by the ocean.
On the slipway of the little harbour, a man is waiting, a canvas bag at his feet. His name is Loïc. He's a lighthouse keeper.
Tonight, he's going back to his island, for a week on watch.
[pause 2s]
The ferryman arrives in his boat, an old wooden launch painted blue, the paint flaking a little at the edges. The engine makes a steady, reassuring sound. Put, put, put.
The two men greet each other with a nod. They've known each other a long time. They don't need to say much.
Loïc steps aboard. He sits at the back, his bag between his knees, and the boat slips gently out of the harbour.
[pause 2s]
The sea is calm. Just a long, lazy swell that lifts the boat, lets it down, and lifts it again.
The wooden bench is warm beneath him, heated by the afternoon sun. Through the soles of his boots, he can feel the slow, steady hum of the engine.
Behind them, the village grows smaller. White houses with blue shutters, the grey church tower, small boats resting on the sand at low tide. Everything becomes small, then distant, then blurred.
The gulls circle above the boat, then drift away toward the rocks. Their cries grow further and further off.
[pause 2s]
Loïc trails his hand over the side. The water is cool, almost cold.
It slips between his fingers, lively and salty. He watches the little drops sparkle in the sun as he lifts his hand out.
The ferryman holds the tiller without a word, eyes narrowed against the light. He knows every rock, every current. He could make the crossing with his eyes closed.
[pause 2s]
Ahead of them, the island draws near.
It's a tiny island, hardly bigger than a field. A lump of pink granite, covered in short grass and heather. And right at the far end, on the point, the lighthouse.
It's tall and white, with a red band at the top. At this hour, the low sun lights it from the side, and it looks almost golden.
The sun sinks slowly toward the horizon. The light turns warm and thick, the colour of honey. It settles on the water in millions of tiny dancing sparkles.
[pause 2s]
The boat draws up against a small stone jetty. Loïc steps onto the damp steps, slippery with kelp. The ferryman hands him his bag.
See you next week, says the ferryman.
See you next week, says Loïc.
And the boat heads off again, put, put, put, drawing a white wake across the golden sea. Loïc watches it go for a while. Then he turns toward the island.
[pause 3s]
A little dirt path climbs between the grasses. It's edged with flat stones, laid there long ago by other keepers.
Loïc walks slowly. He's in no hurry. He has the whole evening ahead of him.
The wind has dropped. All there is to hear is his footsteps on the path, the rustle of the grass, and the sea, all around, breathing against the rocks.
The air smells of sun-warmed heather, and of salt. Now and then a rabbit darts between the tufts of grass, then stops, and watches him go by.
[pause 2s]
At the foot of the lighthouse stands the keeper's cottage. A small, low house of granite, with a slate roof and a door painted green.
Loïc takes a big key from his pocket. The lock is a little stiff.
It has to be turned twice, with the handle lifted slightly. He knows the movement by heart.
The door opens with a small creak.
[pause 2s]
Inside, it smells of wood, of wax, and a little of a house left shut. Loïc opens the kitchen shutters. The evening light pours in, all orange, and settles on the wooden table.
He puts his bag down on a chair. He takes off his jacket and hangs it on the hook behind the door.
Then he kneels in front of the cast-iron stove, in the corner of the room.
[pause 2s]
He opens the little black door. Inside, there's still some grey ash from last week. He pats it down with the poker.

He takes a few sheets of newspaper from the basket, crumples them into balls, one by one, and lays them at the bottom. On top he places dry twigs, criss-crossed, like a little hut. Then two logs of oak, not too big.
He strikes a match. The small yellow flame trembles for a moment, then catches the paper.
The newspaper flares, curls, turns orange. The twigs crackle. And soon, the logs begin to sing softly.
[pause 2s]
Loïc closes the stove door, leaving the vent a little open. He stays crouched for a moment, watching the flames through the small glass window. He can already feel the warmth on his face.
Next, he fills the kettle at the tap. The water comes in fits and starts, a little cloudy at first, then clear and cold. It's rainwater from the cistern.
He sets the kettle on the stove.
[pause 2s]
While he waits, he takes out what he's brought for the week. A loaf of bread. A piece of salted butter wrapped in paper.
Some apples. A packet of tea. A few books.
He puts each thing in its place, unhurried. The bread in the bread bin. The butter in the larder, where it's cool.
The apples in a bowl on the table. The books on the shelf, beside the others.
[pause 2s]
The kettle begins to murmur. Then to whistle softly.
Loïc takes his mug, a big earthenware mug, chipped at the rim, that has always lived here. He drops in a pinch of black tea. He pours the hot water.
A fragrant steam rises to his face.
He sits at the table by the window, and holds the mug in both hands to warm them.
[pause 3s]
Outside, the sun is now touching the horizon. It turns red, then a deep orange. The sea beneath it takes on shades of pink and violet.
Loïc drinks his tea in small sips. It's hot, a little strong. He cuts a slice of bread, butters it generously, and eats it slowly while he watches the sky change colour.
The stove purrs. A log settles with a small, soft thud. The kitchen is warm now.
[pause 2s]
The sun disappears. There's only a strip of orange light left along the water, growing thinner, and thinner still.
Soon it will be time.
Loïc rinses his mug and sets it upside down on the draining board. He takes his torch from the shelf. He puts his jacket back on.
And he goes out, to climb the lighthouse.
[pause 5s]
The lighthouse is right next door, a few steps away. Its door is made of thick wood, strengthened with black iron.
Loïc pushes it. It opens slowly, heavily, and cool mineral air comes to meet him. The smell of stone, slightly damp, and of machine oil.
Inside, it's almost dark. Only a small window, very high up, lets in a last trace of blue light.
Loïc switches on his torch. The circle of light lands on the first steps.
[pause 2s]

The staircase spirals upward, around a central pillar. The steps are granite, worn down in the middle by the feet of all the keepers who came before him. A little hollowed, a little polished, like pebbles.
A brass handrail follows the curve of the wall. It's cool and smooth under his hand.
Loïc sets his foot on the first step. Then on the second.
[pause 2s]
He climbs slowly. One step, then another.
He knows the number by heart, a hundred and twenty-eight steps. But tonight he doesn't count. He simply climbs.
The sound of his footsteps echoes softly off the walls. A small, round echo that rises with him.
One step. Then another.
[pause 2s]
The pillar turns beside him, always on his left. The handrail slides under his right hand.

Every so often he passes a small square window, set deep into the thickness of the wall. Through the first, he sees the keeper's cottage, its slate roof, the smoke from the stove rising straight up into the still air.
He carries on. One step, then another.
[pause 2s]
Through the second window, he sees the whole island. The heather, the little path, the jetty. And the sea all around, a deeper and deeper blue.
He carries on. His breathing is slow and steady.
His legs know the way. He doesn't need to think.
One step, then another. The spiral turns, and turns again. The torchlight dances on the stone.
[pause 2s]
Through the third window, there's almost nothing but sky. A midnight-blue sky, where the first star appears. Just one, all alone, above the horizon.
He carries on. The steps grow a little narrower as he nears the top.
The wall comes closer. The air grows cooler.
One step. Then another. Then the last.
[pause 2s]
Loïc pushes open a small wooden hatch above his head. And he climbs into the lantern room.
It's a round room, glass on every side. All around, there's nothing but sky and sea.
Nothing else. As far as the eye can see.
[pause 2s]

In the centre stands the great lens of the lighthouse. It's enormous, as tall as a man, made of dozens of rings of cut glass, layered like the petals of a flower. Even unlit, it catches the last glints of the day and makes them shimmer softly.
Loïc sets down his torch. He takes off his jacket and folds it on the little bench.
Then he begins the evening routine. The same tasks every evening, in the same order.
[pause 2s]
He takes a soft cloth from the drawer. He wipes the windows of the lantern, one by one, working his way around the room. He removes the salt the wind has left during the day.
One pane. Then the next. Then the next.
Then he wipes the lens. Delicately, from top to bottom, following the curve of each glass ring. The cloth glides without a sound.
He checks the oil level in the mechanism. He winds up the counterweight a little. He listens to the faint ticking of the gears.
Everything is in order. Everything is ready.
[pause 3s]
Outside, the sky is now a deep blue, almost black in the east. In the west there's still a pale glow, green and gold, just above the sea.
Loïc looks at his watch. It's time.
He turns the little copper switch.
[pause 2s]
At first, nothing happens. Then comes a faint hum. And at the heart of the lens, the lamp comes on.
The light grows, white and warm. It passes through the rings of glass, which gather it, focus it, and send it far away, in a great beam reaching out over the sea.
Then the mechanism starts up with a small click. And the lens begins to turn.
Slowly. Very slowly. Without a sound, or almost.
[pause 3s]
The beam sweeps across the sea. It passes over the dark water, slides toward the horizon, then swings back toward the coast, lights up the island's rocks for a moment, and sets off out to sea again.
One turn. Then another. Then another still.
Loïc sits on the little bench, against the glass. He watches.
The beam turns above his head. It passes, it goes, it comes back.
Always at the same pace. Steady as a breath.
[pause 3s]
Night has fallen now. A real night, deep and full of stars. There are hundreds of them.
Thousands. The longer you look, the more appear.
The sea is black and calm. Its surface shows only in the small glints when the lighthouse beam passes over it.
[pause 2s]
Far away, very far, there's a ship. All there is to see are its lights.
A small white light at the top of the mast, a green light on the side. It moves gently, unhurried, toward the south.
Loïc watches it for a long time. The ship can see the lighthouse too. It knows where it is.
It knows where the rocks are. It can carry on its way, untroubled.
[pause 3s]
Further still, along the coast, there's the light of another lighthouse. A small white flash, returning every ten seconds. Like an old friend waving from the other side of the bay.
The beam turns. It passes, it goes, it comes back.
A little later, a small trawler heads home to the harbour, across the bay. Its lights move slowly over the black water. Carried on the still air, there's almost the hum of its engine.
The fishermen are going home. Soon they'll be in bed too, in the houses with the blue shutters.
[pause 3s]
Loïc writes in the big logbook. Clear sky, calm sea, no wind, one vessel offshore, heading south. His handwriting is slow and careful. The pen scratches the paper a little.
Then he closes the logbook, and stays a while longer, looking at the night.
[pause 3s]
In the east, behind the coast, the moon is rising. It's nearly full, a little orange at first, huge just above the hills. Then, as it climbs, it pales, turns white, then silver.
Its light settles on the sea. A long silver path stretches across the water, from the horizon right up to the island's rocks. It trembles a little, in time with the swell.
The lighthouse beam crosses this moon path on every turn. A white light that turns, a silver light that stays still. And between the two, the sea, vast and calm.
[pause 3s]
There's nothing else to do. The lighthouse does its work.
The light turns by itself. The sea breathes below, against the rocks.
[pause 3s]
After a while, Loïc stands. He shrugs his jacket back on. He takes one last look at the lens, turning, bright and calm.
Then he opens the hatch, and goes back down.
One step, then another. The spiral turns the other way this time. The brass rail slides under his left hand.
[pause 2s]
He goes down slowly. The small windows pass one by one, all dark now. In each, now and then, the glow of the beam passes, and is gone.
His footsteps are softer now. As if the staircase itself had fallen asleep.
One step, then another. At the bottom, the door.
The path. The cool night air, smelling of salt and heather.
Above him, the beam sweeps the sky, slowly, silently.
[pause 3s]
Loïc goes back into the cottage. It's cosy.
The stove has warmed the kitchen through. He adds one last log, and closes the vent, so the fire will burn gently until morning.
He turns off the kitchen lamp.
He climbs the little wooden staircase to his bedroom, under the roof.
[pause 2s]
It's a small, simple room. A wooden bed. A thick, checked wool blanket.
A bedside table with a candle and a book. A round window, like a porthole, looking out over the sea.
Loïc undresses and folds his clothes on the chair. He pulls on an old wool jumper that smells of wood smoke.
[pause 2s]
He slips under the sheets. They're cool at first. Then, very quickly, they warm up.
