The wool of the blanket is a little rough under his fingers. It smells of soap, and of the sea wind that dried it on the line last summer.
He blows out the candle.
[pause 3s]
In the dark, he listens.
The waves. Down below, against the rocks.
They come in, they draw back. They come in, they draw back.
[pause 3s]
Through the round window, the glow of the lighthouse passes over the ceiling. A long streak of pale light that glides... and fades. Then comes back.
The waves come in... they draw back.
[pause 3s]
Down on the little shingle beach, the pebbles roll softly as the water pulls away. A gentle sound, like a string of beads slipping slowly through someone's fingers.
The blanket is heavy and warm.
The stove creaks softly, downstairs.
The light passes over the ceiling... and goes.
[pause 4s]
Outside, the whole island is asleep.
The little path edged with flat stones, silvered by the moon.
The tufts of heather, perfectly still. The rabbits, curled up deep in their burrows, ears folded along their backs.
The stone jetty, where the water rises gently with the tide, step by step, without a sound.
[pause 3s]
On the rocks, the seaweed lifts and settles, slowly, in time with the swell. It gleams for a moment whenever the lighthouse beam passes over it.
Across the bay, the village is asleep too. The blue shutters are closed.
The church tower stands in the night, grey on black. In the harbour, the small boats rock at the end of their moorings.
[pause 3s]
The ferryman is asleep in his house by the water. His old blue launch is tied to the quay, and the swell rocks it, very slowly.
And in the middle of it all, the lighthouse keeps watch. Its light turns, and turns again, above the houses, above the boats, above the sea. So that everyone can sleep in peace.
[pause 4s]
Loïc closes his eyes.
[pause 3s]
The waves... against the rocks...
[pause 3s]
The light turning... up above...
[pause 3s]
The ship, far away... going on its way...
[pause 3s]
The stars... thousands of them...
[pause 4s]
The sea, breathing...
[pause 4s]
Softly...
[pause 4s]
Slowly...
[pause 10s]

sessions.title: Summer night in Provence
script: [pause 1.5s]
Before we begin, get yourself nice and settled. Find the position where your body feels most at ease, and let the bed hold you.
Tonight, we're heading south. To an old stone house in the hills, on a summer evening.
There's nothing to remember in this story. No plot, no surprises. Just scents, sounds, and the heat of the day slowly fading.
If you fall asleep before the end, that's perfect. Let my voice carry on without you, like a radio left on very low in the next room.
[pause 4s]
It's the end of a long July day, in Provence.

You arrived here a few days ago, at the farmhouse of a friend who has lent it to you for the summer. A big, low house of pale golden stone, with lavender coloured shutters, and a roof of curved tiles, a little crooked, that have taken on every shade of orange and pink.
All afternoon, it's been very hot. A white, motionless heat that made the air shimmer above the fields. You stayed indoors, in the cool of the thick walls, the shutters half closed.
You read a little. You dozed. You felt the cool tiles under your bare feet.
And now, at last, the heat is beginning to ease.
[pause 2s]
You open the kitchen door, the one that leads out to the garden. The air outside is still warm, but it has changed.
It's softer, lighter. A small breeze is coming down from the hills, and it smells of thyme.
The light has changed too. It's no longer white. It's golden and low, stretching the shadows across the dry earth.
The shadow of the fig tree reaches all the way to the wall. The shadow of the well grows long and thin, like the needle of a sundial.
[pause 2s]
You step outside, barefoot. The flagstones in front of the house are still warm.
Their warmth rises into the soles of your feet, a round, gentle heat, stored up all day long. Then you step onto the dry grass, which crackles softly underfoot, and it's cooler.
You pause for a moment by the old well. You rest your hand on its stone rim, worn smooth by the years, warm as a cheek.
Far below, the dark water holds a small circle of sky. A smell of wet stone and moss drifts up towards you.
You let the bucket down on its rope, and it comes up heavy and dripping. You dip your hands in. The water is cool and clear, and you press your wet palms gently to your cheeks, to your neck.
[pause 2s]
The garden slopes gently down, in small terraces held up by dry stone walls. You take the little gravel path that winds between them.
First, there's the lavender.

Rows and rows of lavender, perfectly round, like purple cushions lined up along the path. The flowers are in full bloom. A few late bees are still humming among them, moving from one stem to the next, heavy and slow, before heading home to the hive.
You pass your hand over the stems, barely brushing the flowers. At once, the scent rises.
A strong, clean, slightly peppery scent that stays on your fingers. You bring your hand to your face, and breathe in.
It's the smell of a grandmother's wardrobe, of sheets folded away with a little cloth sachet. The smell of childhood summers.
[pause 2s]
A little further on, against the wall, grows a big rosemary bush. Its small, needle like leaves are dark green, silvery underneath. You pick a sprig.
You roll it between your fingers. Its scent is more resinous, warmer, like a pine forest in the sun.
There's thyme too, in little grey tufts close to the ground. And sage, with leaves as soft and velvety as a rabbit's ear.
All these scents blend in the evening air. They rise from the earth, still warm, and float around you like an invisible scarf.
[pause 2s]
At the end of the path, on the last terrace, stands the old fig tree.
It's an enormous tree, twisted, with a trunk as grey and smooth as an elephant's skin. Its branches spread very low, almost to the ground, and its big rough leaves cast a thick, green, cool shade.
You step under the branches. Suddenly it's cooler. The air smells of milk and honey, that unmistakable scent of fig leaves after a whole day warming in the sun.
The figs are ripe. They hang beneath the leaves, purple, slightly split, swollen with sugar. You pick one.
It's warm and soft in your hand. You open it with your thumbs. Inside, the flesh is pink, almost red, full of tiny seeds.
You eat it slowly, standing under the tree. It's as sweet as jam.
[pause 2s]
All around you, the cicadas are singing.
They've been singing since morning. All day long their song has filled the air, shrill and unbroken, so constant you stopped hearing it. It was part of the heat, like the light.
But now that the sun is sinking, their song is changing.
It becomes less regular. There are pauses. One cicada stops, then another.
Then they start again, a little softer. Like an orchestra playing its final bars, in no hurry.
You stay there under the fig tree, listening.
The song is running out of breath. It comes in waves now. One wave rising from the big pine by the gate.
Another answering from the other side, among the olive trees. Then a silence. Then another wave, fainter.
And little by little, one by one, the cicadas fall silent.
Only one is left, somewhere in an olive tree. It sings on a little longer, alone, as if it wanted the last word. Then it stops too.
[pause 2s]
And the silence arrives.
Not an empty silence. A silence full of small sounds. The rustle of fig leaves in the breeze.
A bird calling two notes in the distance. The tinkle of a goat's bell, on the far side of the hill.
[pause 2s]
From the bottom of the garden, you can see the whole valley. Wheat fields already harvested, the colour of straw.
Rows of olive trees with silver leaves. Vineyards in neat lines, following the curve of the hills.
And on the hill opposite, a little hilltop village, huddled around its church. Its houses are the same colour as the stone of the hill, so it looks as if they simply grew there.
In the bell tower, a bell begins to ring. Seven strokes, slow and spaced out.
The sound crosses the valley and reaches you, softened by distance. Then the last stroke fades, and the air closes over it.
You walk back up towards the house, unhurried, along the gravel path. You pass the lavender again, and the rosemary. You let your fingers trail over the flowers.
[pause 4s]
In front of the house, there's the arbour.
Four old wooden posts, and over them, a trellis covered with vines. The leaves make a living green roof, pierced with little holes of light.
Bunches of grapes hang among the leaves, still green and hard. They'll be ripe at the end of summer.
Under the arbour stands a long wooden table, grey and weathered by the years, with a bench on either side.
That's where you'll have dinner tonight. A very simple dinner.
[pause 2s]
You go back into the kitchen. It's cool and a little dim, with red terracotta tiles on the floor and beams across the ceiling. Bunches of herbs hang upside down to dry, near the window.
You take a big earthenware dish, glazed yellow. You put in tomatoes from the garden, still warm from the sun, and cut them into wedges.
They're red, fleshy, a little uneven. Their juice runs across the board.
You add a drizzle of golden green olive oil. A few grains of coarse salt that crunch between your fingers. Basil leaves, torn by hand, whose scent fills the kitchen at once.
You also take a piece of goat's cheese, a small round loaf, and a handful of black olives, wrinkled and glossy.
You carry it all outside, to the table under the arbour. You go back for a jug of cool water with a slice of lemon in it. And a glass.
[pause 2s]
You sit down on the bench. The wood is smooth, polished by years of summer meals.
You eat slowly. There's no one to wait for, nowhere to go. Just this meal, and the fading light.
The bread crackles between your teeth. The tomato is sweet and sharp at once.
The olive oil tastes faintly of cut grass. The cheese is fresh, a little lemony.
Now and then you sip some water. It's cold, and you feel its coolness travel all the way down.
A faint smell of woodsmoke drifts in from far away, carried on the evening air. Somewhere down in the valley, at another farmhouse, someone is making their dinner too.
[pause 2s]
The neighbour's cat arrives without a sound, along the top of the wall. A tabby, lean and calm. It jumps onto the bench opposite, sits, and watches you eat, blinking slowly.
You give it a little piece of cheese. It takes it delicately, eats it, then curls up on the warm bench and closes its eyes. It will stay there a while, purring, before slipping away into the night.
[pause 2s]
Above you, through the vine leaves, the sky shifts from pale blue to pink, then to mauve.
A swallow darts past, skimming the arbour, then another. They wheel through the evening sky with little high cries, catching the last insects.
Then, little by little, they too disappear.
The sun has set behind the hill. There's only an orange glow above the ridge, where the cypresses and the pines stand out, black.
[pause 2s]
To finish, you take a peach from the basket. A vineyard peach, with downy, dark red skin. You cut it into slices with a small knife.
The juice runs over your fingers, sweet and fragrant. You eat it piece by piece, taking your time.
When you've finished, you stay sitting, your hands resting on the table. The wood is still warm.
You do nothing. You think of nothing in particular. You watch the garden slowly darken.
The colours go out one by one. The purple of the lavender turns grey.
The green of the fig tree turns black. The golden stones of the house turn blue, then grey.
The silence is deep now. A countryside silence. All you can hear, very far away, is a dog barking twice, then falling quiet.
[pause 3s]
You clear the table, unhurried. You carry the dish, the glass and the jug back to the kitchen. You rinse everything under cool water and set it on the draining rack.
Then you go back outside.
At the end of the terrace, near the low wall, there's an old deckchair in striped canvas, blue and white. You pull it a little further from the house, to where the sky is biggest.
You lie down.
Beneath the deckchair, the flagstones are gently giving back the warmth they've held all day. It rises to you through the canvas, like the warmth of a sleeping animal.
The canvas is taut under your back, supple and firm at once. It takes your shape. You rest your arms on the wooden armrests.
You stretch out your legs. You let your head fall back.
The air is mild now. Neither warm nor cool. Exactly the temperature of your skin, so that you can no longer quite tell where your body ends and the night begins.
[pause 3s]
The sky above you is a very deep blue. An ink blue.
And in that blue, a first star appears.
It's just above the hill, all alone, bright and clear. Perhaps it's a planet.
It doesn't twinkle. It shines, calmly.
You watch it. And while you're watching, a second star appears, a little higher. Then a third.
It's as if someone were lighting them one by one, very slowly, taking their time.
You don't see them arrive. You blink, and there they are.
Five. Ten. Twenty.
Here, far from any town, there's no light to hide them. Little by little, the sky fills up, until it's covered.
[pause 2s]
And then you see it. The Milky Way.
A long, pale, milky scarf crossing the sky from one side to the other. Like a cloud of glowing dust, resting there, motionless, forever.
You lie there, watching.

You recognise the Plough, its seven stars in the shape of a saucepan, the handle pointing towards the hill. You follow the edge of the pan with your eyes, and you find the North Star, alone, faithful, never moving.
Around it, slowly, through the night, the whole sky turns. But you can't see it move.
You'd have to stay there for hours. And you have no wish to count the hours.
[pause 3s]
On the hill opposite, the lights of the village go out, one by one. One window, then another.
People are going to bed. Soon only the little street lamp in the square is left, and the outline of the bell tower against the stars.
The crickets have taken over from the cicadas. Their song is softer, steadier.
A small chirr rising from the grass, from everywhere at once, calm and continuous. As if the earth itself were breathing.
Now and then a shooting star crosses the sky. A very fine, very quick streak of light, gone before you can point at it.
You don't need to make a wish. You just watch it pass.
[pause 3s]
The evening breeze still carries the scents of the garden. Lavender, thyme, rosemary. And a new scent, the smell of the earth cooling, finally breathing out the heat of the day.
At the foot of the deckchair, there's an old wool blanket, folded in four. You unfold it over your legs.
It's soft and a little thick, and it smells of the linen cupboard and of lavender. Its fringes tickle your ankles.
Your breathing is slow. Your arms are heavy on the armrests. Your eyelids are growing heavy too.
The breeze touches your bare arms, your ankles, your face, lightly, like a hand smoothing a sheet. There's nowhere you need to be.
Nothing you need to remember. Only the sky, and the crickets, and the slow, warm night.
[pause 3s]
You could stay there all night. But the air is gently cooling. It's time to go in.
You get up slowly. You fold the deckchair and lean it against the wall. You take one last look at the starry sky.
[pause 4s]
You go into the house. Inside, the thick walls have kept some of the day's coolness.
It's pleasant. The tiles are cool under your feet.
You climb the stone staircase to the bedrooms. The steps are slightly worn in the middle. The wrought iron banister is cool under your hand.
On the landing, a little gecko clings to the wall beside the window, pale and perfectly still, waiting for moths. It doesn't move as you pass. It's part of the house, like the beams and the tiles.

In the little bathroom upstairs, you let cool water run into your cupped hands, and splash it over your face, your neck, your arms. The coolness washes away the dust and the heat of the day. You dry yourself with a cotton towel, a little rough, that smells of Marseille soap.
[pause 2s]
Your room is simple. Whitewashed walls. A chest of drawers in pale wood.
A big iron bed with white sheets. And a window, with its lavender coloured shutters.
You open the window. You push the shutters out, then draw them back, not all the way.
You leave them half open, just enough to let the night air in. Just enough to see a small patch of starry sky.
The song of the crickets comes into the room. And the scent of lavender too, carried on the breeze.
[pause 4s]
You slip into bed.
The sheets are cool. Linen sheets, a little coarse, dried in the sun, still smelling of fresh air. Their coolness on your skin, after the heat of the day, is delicious.
You stretch, long and slow. You feel your legs slide through the cool sheets, all the way to the bottom of the bed.
Then you settle. Your head in the pillow. Your arms by your sides.
[pause 3s]
Through the half open shutters, a small rectangle of sky. Three stars, perhaps four.
Very far off, if you listen closely, you can hear the village fountain. A thin trickle of water running, night and day, into its stone basin.
The crickets sing outside. Chirr. Chirr.
Slowly. Steadily.
[pause 3s]
The breeze moves the shutter, barely. It creaks very softly, then stops.
The lavender... the thyme... the earth cooling...
[pause 3s]
The cool sheets... the heavy body...
[pause 4s]
Outside, the garden is asleep. The lavender, still, in the dark.
The rosemary against the wall. The old fig tree, its figs ripening slowly through the night.
The table under the arbour, empty, beneath the vine leaves.
The deckchair, folded against the wall.
The well, and its shadow that's no longer there.
[pause 3s]
The bees are asleep in their hive, pressed close together, warm, in the scent of wax and honey.
The swallows are asleep under the eaves, in their nests of mud.
The village on the hill opposite is asleep too. Its bell will ring midnight later on, but no one will count the strokes.
[pause 3s]
The olive trees in the valley hold their silver leaves still. The vines follow the curve of the hills, in the dark.
In the kitchen, the bunches of herbs are still drying, upside down, in the dark.
The terracotta tiles keep their coolness. Somewhere, an old clock makes its small, steady sound.
The cicadas are asleep, clinging to the branches of the pines. They'll sing again tomorrow, when the sun comes back. But not now.
[pause 5s]
Now there are only the crickets...
[pause 3s]
and the stars...
[pause 3s]
and the warm night over the hills...
[pause 4s]
The stones of the house, gently giving back their warmth...
[pause 4s]
The half open shutter... the small patch of sky...
[pause 4s]
The sky, immense...
[pause 4s]
The breeze...
[pause 5s]
The crickets, softer now...
[pause 5s]
further away...
[pause 6s]
Everything is calm...
[pause 10s]

sessions.title: The night train
script: [pause 1.5s]
Take a moment to settle in. Lie down however you like, pull the duvet over your shoulders, and let your head find the hollow of the pillow.
[pause 2s]
Tonight's story is a journey. A long night journey by train, from Paris all the way to Italy.
You have nothing to prepare, no ticket to look for, no suitcase to carry. Everything is ready.

And you don't need to reach the end of the journey. Most night travellers fall asleep long before the border. If you drift off along the way, the train will carry on without you, quietly, until morning.
[pause 4s]
It's a winter evening in Paris.
It's cold outside, a dry, clear cold. The pavements gleam under the street lamps. Your breath makes small white clouds in front of your mouth.
You reach the Gare de Lyon a little before nine. You have a small bag over your shoulder, not very heavy. Just what you need for one night and a few days.
You push open the big glass door and step into the hall.
[pause 2s]

It's warmer in here. The hall is vast, with its high, dark glass roof above your head and its big round clocks. Sounds echo under the roof. Footsteps, wheeled suitcases, a distant announcement, the coo of a pigeon perched on a beam.
At this hour, there aren't many people left. The commuter trains have gone. A few travellers remain, like you, leaving for the night. They walk without hurrying. Nobody runs.
You pass a newspaper kiosk pulling down its metal shutter. A bakery, where an assistant is slipping the last croissants into a paper bag.
[pause 2s]

You stop for a moment beside a piano, left in the middle of the hall for travellers. Someone is playing very softly, a slow melody, a few notes that rise into the glass roof and get lost there. You listen for a while. Then you go on your way.
On the big departures board, the white letters flip over one by one with a small clatter. Your train is there, at the top of the list. Night train. Departing at twenty one twelve. Platform M.
You go down to the platform.
[pause 3s]

The train is already there. It's waiting for you, long and dark, under the orange glow of the lamps. Its carriages are midnight blue, with a thin gold line beneath the windows. There are so many of them that you can't see where it ends.
Along the platform, a few staff in uniform wait at the door of each carriage. They hold lists, and they have torches clipped to their belts.
The air smells of cold metal, and faintly of coffee from the platform kiosk.
[pause 2s]

You walk along the train, reading the carriage numbers. The windows glow with a soft yellow light. Behind some of them, you glimpse people settling in. A woman hanging up her coat. An old man opening a book. A child in pyjamas, nose pressed to the glass, giving you a little wave.
You wave back. The child smiles, then disappears behind the curtain, no doubt sent off to bed by a patient parent.
[pause 2s]
Here's your carriage. The attendant checks your ticket, stamps it, and hands it back with a small nod. Have a good journey, he says.
You climb the three metal steps. Inside, it's warm. A narrow corridor with blue carpet runs alongside the compartments. The walls are varnished wood, and brass wall lights give off a golden glow.
You walk down the corridor. The floor creaks a little under your feet. Your cabin is the third one.
You slide the door open. It rolls gently on its runner and closes behind you with a soft, muffled click.
[pause 3s]
The cabin is small, but it has everything. Everything has its place, as on a boat.

There's a berth, already made up. White sheets, pulled tight, folded over a blue wool blanket. A thick, plump pillow. At the foot of the berth, a little ladder, and above, another berth, empty tonight. You have the cabin to yourself.
Under the window, there's a tiny fold down table, and on it, a bottle of water and a little pouch with a flannel and a bar of soap.
In one corner, a steel washbasin, with a mirror and a small tap. Above it, a net for your things. And hooks to hang your coat.
[pause 2s]

Everything is small, clever, well thought out. A handle to hold beside the berth. A little round mirror. A blue night light down by the floor, to help you find your slippers in the dark. You feel as if you're in a den, or a ship's cabin. A place made for shelter.
You put your bag in the net. You take off your coat and your scarf and hang them up. You take off your shoes and tuck them under the berth, side by side.
Then you sit on the edge of the berth.
[pause 2s]

The sheets are cool and a little stiff, like hotel sheets. They smell of clean laundry. The blanket is soft under your hand, thick and slightly fuzzy, the kind of blanket that has kept a great many travellers warm on a great many winter nights.
Above the pillow, there's a small reading lamp with a frosted glass shade. You switch it on. A round, warm light settles on the pillow. Then you switch off the ceiling light.
[pause 2s]
Now the cabin is lit only by that little lamp. It's like a nest. A small world of your own, warm and golden, with the big cold world on the other side of the glass.

You lay your hand flat against the window. The glass is cold and smooth, and through it you can feel the calm chill of the winter night. Then you tuck your hand back under the blanket, where it warms up again straight away.
[pause 3s]
Through the window, you can see the platform. The orange lamps. A porter going by with a luggage trolley. A clock showing ten past nine.
In the corridor, a few doors are still sliding. Voices wishing each other goodnight. Then, little by little, the quiet returns.
A whistle, somewhere in the distance.
The train doors close, all together, with a sigh of air.
[pause 2s]
And very gently, without a jolt, the train begins to move.

At first you can hardly feel it. The platform simply slides past the window, as if it were the one moving. The lamps go by, one after another, faster and faster. Then the end of the platform. Then the night.
The wheels begin their song.
Da-dum. Da-dum. Da-dum.
Slowly at first, rolling over the points with small, soft bumps. Then more and more steadily.
Da-dum. Da-dum.
[pause 5s]
The train leaves the station and crosses the city.

Through the window, Paris passes by, all lit up. Buildings with glowing windows, where you glimpse kitchens, living rooms, people having dinner in front of the television. Wet streets, with red traffic lights reflected on the tarmac. A bridge, and under it the Seine, flowing black and slow, with golden reflections.
The train isn't going very fast yet. It takes its time, as if it wanted to say goodbye.
You stay sitting by the window, watching.
[pause 2s]

The buildings grow lower. Then come houses with little gardens. Warehouses. An empty car park lit by a single lamp. A suburban station, deserted, where the train passes without stopping, its name flashing by too quickly to read.

It's nearly Christmas. In some windows, fairy lights are blinking, red, green, gold. On a balcony, a small decorated tree. In a garden, a light up reindeer, slightly crooked, glowing all alone in the cold.
Then the lights grow fewer. Further apart. One here. Another over there, further off.
And at last, the city is behind you.
[pause 2s]
Da-dum. Da-dum. Da-dum.

The train has reached its cruising speed. It speeds through the night now, steady, sure of its way. You feel a faint, very gentle vibration rising through the berth. And now and then, a slight sway from side to side as the track curves.
[pause 3s]
There's a soft knock at the door. Two small taps.
It's the carriage attendant, a grey haired man in a blue jacket, with a tired smile. He's holding a tray.
Good evening, he says quietly. A herbal tea for the night? Lemon verbena, or lime blossom?

You choose the verbena. He sets a steaming cup on your little table, with a paper napkin. He asks what time you'd like your breakfast. You tell him, not too early. He nods, writes something in his notebook, and wishes you goodnight.
The door closes with its soft, muffled click.
[pause 2s]
You take the cup in both hands. It's hot. The steam smells of lemon and dried grass. You drink in small sips, watching the night go by. Each sip goes down warm and settles in your belly.
On the little table, the cup leaves a small ring of mist. The verbena bag still floats at the bottom, like a tiny boat resting on a golden pond.
[pause 3s]
It's time to get ready for the night.
You stand up and run a little water into the small basin. It's lukewarm. You wipe your face with the flannel. You brush your teeth, holding the edge with one hand because of the gentle sway.
You put on your pyjamas. Soft cotton pyjamas, a little worn, the ones you always take when you travel.
You draw the little curtain across the window, only halfway. You still want to be able to look out from your pillow.
Then you slip under the sheets.
[pause 2s]
They're cool at first. You shiver a little. Then the wool blanket does its work, and very soon warmth gathers around you.
You lie on your side, facing the window. The pillow is thick and soft. You pull the blanket up to your chin.
The little lamp still lights one corner of the pillow. You leave it on, for now.
Da-dum. Da-dum.
[pause 3s]

You listen to the small sounds of the carriage. The faint creak of the wooden panels as the train takes a bend. A curtain ring tinkling against its rail. A door sliding at the far end of the corridor, then closing. Someone coughing softly in the next compartment, then nothing.
These are the sounds of a house on wheels. A house full of sleepers, crossing the night without any fuss.
[pause 3s]
Outside, it's the countryside. A winter countryside, deep in the night.

You can make out huge, flat fields covered in frost. A row of bare trees, black against a sky that's slightly less black. A lone farmhouse with a single lit window. Then nothing. Then another farmhouse.
The sky is clear. A nearly full moon has risen, and it's following the train. Every time you look, it's there, in the same place above the fields. As if it were travelling with you.
Under the moon, the frost glimmers faintly on the fields, with a bluish sheen.
[pause 2s]

The train runs alongside a canal. The water is frozen at the edges, and the ice shines like glass. A barge is moored there, perfectly still, a thread of smoke rising from its little chimney. Someone is asleep inside, warm, rocked by nothing at all.

Further on, a towpath stretches along the water under the bare trees. A bicycle leans against a gate, covered in frost, left there until spring. The train passes, and the canal stays behind, smooth and quiet.
Da-dum. Da-dum. Da-dum.
[pause 3s]

The train passes through a sleeping village. You see, very quickly, a church tower, a square with a fountain, a street of closed shutters. A single street lamp on a corner. No one outside. Everyone is asleep.

Except, perhaps, the baker. At the end of a lane, a small square window is lit, misted with steam. Behind it you can make out an oven, trays, hands covered in flour. Tomorrow morning, the village will wake to the smell of warm bread. But for now, it sleeps.
Then the fields return. The trees. The frost. The moon.
[pause 3s]
A little later, the train crosses a long stone viaduct. Below it lies a lake. A great still lake, black as ink, with the whole moon reflected in it, round and perfect.
The train passes over the lake slowly, arch after arch. You see its reflection gliding across the water, a line of small golden windows moving through the dark, like a necklace of lights.
Nothing moves on the water. Not a ripple, not a bird. Only the moon, and the little golden windows of the train, sliding across it.
On the shore, a few rowing boats are pulled up on the pebbles. A wooden jetty reaches out into the water. Everything is frozen in the cold, and in the silence.
Then the viaduct ends, and the trees come back.
[pause 3s]
Every so often, the train slows down.
It pulls into a small station.

The platform is deserted. There's an empty bench, a round clock showing a little after eleven, a small lamp above the door of the station building. The station's name is written on a blue sign in white letters. A name you don't know. A name you'll forget straight away.
The train stops, with a long sigh of brakes.
[pause 2s]
And for a while, everything is still. The silence is complete. All you can hear, somewhere in the carriage, is the soft hum of the ventilation.
On the platform, a railwayman walks slowly by with a lantern. He looks along the train, from end to end. Then he raises his hand.
And the train sets off again. Gently. Without a jolt.
The little station slides away behind, with its empty bench and its clock. It grows smaller. It disappears.
Da-dum. Da-dum.
[pause 3s]
You switch off the little lamp.
Now the cabin is dark. Only moonlight comes in through the half open curtain, drawing a pale rectangle on the blanket.
Your eyes get used to the dark. You can see the landscape even better. The fields. The woods. A river that gleams for a moment in the moonlight, then hides behind poplars.

On the blanket, the rectangle of moonlight shifts slowly as the track curves this way and that. It slides over your knees, then over your hand, then back again. You watch it without moving, the way you might watch a cat wander across a bed.
Da-dum. Da-dum. Da-dum.
[pause 3s]
Another small station. The train slows, stops. An empty platform, an empty bench, a lamp. A name on a blue sign.
The silence. The stillness.
Then the train moves off again, gently.
Da-dum. Da-dum.
And another one. A platform. A lamp. A name. The silence.
Then the rolling starts again.
[pause 3s]

At one point, during a stop, another train passes on the next track. A goods train, very long, very slow. Its wagons pass your window one after another. A grey tanker. A dark red wooden wagon. A wagon loaded with tree trunks. Another. And another.

They go by with a low, steady, almost sleepy sound. You watch them, without counting. There are so many. Then the last wagon passes, with a little red light blinking at the back. And the next track is empty and dark again.
You've stopped counting the stations. They all look alike. Each one is a small pause in the night, a moment of calm, before the train goes on its way.
[pause 3s]
Little by little, the landscape changes.
The ground begins to rise. The flat fields give way to hills, gentle at first, then steeper. The train slows a little on the climbs. You feel the rise in your body, a slight tilt of the berth.
There are forests now. Great forests of fir trees, dark and dense, lining the track.
And then, on the branches of the firs, you notice something white.
Snow.
[pause 2s]
Only a little at first, in patches along the track. Then more and more. The banks are white. The roofs of the houses are white. The fir trees wear heavy coats of snow on their branches.
The train is entering the mountains.
The air in the cabin seems to change too. Quieter. Softer. As if the snow outside were muffling every sound in the world, and leaving only the gentle rolling of the wheels.
Da-dum. Da-dum. Da-dum.
[pause 3s]
The landscape under the moon has a silent beauty.

Everything is white and blue. The snowy slopes glow softly in the moonlight. The shadows of the firs are dark blue on the snow. In the distance, the peaks stand out against the sky, immense, motionless, covered in glittering ice.

The train follows a narrow valley. Below, a mountain stream runs between snow covered rocks. You can't hear it through the glass. But you can see the water shining, black and silver, between the white stones.

On the other side of the valley, a small mountain village. Wooden chalets with roofs heavy with snow. A church with a pointed spire. Not a single light. The whole village is asleep, buried in snow, like an animal hibernating.
Da-dum. Da-dum.
[pause 3s]

At the edge of a forest, under the moon, a roe deer lifts its head. It watches the train go by without moving, its big ears turned toward the sound. Then it goes back to calmly nibbling the grass poking through the snow.
A little further on, a lone chalet with a single lit window. Someone up there is still awake. Perhaps to put another log on the stove. Perhaps for a glass of water. Then that window goes dark too.
Da-dum. Da-dum.
[pause 3s]
The train enters a tunnel.
Everything goes black. The sound of the wheels changes, deeper, more enveloping. A soft, steady rumble resonating all around the carriage. It's like being inside the mountain.
You close your eyes for a moment. You listen. The rumble wraps around you like a thick wool scarf, and for a moment there's nothing else in the world but that low, kind sound.
Then the train comes out of the tunnel. And the snow and the moon return all at once, dazzling in their softness.
Da-dum. Da-dum. Da-dum.
[pause 3s]
The train climbs slowly, in long curves, toward the pass. It crosses a stone bridge over a ravine. Far below, you can see the valley you've just left, with the thin dark line of the stream.
It begins to snow.

A few flakes at first drift past the window. They dance in the light spilling from the carriages. Then they grow thicker, closer together. They fall softly, silently, on the firs, on the rocks, on the roof of the train.
[pause 2s]
You watch the snowflakes from the warmth of your berth.

Some of them land on the glass. You can see their shape for an instant before they melt. Tiny stars of ice, each one different, with six branches as fine as lace. Then each becomes a drop of water, sliding slowly down the pane.
Outside, it's very cold. But in here, under the wool blanket, it's warm. Your feet are warm. Your hands are warm. Your body is heavy and relaxed, rocked by the motion of the train.
Da-dum. Da-dum.
[pause 3s]

At the top of the pass, the train stops at a station a little larger than the others. It's the border station. The platform is covered in fresh snow, and flakes are falling through the light of the lamps.

Here, the drivers change. Far off, you hear calm voices, doors opening and closing. A woman's voice announces something very softly, in Italian, then in French. You don't try to understand. The words are soft and round, like a song.
Then everything falls quiet again. And the train sets off, and begins to descend, slowly, down the other side of the mountain.
Da-dum. Da-dum.
[pause 3s]

On this side, the valleys are narrower and deeper. Villages cling to the slopes, with houses of grey stone and roofs of heavy slate slabs covered in snow. There are square bell towers, little humpback bridges over the streams, low walls tracing terraces under the snow.

Everything is asleep here too. A single lamp glows over a square, above a frozen fountain. Around it, the snow lies smooth and untouched. Not a single footprint. Nobody has crossed the square since the snow began to fall.
[pause 2s]
The train winds gently down, bend after bend. You feel your body slide, just slightly, toward the foot of the berth, and then back.

In the corridor, every light is out now, except the little blue night light down by the floor. The whole carriage seems to breathe in the same rhythm. The wooden panels barely creak, like an old ship letting itself be carried by the swell.
Da-dum. Da-dum.
[pause 4s]
The rolling of the wheels has become a lullaby.
Always the same rhythm. Always the same song. Da-dum. Da-dum. Like a heart beating slowly. Like a hand gently patting a child's back to send them to sleep.
The berth sways, barely. From right to left. From left to right. Like a cradle.
[pause 3s]

Without deciding to, your breathing has fallen in with the train. One in breath over a few beats of the wheels. One out breath, a little longer, over the next few. You're not counting. It just happened, the way you fall into step with someone walking beside you.
Da-dum. Da-dum.
[pause 4s]
You don't need to look outside anymore. You know the snow is falling. You know the mountain is there, vast and calm. You know the train knows the way.

There's nothing for you to steer, nothing to check, nothing to remember. The driver, right at the front, is keeping watch for you. The attendant, at the end of the corridor, is keeping watch for you. Everyone on this train can sleep.
Da-dum. Da-dum.
[pause 4s]
Your eyelids are heavy.
[pause 2s]
The snowflakes drift past the window.
[pause 2s]
The blanket is warm.
[pause 2s]
Da-dum.
[pause 5s]
Somewhere at the end of these valleys lies the Italian morning. Stone towns, sunlit squares, strong coffee in tiny cups. You'll be there tomorrow. But not now.
Now there's only the night...
the train...
the snow...
[pause 2s]
Da-dum. Da-dum.
[pause 3s]
A little mountain station goes by, all white, asleep...
A platform under the snow... a lamp...
The silence...
[pause 2s]
Then the rolling starts again...
Da-dum...
Da-dum...
[pause 5s]
The fir trees... the moon... the snowflakes...
The little black lake, far behind, with the moon inside it...
The villages asleep under the snow...
[pause 2s]
The deer, at the edge of the wood...
The verbena cup, empty, on the little table...
The long goods train, and its little red light...
[pause 2s]
The stars of snow on the window...
The warmth of the sheets...
The soft weight of the blanket...
[pause 2s]
The smell of clean laundry on the pillow...
The warm wood of the cabin...
The cradle of the train...
[pause 3s]
going down... and down...
[pause 6s]
Da-dum...
[pause 10s]

sessions.title: Yoga nidra for sleep
script: [pause 1.5s]
Tonight, you're taking your time. Thirty minutes, just for you, to go down slowly, step by step, into deep rest.
[pause 2s]

Yoga nidra is sometimes called conscious sleep. You'll lie still and follow my voice from one place to another. Your body will rest more and more deeply. Your mind will stay with me a little longer, listening, the way you might listen to rain on a window.

The practice follows a set path, always the same. You settle in. You plant an intention. You travel through the body, then through the breath. You play with opposite sensations, then with images. And you end in an inner place of rest.
[pause 2s]

The path goes down like a staircase. With each step, the body lets go a little more. You don't need to know where you are along the way. Just follow my voice, without effort, like a small boat drifting down a slow river.
Images may appear on their own, thoughts may blur together, you may lose the thread for a few moments. That's often a sign that sleep is near. Let it happen.

And tonight, unlike the usual practice, there will be no coming back. If you fall asleep along the way, that's exactly what we're hoping for. My voice will carry on for a while, and then sleep will take over.
[pause 3s]
Lie on your back, in the posture of rest. Legs stretched out, slightly apart, hip-width or a little wider. Feet falling loosely outward.
Arms by your sides, a little away from your body. Palms facing up, if that's comfortable, fingers gently curled, like the hands of a sleeping child.
Head in line with your spine, neither too high nor too low. If your neck pulls, add a small cushion. If you feel cold, cover yourself well now. The body often cools down during the practice.
If your back complains in this position, slide a pillow under your knees. And if you really can't stay on your back, lie on your side. The practice will still work.
[pause 4s]
Make any last adjustments. Roll your shoulders a little. Lengthen the back of your neck. Let your hips settle flat. Pull the covers up to your chin, if you'd like.
[pause 2s]

And now, make yourself a small promise. To stay still until the end of the practice. Not stiff, not frozen. Just still, like a stone resting on the bed of a stream, while the water slips gently over it.
If an itch comes, first try simply observing it, without responding. Often it fades on its own. If it insists, move gently, then return to stillness. That's not a mistake, just a small detour.
[pause 2s]
Close your eyes. Let them stay closed, easily, for the whole practice.
Take a deep breath in through your nose...
[pause 3s]
and let it out through your mouth, with a long sigh.
[pause 6s]
Once more. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and as you sigh, let the full weight of your body drop into the bed.
[pause 6s]
One last time, more softly. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out, as if you were setting down a heavy bag at the end of a long day.
[pause 6s]
Then let your breath return to its natural rhythm. It knows how to do this without you.
[pause 3s]
Your body will now stay still, and it's your attention that will travel. Outside first, then closer and closer, until it reaches inside.

Listen to the sounds around you. The most distant ones first. Outside, perhaps, a car, the wind, a night bird, the low murmur of the town. Let your attention reach far away, without holding on to any sound.
[pause 4s]
Then the closer sounds. The sounds of the house. The hum of the fridge, the tick of the radiator, a door somewhere far off, the background hum of the building.
[pause 4s]
Then the sounds of the room. The faint rustle of the sheet as your chest rises. And the sound of your own breath, very close, soft as a wave on sand.
[pause 4s]

Move from one sound to the next, the way you'd wander from room to room in a quiet house. Without lingering. Without trying to work out where they come from. You hear, that's all. And you let each sound go by, the way you'd watch the carriages of a train pass.
All these sounds belong to the night. None of them asks anything of you. They can even become a kind of lullaby, a soft background to rest on.
[pause 4s]

Now become aware of your body lying here. All of it. Feel the points of contact with the bed. The back of your head. Your shoulders. Your elbows. The backs of your hands. Your pelvis. Your calves. Your heels.
[pause 3s]

Feel the weight of each part. The weight of your head, round and heavy in the pillow. The weight of your arms. The weight of your pelvis. The weight of your legs. All that weight handed over to the bed, which holds it effortlessly, all night long if it needs to.
[pause 3s]
Feel your body resting, still, on the mattress. And say to yourself silently... I am awake, and I am practicing yoga nidra. Awake, still, and at ease.
[pause 5s]
Now comes the moment of the sankalpa. It's a resolve, an intention. A short sentence, in the present tense, phrased in a positive way.
A sentence that comes from the heart rather than the head. Something you truly need at this moment in your life.
If nothing comes, you can choose one of these. I am at peace. I deserve rest. I trust myself. I sleep deeply and wake up rested.
[pause 2s]
Avoid sentences built around the word not, like I'm not stressed anymore. The heart hears what you offer it better than what you take away. Say instead, I am calm.
And keep it simple. A few words. A sentence you could whisper to a child to help them drift off.

Take a moment to find it. It doesn't need to be perfect. The one that turns up first is often the right one. And once you've chosen it, keep it for several nights, even several weeks. It's by repeating it that it takes root.
Let the words come to you on their own. Listen to them, the way you'd listen to someone dear speaking very quietly beside you.
[pause 6s]
Now repeat your sankalpa silently, three times, slowly, with all your feeling. The first time... take your time.
[pause 6s]
The second time... a little more slowly still, feeling every word.
[pause 6s]
And the third time... as if you were placing it somewhere deep inside you.
[pause 6s]
Your resolve has been planted. Like a seed laid in soft, dark soil. You don't need to tend it anymore. It will grow on its own, at its own pace.
Don't ask yourself whether it's working, or when. You don't dig up a seed every morning to see if it has sprouted. You leave it in peace, in the dark, and you trust the earth to do its quiet work.
[pause 4s]
Now let's begin the rotation of consciousness.
I'm going to name different parts of your body, one after another. With each name, simply place your attention on that spot, and repeat the name in your mind. Then move on to the next.
There's no need to move, no need to relax anything. Just visit. Like a small light landing on one point, then the next, without lingering.
If you miss a spot, don't go back. Simply rejoin my voice wherever it is. The journey carries on, with or without you, and your body hears it anyway.
[pause 3s]
We begin with the right side.
The thumb of the right hand. The index finger. The middle finger. The ring finger. The little finger. The tips of all five fingers, like five tiny lights.
The palm of the hand. The hollow of the palm. The back of the hand. The wrist. The forearm. The elbow. The inside of the elbow. The upper arm. The shoulder. The armpit.

The right side of the body. The ribs along the right side. The waist. The right hip. The thigh. The knee. The back of the knee. The calf. The shin. The ankle. The heel. The sole of the foot. The arch of the foot. The top of the foot.
The big toe. The second toe. The third. The fourth. The fifth. The whole right side, from the hand all the way down to the foot.
[pause 3s]
Now the left side.
The thumb of the left hand. The index finger. The middle finger. The ring finger. The little finger. The tips of all the fingers of the left hand.
The palm of the hand. The hollow of the palm. The back of the hand. The wrist. The forearm. The elbow. The inside of the elbow. The upper arm. The shoulder. The armpit.

The left side of the body. The ribs along the left side. The waist. The left hip. The thigh. The knee. The back of the knee. The calf. The shin. The ankle. The heel. The sole of the foot. The arch of the foot. The top of the foot.
The big toe. The second toe. The third. The fourth. The fifth. The whole left side, from the hand all the way down to the foot.
[pause 3s]
Now the back of the body.
The right heel, resting on the bed. The left heel. The right calf. The left calf. The back of the right thigh. The back of the left thigh.
The right buttock. The left buttock. The lower back, spreading wide on the mattress. The middle of the back. The upper back.
The right shoulder blade. The left shoulder blade. The space between the shoulder blades. The whole spine, one vertebra after another, from the bottom all the way to the top.
The back of the neck. The back of the head, resting in the pillow. The crown of the head.
[pause 3s]
Now the face and the front of the body.
The forehead. The whole forehead, broad and smooth. The right temple. The left temple. The right eyebrow. The left eyebrow. The space between the eyebrows.
The right eyelid. The left eyelid. The right eye, resting in its socket. The left eye.
The right ear. The left ear. The right cheek. The left cheek. The cheekbones.
The nose. The bridge of the nose. The right nostril. The left nostril. The upper lip. The lower lip. The corners of the mouth. The space between the lips.
The chin. The jaw on the right side. The jaw on the left side. The tongue, resting in the mouth. The teeth. The roof of the mouth. The throat. The hollow at the base of the throat.
The right collarbone. The left collarbone. The right side of the chest. The left side of the chest. The center of the chest, where the heart beats quietly.
The upper belly. The navel. The lower belly. The pelvis. The whole pelvis, like a wide bowl resting on the bed.
[pause 3s]
Now the larger parts.
The whole right leg. The whole left leg. Both legs together.
The whole right arm. The whole left arm. Both arms together.
The whole back. The whole front of the body. The whole head.
The whole body. The whole body together. The entire body, from head to toe, as a single presence.
[pause 5s]
A second time, more lightly, in pairs. Both thumbs. Both index fingers. Both middle fingers. Both ring fingers. Both little fingers.
Both palms. Both wrists. Both elbows. Both shoulders.
Both hips. Both knees. Both ankles. Both heels. All the toes, at once.
Both shoulder blades. Both cheeks. Both eyes. Both ears.
The forehead. The crown of the head.
The whole body. One single shape, calm, lying at rest.
[pause 4s]
Feel your body as a whole. Still. Settled. Present.
Like a stone figure lying in a cool, silent chapel. Or like a long outline drawn in chalk on the bed. You can sense its edges, from head to feet, as one single shape.
Feel, too, the boundary between your body and the air of the room. The skin of your face and hands, touching the air. And all around you, the calm space of the room, wrapping around you like a shell.
[pause 3s]
If you notice that you drifted off for a moment, or lost the thread, that's perfectly fine. Simply come back to my voice, the way you'd find a hand held out to you in the dark.
[pause 5s]
Now become aware of your breath.
Don't change it. Just watch it. The air coming in through your nostrils, a little cool. The air going out, a little warmer. Cool on the way in... warm on the way out.
[pause 4s]
Now notice the breath in each nostril. Perhaps the air flows a little more through the right nostril. Or the left. Or equally through both. There's nothing to correct. Just observe.
[pause 3s]
Imagine you're breathing in through the left nostril and out through the right. Then in through the right and out through the left. Only in your mind. The breath itself stays free and natural.
Left... right.
[pause 3s]
Right... left.
[pause 3s]
Like a very slow pendulum, swinging from one nostril to the other. Left... right.
[pause 3s]
Right... left.
[pause 4s]
Now follow the breath down into your belly. The belly rising as you breathe in, like a small tide coming in. The belly falling as you breathe out, like the tide drawing back from the shore.
[pause 4s]

Now imagine your breath tracing a path between your navel and your throat. As you breathe in, it rises from the navel up to the throat. As you breathe out, it flows back down from the throat to the navel.
Rising... and falling. Like a gentle wave, moving along the center of your body.
[pause 4s]

As you breathe in, the wave passes through the belly, the chest, and reaches the throat. As you breathe out, it leaves the throat, crosses the chest, and comes to rest at the navel. No effort. Just a simple movement of attention.
[pause 5s]
Now we'll add a countdown, from twenty-seven all the way down to one.
To begin, I'll count with you, very softly. After that, you'll carry on alone, at your own pace. If your breath is slower or faster than my voice, follow your breath, not my voice.
Breathing in, twenty-seven.
[pause 3s]
Breathing out, twenty-seven.
[pause 4s]
Breathing in, twenty-six.
[pause 3s]
Breathing out, twenty-six.
[pause 4s]
Breathing in, twenty-five.
[pause 3s]
Breathing out, twenty-five.
[pause 4s]
Breathing in, twenty-four.
[pause 3s]
Breathing out, twenty-four.
[pause 4s]
Breathing in, twenty-three.
[pause 3s]
Breathing out, twenty-three.
[pause 4s]
Breathing in, twenty-two.
[pause 3s]
Breathing out, twenty-two.
[pause 4s]
And now, carry on by yourself, silently. Each number resting on a breath, like a pebble set down on a riverbank.
[pause 8s]

If you get lost, if you're not sure where you are, start again at twenty-seven. If you reach one, begin again at twenty-seven. It doesn't matter if you make mistakes. The count is only a thread to keep the mind busy while the body rests.
The numbers go down, like the steps of an old wooden staircase leading to a cool, quiet cellar. With each step, a little lower. With each step, a little calmer.
[pause 8s]
Breath after breath. Number after number. The in-breath, and the number. The out-breath, and the same number. Then the next one, a notch lower.
If your mind wanders off to the day, to tomorrow, to a conversation, that's normal. Bring it gently back to the number, the way you'd guide a sleepy child back to bed, without a word of reproach.
[pause 8s]
Perhaps the numbers are getting blurry. Perhaps you're not quite sure whether you said fifteen or sixteen. That's perfectly fine. Pick one, any one, and keep going down.
Each out-breath is a little longer than the one before, without you having to make it so. The body slows down by itself, like a clock that nobody winds anymore.
[pause 8s]
Now let go of the count. Let the numbers fade away, like footprints on a beach as the tide comes in to smooth them over. The breath carries on by itself, free.

It doesn't matter where you stopped. Whether you reached one, or started over three times, or got lost along the way, it's all just right. The count has done its job. It kept the mind occupied while the body sank deeper.
[pause 5s]
Now let's awaken some opposite sensations. First, heaviness.
Feel your body becoming heavy. Very heavy.
Your legs are heavy, as if they were made of stone. Your arms are heavy, like lead. Your head is heavy, sinking into the pillow.
Your whole body is so heavy that it sinks into the mattress, deeper and deeper. As if you were slowly settling into warm, welcoming earth.
[pause 3s]

Your eyelids are heavy, like two small stones resting on your eyes. Your cheeks drop. Your jaw sags. Your shoulders press down into the mattress. Your back is as heavy as an oak plank. Your pelvis is as heavy as a sack of wet sand. Your heels sink into the bed.
Even your fingers are heavy. Each finger lying there like a small branch fallen to the ground. Even your tongue is heavy, at the back of your mouth.
This is the heaviness that comes before sleep. The kind you feel sinking into the sofa after a long Sunday outdoors, when you no longer have the strength to get up and turn off the light.
Find that feeling of heaviness. Feel it everywhere. Heavy... heavy... heavier and heavier.
[pause 5s]
Now let the heaviness slip away, and welcome lightness.
Feel your body becoming light. Very light. Light as a feather.
Your legs are so light they could lift up all by themselves. Your arms are floating. Your head is as light as a balloon.
Your whole body is so light that it begins to rise above the bed, slowly, like a cloud drifting over a meadow.
[pause 3s]

Your eyelids are as light as butterfly wings. Your chest lifts on its own, like a balloon filled with warm air. Your hands could float away, like two leaves carried on an autumn breeze. There's no more weight. No more effort. Nothing pulling you down.
You float like a cork on a still pond. Like a dandelion seed, hesitating, suspended in the evening air.
Find that feeling of lightness. Light... light... so very light.
[pause 5s]
Now, warmth.
Imagine it's very hot. You're lying in the sun, in the middle of summer, on a beach of burning sand. The sun is warming your skin. The air is hot in your nostrils.
Feel that heat on your face, on your arms, on your belly. A strong, enveloping heat. Your whole body is warm.

The hot sand under your back, under your legs. Your palms warming up. A drop of sweat beading at your temple. The air shimmering above the sand. Cicadas singing far off in the pine trees. You'd like to move into the shade, but you stay right there, feeling the heat.
[pause 4s]
Now, cold.
Imagine it's very cold. You're outside on a winter morning, in the snow. An icy wind brushes across your face. Your hands are cold, your feet are cold.
Feel that cold on your skin. The tip of your nose, frozen. Your cheeks stinging. Your ears turning red. Your whole body is cold.

The snow crunches under your feet. Your breath makes little clouds in front of your mouth. Your fingers are numb inside your gloves. You feel the cold creeping up your legs, over your shoulders, into your neck. You'd like to go back inside where it's warm, but you stay right there, feeling the cold.
[pause 4s]
And now, try to feel both at once. Your right hand warm, as if resting on a hot water bottle. Your left hand cold, as if pressed against a window pane in winter. Warm on one side, cold on the other.
[pause 3s]

Then the body heavy, sunk deep into the earth... and at the same time, light, floating above. Heavy and light. Both together. Don't try to understand it. Simply let your mind hold these two sensations side by side.
[pause 4s]
And now, let the two sensations meet. Warmth and cold. Heaviness and lightness.
Then let them dissolve, like sugar stirring into a cup of herbal tea. Your body finds its own right temperature again. Neither hot nor cold. Neither heavy nor light. Just resting.
[pause 5s]

Now I'm going to name some images, one after another. For each one, let whatever comes, come. A clear picture, a blurry one, a simple idea, a feeling. It's all just right. And as soon as I name the next image, let the previous one go.
[pause 2s]
A lit candle in a dark room. The flame standing straight and still.
[pause 2s]
A still lake at sunrise. A light mist floating over the water.
[pause 2s]
A cat asleep on a windowsill, curled up in a patch of sunlight.
[pause 2s]
A forest under snow. Not a sound.
[pause 2s]
A mug of hot chocolate, held between two cold hands.
[pause 2s]
A lighthouse at night, on a rock. Its beam slowly turning.
[pause 2s]
Summer rain on a tin roof. Its steady patter.
[pause 2s]
A rowing boat tied to a jetty, barely rocking.
[pause 2s]
An old wooden door, painted blue, the paint flaking away.
[pause 2s]
A field of wheat in the wind, rippling like a golden sea.
[pause 2s]
A paper lantern, rising slowly into the evening sky.
[pause 2s]
A sky full of stars, above a desert.
[pause 2s]
A white feather drifting slowly down, swaying as it falls.
[pause 2s]
A distant mountain, its snowy peak turning pink at sunset.
[pause 2s]
A river flowing between smooth, round stones.
[pause 2s]
A bird perched on a telephone wire, its feathers puffed up against the cold.
[pause 2s]
A wood fire in a hearth. The embers glowing red.
[pause 2s]
A jar of honey, a wooden spoon standing in it.
[pause 2s]
The smile of someone you love.
[pause 2s]
A stone bridge, covered in moss, arching over a stream.
[pause 2s]
A lit window at night, in a small house at the end of a lane.
[pause 2s]
A nest in the hollow of a tree, holding three blue eggs.
[pause 2s]
An old armchair by a window, a soft blanket draped over its arm.
[pause 2s]
A loaf of bread cooling on a kitchen table.
[pause 2s]
A white sheet drying in the sun, billowing in the breeze.
[pause 2s]

sessions.title: Stress as an ally?
script: [pause 1.5s]
Welcome. Today, a slightly unexpected question. What if your stress were trying to help you?
[pause 2s]
Get comfortable, sitting or standing, whatever suits you. And take one breath a little deeper than the others.
[pause 4s]
Here's what happens in your body when you face a challenge. It gears up. Your heart beats faster, your breathing speeds up. Sometimes you feel heat, or butterflies in your stomach.
Most of us have learned to see these signs as a threat. As proof that something is wrong.
Yet this reaction has a very concrete job. It sends more energy and oxygen to your muscles and your brain. Your body is getting ready to act.
It's a bit like warming up a car on a winter morning. The engine runs louder, but only so you can get moving.
[pause 2s]
Researchers, especially in the United States, have studied what changes when people look at this reaction differently.
In several experiments, people about to face a stressful test, like giving a talk or sitting an exam, were told that their pounding heart was a resource. Fuel for the task.
These people often felt more confident. And in some of them, the heart and blood vessels responded more the way they do for a challenge than for a threat.
[pause 1.5s]

Another study tested one simple sentence, said just before singing or speaking in public. I am excited. People who said it seemed a little more at ease than those who tried telling themselves, I am calm.
Why? Perhaps because it's very hard to jump straight from agitation to calm. It's much easier to change the name you give that agitation.
Other research suggests that seeing stress as something that can also help you grow is linked to handling it more calmly from day to day.
[pause 1.5s]

Careful, though. This doesn't mean all stress is good, or that you should put up with everything in silence. Stress that's too intense, or that lasts for months, deserves to be taken seriously, sometimes with the help of a professional.
The idea is simpler. In the face of a one-off challenge, what you tell yourself about your sensations can change how you move through them.
You're not trying to calm down at all costs. You're trying to turn I'm panicking into I'm getting ready.
[pause 2s]
Let's try it together.
Think of something coming up that stresses you a little. Not the worst thing in your life. Something moderate, manageable.
An important appointment, a meeting where you have to speak, a conversation you keep putting off, an exam.
Choose one, and imagine you're there. The place, the people, the moment just before it begins.
[pause 3s]
Now turn your attention to your body. No need to change anything. Just observe.
Your heart, first. Is it beating a little faster, a little harder?
[pause 2s]
Maybe you can feel it in your chest, or in your throat.
Your breath. Is it shorter, higher up in your chest?
Maybe you also feel like moving, tapping your foot, getting up. That's energy looking for a direction.
And heat. In your face, your hands, your belly. Maybe a slight restlessness in your legs, or a knot in your stomach.
[pause 2s]
Whatever you notice is normal. It's your body responding to something that matters to you.

You may notice these are almost the same sensations as excitement, before a concert or a first date. Your body doesn't always know the difference. Often, it's the interpretation that changes everything.
[pause 3s]
Now let's look at these same sensations differently. One at a time.
Your racing heart is sending more blood to your muscles and your brain. You can say to yourself, silently... my body is giving me energy.
[pause 2s]
Your quickening breath is bringing in more oxygen. Tell yourself... I'm breathing to get ready.
[pause 2s]
The heat, the butterflies, they're a sign that this situation matters to you. You wouldn't feel this way about something meaningless.
And now, try this sentence, slowly. My body is getting ready.
[pause 3s]
My body is getting ready. It's on my side.
[pause 3s]
Notice whether anything shifts, even slightly. The sensations may still be there, but they don't feel quite the same.
And if nothing changes, that's fine. This is training, and it grows stronger with repetition.
Think of a musician just before going on stage. Many still get nervous, even after years of performing. They don't wait for the nerves to disappear before they play. They play with them.
[pause 2s]
To support this new view, let's give your body a posture of momentum rather than retreat.
Gently straighten your back. Let your chest open, your shoulders widen a little toward the back. Your head upright, your chin level with the floor.
Place your feet flat, as if you were putting down roots.
[pause 2s]
And now, a steady breath. Not necessarily slow, just even. In for about four seconds, out for a little longer. I'll give you the cues.
In, through your nose...
[pause 4s]
And out, without forcing...
[pause 6s]
You keep the energy, but you give it a direction. Like an athlete on the starting line. Focused, awake, ready to go.
One more. In...
[pause 4s]
And out, smoothly...
[pause 6s]
If you feel at all dizzy, simply go back to your natural breathing.
[pause 1.5s]
Picture yourself in the situation again. This time, with that straight back, that steady breath, and that sentence in mind.
Your heart may still be beating fast, and that's perfectly fine. It's working for you.
See yourself begin, say your first words, make your first move. Not perfectly. Simply there, with your energy.
You can feel your heart beating fast, and at the same time feel your feet on the floor and your steady breath. Both can be there together.
[pause 4s]
Let the image fade. Come back to the room you're in, to the feeling of your feet on the floor.
Notice how you feel about that situation now. A little more drive, perhaps. Or simply a little more clarity.
[pause 2s]

Here's what I'd like you to take with you. When the moment comes and you feel your heart speed up, just before you walk in, pick up the phone or start speaking, plant your feet, stand tall, and say it again. My body is getting ready.
You don't need to make stress disappear to move forward. You can bring it with you, as an ally.

sessions.title: The negativity bias
script: [pause 1.5s]
Hello. Take a moment to arrive here, and let your body find a position where it can settle.
You can sit, lie down, or even stay standing. What matters is being comfortable for the next few minutes.
[pause 2s]
Think about yesterday. What comes back to you first?
[pause 2.5s]
Chances are it's an annoyance. A sharp word, a delay, an irritating email.
And yet that same day surely held some pleasant moments too. A hot coffee, a smile, a ray of sunshine.
Or think of one criticism among ten compliments. Which one do you replay at night while you brush your teeth?
Or this one. On a drive, a hundred polite drivers pass you, and one cuts you off. Guess which one you talk about when you get home.
[pause 1.5s]
That's no accident. Psychologists call it the negativity bias. For the same intensity, a negative event usually leaves a stronger mark than a positive one.
An American psychologist put it in a simple image. For bad experiences, our brain is like Velcro, they stick right away. For good ones, it's more like Teflon, they slide right off.
[pause 1.5s]
This isn't a flaw in your character. It's an inheritance.
For our ancestors, missing a sweet fruit wasn't a big deal. Missing a predator could cost them their life.
Brains that spotted danger quickly, and remembered it, had a survival advantage.

Today there's no predator in the hallway. But the brain keeps scanning for threats, and that can feed a constant background hum of stress. In a way, it behaves like a news channel that mostly reports the bad news.
[pause 1.5s]
The good news is that we can tip the balance back a little.
Research on what's called savoring suggests that taking time to linger on good moments is linked to more positive emotions.
Savoring is what you naturally do with a delicious dessert. You slow down, and make each bite last. You can do the same with a moment in your day.
The idea is simple. A pleasant moment doesn't sink in on its own. But if you stay with it for a few dozen seconds, feeling it in your body, it probably has a better chance of leaving a trace.
We're not denying difficulties, or looking at life through rose tinted glasses. We're simply giving good moments the time to exist.
[pause 2s]
Let's do it now, together.
Close your eyes if you'd like. Take two easy breaths. Let your belly rise as you breathe in...
[pause 4s]
and settle as you breathe out.
[pause 6s]
Once more, at your own pace.
[pause 8s]
Now look for a small, pleasant moment from the last few days. Not a big event. Something simple.
The first sip of coffee. A conversation that made you laugh. Cool, fresh sheets. Sun on your face as you stepped outside. A kind message.
Take the first one that comes. It doesn't have to be perfect.
And if nothing comes, that's fine. You can choose something present. The warmth of your hands, the comfort of your seat, the simple fact of taking this time for yourself.
[pause 3s]
Now relive this moment in detail, as if you were there again.
Where are you? What do you see around you? The colors, the light, the shapes. Who's there with you, if anyone?
[pause 3s]
What do you hear? A voice, music, silence, the sound of the street.
Is there a smell, a taste? A temperature, a texture against your skin? Take your time with each detail. There's no rush.
[pause 2s]
And what were you feeling in that moment? Joy, ease, tenderness, lightness?
Let that feeling come back, even just a little. It doesn't need to be as strong as on the day itself.
[pause 3s]
Now let's stretch this moment out. Stay with it, without moving on. Just for twenty seconds or so.
Find where it lives in your body. Warmth in your chest, perhaps. A smile at the corner of your mouth. Softer shoulders.
There's no right way to feel it. A little warmth, a slight smile, a bit more space... it all counts.
[pause 6s]
If your mind wanders off to a task or a worry, that's normal. That's the Velcro doing its job. Gently come back to your moment.
[pause 4s]
Let the feeling spread, like a patch of light slowly widening inside you.
Breathe in, welcoming this moment...
[pause 4s]
and breathe out, letting it settle into you.
[pause 5s]
If it feels good, let it grow a little. Breathe with it. With each in breath, imagine it taking up a bit more space.
[pause 3s]
Now imagine this moment sinking into you. Like water slowly soaking into a sponge. Or like warmth spreading out from the center of your chest.
There's nothing to force. You simply let this good experience in, and let it find its place.
Some people like to picture placing the moment in a treasured box inside them, where they can come back for it on grayer days.
[pause 5s]
You can say to yourself, silently... This is part of my life too.
[pause 3s]
Notice how that sentence lands in your body. Does it ring true, or feel a little strange? Both are welcome.
[pause 2s]
Now let the image drift away, keeping whatever remains of it in your body.
Notice how you feel. Maybe a little softer. Maybe nothing dramatic, and that's fine. Like a muscle, this ability builds little by little.
Savoring doesn't mean hard moments don't count. They do. But they aren't the whole story.
[pause 2s]
Here's the practice I'd suggest. Three times a day, when a small pleasant moment comes along, pause.
The taste of your lunch, the light at the end of the day, a loved one's voice on the phone.
Even something as small as warm water on your hands, or the smell of bread as you walk past a bakery.
Instead of rushing on to the next thing, stay with it for about twenty seconds. Feel it in your body. Let it sink in. Twenty seconds is roughly three or four slow breaths.
It takes almost no time. But day after day, you're teaching your brain to notice what's going well, too. You may find these moments start catching your attention more easily, almost on their own.
You can also do it at night, once you're in bed. Recall three good moments from your day and linger on each one, instead of replaying what went wrong.
[pause 2s]
Come back gently. Take a slightly deeper breath, move your hands, and open your eyes whenever it feels right.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Your cortisol rhythm
script: [pause 1.5s]
This session works best at the end of the day. If you're listening at another time, the practice will help you prepare your evening ritual.
Get comfortable, and let your breath settle.
[pause 2s]
Cortisol has a bad reputation. It's often called the stress hormone, as if we should get rid of it.
Some people even think of it as an enemy, something to fight, or to keep as low as possible all day long.
In fact, your body needs it every day. It helps mobilize energy, regulate blood sugar, wake you up and meet challenges.
[pause 1.5s]
Above all, it follows a rhythm, set by your internal clock. That clock is a small region deep in the brain that keeps time over roughly twenty four hours.
Here's what happens in your body. The rhythm is like a tide. Cortisol starts to rise in the second half of the night, to prepare you for waking.
Then, within about half an hour of waking up, it reaches a peak. Researchers call this the cortisol awakening response. It's a bit like a boost to help you start the day.
After that, as the hours go by, the tide slowly goes out. In the evening, levels are low, and they reach their lowest point early in the night. That dip makes room for sleep.
[pause 1.5s]

Think of the light on a summer day. It rises in the morning, shines at noon, then slowly fades into evening. Your cortisol curve looks a little like that, except that it gets up a little before you do.
High in the morning, low at night. That's the usual pattern for most people.

Cortisol doesn't work alone. In the evening, as it falls and the light fades, another hormone takes over. Melatonin, which tells your body it's nighttime. The two respond to each other, a little like dance partners.
This rhythm also varies from person to person. Some people are morning types, others are night owls. The point isn't to fit a mold, but to find a regular rhythm that suits you.
[pause 2s]
What can throw this tide off is often our modern way of life.
Bright light late in the evening, from screens and ceiling lights, can tell your clock it's still daytime.
Your clock can't read the time on your phone. It mostly reads light, and bright light says daytime.
Stress that drags on into the evening, emails at ten at night, tense conversations before bed, keeps your body in action mode.
And very irregular hours, going to bed and getting up at very different times from one day to the next, blur your clock's signals.
[pause 1.5s]

Studies have also observed that in people under stress for a long time, this curve tends to flatten. Less difference between morning and evening, less get up and go on waking, more trouble switching off at night.
[pause 1.5s]
On the other hand, a few simple habits help the clock keep time.
Morning light, first. Spending a few minutes outside, or sitting near a window soon after you get up, is one of the strongest signals for setting your internal clock.
Even on a gray day, outdoor light is far brighter than a lit room.
Breaks during the day, too, so you're not tense from morning to night.
And in the evening, slowing down. Dimming the lights, setting screens aside a little before bed, and signaling to your body that the day is over.
In the evening, soft, low light, like a bedside lamp, is a simple way of telling your clock that the day is coming to an end.
Screens aren't forbidden. The idea is mainly to avoid staying under bright light, with content that winds you up, until the very last minute.
None of this is a strict rule. These are invitations to go with your rhythm rather than against it.
[pause 2s]
Let's practice this evening slow down together now.
If you can, dim the lights around you. Switch off the overhead light, keep a small lamp on. If you can't move, simply imagine the room gently growing darker.
[pause 3s]
You can also turn down your screen's brightness, or place your phone face down. If you like, tuck your feet under a blanket, and notice the temperature of the room.
[pause 2s]
Now slow your movements. If you move your hands, move them twice as slowly as usual. As if you were moving through water.
Try it, if you like. Slowly raise one hand, as if it were floating, then lower it, in slow motion. This simple slowness tells your body there's no rush.
[pause 4s]
Rest your hands on your thighs, or on your belly. Feel their weight.
[pause 3s]
Your face can slow down too. Your forehead smooths out. Your eyelids grow heavy. Your jaw loosens.
Your arms grow heavy. Your hands settle. Even your thoughts can slow down, like a conversation winding down at the end of a meal.
[pause 3s]
Now let's lengthen the out breath. It's a simple way to help your body shift into recovery mode.

Here's the rhythm. A calm in breath through your nose, about four seconds. Then a slower out breath, about six seconds, as if you wanted to make a candle flame flicker without blowing it out. I'll guide you, and the silence will keep time.
[pause 1.5s]
Breathe in through your nose, calmly...
[pause 4s]
And breathe out slowly, the candle flame barely moving...
[pause 6s]
Once more. Breathe in, without forcing...
[pause 4s]
And let the air flow out, long and slow, all the way out.
[pause 6s]
A third time, at your own pace. Breathe in... your belly rises...
[pause 4s]
And breathe out... your shoulders drop... your face softens.
[pause 6s]
Carry on at your own pace. With each out breath, imagine the tide going out inside you. The day's tasks recede, like water leaving the sand smooth behind it.
If you feel any discomfort, go back to your natural breathing.
[pause 8s]

Now imagine your body is a house where the lights go off, room by room. The office light goes off, and work thoughts fall quiet. Then the kitchen. The lists, the shopping, the things to plan. All that's left is one small lamp, soft and warm.
[pause 5s]
Can you notice the signs that your body is shifting into evening mode? Lower shoulders. A small yawn, maybe. Warmth in your hands or feet. A wish to slow down even more.
[pause 3s]
There's nothing to achieve. Your body knows how to make this transition. You're simply giving it the right conditions.
[pause 3s]
Feel the day behind you. Whatever isn't finished can wait until tomorrow. Tonight, there's nothing left to solve.
[pause 4s]
Before we finish, let's choose two small habits together. One for the morning, one for the evening.
