For the morning, for example, opening the curtains as soon as you get up, drinking your coffee by the window, or walking outside for a few minutes before your day begins.
Choose the one that feels easiest. The smallest habit is often the one that lasts.
[pause 3s]
For the evening, dimming the lights at the same time every night, leaving your phone in another room, or repeating these long out breaths before bed.
Choose one here, too.
[pause 3s]
Bright mornings, dim evenings. Two simple habits to support your inner tide.
If sleep problems or tiredness have been going on for a long time, don't hesitate to talk to a health professional.
For now, keep this slowness with you. And if you're heading to bed, keep the lights low on the way.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: What stress does in your body
script: [pause 1.5s]
Welcome to this exploration of stress. Over the next eight minutes, you'll understand what happens in your body when stress rises, and then learn how to press the brake.
Settle in however you like. No need to close your eyes yet. Just listen.
[pause 2s]
Picture a smoke detector. It's there to protect you. When it senses danger, it goes off loudly, and that's exactly what we want it to do.
Your brain has an alarm system that works in much the same way. It's very old. We share it with many animals, and it helped our ancestors escape predators.

At the heart of this alarm is a small, almond-shaped area called the amygdala, which picks up anything that looks like a threat. It acts very fast, often before you've had time to think. That's why you can jump before you even understand what's happening.
Think of slamming on the brakes to avoid a cyclist. In a split second, before you've even thought about it, your body has already reacted.
[pause 1.5s]

The trouble is that today, this detector often goes off over a slightly burnt piece of toast. A full inbox, a traffic jam, a comment from a coworker. No real danger to your life, but the alarm sounds anyway.
Your body doesn't always tell the difference between a lion and a presentation in front of your boss. In both cases, it gets roughly the same resources ready.
It's a bit as if your phone sounded the same siren for a text from a friend and for a fire alarm.
[pause 2s]
Here's what happens when the alarm sounds. Two things, as if someone pressed the accelerator.

First, within seconds, your body releases adrenaline. That's what makes your heart beat faster, speeds up your breathing, tenses your muscles, and sometimes gives you sweaty palms or a knot in your stomach.
Meanwhile, anything that isn't urgent takes a back seat. Digestion slows down, for example. Your body puts its resources into action.
Then, a little more slowly, over several minutes, a second pathway takes over. It's a chain linking the brain to small glands sitting on top of the kidneys, and it releases cortisol.
Cortisol mobilizes energy, in particular by raising the sugar available in your blood. It helps your body keep going.
Picture a runner on the starting line. Heart pounding, muscles ready, energy available. That's what adrenaline and cortisol are preparing you for.
All of this is useful, in the short term. It's what lets you react, focus, and push yourself.
[pause 2s]

But an accelerator isn't enough. Your body also has a brake, the recovery system. It slows the heart, relaxes the muscles, gets digestion going again. It tells your body, it's over, you can rest. Scientists call it the parasympathetic nervous system, but you can simply call it the brake.

Normally, after the alarm, the brake takes over. The problem is when the accelerator stays pressed down, day after day. Studies link this kind of prolonged stress with fatigue, poorer sleep, and other effects on health.
The good news is that you can partly press this brake yourself. And one of the most accessible ways is your breath, especially the out-breath.
[pause 2s]
Before pressing the brake, let's learn to notice when the accelerator is down.
If you like, close your eyes, or simply lower your gaze.
Take a natural breath, and begin to scan your body, like a kind detective. You're not trying to change anything, just observing.
Start at the top of your body and slowly work your way down, one area at a time.
Your jaw. Is it clenched? Are your teeth touching?
[pause 2s]
Your forehead, around your eyes. Is there a frown, any tightness?
Your shoulders. Are they hunched up toward your ears, or low and resting?
[pause 2s]
Your breathing. Is it high in your chest, and quick? Or slow, and deep in your belly?
Rest a hand on your belly if you like, to feel where your breath is sitting.
[pause 1.5s]
Your heart. Can you feel it beating? Fast, or calm?
No need to take your pulse. Just notice what you can sense, and what you can't.
Your belly. Is it knotted, tight, or soft?
[pause 2s]
Your hands. Are they clenched, sweaty, cold, or relaxed?
Whatever you find is useful information. There's nothing to fix right now.
Simply note what you find, like ticking off a list. Jaw clenched, yes or no. Shoulders up, yes or no. Nothing more.
[pause 3s]
Maybe you found a few signs of the accelerator. Maybe very few. Either way, you've just done something important. You've checked in with your body.
[pause 1.5s]
Now let's press the brake together. A gentle breath in through the nose, then a longer breath out through the mouth, as if blowing through a straw.
Breathe in gently, without filling your lungs completely...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out slowly, longer than the in-breath.
[pause 6s]
As you breathe out, your heart naturally tends to slow down a little. It's a normal mechanism, and you can use it to your advantage.
Once more. In through your nose...
[pause 3s]
and out, long and slow. Let your shoulders drop with the air flowing out.
[pause 6s]
Carry on like this, at your own pace. A simple in-breath, a longer out-breath. If you feel light-headed, go back to your usual breathing.
With each out-breath, release one of the areas you noticed earlier. Your jaw first. Let a little space open between your teeth.
Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and as the air slowly leaves, let your tongue relax in your mouth too.
[pause 5s]
Then your forehead. It smooths out, like a sheet being shaken flat. Your shoulders settle a little lower.
Your hands open and rest, palms up if that's comfortable. Your belly can soften and move freely with the breath.
Breathe in again...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out slowly. Your breath is the foot resting gently on the brake pedal.
[pause 5s]
Imagine the smoke detector falling silent. The toast is out of the toaster, the window is open, and the air is clear again.
[pause 3s]
Now let your breathing return to normal. And quickly scan again. Jaw, shoulders, breath, heart, belly, hands.
What has changed?
[pause 2s]
Maybe a little more heaviness, warmth, space. Maybe the change is tiny. That's fine. Your brake is training, like a muscle.
[pause 2s]
Here's something to explore next. Everyone has their own warning signals. For some, it's a clenched jaw. For others, a knotted stomach, a held breath, or shoulders creeping up.
Over the next few days, try to spot yours. The very first sign that shows up when the alarm goes off.
It might help to think back to the last time you felt stressed. What did your body do first?
The day you recognize it, you'll know the accelerator is down. And you'll know what to do. One long out-breath, and one area that lets go.
The earlier you spot it, the easier it is to brake. A bit like driving. Easing off gently before a bend takes far less effort than slamming on the brakes at the last moment.
[pause 2s]
If these signals are very frequent, very intense, or get in the way of daily life, talk to a doctor or a psychologist. That's what they're there for.
Gently open your eyes. You now know your alarm, your accelerator, and your brake.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Stress and connection
script: [pause 1.5s]
If you can, settle near something warm. A blanket, a mug, a soft lamp. Take your time to arrive.
Let your breath settle. Feel the places where your body is supported, whatever is holding you right now.
[pause 1.5s]
Breathe in calmly...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out, letting your shoulders grow a little heavier.
[pause 5s]
Once more, at your own pace.
[pause 6s]
When we talk about stress, we usually think of two reactions. Fight or flight. A racing heart, muscles ready to spring.
In the year two thousand, an American researcher, Shelley Taylor, and her team suggested adding to that picture.
The team noticed that, under stress, many humans also do something else. They move closer to others. They take care of the most vulnerable, and they seek support.
The researchers called this tend and befriend. Caring for others, and reaching out.
[pause 1.5s]
Think about what happens after bad news. Often, the first reflex is to call someone, to check on the people we love, to hold our children close. That's exactly it.
Or think of those stormy nights when neighbors who barely say hello suddenly find themselves in the hallway, helping each other out.
Several hormones seem to be involved in this urge to connect, and researchers are still exploring their exact role.
Shelley Taylor's work focused mainly on women. But other teams have observed that, under stress, men also became more cooperative and generous. This tendency seems to exist in all of us.
[pause 1.5s]
And it's more than a nice idea. Connection with others is one of the strongest buffers against stress.
You can think of it as a cushion between you and the hard knocks of life.
In one study, for example, people had to speak in front of a panel. Those who had spent time with a friend just beforehand showed a smaller stress response in their bodies.

Large health studies also show that people with good social ties are, on average, in better health. What matters isn't necessarily how many friends you have, but the feeling that you can count on someone. Studies even suggest that brief, friendly exchanges, with a neighbor or the person at the bakery, can lift our mood.
[pause 1.5s]
So when stress rises and you feel like calling someone, that's not weakness. It's your body reaching for a very old, and often very effective, resource.
And connection works both ways. For many people, offering support seems to do good to the giver as well.
[pause 2s]
Let's explore this together now.
Close your eyes if that's comfortable. Breathe easily.
Breathe in through your nose...
[pause 3s]
and let the out breath last a little longer. Your body settles.
[pause 5s]
Imagine yourself somewhere you feel good. A cozy room, a garden, a corner of the sofa.
[pause 2s]
Now think of someone who supports you. Someone you feel safe with, someone you can be yourself around.
It might be a friend, a family member, a coworker, a neighbor. It might also be someone you haven't seen in a long time, a teacher who believed in you, or even a pet you love.
Choose whoever comes most easily. There's no wrong answer here.
[pause 2s]
Imagine this person near you. Their face, their smile, the way they look at you. Notice the small details. The color of a sweater, a familiar gesture, the sound of their laugh.
[pause 4s]
Then let a second person come to mind. And maybe a third. They take their places around you, in a circle.
If only a few faces come, that's completely normal. One person is enough. You can also include someone who helped you once, even briefly.
[pause 2s]
Look at each of these people, one after the other. Remember a specific moment when they were there for you. A piece of advice, a fit of laughter, a quiet presence.
Hear their voice, perhaps. Something they once said to you that did you good.
[pause 4s]
Feel their presence. They're not asking anything of you. They're simply here, on your side. Let yourself enjoy this, even for a few seconds.
What happens in your body as you imagine them around you?
[pause 2.5s]
Warmth in your chest, maybe. Shoulders softening. Your breath deepening.
Many people feel their body relax just by thinking of someone kind. Simply let yourself taste that feeling.
[pause 4s]
Imagine one of them placing a hand on your shoulder. A warm, reassuring hand. As if to say, I'm here, with you.
If you like, actually rest your own hand on your shoulder, or on your arm. Your body understands this language too.
Let that warmth spread, from your shoulder into your back, then into your chest.
Breathe in slowly...
[pause 3s]
and as you breathe out, let your chest soften into that warmth.
[pause 5s]
If something difficult is weighing on you right now, imagine setting it down in the middle of the circle. You're no longer the only one carrying it. Other eyes are looking at it with you.
You don't have to solve it right now. Just feel that it's a little lighter when it's shared.
[pause 4s]
Now, let's turn things around.
Think of someone you could support today. Someone going through a hard time, facing a stressful moment, or who seems a little isolated lately.
Picture them in front of you. And silently send them a few simple words. I'm thinking of you. I hope you're okay. I'm here.
You don't need to have solutions for them. Often, what helps most is simply feeling seen, and heard.
[pause 4s]
Notice what it does inside you to offer them this attention. Caring for someone often calms us too.
Perhaps a smile, a softness, a quiet sense of pride. Let that feeling settle in over a few breaths.
[pause 4s]
Now let's turn this moment into something concrete.
Of all the people who came to mind, choose one to contact, today or tomorrow. Someone who supports you, or someone you could support.
And choose how. A simple message, a five minute call, an invitation for coffee, a walk.
There's no need for a big conversation, or a perfect one. A quick, I was thinking of you, is often enough to bring two people closer.
For example, I thought of you this morning, how are you doing? Or, fancy a coffee this week?
And if you're hesitating, afraid of bothering them, studies suggest we often underestimate how much an unexpected little message is appreciated. Most people are touched to be thought of.
You can even decide, silently, when you'll do it. Tonight after dinner. Tomorrow on your break.
[pause 2s]
See yourself doing it. Your phone in your hand, the first words you type. And the reply, perhaps, arriving with a smile.
Notice how simple it really is. A few seconds for you, and maybe a bright spot in someone else's day.
[pause 3s]
Notice how you feel now, after this time spent in good company. Maybe a little warmer, a little lighter in the shoulders.
Now let the circle gently fade, keeping its warmth with you. These bonds exist, even when people are far away.
[pause 2s]
Come back to the feeling of your body, your breath, the sounds around you.
And if you're going through a time when loneliness weighs heavily, remember that you can also turn to a doctor, a therapist, or a support line. Asking for help is another way of creating connection.
[pause 2s]
Open your eyes whenever you like. And don't forget your message. Someone, somewhere, may be very happy to receive it.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: The humming breath
script: [pause 1.5s]
For this session, find a spot where a little noise won't bother anyone. We're going to hum together, with our mouths closed.
Sit down, with your back straight and relaxed. Let your shoulders drop, and let your breath find its rhythm.
[pause 1.5s]
Breathe in through your nose...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out calmly.
[pause 4s]
Once more, letting your belly move freely.
[pause 6s]
You may have heard of the vagus nerve. It's become very fashionable in recent years, so let's untangle what's true from what's fuzzy.

The vagus nerve is one of the longest nerves in your body. It starts at the base of the brain, runs down through the neck, and branches out to the heart, the lungs, and a large part of the digestive system.
Its name comes from the Latin word vagus, which means wanderer. It wanders through your whole torso, visiting many of the places where you feel stress.

It's a major communication line, and it runs both ways. It carries messages from the brain to the organs. But it carries even more from the organs back to the brain. How your stomach is doing, how fast your heart is beating, how your lungs are breathing.
[pause 1.5s]
It's part of the recovery system, the one that slows the heart and supports digestion and rest. You could call it your body's brake, working against the accelerator of stress.
This brake is working all the time, even right now. You don't have to switch it on. You can simply give it a little more room.
It's a bit like your foot hovering near the brake pedal when you drive. It doesn't slam on the brakes. It keeps adjusting your speed.

Researchers track its activity through a measure called heart rate variability, the small, natural variations in time between heartbeats. A healthy heart isn't a metronome. It's constantly speeding up and slowing down, along with the breath.
[pause 2s]

So what seems to engage this brake? First, slow exhaling. When you breathe out, your heart slows slightly, and the vagus nerve plays a big part in that. Lengthening your out-breath makes use of a natural mechanism.
You can feel it for yourself some time. Place two fingers on your wrist or your neck, and breathe slowly. For many people, the pulse speeds up a little on the in-breath, and slows on the out-breath.
Next, the voice. The vagus nerve also helps control the muscles of the throat and larynx, the ones that let you speak and sing.
And finally, a sense of safety. A familiar face, a gentle voice, a reassuring presence. All of these seem to help the body step out of alert mode.
[pause 1.5s]
To be honest, you'll sometimes read that you can hack your vagus nerve in a few minutes. The research doesn't go that far.
What we do know is that slow breathing helps many people feel calmer, and that humming is a very natural way to lengthen the out-breath.
A few studies, still small, also suggest that bee breath, a closed-mouth humming practice from yoga, may encourage relaxation. And many people simply enjoy the vibration it creates.
Humming has another advantage. It keeps the mind busy. It's hard to ruminate while you're making a sound and feeling its vibration.
Try worrying about tomorrow's meeting while you hum a long, low note. It's surprisingly hard.
It's a little like singing yourself a lullaby.
[pause 2s]
Let's try it.
One thing before we start. If your nose is blocked, or the sound bothers you, you can simply do the long out-breath, in silence.
Keep your mouth closed, your teeth slightly apart, your tongue resting. Your jaw is relaxed.
Close your eyes, if you like.
[pause 2s]
Start with a simple breath. Breathe in gently through your nose, then out through your nose, without doing anything special.
[pause 6s]
Once more. The air comes in, cool...
[pause 3s]
and goes out, a little warmer.
[pause 4s]
Now let's add the sound. On your next out-breath, hum a low, soft mmm, like when you taste something delicious.
No need to sing in tune, or to be loud. The sound stays soft, almost inward. It happens only on the out-breath. The in-breath stays silent, through the nose.
Breathe in through your nose, letting your belly expand...
[pause 3s]
and hum, for as long as it feels comfortable.
[pause 8s]
Good. Let the sound finish in its own time, and breathe normally for a moment.
Where did you feel the vibration? Maybe in your lips, your nose, your cheeks, or behind your eyes.
[pause 3s]
Notice, too, how the sound changed your out-breath. It becomes longer, steadier, almost effortless.
That longer out-breath is exactly what we were talking about a moment ago.
[pause 2s]
Once more. Breathe in through your nose, without filling your lungs all the way...
[pause 3s]
and hum, letting the sound sink down into your throat and chest.
[pause 8s]
Place a hand on your chest, if you like, to feel the vibration under your fingers. Like a purr.
Notice your shoulders, too. They often soften on their own while you hum.
Your jaw stays soft, your teeth apart. Only your lips are gently closed.
Breathe in gently...
[pause 3s]
and let the sound come.
[pause 8s]
You can try a slightly lower note, or a slightly higher one, to find the one that vibrates most pleasantly for you. Everyone has their own.
Breathe in through your nose...
[pause 3s]
and hum your own note.
[pause 8s]
If you feel dizzy or short of breath, stop and breathe normally. Humming should stay easy, never forced.
[pause 1.5s]
Now let's slow down. With each round, let the sound last just a little longer, without straining. The in-breath stays simple and natural.

If you like, you can also gently close your ears with your index fingers, resting them on the little flap of cartilage at the entrance of each ear. The sound becomes more inward, like listening to a seashell.
If that doesn't feel comfortable, simply keep your hands where they are.
Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
and hum slowly, like a bee drifting away across a garden.
[pause 9s]
One last hum. Breathe in through your nose...
[pause 3s]
and let the sound stretch out to the end of your breath, without going into discomfort.
[pause 10s]
Now let the sound fade away. Breathe naturally, through your nose, without controlling anything.
Stay for a moment in this calm. Notice what remains of the vibration, in your lips, your face, your chest. Like the echo of a bell fading away.
[pause 5s]
Your breath carries on by itself. There's nothing left to do. Just listen to the quiet inside.
[pause 5s]
How is your breath now? Your heart? Your face?
[pause 3s]
Your thoughts may be a little slower, more spaced out, like clouds drifting apart.

There's nothing in particular you should feel. Maybe relaxation, warmth, tingling. Maybe just silence. Everything is welcome. And if you didn't notice anything special, that's fine too. You've discovered a tool, and it gets easier with time.
[pause 2s]
Gently come back. Move your fingers, your shoulders. Open your eyes whenever you like.
[pause 1.5s]
As with any breathing practice, regularity is what counts. A few minutes a day will probably serve you better than one long session now and then.
You can take this humming anywhere a little sound is possible. In the shower, while cooking, before sleep. A few rounds are enough.
And where you can't make noise, at work or on the train, just keep the long, slow out-breath, as if you were humming on the inside. Your voice, even silent, is there to soothe you.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Your window of tolerance
script: [pause 1.5s]
Welcome. This session gives you a simple map for understanding your inner states, and two tools to find your way.
[pause 1.5s]
Sit with your feet on the floor. You can keep your eyes open the whole time. That's part of the practice.
Take a breath, at your own pace.
[pause 3s]
Feel the air coming in through your nose, and your back resting against the chair. You're simply arriving.
[pause 2s]
Clinicians, including the American psychiatrist Dan Siegel, have offered an image called the window of tolerance.
Picture a band, a zone, between two extremes. Inside this zone, you can feel emotions, even strong ones, and still be able to think. You can listen, choose, respond rather than react.
It isn't a state of perfect calm. Inside your window, there can be anger, worry, emotion, excitement. But you stay at the controls.
Think of a river flowing between two banks. The water can be calm or choppy, fast or slow. As long as it stays within its banks, it keeps on flowing.
[pause 2s]
Above the window is over-activation. Your heart pounds, your thoughts race. It's agitation, panic around the corner, anger taking over. Thinking clearly gets hard, and you react on a hair trigger.
Below it is under-activation. Here, it's more like emptiness. A sense of numbness, of being cut off from your feelings, flat. As if someone had turned the dimmer down.
You might want to curl up under the covers, or scroll through your phone without really seeing anything.
Or stare at the same page for ten minutes without taking in a single word.
Both states are protective reactions of your nervous system. They're not flaws, and they're not failures.
[pause 2s]
Here's an example. You get an unpleasant email. Inside your window, you read it, feel the irritation rise, take a breath, and choose how to reply.
Above it, you fire back within a minute, hammering the keyboard, and regret it a little later. Below it, you shut the laptop and can't get anything done for the rest of the evening.
No one stays inside their window all the time. Leaving it is part of life. What matters is knowing how to come back.
[pause 1.5s]
The width of the window varies. Poor sleep, hunger, built-up stress can narrow it. Rest, connection with others, and practice can help widen it.
It's worth saying that this is a model, a map to help you find your bearings, not a precise measurement. But many people find it helps them understand themselves better.

Above all, it points the way. You don't come back to your window the same way when you're too high as when you're too low. Too high, the aim is to come down. Too low, the aim is to come gently back up.
It's like a thermostat. When it's too hot, you don't turn up the heating. When it's too cold, you don't open the window.
[pause 2s]
Let's start by finding where you are. Without changing anything, just notice.
Your energy, first. Is it rather high, jittery? Or rather low, heavy?
[pause 3s]
Your thoughts. Are they racing in every direction? Or slow, foggy, far away?
[pause 3s]
Your body. Is it tense, ready to spring? Or limp, heavy, hard to get moving?
[pause 3s]
Picture a vertical ladder, with your window in the middle. Where are you right now? A bit above, in the middle, a bit below?
[pause 2s]
A rough sense is enough. You don't need to be precise.
There's no right answer. Just information, which you can take in without judgment.
Sometimes you're a bit of both at once, exhausted and on edge. That's common. In that case, start with whichever tool feels most fitting.
And if you're not sure where you are, that's fine too. Just notice your energy right now, and let's move on.
[pause 2s]
Here's the first tool, for times when you're too high. Even if you feel fine right now, try it. Practicing calm is how you remember it in the storm.
What helps when you're too high is anything that slows and grounds you. Contact with the floor, the weight of your body, the out-breath.
Place both feet flat on the floor. Press them down a little, as if you wanted to leave a footprint.
Feel the weight of your legs. Imagine them growing heavy, anchored.
If you're sitting, feel the seat beneath you too, solid, carrying all your weight without any effort.
[pause 2s]
Now, the long out-breath. The exhale lasts about twice as long as the inhale, like a long, easy sigh.
Breathe in through your nose, simply...
[pause 3s]
And breathe out slowly through your mouth...
[pause 6s]
Again. In through your nose...
[pause 3s]
and blow out slowly, letting your shoulders drop.
[pause 6s]
One last time, in...
[pause 3s]
and as the air leaves, think, heavy and slow.
[pause 6s]
If you feel dizzy, simply go back to your natural breathing.
[pause 1.5s]
That's the first tool. Heavy feet, long out-breath. It helps your body press the brake when everything speeds up.
You can use it anywhere. In a meeting, on the train, in a waiting room. No one even needs to notice.
[pause 2s]
Here's the second tool, for times when you feel switched off, empty, drained. Here, the aim isn't to calm down further. It's to gently wake up your senses.
What helps when you're too low is the opposite. Anything that brings a little stimulation, movement, contact with your surroundings.
Keep your eyes open, and look around you. Let your gaze wander slowly across the room, from left to right.
Silently name three colors you can see.
[pause 3s]
Then find an object you hadn't noticed until now. Look at its shape, its texture.
Describe it silently, as if you had to explain it to someone who has never seen it.
You can also rest your hands on a cool surface, a table or a wall, and feel its temperature.
[pause 2s]
Now move a little. Rub your hands together briskly until you feel warmth. Then place them on your thighs, or on your face.
[pause 2s]
Stretch your arms up, or roll your shoulders. Always within what's comfortable, never into pain.
[pause 2s]
And now, a slightly livelier breath. Breathe in a little more fully through your nose, as if smelling something good, and breathe out naturally, without lingering.
A few breaths like that, at your own pace. No faster. The aim is to wake you up, not to leave you breathless.
Breathe in with a little energy...
[pause 2s]
and out.
[pause 2s]
Again, in...
[pause 2s]
and out.
[pause 2s]
One last time, in...
[pause 2s]
and out.
[pause 3s]
If you feel lightheaded, slow down and breathe normally.
That's the second tool. Look, move, breathe a little more fully. It helps your body come gently back up into its zone.
[pause 2s]
Now let's come back to the center. Let your breathing find its own rhythm, neither too fast nor too slow.
Feel your feet on the floor, and at the same time, what's around you. The light, the sounds. Body present, mind available.
Pick out three sounds around you, near or far, while keeping your feet firmly planted.
[pause 3s]
Notice how, here, you can both feel your body and follow my voice. That's the window. Feeling and thinking at the same time.
[pause 2s]
This is what your window feels like. Not necessarily deep calm. More a sense of being here, neither swept away by the storm, nor absent.
Take a few moments to savor it, and to remember it.
Notice the temperature of the air, the weight of your hands, the sounds in the room.
[pause 4s]
Over the coming days, I invite you to spot your own signals that you're leaving the zone.
Going up, it might be a rising voice, a clenching jaw, thoughts going round in circles.
Going down, maybe an urge to give up on everything, a blank stare, a sudden heaviness.
The earlier you recognize them, the easier it is to come back. Heavy feet and a long out-breath when you're too high. Look, move, breathe more fully when you're too low.
[pause 2s]

If you often find yourself outside your window, or go through periods where everything stays switched off for a long time, talking to a therapist or a doctor can really help. This isn't a path to walk without support.
[pause 1.5s]
For now, have a little stretch, and carry on with your day from the center of your window.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Complete the stress cycle
script: [pause 1.5s]
Welcome. This session is a little more active than the others. At one point, I'll invite you to stand up and move. If that's not possible for you, you can do everything sitting down.
To begin, settle in however you like, and take a breath to arrive.
Breathe in through your nose...
[pause 4s]
and out through your mouth, letting your shoulders drop.
[pause 5s]

Have you ever been through this? A hard week comes to an end. The project is handed in, the argument is settled, the exam is over. The problem is gone... and yet the tension is still there. In your shoulders, your stomach, your sleep.
[pause 1.5s]
Two American authors, Emily and Amelia Nagoski, offer a simple way to understand this gap. They separate the stressor from the stress.
The stressor is the cause. Work, money, a conflict, an endless line at the store.
The stress is the reaction in your body. Your heart speeding up, your muscles tensing, hormones circulating.
And here's the key idea. Dealing with the stressor doesn't necessarily deal with the stress. You can solve the problem, and still carry the reaction in your body.
[pause 1.5s]
Think of a gazelle chased by a lion. If it escapes, it's because it ran with all its strength. Its body used up the energy that stress mobilized, then returned to calm. The cycle is complete.
We, on the other hand, face stressors we can neither run away from nor fight. We stay seated in front of a screen, heart pounding, jaw clenched. That mobilized energy has nowhere to go.
It's a bit like starting the car, revving the engine, and then sitting in neutral all day long.
And if these cycles stay open day after day, the tension builds up, a bit like a pile of dishes that never gets washed.
A sink full of dishes isn't a disaster on day one. After a few weeks, it becomes a real weight.
[pause 1.5s]

This is what these authors call an unfinished stress cycle. It's more of an image than a scientific theory in the strict sense. But it fits with well established findings. Physical activity, rest, slow breathing and social connection help the body return to calm.
[pause 1.5s]
So what tells your body the danger has passed?
Moving, first. It's one of the most effective ways. Walking, dancing, running, anything that gets your body working.
Breathing slowly, with long out breaths.
Laughing, really laughing, with someone. Not a polite little laugh. A real fit of giggles, the kind that shakes your belly.
Connection and affection. A warm conversation, a hug that lasts a little while, stroking a pet.
Creating, too. Drawing, singing, writing down what you feel, playing music. Anything that lets what's inside find a way out.
And sometimes, crying. Crying isn't failure. For many people, it's a way of releasing pressure.
[pause 2s]
Today, we'll complete the cycle together, in four steps. Movement, breath, release, safety.
Before we start, notice how you feel on a scale from one to ten, where ten is maximum tension. Just keep that number in mind.
[pause 3s]
Step one, movement. If you can, stand up, and give yourself a little space. If not, stay seated and do the same movements with your arms and upper body.
An important reminder. Never into pain. Always stay within what feels comfortable for you.
[pause 1.5s]
Start walking on the spot, gently. Lift one foot, then the other. Let your arms swing.
You can swing your arms a little more freely, as if you were walking briskly to catch a train. Feel your feet meeting the floor, one after the other.
[pause 4s]
Speed up a little, if it feels good. Lift your knees a bit higher. Feel your heart getting going, your breath deepening.
Your body is doing exactly what it was waiting for. Using up this energy. For your body, it's a bit like finally escaping the lion.
Keep going a little longer. Left, right, left, right. Let your arms follow the rhythm of your steps.
[pause 6s]
Now stop walking, and shake out your hands. As if you were flicking off drops of water.
Shake your arms, your shoulders. Let your whole upper body shake, loosely, like a dog coming out of the water.
You may have seen a dog shake like this after a fright, then trot off calmly. Here, it's simply a way to release the tension built up in your muscles.
[pause 3s]
Wrists loose, fingers relaxed. Shake, shake, as if you were shaking the day off your hands.
One leg, then the other. Shake them gently. And if you feel like making some noise, blowing out, sighing, go for it.
A few more seconds. Your whole body shaking. Letting out the energy that was stuck.
[pause 5s]
And stop. Stay still, standing or sitting. What's moving through you right now?
[pause 3s]
Warmth, tingling, your heart beating.
[pause 3s]
Step two, the breath. As your heart slows down, let's go along with it. Notice how, after effort, your breath naturally wants to lengthen.
Here's the rhythm. A breath in through your nose, about four seconds. Then a long breath out through your mouth, about seven seconds, like a long sigh. I'll just give you the cues.
[pause 1.5s]
In.
[pause 4s]
Out.
[pause 7s]
Once more. In, feeling your belly rise.
[pause 4s]
Out, letting your body come back down, like a wave drawing back.
[pause 7s]
Carry on at your own pace. With each out breath, imagine telling your body, it's over, the danger has passed.
If you feel any dizziness, go back to your natural breathing.
[pause 5s]
One last slow breath. In...
[pause 4s]
and out, all the way, feeling your heart settle back into its easy rhythm.
[pause 6s]
Step three, release. If you were standing, sit down now, comfortably.
We'll tense and then release a few areas of the body. Tensing first often helps you feel the release more clearly. Keep breathing normally while you tense.
Make fists. Tight, but without hurting yourself. Hold the tension for a few seconds...
[pause 4s]
And let go. Let your hands open, and feel the difference.
[pause 3s]
Now lift your shoulders up toward your ears. Squeeze, and hold the tension...
[pause 4s]
And let them drop, all at once. Heavy.
[pause 2s]
Your legs, now. Press your heels into the floor, tighten your thighs...
[pause 3s]
and let go. Feel your legs growing heavy, as if after a long walk.
[pause 2s]
Scrunch up your whole face, as if you'd bitten into a very sour lemon. Eyes, nose, mouth.
[pause 3s]
And release. Your forehead smooths, your cheeks soften, your jaw falls slightly open.
[pause 3s]
Now let your whole body grow heavy in your seat. Arms, legs, back. Nothing to hold, nothing to do.
Your breath moves on its own. Your body is held by the seat beneath you.
[pause 4s]

Step four, safety. Place one hand on your heart and the other on your belly. Or both on your chest. You can also cross your arms and rest your hands on your shoulders, as if giving yourself a hug. Choose whatever you prefer.
Feel the warmth of your hands. The gentle movement of your breath under your palms.
Many people find this simple touch comforting. It's a gesture we make instinctively to console someone. Today, you're offering it to yourself.
[pause 2s]
You can say to yourself, silently... I'm safe, here and now. Or, it's over, I can rest.
Choose the words that feel true for you.
[pause 4s]
If those words don't feel true today, that's okay. Just keep the warmth of your hands, and the feeling of your breath.
Your body knows how to find its way back to calm. You're simply helping it find the path.
[pause 3s]
Now gently lower your hands, and notice how you feel.
Think back to the number you had in mind at the start, between one and ten. Where are you now?
[pause 3s]
Maybe the number has gone down. Maybe it's hardly moved, and that's useful information too. Sometimes built up stress takes several cycles, several days, to unwind.
What you've just done, you can do again every day, in one form or another. What matters is choosing what suits you.

Maybe a brisk walk on your way home from work. Ten minutes of dancing in your kitchen. A fit of laughter with a friend. A long hug with someone you love. Or a few slow breaths, a hand on your heart, before you sleep.
Choose something that's realistic on a busy day, not just on a perfect one.
This isn't one more chore on your list. It's a way of telling your body, every day, that you're listening.
Think of one or two ways that feel like you, and that you could slip into your day, even briefly.
[pause 3s]
And if you feel that tiredness and tension have been settling in for a long time, despite everything, don't hesitate to talk to a doctor or a therapist. Exhaustion deserves to be taken seriously.
[pause 2s]
For now, take one last deep breath.
[pause 5s]
You've given your body what it needed. The end of the story.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Before you speak up
script: [pause 1.5s]
In a few minutes, you're going to speak. A presentation, an interview, or just that point you need to make in a meeting.
And your body already knows it. Keep your eyes open. We're going to work with it, not against it.
[pause 2s]
Start by noticing what's happening, without changing anything. Is your heart beating faster, harder?
[pause 2s]
Your hands might be cold, or a little clammy. In your stomach, maybe there's that small knot, that fluttering.
That's stage fright. Almost everyone feels it, including the people who look perfectly at ease up there.
You don't need to make it disappear. That would be hard anyway, just minutes before you go on.
These few minutes are for something else. Turning that energy into an ally instead of an enemy.
[pause 3s]
Here's another way to see it. That racing heart is sending more oxygen to your brain and your muscles.
Your body isn't betraying you. It's getting ready, because this moment matters to you.
It's the same energy as the excitement before setting off on a trip. The same chemistry, with a different label.
You can say it to yourself. My body is getting ready. This energy is here to help me.
Some studies suggest that simply relabeling nerves as excitement can help people perform better than trying to force themselves to calm down.
[pause 3s]
Now, your feet. Place them flat, about hip width apart. If you're standing, spread your weight evenly across both legs, knees soft.
Feel your heels, your toes, the whole sole of each foot. Press very gently into the floor, as if to feel it holding you.
[pause 2s]
Then grow a little taller. Imagine a thread gently drawing the top of your head toward the ceiling.
Open your chest. Let your shoulders drop and widen, away from your ears.
Unclench your hands. Let your arms hang freely, or rest your hands, palms open.
[pause 2s]
If you're somewhere private, you can even raise your arms for a few seconds, like a runner crossing the finish line. Then let them float back down.
[pause 2s]
This is the posture of someone who has room to be here. You're allowed to take up space.
An open posture helps your breathing too. Your ribcage has room, and the breath drops more easily.
[pause 2s]
Now the breath, which will steady your voice. Place one hand on your belly, just below your navel.
Breathe in through your nose and let your belly press gently into your hand...
[pause 3s]
Then breathe out through your mouth, slowly, longer than the in breath. Your belly sinks back.
[pause 6s]
Again. A calm breath in, about four seconds...
[pause 4s]
And out, about six, without straining.
[pause 6s]
A third time. Breathe in...
[pause 3s]
And let your throat open as you breathe out, like a quiet, hidden yawn.
[pause 6s]
If you feel any discomfort or lightheadedness, go back to your natural breathing. That's perfectly fine too.
If you can, hum softly on the next out breath, lips closed. A gentle mmm.
[pause 5s]
Can you feel the vibration in your lips, your nose, your chest? Your voice is right there, warm and grounded.
[pause 2s]
A steady voice comes from a low breath and a relaxed throat. That's why we take this time, however short.
[pause 2s]
Now picture your entrance. Just the first few seconds.
You walk into the room, or the camera turns on. You see the faces, the screen, the table.
You take your place. Your feet find the floor, just like now.
You let one breath pass before you speak. That short silence isn't empty. It's you setting the pace.
And you say your first sentence. Slowly. Hear it in your head, in your steady voice.
[pause 3s]
Picture a small hiccup, too. A word that slips away, a slide that won't load.
You pause, you breathe, you pick it back up. It happens to everyone, and it's easy to recover from.
[pause 2s]
Run through that entrance one more time, even more calmly.
This time, notice your easy breath and your low shoulders as you speak.
[pause 5s]
Finally, choose an intention. One thing you want people to remember.
Not all of your content. The heart of your message, in one simple sentence.
Say it to yourself now, as if you were explaining it to a friend over coffee.
[pause 4s]
If you lose your thread while you're speaking, that's where you'll come back to. It's your anchor.
And remember, the people listening aren't looking for perfection. They want to understand what you have to say.
[pause 2s]
Your heart may still be racing, and that's fine. Your body is ready, your feet are grounded, your voice is there, and so is your message.
One last long out breath.
[pause 5s]
This is your moment. Go for it.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: After criticism
script: [pause 1.5s]
You've just heard something that hurts. Negative feedback, a tough performance review, a passing comment that stuck with you.
And it stings. That's human. Nobody likes hearing that their work isn't good enough, even when the criticism is fair.
[pause 2s]
Find a place where you can have a little quiet. Sit down, with your back supported and your feet on the floor.
You can close your eyes, or lower your gaze to a spot in front of you.
Take one breath that's a little slower than the others. Nothing more for now.
[pause 3s]
Let the air come in and go out at its own pace. Feel the chair beneath you, your feet against the floor.
These are simple, steady things. They were here before that feedback, and they'll be here after.
If your mind drifts back to the scene, that's normal. Just come back to the feel of your feet, one more time.
[pause 2s]
Now let's look for where that criticism has landed in your body.
For some people, it's heat in the face, in the cheeks or the ears. For others, a lump in the throat, a weight on the chest, a hollow feeling in the stomach.
Where is it for you, right now?
[pause 3s]
It doesn't have to be clear. A vague impression is enough.
When you find a spot, stay next to it. You don't have to dive in.
Imagine your breath flowing toward that area. As if each inhale gave it a little more room, and each exhale softened it.
You don't have to make the feeling go away. It can stay as long as it needs to. You just breathe alongside it, the way you'd sit beside someone who's hurting.
[pause 3s]
If you like, rest a hand on that spot. Or over your heart, or on your arm. A warm, simple touch.
It's the gesture you'd offer a friend coming out of a hard meeting.
Now say to yourself, in the kindest voice you have... this is hard to hear.
Let the words land. You're not complaining. You're simply naming what's true.
[pause 3s]
You can add... I'm not the only one who goes through this. Everyone, at some point, gets criticism that hurts.
And maybe... what do I need, right now? A little patience with myself. A little time.
[pause 2s]
This isn't letting yourself off the hook. It's what allows you to look at the criticism without getting defensive, and without crumbling.
When we talk to ourselves harshly, we tend to shut down. When we're gentle, we can actually face what happened.
[pause 3s]
Now that the sting has eased a little, let's sort things out together.
Think back to what was actually said. Not everything you felt. Just the words, the facts.
For example, the report came in two days late. Or, the presentation needed more data. Those are facts.
And then there's what your mind made of them. I'm useless. I'll never get this right. They're going to realize I don't belong here.
That's not what was said. It's an interpretation. A sweeping judgment added on top of specific feedback.
In a matter of seconds, a comment about one report becomes a verdict on who you are. It's a very common shortcut when we feel under attack.
Try to separate the two, like sorting two piles of paper on a desk. On one side, what was really said. On the other, the story you're telling yourself.
[pause 3s]
Look at the pile of facts. If you could keep just one useful thing, what would it be?
[pause 2s]
A piece of information that can help you grow, even a little. A concrete point, something you can act on.
Choose it. Just one. The rest can be set aside for today.
You can even turn it into a small action. Next time, I'll flag it as soon as I sense the deadline is tight.
And if part of the criticism feels unfair, you're allowed to think so. You can bring it up later, once things have cooled down.
As for the pile of judgments about yourself, you don't need to keep it. It teaches you nothing new. It just hurts.
[pause 3s]
To rebalance the scales, bring to mind a recent success. Something that went well in the last few weeks.
A project wrapped up, a happy client, a colleague you helped, a problem you solved.
Replay that moment in a little detail. Where you were, what you did, how it felt.
[pause 3s]
That success is just as real as today's criticism. Both are part of your work.
You don't have to choose between them. You can see something to improve and, at the same time, know what you do well.
[pause 2s]
Come back to your breath. Notice the place in your body you visited earlier. Has anything shifted, even a tiny bit?
[pause 3s]
If the sting is still there, that's normal. It will fade in its own time.
You might also offer yourself something kind in the next hour. A glass of water, a short walk, a message to someone you trust.
[pause 2s]
Wiggle your fingers, roll your shoulders, and come back to the room around you.
That feedback was about a piece of work, at one moment in time. It doesn't define who you are. You're much bigger than a few sentences.
And you leave with the one useful thing you chose to keep.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: The commute home
script: [pause 1.5s]
Before we begin, a quick note. This session is meant for public transport, walking, or the passenger seat. Never while driving, and never on a bike.
Keep your eyes open the whole time. If you're walking, your attention always goes first to crossings and intersections.
[pause 2s]
There. The workday is behind you. This commute is an airlock. A space between the person you were at the office and the person you'll be tonight.
With a phone in your pocket, work tends to follow us everywhere. For these few minutes, you can leave the emails where they are. They won't go anywhere before tomorrow.
[pause 1.5s]
Take a breath that's a little longer than the others...
[pause 3s]
and let it out slowly.
[pause 5s]
Start by feeling the movement. If you're on a train, a subway, or a bus, notice the little jolts, the speeding up, the braking.
Your body adjusts to each one, without you having to think about it.
If you're walking, feel the rhythm of your steps. Heel, sole, toes. Left, right.
[pause 2s]
This journey has its own speed, and for once, there's nothing to rush. The train will get there when it gets there. Your feet will carry you home.
Notice where you're supported. Your feet on the floor, your back against a seat, or your hand on a pole. Feel the temperature of the metal, the texture of the fabric.
Let your eyes rest on what's around you, without latching on. A window, building fronts, people, a patch of sky.
[pause 3s]
There may be noise. Announcements, conversations, the rumble of the tracks, traffic.
You don't need to push it away. It's part of the journey. It passes, like everything else.
If you're wearing headphones, let my voice blend with those sounds, without shutting out the world completely.
And if your stop is coming up or you need to change lines, keep one ear on the announcements. You can pause this anytime.
[pause 2s]
Now let your day roll past, like the scenery outside the window.
The morning, the first emails. A meeting. Lunch. A moment of frustration, maybe. A pleasant moment, too.
You watch these images go by, without stopping on any of them. Like buildings sliding past outside. They appear, then disappear behind you.
[pause 2s]
One image may come back more than the others. It's often the one that mattered most, for better or worse.
You can give it a glance, a small inner nod, the way you'd wave to someone across the street. Then let it slip away with the next one.
This isn't the moment to analyze what happened. Just to acknowledge that the day took place, with its highs and lows.
[pause 3s]
Let's use the journey itself to set down what still feels heavy.
At each stop, or each street you cross, you'll leave one worry behind.
Pick the first one. An email you haven't answered. A comment that annoyed you. A project that's stuck.
[pause 2s]
At the next stop, when the doors open, imagine that worry stepping off the train. It stays on the platform. You keep going.
If you're walking, leave it at the next corner, sitting on a bench.
It may feel a little simple. But giving a worry a concrete place often helps the mind stop carrying it around.
[pause 3s]
Now a second worry. Maybe a smaller one. A task that's dragging on, a meeting tomorrow.
At the next stop, at the next street, it gets off too. It'll still be there tomorrow if you need it. It doesn't need to come home with you.
And if there's a third, do the same. You don't need to empty everything. Just travel a little lighter.
[pause 2s]
What does it feel like each time a worry stays behind?
[pause 2s]
Maybe nothing dramatic. Maybe a breath that comes a little more easily.
And if a worry climbs back on board, which happens a lot, that's fine. You notice it, and you set it down again at the next stop.
[pause 2s]
Come back to your breath. Let the exhale become a little longer than the inhale, naturally.
Breathe in easily through your nose...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out slowly, as if you were cooling a spoonful of hot soup.
[pause 6s]
With each exhale, let your shoulders drop a little. They may have spent the day up by your ears, at your screen or in meetings.
Relax your jaw, too. And your hands, if they're gripping a bag or a phone. Keep just the hold you need to stay safe.
If you feel any discomfort, simply return to your usual breathing.
Notice how your body follows the motion of the journey without resisting. It sways, adjusts, lets itself be carried. You can do the same with what's left of the day.
[pause 3s]
Now think about what's waiting for you when you arrive.
Maybe people. A partner, kids, a roommate, a pet who'll greet you at the door.
Or maybe a moment for yourself. A meal, a hot shower, a book, the couch, some quiet.
Imagine the exact moment you arrive. The sound of the key, the smell of home, the light in the hallway. The first thing you'll say, or the first thing you'll do.
[pause 2s]
Choose one image. And let yourself look forward to it. Feel what it's like, in your body, to be heading toward something good.
[pause 3s]
For those people, or for that moment, which version of yourself do you want to bring home?
[pause 2.5s]
Maybe more present. More patient. More available. Or simply more rested.
There's no need to be perfect. Just to arrive a little more whole.
The people waiting for you don't need the rushed version of you from the office. They need you, with a little more calm.
[pause 2s]
The journey is nearly over. Get ready to arrive.
When you reach your door, before you turn the key, take one conscious breath.
That doorstep is your threshold. On one side, work. On the other, your life.
As you step across it, you can say to yourself, I'm home.
Say it simply, as a small marker that the workday is over.
[pause 2s]
Once you're inside, set your bag down a little more slowly than usual. Change your shoes, take off your badge, like taking off a costume. Small signals, but your body understands them.
[pause 1.5s]
Tonight, you come home with your hands a little freer, and your heart a little more open.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Impostor feelings
script: [pause 1.5s]
Maybe you've just started a new role, earned a promotion, or taken on a project that feels too big for you.
And somewhere, a small voice whispers that you don't belong here. That one day, someone is going to figure it out.
If so, this session is for you. We're not going to silence that voice. We're going to learn to live alongside it.
[pause 2s]
Get comfortable, with your back supported and your feet on the floor. Close your eyes if you like, or keep a soft, lowered gaze.
Take a few slow breaths. Breathe in through your nose...
[pause 3s]
and breathe out gently, without forcing.
[pause 5s]
Let your breath find its rhythm. The air coming in, slightly cooler. The air going out, slightly warmer.
Feel where you touch the chair, and the floor. Your body is here, right now. It has nothing to prove.
[pause 2s]
Simply being here, willing to look this thought in the eye, already takes a bit of courage.
You don't need to feel confident to do this. You just need to be curious for a few minutes.
[pause 2s]
Now let's do something a little unusual. Instead of pushing this thought away, we're going to invite it in.
Let the sentence come that your mind tells you in those moments. The one that shows up most often.
Maybe it's, I'm not good enough. Or, I just got lucky. Or, sooner or later they'll find out I have no idea what I'm doing.
Find your own version, in your own words.
Don't pick the harshest one you can imagine. Just the familiar one, the one you actually hear.
[pause 3s]
Listen to it. What's the tone of that voice? Urgent, mocking, cold, anxious?
[pause 2s]
How long have you known it? Maybe since school, or your first jobs. It's not a newcomer. It's an old habit of your mind.
Notice what it does in your body, too. Maybe a tightening in your stomach, heat in your chest, a weight on your shoulders.
You don't have to do anything about it. Just observe it, with curiosity, like a scientist studying something interesting.
Often we try to shut this voice up, or prove it wrong. And the more we fight it, the more room it takes up. Here, we do the opposite.
[pause 2s]
Here's a first step toward a little distance. Instead of thinking, I'm not good enough, you're going to say to yourself, I notice I'm having the thought that I'm not good enough.
Try it with your own sentence. I notice I'm having the thought that... and then your thought.
[pause 3s]
Feel the difference. The thought is still there. But now there's a little space between it and you. You're the one noticing it.
You are not the thought. You're the space it appears in, like the sky a cloud drifts across.
You can go a step further. Tell yourself, there's my mind, telling me the impostor story again.
Like an old song the radio keeps playing. You know every word. You don't have to sing along.
Each time you name the thought this way, you're practicing watching it pass, instead of getting swept away by it.
[pause 2s]
Now let's play a little. Take your sentence again, but this time, hear it in a cartoon voice.
A tiny, squeaky, nasal voice, like a very small character. Or a very deep, very slow voice, like a record winding down.
Let that voice say your sentence. They're going to find me out...
You can also picture it written in big, colorful letters on a balloon, drifting slowly off into the sky.
[pause 3s]
What happens? Maybe a slight smile. Maybe the sentence feels a little less threatening.
[pause 2s]
The words are the same. But you hear them for what they are. Words. Not facts. Not the truth about you.
If this exercise doesn't do much for you today, that's fine. Simply observing is already enough.
[pause 2s]
Here's something important to know. This feeling is extremely common, especially among capable, conscientious people.
Brilliant students, doctors, researchers, celebrated artists have all described this same voice.
It often shows up precisely when you're growing, when you're taking on new responsibilities. It's not a sign that you don't belong. More likely a sign that you're stepping outside familiar ground.
It's often the people who think hardest about their work who doubt themselves the most. Your doubt may mostly be a sign that you take things seriously.
Feeling like an impostor and being one are two very different things.
[pause 3s]
Now let's gather some evidence. Not feelings. Concrete facts.
Think of a first piece of evidence that you belong. A skill you've mastered. A problem you solved. A specific piece of positive feedback someone gave you.
Let it come with details. The moment, the people, what you did.
[pause 3s]
A second piece of evidence. Maybe the reason you were chosen. A degree, an experience, a quality others have noticed in you.
Someone decided to trust you with this role or this project. They surely had their reasons.
[pause 3s]
And a third. Something difficult you've already been through. A situation where you didn't know how, and you learned along the way.
You've never known everything in advance. Nobody does. We learn by doing.
Every capable person you admire was once a beginner, figuring it out as they went.
Keep these three pieces of evidence close. They're just as real as that little voice. More real, in fact, because they actually happened.
If your mind answers yes, but, to each one, notice that too. It's the same voice again. You can let it talk, and keep the evidence anyway.
[pause 2s]
Now, one last question. Why does this work matter to you?
Not for your title, or for what other people think. For you.
[pause 2s]
Maybe because you love to learn. Because you want to help people. Because you enjoy creating, solving, teaching, building.
Let what's true for you come forward. A value, a single word.
It doesn't need to be grand. Something simple and honest is enough.
Feel what it's like to connect with that. Maybe a kind of calm, a steadiness, deeper than the doubt.
[pause 4s]
That's your compass. Not the doubting voice. When it comes back, and it probably will, you can turn toward what matters to you.
[pause 2s]
Come back to your breath. Feel your body in the chair, your feet on the floor.
Notice how you feel now. The thought may still be there, a little in the background. That's okay.
[pause 2s]
If you like, choose one small step for tomorrow. A question you dare to ask, an idea you share in a meeting, even an imperfect one.
You don't need the voice to disappear in order to move forward. It can ride along in the car. But you're the one driving.
Next time it speaks up, you can simply tell yourself, ah, there's the impostor story. Thanks, mind. And carry on with what you were doing.
Doubt and competence can live side by side. Many people do excellent work while still hearing that voice now and then.
[pause 2s]
Gently move your hands, your shoulders. Open your eyes, if they were closed.
The thought can stay. You keep moving forward anyway.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Sunday evening dread
script: [pause 1.5s]
It's Sunday evening. The light is fading, and with it, maybe, that little knot rising in your stomach as you think about tomorrow.
If that's what you're feeling, you're far from alone. So many people know the moment when Monday shows up early.
Maybe it started late this afternoon. A small dip in mood, an irritability with no clear reason. Then your thoughts began drifting toward the week.
[pause 2s]
Get comfortable, wherever you are. On the couch, on your bed, in an armchair. Let your body sink in a little.
You can close your eyes, or let your gaze rest somewhere in front of you.
[pause 1.5s]
Over these eight minutes, we'll do two simple things. Put the coming week away. Then come back to the Sunday you're actually living.
[pause 1.5s]
Breathe easily. In through your nose...
[pause 3s]
And out slowly, as if blowing on a candle without making the flame flicker.
[pause 5s]
Once more. In...
[pause 3s]
and let the exhale last a little longer.
[pause 5s]
Now notice where this dread lives in your body. Often it's a tightness in the stomach or chest, sometimes a restlessness in the legs.
Rest a hand there, if you like. Just to say, I see you.
[pause 3s]
First, know this. This anticipation isn't a flaw. It's your brain doing its job.
It's trying to protect you by preparing for the week ahead, scanning for problems. It's just a little overeager, and a little early.
You can thank it, silently. Thanks, I know you mean well. But right now, it's still Sunday.
Your brain hears you. It may not settle right away, and that's okay. You can keep reminding it, gently, as many times as you need.
[pause 3s]
Now notice the thoughts circling around Monday. You don't need to follow them or solve them. Just watch them go by.
Each time a thought about the week appears, count it. One. Then the next, two. And so on.
Monday morning's meeting. The email you haven't answered. That overdue project. That difficult colleague.
Maybe even a vague feeling with no clear content, just a general heaviness. Count that too.
[pause 2s]
You count them without stepping inside. Like counting the cars of a passing train.
Notice their shape, too. They often start with what if. What if the meeting goes badly. What if I don't have time. Questions about a future that doesn't exist yet.
[pause 3s]
There may be a lot of them. Or maybe it's the same one, coming back again and again. Both are normal.
[pause 1.5s]
Now let's give them somewhere to go. Picture a notebook. A real notebook, with a cover you choose.
On the first page, at the top, write Monday, nine in the morning.
It's an appointment. On Monday at nine, you'll deal with everything written in this notebook. Not before.
Your brain needs to know these things won't be forgotten. That's why it keeps bringing them up. By giving them a specific appointment, you show it they're in safe hands.
[pause 3s]
Now take each thought you counted, and write it in the notebook. Just a few words.
Team meeting. Reply to the client. Finish the presentation. Whatever comes.
If a thought feels huge, shrink it down to its first step. Not the whole project, just the first phone call.
With each line, you can tell yourself, it's noted. I'll think about it Monday, at nine.
[pause 3s]
If a thought comes back later this evening, you'll know what to tell it. You're already in the notebook. See you Monday.
If you like, you can write this notebook for real after the session. For many people, that really helps the mind let go.
[pause 1.5s]
Before you close the notebook, choose one preparatory action. Just one, simple and concrete, something you can do tonight in under five minutes.
Lay out your clothes for tomorrow. Put your badge in your bag. Set your alarm. Write down Monday's first task.
Or nothing at all, if everything's ready.
Decide on it now. You'll do it right after this session, and then it's done.
The goal isn't to prepare the whole week. It's to show your mind you've got it handled, just enough so it can rest.
Small, concrete steps like this often calm the mind more than hours of going over the week in your head.
[pause 3s]
And now, close the notebook. Imagine the sound of the cover closing. Put it on a shelf, away from you.
The week is put away. It will wait until Monday.
[pause 2s]
Does anything loosen, even a little, now that the week is up on the shelf?
[pause 3s]
Come back to the present. To this Sunday evening, which is still here.
Start with the room around you. If your eyes are open, notice three things you can see. A color, a light, a familiar object.
If they're closed, simply picture the room as it is right now.
[pause 2s]
Now listen. What sounds are there tonight? A television in another apartment. A passing car. The heating. The silence.
Let these Sunday sounds come to you.
[pause 3s]
And feel your body. Your weight on the couch or the bed. The texture of a cushion, a blanket, your clothes.
Notice the places where you feel good. Maybe warm feet. Maybe relaxed hands.
And your breath. Let it be slow and easy. A Sunday breath, with no schedule, no rush.
[pause 3s]
Each time your attention drifts toward tomorrow, and it will, just bring it back to what you feel right here.
[pause 1.5s]
Now think back to a good moment from this weekend. Even a tiny one.
Coffee at a café. Sleeping in. A meal with people you love. A walk, a movie, a fit of laughter, a moment alone.
Choose one, and relive it in detail. Where were you? What did you see, hear, feel?
[pause 3s]
Savor it. Notice what it does in your body to think back on that moment. Maybe some warmth, a smile.
You can stretch the memory out. If it was a meal, find the taste again. If it was a walk, the light, the air on your face. If it was laughter, the voices of the people with you.
[pause 2s]
That moment really happened. It's part of your week, just as much as Monday is.
The mind tends to hold on mostly to what worries it. Taking time to savor a good memory helps rebalance the scales a little.
And there may still be one more good moment possible tonight. Something warm to eat, an episode of your show, a phone call, a bath. Something simple, to savor the same way.
[pause 2s]
Gently come back to your breath. Notice how you feel now, compared to the beginning.
Maybe the knot is still there, a little smaller. Maybe it's gone. Either is fine.
[pause 2s]
Gently move your hands, your feet. Open your eyes, if they were closed.
If the knot comes back later, you know what to do. One breath. A reminder, it's in the notebook. Then come back to what you're living right now.
Monday has its appointment. You'll do your one small action, and then you're done.
And tomorrow morning, if the knot is there when you wake up, you can come back to this notebook and these few breaths.
[pause 1.5s]
Tonight is still the weekend. Your evening is still yours.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Lunch break
script: [pause 1.5s]
It's time to eat. And for once, you're really going to eat. Not in front of a screen, not reading emails, not thinking about this afternoon's meeting.
For these ten minutes, there's only you, your meal, and this moment.
It doesn't have to be a special meal. Something homemade, a salad in a plastic tub, a sandwich grabbed on the run... it all works. What matters is how you eat it.
[pause 2s]
Start by settling in. If you can, step away from your desk. A break room, a bench outside, a quiet table.
Put your phone face down, or slip it into your pocket. Close your laptop if you're at your desk.
Set your meal in front of you. And sit comfortably, feet on the floor, back upright without being stiff.
If you're eating with colleagues, you can listen with one earbud, or simply keep the idea in mind. Eat a little slower, and notice the flavors.
[pause 2s]
Before the first bite, let's take three breaths together. To shift from work mode to meal mode.
Breathe in slowly through your nose. Maybe you can already smell what's in front of you...
[pause 4s]
and breathe out gently through your mouth.
[pause 5s]
Second breath. Let your shoulders drop as you exhale.
[pause 7s]
And a third. Notice your stomach as you breathe.
[pause 6s]
Are you hungry? A little, a lot?
[pause 2.5s]
Is it your stomach that's hungry, or is it more tiredness, stress, habit? There's no right or wrong answer. Just an observation.
This quick check on your hunger is useful. Later on, it'll help you notice the moment you've had enough.
[pause 2s]
Now look at your food. Really look. As if you were seeing it for the first time.
What colors are there? The green of lettuce, the golden crust of bread, the red of a tomato, the white of rice.
Count the different colors, if you like. Even a simple sandwich often holds more than you'd think.
Notice the textures. What's smooth, what's crunchy, what's glossy, what's matte.
Look at the way the light falls on the food. The small shadows, the highlights.
[pause 3s]
Now bring your face a little closer, or lift your plate slightly. Breathe in the smells.
Close your eyes for a moment, if you can. Your sense of smell sharpens when your eyes rest.
Maybe spices, herbs, something toasted, a sweet or tangy note.
Notice if your mouth starts to water. Your body is already getting ready to eat. A smell is all it needs.
[pause 3s]
Take your first bite. But before you put it in your mouth, look at it for a moment, on your fork or between your fingers.
Then bring it to your lips, slowly. And place it on your tongue, without chewing right away.
[pause 2s]
Notice the first taste. Is it salty, sweet, sour, bitter? A mix of all of them?
Notice the temperature. Hot, warm, cool.
Notice, too, where on your tongue the flavor is strongest. The tip, the sides, the back.
Every mouth is different. There's no right place, only what you notice.
[pause 3s]
Now begin to chew. Very slowly.
Notice how the texture changes. What was firm turns tender. The flavors open up, shift.
Maybe a taste you hadn't noticed appears. A spice, an herb, a small hidden note.
Keep chewing, without hurrying. Longer than usual.
How many times do you usually chew before swallowing? This time, go a little further. No need to keep track. Just enough to feel the difference.
[pause 3s]
And when it feels right, swallow. Feel the food travel down your throat, and then nothing.
Notice the taste that lingers in your mouth afterward.
That was a single bite. But maybe more flavor than in an entire meal eaten at your screen.
[pause 2s]
Now put down your fork. Or your sandwich, if that's what you're eating. Really set it down, on the plate or the table.
Between bites, your hands are free. It's a small gesture, but it changes everything. It breaks the habit of eating on autopilot.
Take a breath, hands resting.
[pause 4s]
You might notice a little impatience, an urge to grab the next bite quickly. That's the pace of work still running inside you. Let it slow down, bite by bite.
[pause 3s]
Then take another bite, at your own pace, keeping that same attention.
With each bite, you can focus on a different sense. Taste first. Then texture. Then sound, the crunch, the softness.
For this bite, choose taste. Let it unfold, from the first contact to the last trace on your tongue. For the next one, choose texture. The melt, the crunch, the grain.
[pause 3s]
If your mind drifts back to work, to an email, to what's waiting for you later, that's normal. It happens to everyone.
Just notice that you've wandered off. Then come back to the taste of what's in your mouth. That's your anchor.
And remember to set your fork down between bites. No need to be perfect. Just do it more often than usual.
[pause 3s]
Keep eating calmly. You might think about where this meal came from. The hands that grew it, transported it, cooked it.
All that journey, just to end up on your plate, this lunchtime.
No need to dwell on it. Just a moment of appreciation, and then back to the taste.
Between bites, look around you, too. The daylight, the people, a patch of sky. For a few minutes, you're somewhere other than your desk.
[pause 3s]
As the meal goes on, start noticing your stomach. Is it filling up? Has the hunger from the beginning changed?
Fullness arrives gradually. We often notice it too late, because we eat too fast.
Take a moment between bites to ask yourself, am I still hungry? Or am I eating out of habit?
[pause 2.5s]
On a scale of one to ten, where is your hunger now? A rough guess is enough. It's a way to get used to listening to that signal.
Five might mean comfortably hungry, eight pleasantly full. There's no target, only listening.
If you're still hungry, keep going, and enjoy it. If you're satisfied, you're allowed to stop. Even if there's food left on the plate.
[pause 3s]
Notice, too, whether the taste changes. Often, the first bites are the most intense. Then the pleasure fades a little, as your body is satisfied.
That's a valuable signal. Your body is telling you it has what it needs.
Eating more slowly gives those signals time to arrive. That's often why we feel lighter after a calm meal.
[pause 2s]
When you're finished, or nearly, put your fork down one last time. Push your plate away a little.
And take a few minutes for yourself, before you go back to work.
Let your back lean against the chair. Let your hands rest on your thighs, or on your belly.
Feel the warmth of the meal in your body. The feeling of being nourished.
[pause 3s]
Let your belly be free. Loosen your belt if you need to. Digestion can begin quietly, with nothing for you to do.
Maybe a silent thank you. For this meal, for this moment, for your body, which will turn it into energy.
Notice your energy, too. Maybe a little drowsiness, which is normal after eating. Or a fresh sense of calm.
[pause 2s]
Now lift your eyes. Find the farthest point you can see. Through a window, down a street, at the far end of the room.
Let your gaze rest there, soft and relaxed. Your eyes have spent all morning inches from a screen. Let them see far.
[pause 4s]
Breathe easily. Let your breath be slow and steady, the way it is after a good meal.
Notice the sounds around you. Voices, cutlery, the street, the wind. You don't need to respond to any of them.
[pause 4s]
If you have a little time left, you might take a short walk after eating. Outside, or just to the window. Many people find it softens that early afternoon slump.
Before you go back to work, choose an intention for the afternoon. Not a task, more a way of being.
Maybe, take things one at a time. Or, stay calm when the unexpected happens. Or, take a real break around four.
Choose a simple intention, in just a few words.
[pause 3s]
You can even link it to a gesture. Placing your feet flat on the floor, for example, every time you sit down at your desk. A small reminder, to find this calm again in an instant.
That link between gesture and intention grows stronger every time you use it. After a few days, it can become almost automatic.
Keep it with you. And when you get back to your desk, bring a little of this rhythm, this slowness, with you too.
[pause 2s]
You don't need ten minutes to find this calm again. One slow breath before you reopen your inbox can already be enough.
When the afternoon gets busy, remember this moment. A slow bite, a faraway gaze. You know now that you can slow down, even in the middle of a full day.
Your body is nourished, your eyes have seen far, your mind has had a break.
Enjoy your afternoon.
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Running on empty
script: [pause 1.5s]
Tonight, you don't have to do anything. Not even meditate well. Not even stay focused until the end.
[pause 2s]
If you fall asleep, that's fine. If your mind wanders off, that's fine too. My voice can simply keep you company, like a radio playing in the next room.
There's no goal here, and no right way to do this. Just a moment when, for once, no one expects anything from you.
[pause 2s]
If you can, lie down. On your bed, on the couch, even on a rug on the floor. Somewhere your body can rest completely.
Slip a pillow under your head, and another under your knees if your back needs it. Pull a blanket over you if you're a little cold.
If you can't lie down, that's okay. Settle into an armchair, with your head supported, and let it hold your weight.
[pause 3s]
And let yourself be held. You don't need to sit up straight anymore, or keep up appearances. The bed, the floor, the couch can do that for you.
Feel the places where your body is supported. The back of your head. Your shoulders. Your back. Your hips. The backs of your legs. Your heels.
[pause 3s]
Each of these places can become a little heavier. As if you were handing over your weight, little by little, to whatever is beneath you.
You don't have to make it happen. Gravity takes care of it on its own.
You might notice the mattress or the cushions shaping themselves around you, filling in the gaps. There's no need to hold yourself together right now.
[pause 4s]
The tiredness is here. Maybe a very deep tiredness. The kind that isn't only in your muscles, but in your head too, and sometimes in your heart.
You don't need to fight it, or understand it tonight. You can simply acknowledge it. Yes, I'm running on empty.
[pause 3s]
Maybe it comes with something else. Irritation, sadness, a sense of emptiness, or the feeling of being at the end of your rope. All of that can be here. Nothing needs to be fixed tonight.
You don't have to describe it, or find a reason for it. Let it be here, beside you, without a fight.
[pause 2s]
This exhaustion isn't a weakness. It simply means you've given a lot. That you've held on for a long time, maybe longer than you would have wanted.
Many people go through stretches like this. You're not the only one feeling this way, even if tonight it can seem like it.
[pause 3s]
Your breath can do whatever it likes. No need to breathe deeply, or slowly. Let it come on its own.
Maybe notice, just for a moment, the gentle movement of your belly, or your chest. Rising. Falling.
[pause 4s]
Your body breathes without you. It has always known how, even at night, even when you're not thinking about anything. You can trust it.
